The industry combined ratio rose from 100.6 in 1979 to an estimated 103.5 in 1980, and underwriting losses will mount significantly in 1981 and 1982.
A largely unreported problem may prolong and intensify the coming industry agony, driving insurers to redouble efforts to write business just as underwriting losses hit records.
Falling bond prices and amortized-cost accounting hide that many insurers' bonds, at two to three times net worth, leave some large companies with nominal or negative market-value net worth.

stance.quote: short-term forecasts of stock or bond prices are useless

summary: Insurers' bonds could rise and restore stated net worth or fall further; short-term forecasts of stock or bond prices tell nothing about the future.
Insurers treat bond price declines as irrelevant because bonds repay at maturity, yet any sale books the loss immediately and cuts published net worth.
Unwillingness to recognize bond losses can block sensible moves, such as shifting from tax-exempt to taxable bonds when large underwriting losses are in prospect.
Insurers' bonds are funded by the float of policyholder money; if business volume shrinks they must sell bonds, turning unrealized losses into realized ones that decimate net worth.
An insurer with bond losses near net worth and inadequate rates can either keep pricing to cover expense and expected loss costs per dollar of premium, or write business regardless.
Pricing for adequacy loses annual-renewal business to competitors, shrinking premiums and liabilities, forcing bond sales to match, and partly exposing the hidden loss of net worth.
Some insurers would sell stocks or recently bought bonds instead of their worst bonds, an ostrich-like course unlikely to pay off long term.
The second option is 'asset maintenance' underwriting: keep writing terrible business at inadequate rates to preserve premiums and assets, beyond mere 'cash flow' underwriting.

stance.quote: as long as many large insurers feel compelled to choose that second option, there will be no better day for underwriting

summary: Large insurers will choose to maintain volume regardless of price, so competitors must meet those prices and underwriting will not improve while troubled rivals sell at any price.
Insurers unwilling to realize bond losses may be frozen in their investment posture for a decade and also lose underwriting options.
Berkshire's net worth relative to premium volume is the strongest among large stockholder-owned property-casualty groups, though maturities are mismatched and it also lost money on bonds.
Berkshire's capital and investment flexibility give it staying power and options, but it cannot escape the hostile pricing environment hurting the entire industry.

stance.quote: underwriting margins relative to the industry were at an all-time high

summary: National Indemnity's 1980 volume was flat with record relative underwriting margins; volume will fall in 1981 but Berkshire protects jobs and its underwriting discipline.
Home and Auto keeps replacing a diminishing number of auto policies with small-premium general liability volume, expanding slowly as underwriting results warrant.

stance.quote: The reinsurance business continues to reflect the excesses and problems of the primary writers.

summary: Reinsurance magnifies primary insurers' excesses: easy entry, large advance premiums and delayed loss reports make early cash feel euphoric, like a first credit card.

stance.quote: transforming the reinsurance market into “amateur night”

summary: High interest rates make reinsurance cash flow alluring, so underwriting will be poor for years and a super catastrophe could bankrupt some; Berkshire expects no reinsurance premium growth.
The Homestate group's underwriting is well below average outside Kansas; Insurance Company of Iowa, losing money yearly since 1973, stopped writing and merged into Cornhusker Casualty.

stance.quote: Cypress Insurance Company, run by Milt Thornton, continues its outstanding record

summary: Cypress's underwriting far outpaces competitors; Berkshire expects significantly lower insurance volume and poorer underwriting in 1981, with results somewhat better than the industry's.

stance.quote: these lines could not generate adequate returns related to investment

summary: Berkshire terminated Waumbec Mills, admitting a costly delay, and cut New Bedford looms by a third, abandoning undifferentiated high-volume lines that could not earn adequate returns.
The remaining textile operation was split into manufacturing and sales divisions and doubled capacity in its best segment with used looms; another tough year is expected.

stance.quote: Ben Rosner’s record at Associated Retail Stores continues to amaze us.

summary: Associated's earnings stayed excellent and turned into cash in a poor retailing year; Berkshire swapped Rockford Bancorp, owner of Illinois National Bank, for its own shares.
The bank disposition by share exchange let every Berkshire shareholder keep a proportional interest in the bank, as in a spinoff; 24 of about 1,300 holders chose the proportional exchange.
Thirty-nine more shareholders overexchanged Berkshire shares for bank stock, and the Chairman took the remaining 3% of Bancorp's shares as exchanger of last resort.
Bancorp will be a simple holding company owned by 65 shareholders by conscious choice; in August 1980 Berkshire sold $60 million of 12 3/4% notes due 2005.
Berkshire borrowed without an immediate need, expecting opportunities to use the money, possibly when credit is very expensive or unavailable, so it wants plenty of financial firepower.

Berkshire prefers acquiring businesses that generate cash; as inflation intensifies, many companies must spend all internal funds to maintain volume, so attractive reported earnings never become free cash.
Few acquisitions meet Berkshire's standards; it will keep plenty of liquidity, moderate properly structured debt and abundant capital strength, accepting a somewhat lower return on equity.
Illinois National Bank had enough cash in 1933 to pay all depositors in full and, under its founder, regularly ranked first nationally in profitability.
1981 operating earnings of $39.7 million were 15.2% of beginning equity versus 17.8% in 1980; the new shareholder-designated charitable contribution plan cut earnings by about $900,000.
Berkshire's share of undistributed earnings of companies it does not control is not included in operating earnings, a concept explained in the 1980 report.
Berkshire believes unrecorded undistributed earnings of non-controlled holdings will become tangible shareholder value just as surely as retained earnings of controlled subsidiaries.
Retained earnings convert into capital gains irregularly: poorly where used unproductively, richly where returns are high; a skillfully chosen group should do well.

Berkshire's non-controlled interests have better economics than its controlled businesses, because small portions of exceptional businesses are available at reasonable prices while whole ones rarely are.

Berkshire is comfortable with whole businesses and marketable minority stakes; acquisitions aim at real economic benefits, not size or reported numbers, and insurance and trading stamp liquidity mandate securities holdings.
Berkshire would rather own 10% of a wonderful business at X than 100% at 2X; high-premium takeovers are driven partly by managers' animal spirits.
Organizations measure and pay managers by size rather than profitability, as Fortune 500 managers cite sales rank, which fuels acquisition for size.
Acquirers assume their management will improve a target's profitability, the only reason shareholders would pay a 2X takeover cost rather than buy at the X market price.

stance.quote: We’ve observed many kisses but very few miracles.

summary: Investors can buy toads at toad prices; paying double for managerial kisses rarely produces miracles, though some acquisition records, in two major categories, have been dazzling.
Some acquirers excelled by buying inflation-adapted businesses that can raise prices easily and absorb large dollar volume growth with little added capital.
Very few enterprises have both inflation-adapted characteristics, and competition to buy them has become fierce to the point of being self-defeating.

stance.quote: a real managerial “twofer”

summary: A second category of acquirers is managerial superstars, such as Tom Murphy of Capital Cities, who can turn toads into princes and make few deals.
These top managers have made very few deals recently and often found repurchasing their own shares the most sensible use of corporate capital.
Berkshire's chairman is no turnaround superstar, and its acquisition activity in the inflation-adapted category has been sporadic and inadequate: preaching outran performance.
Buying toads cheaply failed; Berkshire did well with princes bought as princes, and occasionally bought fractional stakes in obvious princes at toad-like prices.
Berkshire seeks whole businesses at sensible prices assuming past trends continue, may pay fancy prices for inflation-adapted businesses, but will not pay much for its own supposed contribution.
In 1981 Berkshire nearly made a major purchase but the demanded price would have left its owners worse off, so it passed: a larger empire, poorer citizenry.
Berkshire had no whole-business purchase in 1981, expects occasional non-voting partnership offerings, and currently finds values easiest in open-market fractional positions in excellent franchises.
Undistributed earnings of minority holdings should produce full value; if not, the error lies in the management joined, the business's future economics, or the price paid.
Berkshire has made plenty of mistakes in controlling and non-controlling purchases, mostly misjudged future economics; the chairman's rosy aluminum-business view had to be reversed within months.
Mistakes are corrected far faster in marketable securities than in controlled subsidiaries, so lack of control often turned out to be an economic plus.

Unrecorded ownership earnings exceed reported operating earnings; four holdings alone, GEICO, General Foods, Reynolds and Washington Post, will contribute over $35 million of undistributed earnings in 1982.
Long-term performance values insurers' equities at market less taxes on unrealized gains; unreported ownership earnings have so far found their way, irregularly, into net worth.
Over seventeen years book value rose from $19.46 to $526.02 per share, 21.1% compounded; Berkshire expects that rate to drift down.
Net worth rose $124 million, about 31%, in 1981, over half from GEICO's market performance; securities gains outstripped growth in underlying business values.

stance.quote: Like virginity, a stable price level seems capable of maintenance, but not of restoration.

summary: Inflation makes Berkshire's long-term record illusory for owners; Buffett applauds Volcker and moderating price indices but remains negative on long-term inflation.
Because currency values keep being destroyed, Berkshire's efforts will fill shareholders' wallets better than their stomachs.
Equity investment is justified by managerial skills adding earnings above passive fixed-income returns and by greater risk deserving higher returns, so a value-added bonus seems natural.
Decades ago a 10% return on equity made a good business, since bonds yielded 5% taxable and 3% tax-exempt, even after taxes cut it to 6-8%.
In that earlier era business earned about 11% on equity and stocks sold at over 150 cents on the dollar of book value, so equity investment added substantial value.
That day is gone, but investors and managers cling to historic p/e ratios and valuation yardsticks; when economic change is great, yesterday's assumptions are costly.
In 1981 long-term taxable bonds yielded over 16% and tax-exempts 14%, while American business earned only about 14% on equity, which taxes reduce further.
At late-1981 rates a typical business paying out all earnings gives a 50%-bracket investor a 7% tax-exempt equivalent, worth perhaps fifty cents on the dollar.
If a typical business retains all earnings, 14% growth in earnings and price still requires a capital gains tax of up to 20%, leaving a poorer return than passive alternatives.
Unless passive rates fall, companies growing earnings per share 14% a year with no dividend are an economic failure for individual holders, since passive capital outearns active capital.
Most American businesses are currently economically bad, earning individuals less after tax than the tax-exempt passive rate, so American equity capital in aggregate adds no value for them.
Corporations are not doing worse; return on equity improved a few points in the decade, but passive returns rose much faster, and few industries show prospects for big gains.
If long-term inflation is tempered, passive returns should fall and American equity's position improve; inflation also forces low-return businesses to retain earnings, punishing their owners.
A rational bondholder would not reinvest coupons in 5% bonds at par when similar bonds trade at forty cents; likewise good money should not be thrown after bad.
Logically, high-return companies should retain most earnings while low-return companies should pay high dividends so owners can redeploy capital, as the parable of the talents illustrates.
Under rising prices the unattractive low-return business must retain every nickel just to continue operating as before, the reverse of what logic would prescribe.

stance.quote: inflation acts as a gigantic corporate tapeworm

summary: Inflation consumes investment dollars for receivables, inventory and fixed assets just to match last year's unit volume, taking the largest share from the least prosperous enterprises.
A business earning 8-10% on equity has no leftovers for growth, debt reduction or real dividends; some disguise this with dividend reinvestment plans or share issues.
Berkshire retains earnings for offensive reasons and still barely clears the after-tax passive-return crossbar with its historic 21% return, so its value-added could turn negative.
The table shows sources of reported earnings: Berkshire owns about 60% of Blue Chip, which owns 80% of Wesco; unusual asset sale gains are grouped with securities transactions.
Table: 1981 and 1980 operating earnings by source, including insurance underwriting and investment income, textiles, Associated Retail, See's and Buffalo Evening News.
Table: 1981 and 1980 operating earnings of Buffalo News, Blue Chip, Wesco, Mutual Savings, Precision Steel, interest, other and the divested Illinois National Bank, with sub-totals.
Table: totals of operating earnings, sales of securities and unusual assets, and total earnings of all entities for 1981 and 1980, pre-tax and after-tax.
Undistributed earnings of non-controlled companies are as important as reported operating earnings; only distributed dividends reach the table, mainly through insurance net investment income.
Table: Berkshire's proportional 1981 holdings in non-controlled companies, with shares, cost and market value, from Affiliated Publications and Alcoa through GEICO, Handy & Harman and Media General.
Table: remaining 1981 non-controlled holdings (Ogilvy, Pinkerton's, Reynolds, SAFECO, Washington Post) and totals of $351.7 million cost and $639.2 million market for common stocks.
Property-casualty insurance is Berkshire's largest area of both controlled and non-controlled activity, so commentary on industry developments follows.
1982 will certainly be the worst underwriting year in recent history, already guaranteed by current pricing behavior and the term nature of insurance contracts.
Policies average a little under twelve months with prices frozen, so premiums written this year set about half of next year's earned premiums and pricing mistakes linger.

Double-digit industrywide premium-written growth bodes well for current and next-year profitability, while small volume gains quickly worsen underwriting results, as expected in an inflationary world.
Best's data cover nearly the entire industry; a combined ratio compares operating and loss costs with premiums, below 100 meaning an underwriting profit and above 100 a loss.
Table: industry yearly change in premiums written and earned and combined ratio after policyholder dividends, 1972 to 1981, from Best's.
Current pricing promises devastating results if the industry's luck with hurricanes and reduced driving ends; underwriting has worsened despite good luck.
Monetary and social inflation, with courts stretching coverage, are unstoppable and will relentlessly raise the cost of repairing property and people.
Industry premium growth of at least 10% a year is needed to stabilize record underwriting losses expected from mid-1982; each point below that quickens deterioration.
Insurers holding bonds at inflated accounting values must keep volume up by selling policies at nonsensically low prices, fearing a volume drop more than an underwriting loss.
All insurers face pressure from the most threatened competitor plus worship of size and fear of losing share, so no major insurer turns down business and prices stay under pressure.

stance.quote: very large, although obviously varying, underwriting losses will be the norm for the industry

summary: Buffett rejects a regular underwriting cycle: large underwriting losses will be the industry norm, and the best future years may look substandard against the past decade's average.

Berkshire's insurers sacrificed volume but kept substantial underwriting superiority over the industry; low volume continues, and its financial strength could become an operational asset if industry fear prevails.

stance.quote: GEICO is a brilliantly run implementation of a very important business idea.

summary: GEICO's operating efficiency leaves it more protected than other insurers; 95.6% of 932,206 eligible shares responded to the new shareholder-designated contributions program.
Over 3% of shareholders wrote letters, all but one approving the designated-contributions program; participation exceeded any solicited shareholder response, with no return envelope provided.
Shareholders valued deciding where charitable gifts go; none asked officers to decide for them or to match directors' own charity contributions.
Shareholders designated $1,783,655 of contributions distributed to about 675 charities; subsidiaries also make local contributions chosen by their managers.
In perhaps two or three years in ten, poor tax deductions mean no program; otherwise holders on the September 30 list designate contributions after about October 10.
A Treasury ruling in early October 1981 allowed the program but excluded nominee-registered shares, so some shareholders missed participating.
Berkshire wrote to all owners promptly so nominee-name holders could re-register before the November 13 record date, urging brokers to forward the letter.
Many nominee holders never received Berkshire's letter or got it too late; one large brokerage held it three weeks, leaving sixty clients, about 4% of holders, unable to participate.
To join future designated contributions, register shares in your own name before September 30; even nominee holders should register one share to receive corporate news at the same time.
Charlie Munger, Vice Chairman of Berkshire and Chairman of Blue Chip, conceived the designated-contributions program; he and Buffett manage all controlled companies as partners.
adjudication_note: Credits Munger with the shareholder-contributions program and states how the controlled companies are managed, governance facts for owners; the warm sign-off makes has_personal true but does not change the scope.

summary: Operating earnings of $31.5 million in 1982 were 9.8% of beginning equity, down from 15.2% in 1981, due to weaker underwriting, equity growth and non-reported partial-ownership earnings.
Operating earnings over equity capital was once the key yardstick of managerial performance, but its usefulness for Berkshire has greatly diminished.
Managers facing poor results redraw the bullseye; Berkshire prefers fixed long-lived targets but drops the operating earnings over equity measure because of its partial holdings.
Accounting earnings include share of earnings only for holdings of 20% or more; below 20% only dividends count and undistributed earnings are ignored.
GEICO, 35% owned, adds only $3.5 million of dividends to reported earnings while $23 million of its undistributed 1982 earnings is excluded, so accounting can misstate economics.
Had GEICO earned $100 million more and retained it all, Berkshire's reported earnings would be unchanged; accounting earnings can seriously misrepresent economic reality.
Economic earnings include all undistributed earnings regardless of ownership percentage; their value depends on how effectively retained earnings are used.
Capital-intensive businesses fully credited with retained earnings under accounting can have minor or zero economic value; accounting numbers are the beginning, not the end, of valuation.
Under-20% ownership positions are small for most firms but large and growing for Berkshire, which limits the significance of its reported operating earnings.
Berkshire's share of undistributed 1982 earnings of GEICO, General Foods, Washington Post and R.J. Reynolds exceeded $40 million, above the $14 million of dividends it reported.
Retained earnings have translated into at least equal market value overall, but unevenly, irregularly in timing and with indeterminate taxation on realization.
Uneven translation of retained earnings into market value benefits value investors buying fractional business interests in an auction market driven by manic-depressive behavior.
Berkshire selects businesses where each retained dollar becomes at least a dollar of market value; overachievers among holdings have so far more than offset laggards.
Buying 100% of good businesses at reasonable prices is harder than buying fractional interests at attractive prices.

stance.quote: managerial intellect wilted in competition with managerial adrenaline

summary: Buffett was relieved not to take part in the large 1982 acquisitions made by others, where managerial adrenaline overrode intellect.
A large purchase Berkshire committed to in 1982 failed to complete for reasons outside its control, which Buffett sees as the year's main accomplishment.
Berkshire's partial-ownership approach needs attractive businesses at attractive prices, so it needs a moderately priced stock market; too high a price can undo a decade of good results.
If stocks rise much higher, Berkshire cannot deploy capital in partial ownership; in 1972 its insurers held only $18 million of equities versus 80% of investments in 1982.
High stock prices would flatter Berkshire's results temporarily but hurt its long-term prospects, and early traces of this problem are visible.
Net worth rose $208 million, or 40%, in 1982; book value grew from $19.46 to $737.43 per share over 18 years, 22.0% compounded, a rate that will diminish.
Berkshire aims for a long-term return well above the average large American corporation by buying partial or total stakes in favorably situated businesses with price discipline.

stance.quote: we are more impressed than ever by the strength of GEICO’s basic business idea and by the management skills of Jack Byrne.

summary: $79 million of the $208 million 1982 net worth gain came from a higher GEICO share price, which outpaced its underlying value growth; Buffett praises Jack Byrne.
GEICO's market value rose more than its intrinsic value over two years; Buffett expects substantial future value gains with eventual full market recognition.
Partially owned businesses may perform poorly in the market in some years and net worth could shrink, but Berkshire would add to holdings at better prices if it has cash.
Introduces the table of Berkshire's reported earnings sources, including its roughly 60% of Blue Chip Stamps, which owns 80% of Wesco Financial, with unusual gains shown separately.
Table: 1982 vs 1981 earnings by entity (insurance underwriting and investment income, textiles, See's, Buffalo News, Blue Chip, Wesco, Mutual Savings, Precision Steel), pre-tax and after tax.
Table (continued): Buffalo News, Blue Chip, Wesco, Mutual Savings, Precision Steel, interest and other, with operating earnings of $41.1 million and securities gains of $36.7 million for 1982.
Table: total earnings of all entities in 1982 and 1981, $77.8 million versus $98.5 million pre-tax and $46.4 million versus $62.6 million after tax.
Buffalo News Sunday circulation grew 35% in six years, from the Courier-Express's 272,000 to 367,000, with little change in households.
Buffalo's rising share of households buying a Sunday paper is unmatched elsewhere; Buffett credits the key Buffalo managers.
Undistributed earnings of non-controlled holdings are now as important as reported operating earnings; introduces a list of holdings whose dividends only are counted.
Table: Berkshire's non-controlled common stock holdings at yearend 1982 with shares, cost and market value, incl. GEICO, Washington Post, R.J. Reynolds, General Foods and Time.
Table (continued): Washington Post stake, subtotal of $402 million cost and $912 million market, other holdings and total common stocks of $424 million cost and $946 million market.
Footnotes to the holdings table; the largest unrealized gains are in Washington Post and GEICO, which Buffett first knew at ages 13 and 20, rewarding returning fidelity.
Property-casualty insurance is Berkshire's largest business; the updated industry table signals poor 1983 underwriting results.
Table: 1972-1982 property-casualty industry yearly change in premiums written and earned and combined ratio, rising to an estimated 109.5 for 1982.
Best's data cover the whole industry; a combined ratio below 100 means an underwriting profit and above 100 a loss.
With industry premium growth well below 10% and insured losses rising at least that fast, underwriting results will deteriorate next year.

stance.quote:
the reaction of weak managements to weak operations is
often weak accounting.

summary: The 1982 combined ratio of 109.5 is a best case; insurers can show almost any profit through long-tail business, reserving or fast growth, and some masked deterioration.
Reserving practices weakened in 1982 so the true combined ratio is likely worse; Buffett disagrees that the cycle will steadily improve after 1983-84 because of changed competition.
Industries with overcapacity and a commodity product are prime candidates for profit troubles unless prices or costs are administered by government, collusion or cartels.
Price administration can be legal through government, illegal through collusion, or extralegal like OPEC-style cartels, as with trucker pricing and deposit costs until recently.
Where full competition, ample capacity and indifferent buyers prevail, industry economics are unexciting or disastrous, so vendors stress brand; candy bars work, sugar does not.
Where differentiation is impossible, only wide sustainable cost advantages earn good returns; persistent overcapacity without administered prices means poor profitability.
Overcapacity corrects slowly and the rebound breeds new expansion; commodity industries' profits depend on the ratio of tight to ample years, as in Berkshire's textile business.
Capacity-tight conditions can last long when demand outruns forecasts or when adding capacity needs long lead times.
Insurance capacity can be created instantly by capital plus an underwriter's signature, and the product is undifferentiated, so overcapacity prevails except under fear of survival.

stance.quote: seem to be a textbook case of an industry usually faced with the deadly combination of excess capacity and a “commodity” product.

summary: Insurance looks like a textbook case of excess capacity combined with a commodity product.
From 1950 to 1970 the industry combined ratio averaged 99.0 thanks to regulated quasi-administered pricing and agent-focused competition rather than price competition.
Historically the big insurers' rates were negotiated between industry bureaus and state regulators, so giants charged identical prices and could not legally cut filed rates.
Regulator-agreed prices included profit allowances, so insurers could legally price their way to profitability despite overcapacity, unlike most businesses.
That regulated pricing era is over: new capacity outside the old structure uses price as a weapon, and customers learned insurance is no longer a one-price business.
Future insurance profitability depends on current competitive conditions; better underwriting results need a major narrowing of the gap between demand and supply.
Insurance supply, meaning underwriters' willingness to sign, must shrink for profits to improve, and poor profit levels alone will not cause that contraction.
Major capacity withdrawals need a megadisaster; until then insurance will not be very profitable, but Berkshire expects great opportunities when supply contracts.
Berkshire's 1982 underwriting deteriorated more than the industry's, mainly in National Indemnity's traditional lines; Buffett expects only average, and poor, results in 1983.

stance.quote: Both Milt and Floyd simply are incapable of being average.

summary: Cypress and Kansas Fire and Casualty have produced an underwriting profit every year since joining Berkshire; Mike Goldberg took over parent responsibility for insurance operations.

stance.quote: We are happy with every aspect of this operation.

summary: GEICO's cost advantage makes it a high-profit exception in a commodity industry; Berkshire's 35% interest equals about $250 million of premium volume, above its direct volume.
Berkshire and Blue Chip may merge in 1983 by stock exchange; Berkshire issues shares only if it receives as much intrinsic value as it gives.
Managers' acquisition cravings often arise when their own stock trades below intrinsic value, forcing a choice between expanding their domain and protecting owners' wealth.
Sellers always demand full business value, but a buyer paying with stock that trades below intrinsic value pays with undervalued currency.
A buyer issuing shares sells part of itself at market price, which may be half of intrinsic value, though selling its whole business would earn full value.
Issuing undervalued stock to buy fully valued property gives up $2 of value for $1, turning a marvelous business into a terrible buy; bankers will rationalize it.
Rationalization (a) that the target will be worth more later ignores that the old business being traded away also grows in value.
Rationalization (b) 'we have to grow' ignores that issuing shares shrinks existing owners' interest, e.g. Berkshire's stakes in See's and National Indemnity; farm merger analogy.
Managers who expand their domain at owners' expense might better consider a career in government.
Rationalization (c) of paying 51% in stock and 49% in cash for sellers' tax-free exchange still harms old owners, and sellers' wishes should not determine the buyer's interests.
Value for old owners is protected in stock mergers by a true business-value-for-business-value exchange like Berkshire-Blue Chip, an exception since such deals are hard to do.
A second route is issuing stock at or above intrinsic value; many 1965-69 mergers worked this way, leaving acquired shareholders holding inflated currency, the reverse of post-1970 activity.
In recent years only companies in glamorous or promotional businesses valued at or above intrinsic value could use stock profitably for acquisitions.
A third route is to repurchase shares equal to those issued in a merger; such damage-repair buybacks are recommended, though buybacks that directly enhance owner wealth are preferred.
Merger dilution is calculated on pro forma book value and earnings per share, and projections are supplied to justify any price when the CEO wants a deal.
When pro forma calculations show an acquisition as anti-dilutive for the acquirer, no comment is thought necessary.
Near-term EPS dilution is overemphasized: non-dilutive mergers can destroy value and dilutive ones enhance it; dilution in intrinsic business value is what counts.
A stock merger means part of the acquirer is sold to buy the target; later stock or convertible sales to fund or repair the deal count in its cost.
Corporate mating can lead to corporate pregnancy: the financing consequences of a deal should be faced before it is done.
Managers should ask whether they would sell 100% of their business on the terms offered for part of it; small stupid capital transactions accumulate into a major stupidity.
Hypothetical investment-company merger: X, at 50% of asset value, issuing shares for Y's assets trades $2 of value for $1, which the SEC would forbid.
Industrial and financial mergers have destroyed acquirer value as dramatically as the investment-company example; using the same yardstick for both businesses would prevent it.
Value-diluting share issuance is a double whammy: the intrinsic value loss from the merger, then a lower market valuation because of the management's record.
Once management shows insensitivity to owners, shareholders suffer a lasting low price/value ratio regardless of assurances that the dilution was a one-time event.
Assurances after diluting issuance are treated like a bug-in-the-salad excuse; the highest market prices go to companies whose managers never issue shares on unfavorable terms.
Berkshire, Blue Chip and Wesco issue shares only for equal business value; acquisition criteria begin with purchases earning at least $5 million after tax.
Remaining acquisition criteria: management in place, simple businesses, a stated price, no unfriendly deals, five-minute answers; cash preferred but stock considered on fair terms.
95.8% of eligible shares joined the shareholder-designated contributions program with $1 per share available versus $2 in 1981; a Blue Chip merger could allow larger amounts.
Berkshire runs from a five-person headquarters whose compact organization lets Buffett and Munger spend time managing the business, with Munger working from Los Angeles.
Phil Liesche of National Indemnity and Ben Rosner of Associated Retail Stores retired; National Indemnity has been the most important operation in Berkshire's growth.
Both retiring managers ran their businesses as if they owned them outright; attracting managers of that character is what secures Berkshire's future.
Registered shareholders grew from about 1,900 to 2,900, mostly through the Blue Chip merger, prompting a summary of the business principles governing the manager-owner relationship.
Berkshire treats shareholders as owner-partners, and its directors are major shareholders with over half of family net worth in Berkshire at four of five.
The long-term goal is to maximize per-share intrinsic business value growth, measured per share not by size; the rate will diminish but should beat the average large corporation.
Berkshire prefers directly owning diversified cash-generating businesses, second choice owning parts of them via insurers' stock purchases, with allocation set by price and insurance capital needs.
Because of two-pronged ownership and accounting limits, consolidated reported earnings say little about economic performance; Berkshire reports each major controlled business instead.
Accounting does not drive decisions: Berkshire prefers $2 of unreportable earnings to $1 of reportable ones, since whole businesses cost double the pro-rata price of small portions.
Berkshire rarely uses debt, structures it long-term fixed rate, and rejects opportunities rather than over-leverage, a conservatism that has penalized results.
No managerial wish list at owner expense; retention is tested by whether each retained $1 delivers at least $1 of market value, applied on a five-year rolling basis.
Berkshire issues stock only for equal business value, applying the rule to all forms including stock options and convertibles, not just mergers or offerings.
Berkshire will not sell good businesses at any price and is reluctant to sell sub-par ones that still generate cash, and doubts capital-spending turnarounds of poor businesses.
Major investment in a terrible industry is like struggling in quicksand, yet Berkshire would rather have results penalized than play gin rummy by discarding its least promising business each turn.
Berkshire commits to candid reporting of pluses and minuses important to business value, telling owners what it would want to know in their position.
Berkshire discusses marketable securities only as legally required, since good investment ideas are valuable and can be copied; the 1983 high point was buying control of Nebraska Furniture Mart.
Nebraska Furniture Mart generates over $100 million of annual sales from one 200,000 square-foot store, selling more than all Omaha competitors combined.

stance.quote:
It’s the ideal business - one built upon exceptional value to the customer that in turn translates into exceptional economics for
its owners.

summary: Nebraska Furniture Mart buys brilliantly and operates at expense ratios competitors cannot match, passing savings to customers: an ideal business built on exceptional customer value.
Berkshire bought 90% of Nebraska Furniture Mart in 1983, leaving 10% with family managers and optioning 10% to key young family managers; Mrs. B still sells carpet at 90.
Book value per share rose 32% in 1983, from $737.43 to $975.83; Buffett prefers a five-year test and warns if gains trail American industry's return on equity.
Over 19 years book value grew from $19.46 to $975.83 per share, 22.6% compounded; this rate cannot be sustained at Berkshire's present size.
Berkshire reports book value as a conservative proxy for intrinsic value growth; it is easy to calculate but the two measures have very different meanings.
Book value records capital put in, while intrinsic value is future cash output discounted to present value; equal educational spending illustrates how equal input yields different value.
In 1965 book value of $19.46 per share overstated intrinsic value because it was all low-return textile assets; today intrinsic value far exceeds book value.
One reason intrinsic value exceeds book: stocks held outside insurers are carried at cost, hiding a $70 million pre-tax excess of market value at yearend 1983.
Second reason: several Berkshire businesses have economic Goodwill far larger than the accounting Goodwill on the balance sheet; the appendix explains the difference.
Buffett's thinking on Goodwill changed from his early bias toward tangible assets, a bias that caused many business mistakes of omission.

stance.quote:
my present strong preference for
businesses that possess large amounts of enduring Goodwill and
that utilize a minimum of tangible assets.

summary: Experience produced Buffett's strong preference for businesses with large enduring Goodwill and minimal tangible assets, escaping old ideas.
Buffett and Munger believe Berkshire has very significant economic Goodwill value beyond its book value; the appendix covers Goodwill's business aspects.
Introduces the 1983 earnings table; Berkshire's stake in Blue Chip rose from 60% to 100% and in Wesco from 48% to 80%, so the first columns best show performance.
Realized capital gains for any single year are meaningless, but aggregate realized and unrealized gains over years matter; Goodwill amortization is shown as a separate item.
Table: 1983 vs 1982 earnings by entity (insurance, Berkshire-Waumbec, Associated Retail, Nebraska Furniture Mart, See's), pre-tax and after tax, start.
Table (continued): See's, Buffalo News, Blue Chip, Wesco, Mutual Savings, Precision Steel, interest, special GEICO distribution, contributions, goodwill amortization and other.
Table: Berkshire's operating earnings, securities gains and total earnings for 1983 and 1982, pre-tax and after tax.
A special $21 million GEICO tender-offer distribution was treated as a dividend, taxed at an effective 6.9% federal rate for corporations versus 28% on capital gains.
Even with the special item, GEICO's 1983 dividends were below Berkshire's share of GEICO earnings, so counting the redemption proceeds in reported earnings is appropriate.
Retained earnings of investees are not in reported earnings, but over time they should raise market prices and Berkshire's intrinsic value dollar for dollar.
Berkshire has received far more than a dollar of market value gain for every dollar of earnings retained by its investees.
Introduces the table of Berkshire's yearend 1983 net holdings of marketable equities, counting 100% of Berkshire's and 80% of Wesco's holdings.
Table: yearend 1983 marketable equity holdings with shares, cost and market, including GEICO, Washington Post, General Foods, Time and R.J. Reynolds.
Table (continued): subtotal of $558.9 million cost and $1.29 billion market, other holdings, and total common stocks of $566.3 million cost and $1.31 billion market.
Berkshire expects about $39 million of dividends from its holdings in 1984 and roughly $65 million of attributable retained earnings, which may not affect prices immediately.
The controlled businesses to discuss are Buffalo Evening News, See's and the Insurance Group; the paper's name changed to Buffalo News when a morning edition began.
Buffalo News somewhat exceeded its 10% after-tax margin target in 1983 thanks to a fully used loss carry-forward and a drop in newsprint cost, with margins about average for newspapers.
Buffalo's heavy-industry economy was hit by the recession, and the paper's retail advertisers have shrunk in number and cut linage.
Buffalo News' strength is public acceptance: it ranked first in weekday household penetration among the 100 largest US papers in the six months to September 1983.
Among large papers that have a city to themselves, Buffalo News is at the top nationally for penetration, far ahead of better-known dailies.
Buffalo News ranks third in Sunday penetration; Sunday circulation was 314,000 in 1970 falling to 270,000 in 1976, versus 376,000 currently.
Penetration ratio is the best measure of a newspaper's franchise, since high-penetration papers are efficient buys for local retailers; three factors explain the News' acceptance.
The News benefits from a stable population and an editorial quality reputation that made the Sunday paper succeed; without Sunday it would not have survived.
The News' news hole was 50% of content in 1983 versus a high-30s average, giving readers over 25% more news; Berkshire will keep it despite others cutting for margins.
A full serving of news makes the paper more valuable to readers and supports its unusual penetration ratio.
Buffalo News preprint lines rose from 9.3 to 16.4 million and revenues from $3.6 to $8.1 million in 1983, helped by the Courier-Express closing, while ROP gains will be hard.
The shift from ROP advertising to preprints hurts economics: preprints are less profitable, more open to competition and reduce space for news.

stance.quote: The financial results at See’s continue to be exceptional.

summary: See's financial results remain exceptional with a valuable consumer franchise; raw material costs are beyond control because Berkshire always buys the finest ingredients.
See's non-raw-material costs per pound have risen faster than general prices, but better cost control is expected to hold 1984 growth below inflation under Chuck Huggins.
Table: See's 1974-1983 sales, after-tax operating profits, pounds of candy sold and stores open; 1983 sales $133.5 million, profit $13.7 million.
Table (continued): See's sales, after-tax profits, pounds sold and stores open for 1975, 1974, 1973 and 1972.
See's second problem is no meaningful gain in pounds sold, an industry-wide weakness; See's used to outperform the industry on volume but no longer does.
See's retail poundage was flat for four years and down 0.8% same-store in 1983, cumulatively about 8% since 1979; dollar volume grew via price increases and quantity orders plateaued.
Buffett is unsure whether See's flat volume reflects pricing, a static industry, the recession or its high market share; the 1984 price rise is modest, with no volume forecast.

stance.quote:
our candy is
preferred by an enormous margin to that of any competitor.

summary: See's candy is preferred by a wide margin in the West, with customer service from company-run shops as good as the product, despite the flat volume problem.
Modest 1984 price rises mean See's profits will be flat versus 1983; Berkshire's own insurers had terrible results from Buffett's earlier mistakes while GEICO shot the lights out.
Table: 1972-1983 industry yearly premium growth and combined ratio, with 1983 estimated at 111.0 and called the worst underwriting year in a long time.
Best's data cover the entire industry; combined ratio is losses plus expenses over premiums, with a ratio below 100 an underwriting profit and above 100 a loss.
Buffett expects 1983's poor industry experience to be typical for years; industry premiums must grow about 10% a year merely to hold loss ratios, given pessimism on inflation.
Berkshire's 1983 combined ratio was 121; insurance results reflect decisions made two or more years earlier because of the business's long lead time.
Roland Miller improved results at National Indemnity and National Fire and Marine as competitors worsened, and Continental Divide Insurance under Tom Rowley looks like a winner.
Berkshire is entering reinsurance where the buyer's priority is the seller's long-term creditworthiness, which Buffett believes makes its financial strength the top choice.
Structured settlements, which pay injured claimants periodically for life with tax advantages, are a major reinsurance source where Berkshire's unmatched financial strength is the selling point.
Berkshire's financial strength should win business from insurers transferring blocks of loss reserves for lump sums, where competitors' finances look materially weaker.
Structured settlements and loss reserve assumptions generate large investment income relative to premiums, so they get a separate line, are excluded from the combined ratio and front-end no profit.

stance.quote:
Its
superiority reflects the combination of a truly exceptional
business idea and an exceptional management.

summary: GEICO wrote at a 96 combined ratio in 1983, after a large policyholder dividend accrual, versus 111 for the industry, reflecting an exceptional business idea and management.

stance.quote:
Lou Simpson is the class of the
field among insurance investment managers.

summary: GEICO shows underwriting discipline and new business gains; Berkshire's one-third interest equals $270 million of premiums, 80% above its own volume, but its own operation still needs improvement.
Berkshire does not split its stock because it wants a price rationally related to intrinsic value, which depends on rational shareholders.
Emotional holders create silly stock prices, which can help Berkshire when trading other stocks but harm it in its own shares, so it tries to minimize them.
Berkshire attracts high-quality shareholders by consistently communicating its business and ownership philosophy and letting self-selection work, like an opera versus a rock concert.
Berkshire's policies and communications try to attract long-term owners focused on business results rather than market prices, and to dissuade others.
Over 90% to 95% of shares are held by owners from five years ago, and over 95% by holders for whom Berkshire is double their next largest holding.
At $1,300 per share almost anyone can afford Berkshire; a split would attract impressionable buyers who prefer paper to value and would downgrade the shareholder group.
Shareholders who buy for non-value reasons sell for non-value reasons, accentuating price swings unrelated to underlying business developments.
Berkshire avoids policies that attract short-term stock-price buyers so that owners can sell in a market of rational informed investors.

stance.quote:
A hyperactive stock
market is the pickpocket of enterprise.

summary: High share turnover and 'liquidity' praised by brokers benefit them, not investors; a hyperactive stock market is the pickpocket of enterprise.
At 100% annual turnover and 1% commissions each way, owners pay 2% of net worth yearly to transfer ownership, losing one-sixth of a 12% return as frictional cost.
Frictional trading costs are the equivalent of a 16 2/3% tax on corporate earnings that investors impose on themselves through market activity.
A year of 100-million-share days at 15 cents per share each way would cost investors about $7.5 billion, roughly the 1982 profits of Exxon, GM, Mobil and Texaco.
The four giants had $75 billion of net worth; investors forfeit that capital's earnings to trading, plus over $2 billion of fees equal to five big banks' earnings.

stance.quote:
casino-type markets and hair-trigger investment management act as
an invisible foot that trips up and slows down a forward-moving
economy.

summary: Buffett rejects the argument that active trading improves capital allocation: casino-type markets and hair-trigger investment management are an invisible foot that slows the economy.
Berkshire's bid-ask spread is about 2%, so round-trip trading costs average no more than 2% against the far higher costs of hyperactive stocks.
Berkshire's turnover of about 3% costs owners 0.06% of market value, or $900,000 yearly; splitting would raise that cost and weaken the link between price and intrinsic value.
Berkshire repeats its acquisition criteria, as repetition is a key to advertising results.
Acquisition criteria: purchases earning at least $5 million after tax, consistent earning power, good returns on equity with little debt, management in place, simple businesses and a stated price.
Berkshire does no unfriendly takeovers, promises confidentiality and a five-minute answer, prefers cash but may issue stock for equal intrinsic value, and offers sellers a good home.
96.4% of eligible shares joined the 1983 designated contributions program, giving $3,066,501 to 1,353 charities; holder participation lagged because of new merger shareholders.
Shares must be registered in the owner's name by September 28, 1984 to join the 1984 program; the Blue Chip merger drew under 0.1% dissent and gave some tax efficiency.
Berkshire has 1,146,909 shares versus 1,137,778 in 1965, so every 1% owner then now owns 0.99%, with all added assets acquired with virtually no net dilution.
The appendix defines economic and accounting Goodwill apart from everyday goodwill; a well-liked business like pre-breakup AT&T can have no economic Goodwill.
Under purchase accounting, any price above the fair value of identifiable net assets is booked as 'excess of cost over equity in net assets acquired', called Goodwill.
Accounting Goodwill from purchases before November 1970 can stay on the balance sheet without amortization charges against earnings.
Goodwill from purchases since November 1970 is amortized over at most 40 years through non-deductible charges to earnings, a hit to after-tax income roughly double that of other expenses.
Blue Chip Stamps bought See's early in 1972 for $25 million when See's had about $8 million of net tangible assets and earned about $2 million after tax.
Businesses are worth far more than net tangible assets when they earn well above market returns on them; the capitalized value of that excess return is economic Goodwill.
See's earned 25% after tax on net tangible assets without leverage, a return due to intangible assets such as consumer reputation rather than inventory or fixed assets.
A consumer franchise lets product value, not production cost, set price; other Goodwill sources are unregulated governmental franchises like TV stations and an enduring low-cost position.
Blue Chip's $17 million of See's Goodwill is amortized at $425,000 yearly, falling to about $12.5 million by 1983, with Berkshire's 60% share about $7.5 million.
The 1983 Blue Chip merger required purchase accounting rather than pooling, spreading the market value of shares given over the net assets acquired.
The Blue Chip merger created $51.7 million of Goodwill: $28.4 million for See's and $23.3 million for Buffalo Evening News; See's amortization runs about $1.0 million yearly.
Different purchase dates and prices give two pieces of the same See's asset vastly different values and amortization charges; Buffett offers no better accounting system.
See's earned $13 million after tax on about $20 million of net tangible assets, so amortization charges were not true economic costs and economic Goodwill grew.
Future amortization charges also will not match economic costs; See's Goodwill is likely to increase in nominal terms because of inflation.
True Goodwill rises with inflation: See's earned $2 million on $8 million of tangible assets, while a mundane business needing $18 million for the same earnings has little Goodwill.
Berkshire paid $25 million for See's against $18 million for the mundane business of equal earnings, justified by anticipating continuous inflation in 1972.
If the price level doubled, both businesses would need to double nominal earnings to $4 million to stay even with inflation, seemingly easy by doubling prices.

stance.quote: The motivation for this investment is the survival of the business, not the prosperity of the owner.

summary: Inflation forces businesses to double their investment in receivables, inventories and fixed assets to double sales, with no improvement in return rate: survival, not owner prosperity.
After doubling, the mundane business needs $18 million more capital and is worth $36 million, gaining a dollar for each new dollar, while See's needs only $8 million more.

stance.quote: Any unleveraged business that requires some net tangible assets to operate (and almost all do) is hurt by inflation.

summary: See's earning $4 million would be worth $50 million, gaining over $3 for each $1 invested; any business needing tangible assets is hurt by inflation, asset-light ones least.

stance.quote: Asset-heavy businesses generally earn low rates of return

summary: The traditional view that asset-heavy businesses protect against inflation is wrong: such businesses earn low returns that barely fund their own inflationary needs.
Great fortunes built during inflation came from lasting intangibles with few tangible asset needs, especially communications; during inflation Goodwill is the gift that keeps giving.
Spurious accounting Goodwill arises when an overexcited management overpays; the silly price sits in Goodwill and is amortized as if it were a sensible asset.
Hypothetical: a company with $20 per share of tangible net worth earning $5 per share, a 25% return, could sell for $100 per share or more because of its franchise.
An investor paying $100 per share who imputed $2 yearly Goodwill amortization would see 'true' earnings fall to $3, which shows accounting amortization is a poor guide.
In judging operating results, amortization charges should be ignored: earnings on unleveraged net tangible assets best show a unit's economic attractiveness and its Goodwill value.
In evaluating acquisitions, purchased Goodwill should be kept at full cost including full intrinsic value of consideration given; the Blue Chip merger cost exceeded the $51.7 million booked.
The true cost of the Blue Chip merger exceeded book because the market value of Berkshire shares given up was below their intrinsic value, which defines true cost.
Operations that look good as businesses may look poor as purchases; a good business is not always a good purchase.
Berkshire seeks businesses with excellent operating economics and reasonable purchase returns, ignoring accounting; yearend 1983 net accounting Goodwill was $62 million, far below economic Goodwill.
Net worth rose $152.6 million, or $133 per share, in 1984, a 13.6% gain in book value to $1,108.77, versus 22.1% compounded over twenty years from $19.46.
A mushrooming capital base drags returns; earning even 15% over the next decade requires about $3.9 billion of profits and a few big ideas that Buffett lacks.
Introduces the table of Berkshire's reported earnings sources; ownership changes at the 1983 Blue Chip merger make the first two columns the best measure of underlying performance.
Unusual asset-sale gains go with securities transactions outside operating earnings; annual realized gains are meaningless but aggregate gains matter; Goodwill amortization is a separate item.
Table: 1984 vs 1983 earnings by entity (insurance underwriting and investment income, Buffalo News, Nebraska Furniture Mart, See's), pre-tax and after tax.
Table (continued): 1984 vs 1983 earnings of See's, Associated Retail, Blue Chip, Mutual Savings, Precision Steel, textiles, Wesco, goodwill amortization, interest, contributions and other.
Table: 1984 operating earnings of $87.7 million before special GEICO and General Foods distributions and securities gains, giving total earnings of $200.5 million pre-tax versus $147.9 million.
The special GEICO distribution was reclassified and reduced in the earnings table, a change of form not substance whose background Buffett explains.
In 1983 GEICO bought back stock by tender while Berkshire sold GEICO 350,000 shares for $21 million, leaving its ownership percentage unchanged in a proportionate redemption.
The $21 million GEICO redemption was taxed at the 6.9% inter-corporate dividend rate and was far less than Berkshire's undistributed GEICO earnings, so it economically equaled a dividend.
Berkshire highlighted the material GEICO distribution to shareholders and auditors Peat Marwick's Omaha office and Chicago reviewing partner agreed with the dividend presentation.
In 1984 a nearly identical General Foods transaction gave Berkshire $21,843,601 cash while its ownership stayed at exactly 8.75%, again far less than retained earnings.
Peat Marwick's New York office wanted the GEICO and General Foods redemptions accounted as stock sales with capital gains, not dividends, though it agrees they were dividends for tax.
Berkshire disagrees but adopted the auditor's view and restated 1983 to avoid a qualified opinion; intrinsic value, ownership, cash and taxes are unaffected.
Berkshire signed another General Foods contract keeping its stake unchanged, which secures dividend tax treatment, but will account for the redemptions as stock sales.

stance.quote:
no alternative action
can benefit shareholders as surely as repurchases.

summary: Repurchases are at least equally favorable for non-selling shareholders; when strong companies' shares trade far below intrinsic value, no alternative benefits shareholders as surely.
Buffett endorses price-driven repurchases but finds 'greenmail' repurchases, paid by innocent shareholders to extortionist holders and insiders, odious and repugnant.
In greenmail, the transient shareholder and management each give speeches while the innocent shareholder mutely funds the payoff.

stance.quote:
major repurchases at prices well below per-share intrinsic business
value immediately increase, in a highly significant way, that
value.

summary: Berkshire's largest holdings repurchased stock when price was below value; repurchases well below intrinsic value immediately raise per-share value, often $2 of value for $1, beating acquisitions.
Repurchases below business value show management favors shareholder wealth over expanding its domain, lifting expected returns and aligning market price with intrinsic value.
Investors should pay more for a business run by a demonstrably pro-shareholder manager than one run by a self-interested manager.
A manager who turns away from clearly beneficial repurchases reveals his motives however loudly he speaks of maximizing shareholder wealth, and the market rightly discounts his assets.

stance.quote:
shareholders have had their interests in outstanding
businesses materially enhanced by repurchases made at bargain
prices.

summary: Berkshire prospered from large repurchases by GEICO, Washington Post and General Foods, its three largest holdings, and by Exxon, its fourth, and likes shareholder-conscious managements.
Introduces the table of Berkshire's yearend 1984 net holdings of marketable equities, excluding minority interests in Wesco and Nebraska Furniture Mart.
Table: yearend 1984 common stock holdings with shares, cost and market value, including GEICO, General Foods, Exxon, Washington Post and Time.
Table (continued): subtotal of $573.3 million cost and $1.23 billion market, other holdings, and total common stocks of $585 million cost and $1.27 billion market.
Equity investments meeting Berkshire's qualitative and value-versus-price standards are harder to find than in over ten years, and doing nothing is the hardest task.
Nebraska Furniture Mart's net sales rose $14.3 million to $115 million from its single Omaha store, the largest home furnishings volume in the US; Blumkin family tribute.
NFM's gross margin is about half Levitz's 44.4% and operating expenses are 16.5% of sales versus 35.6% at Levitz, allowing low mark-ups.

stance.quote: the NFM operation is simply extraordinary

summary: NFM's efficiency and volume buying yield excellent returns while saving customers at least $30 million yearly, widening its geographic reach and growth beyond Omaha.
The Blumkins' business secrets: hard work, a realistic view of their competence, ignoring tempting deals outside it, and high-grade behavior; Mrs. B says 'sell cheap and tell the truth'.
Berkshire bought 90% of NFM for a $55 million check without an audit, inventory count or title checks, relying on Mrs. B's word.
Table: See's 1975-1984 sales, after-tax operating profits, pounds of candy sold and stores open; 1984 sales were $135.9 million and profit $13.4 million.
Table (continued): See's sales, profits, pounds and stores for 1972 to 1976.

stance.quote:
The success of See’s reflects the combination of an exceptional
product and an exceptional manager, Chuck Huggins.

summary: See's success did not come from a rising tide: many boxed-chocolate rivals lost money or were marginal, and only one good-sized competitor was highly profitable.
See's 1984 per-pound price rose only 1.4% to $5.49 and non-raw-material costs only 2.2%, but volume declining same-store forces more shops to hold volume, pressuring costs.
See's same-store volume fell 1.1% in 1984 while total shop volume rose 0.6% from added stores.
See's is increasingly seasonal: the four weeks before Christmas bring 40% of volume and about 75% of profits, with Easter and Valentine's smaller.
See's refuses preservatives or freezing that rivals use to smooth production, accepting production headaches, and introduced six candy bars to fight mall food vendors.
See's aims to hold 1985 cost increases below inflation with prices up 6%-7%; Buffalo News profits beat expectations in 1984 as total hours fell 2.8% and costs rose only 4.9%.
New 1984 union contracts gave Buffalo News a catch-up wage increase, justified by unions' cooperation during the unprofitable 1977-1982 struggle with the Courier-Express.
The catch-up wages take full effect in 1985 and newsprint prices are less favorable, so Buffalo News expects at least a minor margin contraction.
Buffalo News circulation is concentrated in the area useful to advertisers, unlike regional papers with wasted circulation that costs money without earning ad revenue.
Buffalo News penetration of the retail market is exceptional, ranking first weekday and second Sunday among the 100 largest papers, though household decline trimmed weekday circulation.
The News' news hole was 50.9% in 1984 versus a 35%-40% norm, with newsroom employment maintained and newsroom costs up 9.1% against overall costs up 4.9%.
The extra news hole raises news costs relative to revenue, but the gap versus peers is about three points against pre-tax margins often ten times larger.

stance.quote:
The economics of a dominant newspaper are excellent, among
the very best in the business world.

summary: Dominant newspapers earn excellent profits, among the best in business, whether first-class or third-rate; quality may have mattered in achieving dominance, as at the News.
Once dominant, a newspaper prospers whether good or bad because even a poor paper retains essential 'bulletin board' value for readers and advertisers.
Since the market imposes no standards, management must: the News spends above average on news; the passage then introduces the insurance industry premium and combined-ratio table.
Table: 1972-1984 industry yearly change in premiums written and combined ratio after policyholder dividends, with 1984 estimated at 117.7.
Best's data cover practically the entire industry; a combined ratio below 100 shows an underwriting profit and above 100 a loss.
Berkshire has said industry premiums must grow about 10% yearly to hold the combined ratio steady, assuming stable expenses and losses growing 10% from volume, inflation and expanding court rulings.
Industry premiums rose only 30% since 1979 instead of the 61% needed to hold the combined ratio at 100.6, leaving 117.7 in 1984; premium growth drives underwriting profit.
With 1985 premium growth over 10% the combined ratio should ease, but returning to 100 would need five years of 15% increases, so Buffett expects 108-113 ratios.
Berkshire's 1984 combined ratio was a humbling 134, the third straight year worse than the industry; improvement is expected in 1985 as Goldberg corrects earlier mistakes.
Poor results in Berkshire's lines have subdued competitors, letting it raise prices significantly in important lines in the second half of 1984 with little business lost.
Berkshire's premier financial strength may now make a competitive difference: it is almost certainly the strongest property/casualty operation, with capital far above larger rivals.
Berkshire's policy is to keep that superior capital, since an insurance buyer holds only a promise that should withstand depressed markets and poor underwriting together.
Financial strength is an asset in structured settlements and loss reserve assumptions, where claimants need confidence of payments for decades and few insurers qualify.
Funds held against assumed liabilities in these new lines grew from $16.2 to $30.6 million in 1984; Columbia Insurance received added capital and returns should be satisfactory.
GEICO had excellent unit growth in 1984 with underwriting still far better than the industry; Berkshire's 36% stake equals $320 million of GEICO's $885 million premium volume.
GEICO's stock outperformed its business in earlier years but in 1984 its carrying value was flat while intrinsic value rose substantially.
GEICO was 27% of net worth, so its static market value held back 1984's gain, but Buffett prefers rising business value to soaring market value: judge business, not market performance.

stance.quote:
GEICO has a major, sustainable
competitive advantage.

summary: GEICO has a major sustainable competitive advantage in low-cost auto and homeowners insurance, rare in financial services; other GEICO endeavors have not matched its core profitability.
Lou Simpson invests GEICO's funds with below-average risk and has produced returns by far the best in the insurance industry.
Property/casualty financial statements give at best a first rough draft of earnings and condition, so shareholders should understand reporting weaknesses.
Insurer costs depend on claim losses that are exceptionally hard to estimate, sometimes unknown for decades.
Reported loss expense combines paid losses, estimates for reported unsettled losses, IBNR estimates and revisions of past estimates.
Reserve errors must eventually be corrected, misstating the correction year's earnings: a 1979 claim reserved at $10,000 and settled at $100,000 in 1984 charges $90,000 to 1984.
If such a claim were the only 1979 business, Berkshire would have misled itself on costs and shareholders on earnings.
Insurers adjust case reserves with bulk or supplemental reserves aiming for a total with an equal chance of proving slightly too high or too low.
Eventual payments of all losses before the statement date should show reserves as slightly high or slightly low with equal probability.
Berkshire's supplemental reserves in recent years have not been adequate, and Buffett shows the size of the errors so owners can judge possible systemic bias.
Table: Berkshire's underwriting results 1980-1984 as reported versus corrected one year later, e.g. 1983 reported loss $33.2 million, corrected loss $51.0 million.
Excluding structured settlements, 1984's $45.4 million pre-tax underwriting loss is $27.6 million from 1984 business plus $17.8 million of added loss on 1983.
Berkshire's reserving errors made underwriting look better than it was, reducing urgency and causing overpaid income taxes on overstated earnings, which Buffett regrets.
Berkshire's casualty and reinsurance weighting makes loss costs harder to estimate; it underestimated juries and courts making deep pockets pay and the contagious effect of publicity.
Berkshire's worst under-reserving was in reinsurance, where it set reserves on ceding companies' information, so their mistakes became its own.
Berkshire tries to include all 'rented suit' liabilities in current statements but its record of past errors warrants humility and suspicion; it will keep reporting the errors yearly.
Beyond honest reserving errors, insurers facing bad results took optimistic views of unpaid losses or used transactions to hide true current loss costs.

External auditors cannot effectively police property/casualty insurers' statements; an insurer with liabilities above assets must volunteer that, an honor system where the corpse files the death certificate.
Insurers can be broke but flush with cash; insolvent 'walking dead' insurers keep writing business at any price hoping to get lucky, and managers face little penalty.

stance.quote: the losses mount, the managers keep their jobs and perquisites.

summary: Managers face little extra penalty for large shortfalls, so they keep their jobs and perks while losses mount.
Berkshire suffers from price-cutting by the 'walking dead' and later pays a share of insolvent insurers' deficiencies through state guarantee funds, with risk of cascading insolvencies.
Dangers from insolvent insurers could be limited if state regulators identify and terminate them promptly, but progress has been slow.
From October 1983 to June 1984 Berkshire's insurers bought large amounts of WPPSS Projects 1-3 bonds, though Projects 4 and 5 defaulted on $2.2 billion in 1983.
Problems directly affecting Projects 1, 2 and 3 could weaken or destroy a credit position otherwise strong because of Bonneville Power Administration guarantees.
Despite the negatives, Buffett and Munger judged the WPPSS bond risks, at the low prices paid, to be more than compensated by profit prospects.
Berkshire buys stocks for its insurers using criteria for buying entire businesses, an approach scorned by academics but rewarding in practice; owning a group of undervalued pieces tends to pay.
Berkshire's $139 million WPPSS investment earns $22.7 million after tax, 16.3% on unleveraged capital, economics unavailable in operating businesses that sell at large premiums to capital.
$22.7 million of after-tax earnings would normally cost $250-300 million in a negotiated business deal, double what Berkshire paid for the same earnings from WPPSS bonds.
WPPSS has a slight risk of being worth nothing or interrupting interest, and its value is capped at the $205 million face value, only 48% above Berkshire's price.
The bonds' capped upside matters, but most operating businesses also have limited upside unless more capital is invested, since returns on equity rarely improve even with inflation.
Reinvesting a 12% bond's coupons grows like a business retaining 12% earnings: a $10 million 30-year zero-coupon 12% bond and such a business both reach $300 million by 2015.

stance.quote:
paid 100 cents on the dollar for that abominable
business.

summary: Treating bonds as businesses avoids staggering errors; in 1946 buyers of 20-year AAA tax-exempt bonds yielding about 1% bought an abominable 'business' earning 1% on book.
In 1946 good businesses were available near book value earning 10%-15%, yet bond buyers locked in terms outrageously inadequate by business standards for the next two decades.
Graham's The Intelligent Investor ends with 'Investment is most intelligent when it is most businesslike', which Buffett calls the best investing book ever written.
The WPPSS commitment carries real, hard-to-evaluate risk; with few such decisions a year, Berkshire could look foolish in any given year even if long-term results are fine.
Most managers avoid unconventional decisions to escape pink slips, but Buffett and Munger, owning 47% of Berkshire, act with its money as with their own.
Concentrating insurers' investments, including WPPSS, is appropriate only because Berkshire's insurance business has exceptional financial strength; most insurers could not withstand a big error.
Financial strength lets Berkshire hold large blocks of a few well-studied securities; concentration should give superior results, tempered by size, and owners share the risk.
Berkshire bought less than 3% of WPPSS Projects 1-3 bonds despite trying to buy nearly all, and will not inform shareholders of changes in its position until long after completion.
A couple of coat-tail riders could have cost Berkshire $5 million on WPPSS, so it comments on its securities activity to no one unless legally required.

stance.quote:
we
dislike the purchase of most long-term bonds under most
circumstances

summary: Berkshire dislikes most long-term bonds, which are only as sound as the dollar; Buffett sees substantial inflation ahead and a small chance of runaway inflation.
Huge deficits are a dangerous, hard-to-reverse fiscal policy; without reversal high inflation will be delayed but not avoided and could spiral upward.
In runaway inflation bonds suffer far more than a diversified stock portfolio, so an all-bond portfolio has an unacceptable wipe-out risk and Berkshire buys long bonds only rarely.
Companies report dividend policy without explaining why it suits owners; managers and owners should think hard about when to retain or distribute earnings.
Not all earnings are equal: in asset-heavy businesses inflation makes part of reported earnings 'restricted' and undistributable; paying them out leads to oblivion unless new equity is raised.
Restricted earnings are conscripted by the business however poor its prospects; Consolidated Edison retained earnings that turned into 25 cents of market value each under punitive regulation.
Con Edison kept reinvesting most earnings despite this gold-into-lead process while its slogan proclaimed 'Dig We Must'.
Unrestricted earnings can be retained or distributed, and management should choose whichever course makes more sense for the owners.
The only valid reason to retain unrestricted earnings is a reasonable prospect that each retained dollar creates at least a dollar of market value, needing returns above investors' alternatives.
Bond analogy: with a 10% perpetual bond whose coupon can be reinvested, taking cash is foolish when market rates are 5% since the reinvested bonds are worth more.
At 5% interest rates no rational bondholder would take cash, even one needing money, since taking bonds and selling them yields more.
At 15% rates a rational investor takes the 10% coupon in cash, because reinvested bonds would be worth far less and can be bought at a discount.
Owners should similarly judge whether unrestricted earnings be retained or paid out by guessing returns on reinvestment: reinvest if returns will be high, distribute if low.
Managers reason like owners when deciding subsidiary payouts to the parent, but often cannot put themselves in shareholders' shoes for parent-level payouts.
A CEO makes a 5% subsidiary send cash to a 15% one but, with his own 5% incremental returns against 10% market rates, imposes a historical payout on parent shareholders.
Such CEOs demand full explanations from subsidiaries for retention but seldom give owners a similar analysis for the whole company.
Incremental returns may be distorted by a core business: outstanding businesses throw off excess cash, and poor outside investments are hidden by very high returns on small core capital needs.
Like a Pro-Am golf team's best-ball score, a company's overall return can look respectable because of a dominant core business despite hopeless amateurs elsewhere.
Many companies with good returns misallocate retained earnings, camouflaging repeated failures such as high-priced acquisitions of mediocre businesses behind a marvelous core business.
Shareholders would be better off if earnings were retained only to expand the high-return business, with the rest paid as dividends or used for repurchases; managers should be held accountable.

Dividends should be consistent and reflect long-term earnings and incremental return expectations; withheld earnings must earn their keep, and if unwisely retained, managers have likely been unwisely retained too.
Berkshire has historically earned above market rates on retained earnings, creating over a dollar of market value per dollar retained, so any distribution would have hurt shareholders.

Early distributions could have been disastrous: Berkshire (textiles), Diversified Retailing (department stores) and Blue Chip (trading stamps) paid little or no dividends, retaining the capital that built Berkshire.

Berkshire, Diversified Retailing and Blue Chip's cornerstone textile, department store and trading-stamp businesses earned almost nothing, shrank or lost money; better businesses overcame these origins, so diversification served well.
Berkshire will retain all earnings while prospective returns beat a dollar of market value per dollar retained, else distribute surplus; it judges history on a five-year rolling average.
Berkshire plans to use retained earnings to build insurance capital since rivals are weak; industry premium volume should exceed $15 billion in 1985 versus under $5 billion in 1983.
A shareholder found a company meeting Berkshire's tests in 1984 but a chance complication prevented a deal; the 'business wanted' ad is repeated.
Acquisition criteria: purchases earning at least $5 million after tax, consistent earning power, good returns with little debt, management in place, simple businesses and a stated price.
Berkshire does no unfriendly takeovers, offers confidentiality and five-minute answers, prefers cash but may issue stock for equal intrinsic value, and offers sellers a good home.
97.2% of eligible shares joined the 1984 shareholder-designated contributions program, giving $3,179,000 to 1,519 charities; shareholders get an advisory vote.
New shareholders must register shares in the actual owner's name by September 30, 1985 to take part in the 1985 contributions program.

stance.quote:
Quite simply, they are tops in both
ability and integrity.

summary: Berkshire agreed in March 1985 to buy three million Capital Cities Communications shares at $172.50, contingent on Capital Cities acquiring ABC; Buffett admires Murphy and Burke.
1985 saw Berkshire buy a major Capital Cities/ABC position, acquire Scott & Fetzer, enter Fireman's Fund insurance participation and sell its General Foods stock.
Net worth rose $613.6 million, or 48.2%, in 1985; per-share book value grew from $19.46 to $1,643.71 over twenty-one years, 23.2% compounded, a rate that will not repeat.
