The rate can't recur because the stock market offers little opportunity versus 1964-84; Berkshire's insurers cannot find significantly undervalued equities to buy, unlike a decade ago.
Current market prices generously appraise Berkshire's holdings' strong economics, so its insurers have no chance of future portfolio gains on the scale of the past.
The second negative is size: equity capital is over twenty times its level ten years ago, and high-return companies with $1 billion of equity could not keep earning 20%.
Such companies could not find enough high-return opportunities to reinvest all earnings, though shareholders would have been far better off if they could have.
To earn 15% annually Berkshire now needs $5.7 billion of profits over ten years versus $3.9 billion last year, a 48% increase matching capital growth.
Buffett and Munger are reasonably optimistic about returns beyond corporate America's, retaining all earnings, but will need far more good fortune to average 15% than past 23.2% required.
Berkshire shares historically sold modestly below intrinsic value; recently the discount disappeared and sometimes a modest premium prevails.
Elimination of the discount means market value rose faster than business value, good for holders but bad for new owners, who must maintain any premium to match the company's results.
Buffett prefers a market price that approximates business value; wild swings do not change aggregate owner gains, but long mispricing distributes business gains inequitably among owners.
Berkshire's market value has tracked business value more consistently than any other public equity Buffett knows, thanks to rational individual shareholders unlike institution-dominated peers.

stance.quote:
stocks heavily owned and constantly monitored by
institutions have often been among the most inappropriately
valued.

summary: Institutions with large professional staffs do not stabilize markets: stocks heavily owned and monitored by institutions have often been among the most inappropriately valued.
Berkshire's earnings sources table shows the major sources of reported earnings; Buffett and Munger focus on segment figures and never prepare consolidated numbers for internal use.
Segment information is essential for investors in multi-line businesses; managers long withheld it until the SEC ordered disclosure of segment data.
Goodwill amortization is shown as a separate item rather than charged to specific businesses; segment and Goodwill details appear elsewhere in the report.
Table: 1985 vs 1984 pre-tax and after-tax earnings by entity, including insurance, Associated Retail, Blue Chip, Buffalo News, Mutual Savings, Nebraska Furniture Mart and Precision Steel.
Table (continued): See's, textiles, Wesco, goodwill, interest, contributions, other, operating earnings of $125.4 million, and special Washington Post and General Foods distributions.
Table: 1985 securities sales gains of $468.9 million pre-tax and total earnings of all entities of $613.4 million pre-tax versus $200.5 million in 1984.
1985 earnings include unusually large securities-sale gains, which like a graduation ceremony recognize years of growth in the year of sale and so say little about that year's performance.
Gains on stock held by insurers hit net worth annually, but reported capital gains or losses in any single year are meaningless as a measure of current performance.
$338 million of the $488 million realized 1985 gain came from selling General Foods, bought in 1980 below business value, after Philip Morris offered full value.

Berkshire seeks attractive purchases, not attractive sales: bargain price, fine economics and a shareholder-focused management build value even though only a buyer paying full value produces reported earnings.

Special Washington Post and General Foods distributions arise when Berkshire sells shares back as the company repurchases, keeping its ownership percentage unchanged, and the IRS treats them as dividends.
Corporations pay much lower taxes on dividends than on capital gains, a gap a House-passed tax bill would widen; Berkshire again reports these distributions as capital gains.
Berkshire agreed to proportional share sales only when managements proposed them; non-selling holders benefit as repurchases are made below intrinsic value, with the tax benefit as a bonus.
Munger stresses studying mistakes; Buffett has supplied ample material, especially in textile and insurance businesses, and first discusses a failure at a smaller business.
Berkshire decided in July 1985 to close its textile operation, largely completed by yearend.
When Buffett Partnership bought Berkshire 21 years earlier, $22 million of net worth was all textiles; nine prior years of $530 million sales produced a $10 million loss.
Southern non-union textile plants seemed advantaged when Berkshire bought; Ken Chace and Garry Morrison proved excellent managers equal to those at more profitable businesses.
Cash from textiles funded the 1967 purchase of National Indemnity through earnings and reduced inventories, receivables and fixed assets; textiles never became a good earner even in upturns.
Diversification shrank textiles' drag on returns; Berkshire stayed for employer, management, labor and modest-cash-return reasons stated in the 1978 report.
Buffett had said Berkshire would keep supporting textiles despite more attractive uses of capital, as long as the stated conditions prevailed.
Buffett was very wrong about modest cash returns: after 1979 textiles consumed major cash, and with no buyers interested by mid-1985 liquidation was the only option.
Buffett will not close sub-normal businesses just to raise returns, but will not fund an operation facing unending losses.

stance.quote: But in the end nothing worked and I should be faulted for not quitting sooner.

summary: Berkshire's textile operation failed despite reworked products and the Waumbec Mills acquisition; Buffett says he should have quit sooner, as 250 textile mills closed since 1980.
Buffett admits he believed what he preferred to believe about the textile business instead of letting the intellect lead.

stance.quote: The domestic textile industry operates in a commodity business, competing in a world market in which substantial excess capacity exists.

summary: Domestic textiles is a commodity business facing excess world capacity and low-wage foreign competition; Berkshire's poorly paid workers were not to blame for the closing.
Textile unions accepted the cost disadvantage and behaved cooperatively through liquidation; Buffett notes an unreasonable union might have forced earlier closure and saved losses.
Large textile capital projects looked like winners on standard return tests, often better than spending in the candy and newspaper businesses.
Promised benefits from textile capital spending were illusory: when competitors spent too, lower costs became industry-wide lower prices and returns stayed anemic.
Berkshire faced a miserable choice: heavy textile investment meant terrible returns on growing capital, while refusing to invest meant becoming uncompetitive.
Burlington Industries, the largest textile company, had 1964 sales of $1.2 billion against Berkshire's $50 million, with its stock at 60 versus Berkshire's 13.
Burlington stayed in textiles, reaching 1985 sales of about $2.8 billion after roughly $3 billion of capital expenditures over 1964-85, probably rational decisions.
Despite heavy spending Burlington lost real sales volume and returns; its stock at 34 is near its 1964 level while the CPI tripled, cutting purchasing power by two-thirds.

stance.quote: a textile company that allocates capital brilliantly within its industry is a remarkable textile company - but not a remarkable business.

summary: Burlington shows how brain power applied to a faulty premise devastates shareholders; brilliant capital allocation inside a poor industry does not make a good business.
A good managerial record depends more on the business you are in than on how well you row; better to change boats than patch a leaking one.
The early-1986 auction of Berkshire's textile machinery is an investment postscript for those who weight book value or replacement value heavily.
Textile equipment that cost about $13 million, with $866,000 book value and $30-50 million replacement cost, sold for $163,122 gross and netted less than zero.
The economic goodwill of two Buffalo paper routes or one See's store exceeds what Berkshire's large pile of textile tangible assets fetched at auction.
Nebraska Furniture Mart, See's and the Buffalo Evening News earned $72 million pre-tax in 1985 versus about $8 million fifteen years earlier, before acquisition.
The three businesses raised earnings by $64 million while needing only about $40 million more invested capital, after starting from excellent returns on capital.
Economic goodwill let the three businesses grow earnings with little capital in inflation, while the average U.S. business needed about $5 of capital per $1 of added pre-tax earnings.
An average business would have needed over $300 million of extra owner capital to match the earnings gain of Berkshire's group of three.
Quadrupling earnings by putting up more capital is no managerial achievement; CEOs are praised for growth that merely reflects retained earnings and compounding.
CEO praise is deserved only if return on capital was superior; a savings account at 8% reinvesting interest would quadruple earnings in 18 years.

stance.quote: Many corporate compensation plans reward managers handsomely for earnings increases produced solely, or in large part, by retained earnings

summary: Compensation plans and ten-year fixed-price options reward managers for earnings growth that comes from retained earnings, often at companies paying small dividends.
Example of a $100,000 savings account earning 8% whose trustee pays out only one-quarter of interest, illustrating inequities in retained-earnings-based pay.
Under a 25% payout the account reaches $179,084 in ten years, with earnings up 70% to $13,515 and dividends rising from $2,000 to $3,378.

stance.quote: they have gained in value simply because management retained earnings, not because it did well with the capital in its hands.

summary: A trustee holding a ten-year fixed-price option profits from retained earnings alone; many corporate stock options gain value only because management withheld earnings.

stance.quote: Managers actually apply a double standard to options.

summary: Managers never grant ten-year fixed-price options on a business to outsiders, who would have to pay for capital added during the option period.

stance.quote: Managers regularly engineer ten-year, fixed-price options for themselves and associates

summary: Managers grant themselves ten-year fixed-price stock options that ignore retained earnings and the cost of capital, profiting without real performance.

stance.quote: A managerial Rip Van Winkle, ready to doze for ten years, could not wish for a better “incentive” system.

summary: Stock options sometimes reward talented managers but are irrevocable and blind to performance, so a sluggard is paid exactly like a star.
Chrysler objected when the long-term options it gave the U.S. Government for loan guarantees paid off richly, though no manager objects to windfalls on their own options.

stance.quote: No owner has ever escaped the burden of capital costs, whereas a holder of a fixed-price option bears no capital costs at all.

summary: Options do not put managers and owners in the same boat: owners bear capital costs and downside risk, while fixed-price option holders bear neither.
Option holders benefit from a no-dividend policy, while owners should favour full payout; Buffett criticizes the indiscriminate use of options, not options in all circumstances.
Stock options should go only to managers with overall responsibility; managers of limited areas should be paid on results under their own control.
Options should carry a retained-earnings or carrying-cost factor and be priced realistically, not at depressed market prices or tax-code minimums.
Owners are not served by selling part of the business at a bargain price to outsiders or insiders, so options should be priced at true business value.
Some admired managers disagree and use fixed-price options to build owner-minded cultures; where such a culture works it may be left intact.
Berkshire pays key managers bonuses for meeting targets in their own units, regardless of Berkshire's stock price, with performance defined by each business's economics.
Berkshire unit bonuses can reach five times base salary or more, one possibly topping $2 million in 1986, with no cap and no weight on seniority or age.
Berkshire managers can use bonuses or borrowed money to buy Berkshire stock, accepting the risks and carrying costs of real owners; many hold large positions.
Nebraska Furniture Mart's low-cost operation and best values let it set a new sales record in 1985 despite a worsening farm economy.

stance.quote: industry trends are not good, and we continue to experience slippage in poundage sales on a same-store basis.

summary: See's has unmatched store volumes but same-store poundage is slipping, pressuring per-pound costs; only modest price increases are planned and margins will narrow without stabilization.
Buffalo News linage rose in 1985 only through lower-margin preprints while ROP advertising declined; costs stayed controlled and household penetration remained exceptional.
See's, the Buffalo News and Nebraska Furniture Mart have no management problem thanks to their long-serving managers, whom Buffett praises.
Table: insurance industry yearly change in written premiums and combined ratio after policyholder dividends, 1972 to 1985 estimated.
The combined ratio compares losses incurred plus expenses with premium revenue; below 100 is an underwriting profit and above 100 a loss.
Industry insured losses grew 16% in 1984 and 17% in 1985, over 13 points above inflation, a modern record that blocked a combined-ratio drop.
The 1985 loss surge was not from catastrophes, about 2% of premiums, or more exposure units, but partly from industry reserve additions admitting earlier under-reserving.

stance.quote: Nevertheless, the short-term outlook is good.

summary: Judicial inflation is a wild card for insurers, but premium growth accelerated through 1985 and the industry combined ratio should fall sharply in 1986 barring a supercatastrophe.
Commodity businesses earn well only when prices are fixed or capacity is short, and managers quickly add capacity, so the insurance profit gain is short-lived.
Insurance is now priced as a commodity because policyholders focus on price and the old cartel-like pricing is gone, so prices pay off only when capacity is tight.
Insurance capacity is an attitude tied to capital, not a physical fact; capital can be raised instantly, so any capacity shortage is quickly eliminated.

stance.quote: it won’t be long before serious price-cutting appears and next a fall in profitability.

summary: About 15 insurers raised over $3 billion in 1985 and capital-raising accelerated in 1986; continued capacity additions will bring price-cutting and lower profitability.
Berkshire's industry-best capital position became a competitive advantage as the market tightened; premium volume more than tripled in 1985 after a long stagnation.
A flight to quality drew large insurance and reinsurance buyers to Berkshire's strong capital, and its ability to insure substantial risks also set it apart.
Insurers writing large risks traditionally keep a small net line and pass most of the risk to excess-of-loss reinsurers, as in a $25 million D&O policy retaining $1 million.
A company issuing large policies while retaining little risk writes a large gross line but a small net line.
Dividing premium among risk layers between issuer and reinsurers is hard; past loss experience is the usual guide for what reinsurers need for fair compensation.
Reinsurers' long-tail losses make experience an imperfect guide, and huge unprecedented court awards make extrapolating from past data a formula for disaster.
Issuers keeping a small net line kept more premium than risk and sometimes profited on business unprofitable to issuer and reinsurers combined, especially in malpractice, D&O and products liability.
Issuing companies stayed enthusiastic about writing business long after gross premiums became woefully inadequate.
In 1984 a leading large-risk issuer wrote $6 billion, kept about 40%, and ran a combined ratio under 110 while its reinsurers lost over $1.5 billion at over 140.
The issuer-versus-reinsurer gap came from ordinary insurance losses, not catastrophes, and Buffett predicts the 1985 report will show the same unbalanced results.
After repeated unpleasant surprises in long-tail casualty lines, many reinsurers are quitting regardless of price, causing a dramatic pullback of reinsurance capacity.
With reinsurance withdrawn, issuing companies can no longer commit reinsurers for tens of millions per policy, so their gross capacity has shrunk toward their small net capacity.
Berkshire never laid risk off at a profit but now has the underwriting capability others lack, willing to risk $10 million of its own money on a single event.
National Indemnity's mid-1985 ad for policies with $1 million minimum premiums drew 600 replies and about $50 million of long-tail premiums, with underwriting success unknown for five years.

stance.quote: this period of tightness will pass; insurers and reinsurers will return to underpricing.

summary: The tight insurance market will pass and insurers will underprice again, but Berkshire's insurance segments should do well for a year or two under improved management.
Berkshire's combined ratio improved from 134 in 1984 to 111 in 1985 but still reflects past misdeeds; loss development again shows significant underreserving at end of 1984.
Nearly all 1984 underreserving was in reinsurance, mainly a few contracts discontinued years ago, though Buffett warns the 'except for' excuse is a trap.
Managers should drop 'except for' excuses and count all losses; the wise manager learns most lessons from others' experience rather than personal mistakes.

stance.quote: its record was far better than that of virtually all its major competitors.

summary: GEICO, 38% owned, had excellent 1985 premium growth and investment results but poor underwriting as auto and homeowners lines deteriorated; Jack Byrne left for Fireman's Fund.
Jack Byrne's lasting GEICO benefit came from finding successors Bill Snyder and Lou Simpson; Berkshire followed him to Fireman's Fund, where he is CEO.
From September 1, 1985 Berkshire took a 7% share of Fireman's Fund business in force under a four-year quota-share contract, reimbursing losses for many years afterward.
Under the Fireman's Fund contract premiums are remitted promptly and Berkshire reimburses expenses and losses, keeping the resulting funds for investment; Berkshire has no role in its underwriting.
Fireman's Fund writes about $3 billion; Berkshire received $92.7 million of its $1.324 billion unearned premium reserve and paid $29.4 million of expenses, with Wes-FIC taking two-sevenths.

Berkshire's insurance tables gained a Major Quota Share Contracts line showing rough 1985 Fireman's Fund results; a second quota-share contract signed after yearend should exceed $50 million of 1986 volume.
Introduces the yearend 1985 net holdings in marketable equities, listing positions over $25 million and excluding minority interests of Wesco and Nebraska Furniture Mart.

Table: yearend 1985 common-stock holdings (Affiliated Publications, ABC, Beatrice, GEICO, Handy & Harman, Time, Washington Post) with shares, cost and market value; total cost $275 million, market $1,198 million.
Over the past decade the market shifted from ignoring great businesses to recognizing them; the Washington Post Company is an excellent example.

Berkshire bought its Washington Post stake in mid-1973 at no more than one-quarter of per-share business value, a $100 million market value against $400-500 million intrinsic value, following Ben Graham.

stance.quote: the stock market was totally efficient, and therefore calculations of business value - and even thought, itself - were of no importance in investment activities.

summary: Early-1970s institutions ignored business value because academics taught that the market was efficient, which gave value investors an advantage.
By yearend 1974 Berkshire's Washington Post stake was down 25%, $8 million market value against $10.6 million cost, though business value grew and the stock traded below 20% of it.
Kay Graham repurchased large amounts of Washington Post stock at bargain prices and raised business value, giving Berkshire a triple dip from business growth, buybacks and a narrowing discount.
Berkshire still holds all Washington Post shares bought in 1973 except those redeemed in 1985; redemption proceeds plus yearend market value total $221 million.

stance.quote: Her stunning business success has in large part gone unreported but among Berkshire shareholders it should not go unappreciated.

summary: The $10.6 million in Washington Post would have been worth $40-60 million in other media stocks; the extra $160 million came largely from Kay Graham's superior managerial decisions.

stance.quote: there is no way that the value can progress from that level at a rate anywhere close to the rate possible when the company’s valuation was only $100 million

summary: Berkshire will hold Washington Post indefinitely, but at a $1.8 billion market value future returns are far below those from the $100 million valuation, as with its other bid-up holdings.
The large yearend Beatrice position is a short-term arbitrage holding, a parking place for cash used when Berkshire has more money than ideas, though deals can fail.
Insurance subsidiaries held about $400 million of tax-exempt bonds, $194 million of them WPPSS 1, 2 and 3, with a $62 million unrealized gain and $30 million yearly tax-exempt income.

stance.quote: I think it is the best of any publicly-owned company in the country.

summary: Right after yearend Berkshire bought 3 million Capital Cities/ABC shares at $172.50, a price set in March 1985, citing its management as the best of any public company.
Berkshire's stock purchase helped Capital Cities finance its $3.5 billion acquisition of ABC, whose economics will be unexciting for several years; Berkshire is patient.
Berkshire agreed that Capital Cities' CEO votes its stock and restricted sales of its block without management approval, as it did earlier at GEICO and Washington Post.

stance.quote: We feel the long-term economic prospects for these businesses - and, thus, for ourselves as owners - are enhanced by the arrangements.

summary: Despite forgoing premium prices for large blocks, Berkshire says sale restrictions enhance long-term owner value by letting first-class managers avoid distraction from revolving-door capitalists.
Widely diffused voting ownership makes corporate instability inevitable; limiting Berkshire's blocks promotes stability, which with a good manager and business supports a rich financial harvest.
Berkshire's ownership agreements tell managers there will be no surprises and give them a corporate commitment that survives Buffett's departure.

stance.quote: it’s no field for bargains.

summary: Capital Cities was bought at a full $172.50 amid near-manic media enthusiasm, though Buffett sold Berkshire's earlier holding at $43 in 1978-80.
Berkshire bought Scott Fetzer for about $320 million plus $90 million of existing debt; it has $700 million of sales across 17 businesses with good to excellent returns on capital.
World Book is about 40% of Scott Fetzer's sales and slightly more of income, and sells more than twice as many encyclopedia sets as its nearest competitor.
World Book's top-rated encyclopedia sells below competitors' prices; that value combination helped justify the Scott Fetzer price despite weakening direct-selling results.
Scott Fetzer CEO Ralph Schey cut the company from 31 businesses by disposing of poor fits and bought World Book in 1978; Buffett calls his capital-allocation record superb.
Scott Fetzer had been a sale candidate since early 1984; a mid-1985 ESOP-based plan approved by shareholders was scuttled after closing difficulties.
Buffett wrote Scott Fetzer's CEO after its ESOP deal collapsed and signed a contract within weeks; with insurance growth, 1986 revenues should top $2 billion, over double 1985.
Berkshire has no acquisition master strategy or planning staff and simply acts when something sensible appears; it raised its minimum profit requirement so deals measurably affect results.
Acquisition criteria: at least $10 million after-tax earnings, consistent earning power, good returns on equity with little debt, management in place, simple businesses and a stated price.
Berkshire avoids unfriendly takeovers, offers confidentiality and fast answers, and prefers cash but will issue stock when it receives as much intrinsic value as it gives.
Berkshire is not attracted by the frequent proposals that fail its tests: new ventures, turnarounds, auction-like sales and deals expected to work out once parties meet.
Berkshire also negotiates purchases of large non-controlling stock blocks when comfortable with the economics and management integrity, preferring commitments well above $50 million.

96.8% of eligible shares joined the 1985 designated-contributions program, giving $4 million to 1,724 charities; a shareholder plebiscite strongly supported current contribution and dividend policies.
New shareholders should read the shareholder-designated contributions description and register shares in the owner's name by September 30, 1986 to be eligible for the 1986 program.
adjudication_note: Eligibility rules of the shareholder-designated contributions program are shareholder_programs content, and the same paragraph in the 1984, 1991-1997 letters is annotated financial, so the QA row is right.

summary: To comply with the Bank Holding Company Act, Berkshire divested Illinois National Bank by letting shareholders choose between Rockford Bancorp shares and Berkshire shares at a set exchange ratio.
The Illinois National divestiture used a cut-the-cake method: Buffett set the exchange terms and shareholders chose which piece, Berkshire or Rockford, they preferred.
Illinois National was sold in fall 1985, and Rockford shareholders' liquidation proceeds per share will about equal Berkshire's per-share intrinsic value then, indicating a fair five-year split.
Net worth rose $492.5 million or 26.1% in 1986; per-share book value grew from $19.46 to $2,073.06 over 22 years, 23.3% compounded, with shares outstanding up under 1%.
Berkshire's book value has been a reasonable but conservative proxy for business value; in 1986 business value probably grew faster than book value, though that figure is soft within 10%.
Key managers raised earnings dramatically using little added capital outside insurance, building unrecorded economic goodwill that boosted business value relative to book value in 1986.
Buffett says his performance trailed the managers' because he could not skillfully deploy much of the capital their businesses generated.
Buffett and Munger's first job is to attract and keep outstanding managers, who usually came with the acquired companies, and mainly not get in their way.
Berkshire's key managers work for love of the job, not money, and think like owners, which Buffett calls the highest compliment for a manager.
Right players make any team manager look good; Berkshire follows Ogilvy's view that hiring people bigger than yourself builds a company of giants.
With able, high-character managers many can report to one executive, so Buffett and Munger could handle double Berkshire's number of managers if they had the same qualities.
Berkshire works only with people it likes and admires, which improves results and enjoyment; working with disagreeable people is like marrying for money.
Capital allocation is Berkshire's second job and matters more than usual because it earns about 23% and retains everything; misallocating retained earnings would quickly damage its economics.
If retained earnings are used unproductively Berkshire's economics deteriorate quickly, while a company adding about 5% to net worth annually changes far more slowly.
Capital allocation was tough in 1986; the only acquisition was Fechheimer Bros., a company with excellent economics but small, using about 2% of Berkshire's net worth.
With no new ideas in marketable equities, Berkshire's main 1986 capital moves were paying off debt and stockpiling funds; a few blank years in allocation would slow its growth.
Berkshire hopes to buy an operating business every couple of years, but only large ones matter; stock prices leave little to buy for insurers, and timing of change is unknown.
Berkshire's returns will drop because of size; its 15% return-on-equity hope despite negative tax law changes needs net worth to rise $7.2 billion in ten years.
The 1986 earnings-sources table adds four lines for the Scott Fetzer and Fechheimer acquisitions, showing World Book and Kirby separately, and drops separate reporting for smaller businesses.
Goodwill amortization is shown as a separate aggregate item rather than charged to businesses; the Scott Fetzer and Fechheimer acquisitions raised the 1986 amortization charge.
Scott Fetzer required GAAP purchase-price adjustments; the table shows unit earnings before them, which Berkshire views as more useful to investors than GAAP figures.
Table: 1986 and 1985 pre-tax and after-tax earnings by source, covering insurance underwriting and investment income, Buffalo News, Fechheimer, Kirby, NFM, Scott Fetzer, See's, Wesco and World Book.

Table: continuation of 1986 and 1985 earnings by source (See's, Wesco, World Book), goodwill amortization, debt interest, shareholder contributions, operating earnings $195.9 million and securities sales.
Table: special Washington Post distribution, sales of securities and total earnings of all entities, $412.1 million pre-tax in 1986 versus $613.4 million in 1985.

stance.quote: Operating results at The Buffalo News continue to reflect a truly superb managerial job by Stan Lipsey.

summary: Operating earnings rose in 1986; the Buffalo News improved margins for a third year through falling man-hours and tight cost control despite below-industry advertising rate increases.
The Buffalo News keeps a 50% news hole versus about 40% at comparable papers, delivering at least 50% more news for the same number of ad pages despite cost control.
The Buffalo News has the highest weekday penetration among the top 50 papers and leads on Sundays, versus the Courier-Express's 271,000 circulation and 63% penetration ten years earlier.

stance.quote: Despite our exceptional market acceptance, our operating margins almost certainly have peaked.

summary: The Buffalo News Sunday paper reached 83% penetration and 100,000 more copies than the Courier-Express, but margins have peaked with a newsprint price increase and moderate 1987 rates.
Ten years after the purchase, the Buffalo News has delivered financial rewards far above expectations, helped by editor Murray Light and manager Stan Lipsey through its difficult early years.
Nebraska Furniture Mart's 1986 net sales rose 10.2% to $132 million versus $44 million ten years earlier, explained by its widening reputation for rock-bottom prices and broad selection.
Nebraska Furniture Mart is expanding its warehouse capacity by about one-third to prepare for further sales gains.
See's pounds sold rose about 2% in 1986 and same-store pounds stabilized after six years of decline; margins held with minimal price increases and strong Christmas sales.

stance.quote: Few major retailing companies have been able to sustain such a customer-oriented spirit

summary: See's one-of-a-kind personality comes from taste, moderate price, controlled distribution and service; profits should stay level with only very modest price increases matching cost rises.
World Book, largest of Scott Fetzer's 17 operations, grew unit volume a fourth straight year with encyclopedia sales up 7% on 1985 and 45% on 1982; Ralph Schey earns praise.
World Book dominates U.S. direct-sales encyclopedias, priced under 5 cents per page, with editing that ranks 44,000 words by difficulty so entries stay readable.

stance.quote: If you want the best, you buy a Kirby.

summary: World Book salespeople are mostly teachers or ex-teachers; Kirby had a fourth straight year of unit gains, up 4% on 1985 and 33% on 1982, with a durable premium product.
Some historically successful direct-sales companies have stumbled as working women changed the market, but Kirby and World Book have responded successfully.
Berkshire keeps descriptions of major units brief to avoid repetition, noting about 98% of stock at each yearend is owned by holders from the prior year-start.
Berkshire's major business units share very strong market positions, very high returns on capital employed and the best operating managements.
Berkshire's annual 'business wanted' ad paid off in 1986 when Fechheimer's chairman, a shareholder, wrote that his company met the tests and they met after 1985 results were compiled.
Fechheimer, a uniform maker and distributor founded in 1842, was highly successful under the Heldman family's management from 1941 onward.
Fechheimer was sold in a 1981 leveraged buyout; operations stayed successful, debt was substantially paid down and equity value soared before the venture capitalists chose to sell.

stance.quote: Its economic record is superb

summary: Berkshire quickly bought about 84% of Fechheimer at a price based on a $55 million valuation of the whole business, with the Heldman family staying as partners.
The Fechheimer purchase resembled Nebraska Furniture Mart: sellers wanted funds elsewhere, family managers stayed as owners, and the family wanted a buyer who would not resell.
Berkshire judges acquisitions by a business's economic characteristics and its people rather than plant visits; Fechheimer stood out on both, with next-generation managers ensuring continuity.
Fechheimer's only drawback as an acquisition prototype is its size; Berkshire raised its minimum after-tax earnings threshold for acquisitions from $5 million to $10 million.
Acquisition criteria: at least $10 million after-tax earnings, consistent earning power, good returns on equity with little debt, management in place, simple businesses and a stated price.
Berkshire avoids unfriendly takeovers, promises confidentiality and fast answers, and prefers cash but will issue stock when receiving as much intrinsic value as it gives.
Berkshire is not attracted by frequent proposals that fail its tests: new ventures, turnarounds, auction-like sales and deals promoted as sure to work out.
Berkshire also negotiates purchases of large non-controlling blocks when comfortable with the economics and management integrity, preferring commitments many times $50 million.
Table: insurance industry premium growth, combined ratio, incurred-loss growth and GNP deflator inflation, 1981-1986.
The combined ratio compares losses plus expenses to premiums; counting float income, a combined ratio of 107-112 typically yields overall break-even before earnings on shareholder funds.

When industry premiums grow only 4-5%, underwriting losses mount; social and judicial inflation, ballooning verdicts and expanded coverage, are the culprits, and revenues must grow near 10% to hold profitability.
Berkshire believes industry revenues must grow close to 10% annually just to hold profitability, even though general inflation runs only 2-4%.

stance.quote: also predicted that prosperity would be fleeting.

summary: Industry premiums outgrew losses in 1986, cutting the underwriting loss, but premium growth slowed from 27.1% to 18.7% across the year and may fall below 10% by mid-1987.

stance.quote: Thereafter the industry is likely to head south in a hurry.

summary: Industry underwriting should improve again in 1987 as price rises reach revenues with a lag, but the improving trend will probably end by late 1988 or early 1989.
Insurance pricing behaves like a commodity business: high profits occur only in shortage, then insurers issue shares to build capital, capacity soars and prices fade.
Insurance leaders ask colleagues to price more 'statesmanlike' to even out cycles, wishing for the steadily rising prices of a Wall Street Journal-type franchise.

stance.quote: What’s needed is not more statesmen, but less corn.

summary: Appeals for pricing discipline are as futile as asking corn growers to restrain themselves; capital raised in two years expanded insurance capacity, which will depress prices and profits.
Berkshire's insurance operation did well in 1986 and should in 1987, helped by industry conditions and by Mike Goldberg's ability as manager.
Berkshire's statutory combined ratio fell from 111 in 1985 to 103 in 1986, and it was probably the fastest-growing top-100 insurer even excluding the Fireman's Fund quota-share premiums.
Berkshire was the slowest-growing large insurer before 1985 and shrank; its volume swings reflect other insurers coming and going, while it always stands ready to write high-limit coverage.
When many insurers slash prices below expectable costs, customers leave Berkshire for temporary bargains, so its premium volume swings with competitors' behavior.

Berkshire's price firmness hurts neither consumers nor employees; its no-layoff practice during cyclical slowdowns in insurance premium volume serves its self-interest by keeping employees from chasing volume.
National Indemnity's monthly volume rose from about $5 million in late 1984 to $35 million by early 1986, then fell to $20 million as new competitors cut prices.
Berkshire must pay part of bankrupt insurers' unpaid losses through state guaranty funds, while the same managers now write similar business under a new name.
Berkshire's large-risk business with $1-3 million premiums expanded in 1986 and will be volatile; its structured settlement business is near-dormant because current prices make no sense.
The 1986 loss reserve development table shows Berkshire's yearend 1985 liabilities were again understated, making three years in a row of reserving error.

stance.quote: the term is a euphemism for what should more properly be called "correction of previous untruths"

summary: 'Reserve strengthening' is a euphemism for correcting earlier untruths; Berkshire tried hard to reserve accurately at the end of 1986 as in 1985, and time will tell.

stance.quote: It’s a treacherous business and a wary attitude is essential.

summary: Despite reserving difficulties and commodity economics, Berkshire expects its insurance business to grow and make significant money, but irregularly and with major unpleasant surprises.
Berkshire's insurance advantages are attitude, capital and developing personnel, plus a possible long-term edge in investing float; the business requires all of them to prosper.

stance.quote: GEICO’s book of business is one of the best in the world of insurance, far better indeed than Berkshire’s own book.

summary: GEICO, 41% owned, improved its combined ratio to 96.9 with 16% premium growth and shrank its share count 5.5%; Berkshire's share of premiums exceeds $500 million.
GEICO's rock-bottom costs are its key advantage: underwriting plus loss adjustment expense was 23.5% of 1986 premiums, about 15 points below many majors, including Allstate and State Farm.

stance.quote: the company’s future will be brilliant indeed.

summary: GEICO's cost gap is a moat around a valuable franchise; its expense ratio fell from 24.1% to 23.5% from 1985 to 1986 under Bill Snyder and will likely fall further.
Lou Simpson's GEICO equity portfolio beat the S&P 500 every year 1980-1986, for example 38.7% versus 18.6% in 1986; the passage gives the yearly comparison.

stance.quote: GEICO is an exceptional business run by exceptional managers.

summary: Simpson's results came from buying undervalued common stocks unlikely to produce permanent loss and collectively close to risk-free; GEICO is an exceptional business with exceptional managers.

stance.quote: at best, the bonds are mediocre investments.

summary: Insurance companies bought about $700 million of 8-12 year tax-exempt bonds in 1986 as the least objectionable alternative, though Buffett sees them as mediocre and likes neither stocks nor bonds.
Insurance companies investing incoming money have five options: long-term stocks, long-term bonds, medium-term bonds, short-term cash equivalents and short-term arbitrage.
Stocks can deliver grand-slam gains when good companies sell well below intrinsic value; Berkshire finds none now, which is not a market prediction as it cannot foresee market direction.

stance.quote: we simply attempt to be fearful when others are greedy and to be greedy only when others are fearful.

summary: Fear and greed outbreaks are unpredictable in timing and degree, so Berkshire does not try to anticipate them; it aims to be fearful when others are greedy and vice versa.

stance.quote: Unfortunately, however, stocks can’t outperform businesses indefinitely.

summary: Wall Street euphoria has uncoupled stock gains from business performance; because of costs, stockholders as a whole must underperform the roughly 12% equity return American business earns.

stance.quote: Our aversion to long-term bonds relates to our fear that we will see much higher rates of inflation within the next decade.

summary: Berkshire avoids long-term bonds except WPPSS 1-3, held at $218 million cost and $310 million market with $31.7 million tax-exempt income, fearing inflation and currency instability.
Berkshire buys only a few large, publicly announced arbitrage deals and does not bet on the come, so profits are small and disappointments few.
Yearend arbitrage included Lear-Siegler and a $145 million Unilever receivable; arbitrage has returned many times Treasury bills as a cash parking place, though one bad deal could change that.
Berkshire views medium-term tax-exempt bonds as an alternative to short-term Treasuries, accepting risk of loss on early sales for much higher after-tax returns in what it calls a close call.
Even a fairly large loss on selling the bonds could still leave a higher after-tax return than repeatedly rolling over Treasury bills.

stance.quote: our expectations for both the stocks and bonds we now hold are exceptionally modest, given current market levels.

summary: Expectations for Berkshire's stocks and bonds are exceptionally modest; high interest rates could force bond sales at a loss but would hurt common stocks more and create better equity values.

Table: yearend 1986 common-stock holdings over $25 million (Capital Cities/ABC, GEICO, Handy & Harman, Lear Siegler, Washington Post) with shares, cost and market; total cost $655 million, market $1,874 million.

stance.quote: we expect to keep permanently our three primary holdings

summary: Berkshire expects to hold Capital Cities/ABC, GEICO and Washington Post permanently, even if overpriced, just as it would not sell See's or the Buffalo News at a far higher price.
Berkshire's permanent-holding attitude is old-fashioned against modern managers who treat businesses as a restructurable portfolio, dumping businesses but never the officers who bought them.

stance.quote: we will stick with our ‘til-death-do-uspart policy.

summary: Investment managers trade hyperactively, but Berkshire sticks with permanent holdings, which produce decent results and let managers of its investees run their businesses undistracted.
Berkshire paid $23.7 million for about 50% of NHP, a developer, syndicator, owner and manager of multi-family rental housing, falling to slightly over 45% if options are exercised.

NHP descends from a 1967 presidential commission on multifamily housing for low- and moderate-income tenants; one of its entities has presidentially appointed directors and reports annually to the President.

Over 260 corporations invested $42 million in NHP's original entities, which developed subsidized rental property through partnerships financed by non-recourse mortgages and tax-motivated limited partners.

NHP broadened into market-rate apartments and Washington single-family homes with about $50 million revenue; it oversees 500 partnership properties costing over $2.5 billion and earns about $16 million from management.
NHP owns residual interests in its partnerships; those on deep-subsidy properties are unlikely to be valuable, but others could prove quite valuable if inflation heats up.
The Tax Reform Act of 1986 halted tax-oriented syndication, so NHP now seeks equity or residual stakes in non-subsidized rentals with institutional partners; Weyerhaeuser holds about 25%.

stance.quote: the net financial effect for Berkshire is negative

summary: The 1986 Tax Reform Act slows Berkshire's business value growth; shareholders keep 72 cents per dollar of gain instead of 80 as the capital gains rate rises to 28%.
The corporate ordinary income tax rate falls from 46% in 1986 to 34% in 1988, a positive for Berkshire and for investees Capital Cities/ABC and the Washington Post.
The 'pipeline' theory holds that corporations merely pass corporate taxes to consumers, implying a rate cut would not help profits but would flow through to lower prices.
Proponents of the pipeline theory must conclude that corporate tax decreases will not raise profits but will lead to correspondingly lower consumer prices.
Opponents say corporations absorb their taxes; the question of whether Berkshire, Washington Post and Cap Cities keep corporate rate-cut benefits or pass them to customers matters to investors.
Who benefits from corporate tax cuts depends on franchise strength and whether profits are regulated: for regulated electric utilities, tax changes flow mainly into prices rather than profits.
In price-competitive industries with weak franchises, the market regulates after-tax profits, so tax changes eventually affect prices more than profits.
Unregulated businesses with strong franchises keep the benefit of tax cuts for the corporation and shareholders, like an electric company without a regulator.
Many Berkshire businesses and investees have strong franchises, so their tax reductions mostly end up with Berkshire rather than customers, as with a top brain surgeon's fees.
Scheduled 1988 tax rates look unrealistic and will create a Washington fiscal problem incompatible with price stability; within about five years higher taxes or inflation, or both, are likely.
Raising the corporate capital gains rate from 28% to 34% hurts Berkshire, whose three main holdings, over $1.7 billion or 75% of net worth, yield only about $9 million income.
The higher rate hits $1.2 billion of unrealized gains; a GAAP rule delays the effect, but when it changes about $73 million moves from net worth to deferred taxes.

Insurers face heavier tax on dividend and interest income: 20% of dividends taxable instead of 15%, plus extra tax on post-August 1986 stock dividends and tax-exempt interest for property/casualty companies.
The investment-income tax changes will eventually cut Berkshire's insurance earning power by at least 10%; new rules also require discounting loss reserves and taxing 20% of unearned premiums.
The new reserve and unearned-premium rules leave the annual tax accrual unchanged but accelerate payments, ending tax deferral and significantly cutting insurance profitability.
An apparent inconsistency: tax changes should pass through to customers in price-competitive industries, yet they will hurt Berkshire's intensely price-competitive property/casualty profits.

Insurers face unequal tax equations from the alternative minimum tax, large loss carry-forwards and consolidated returns, producing widely varying marginal rates across the property/casualty industry.
In most price-competitive industries such as aluminum, autos and department stores, major players face similar tax equations, unlike property/casualty insurers.
Without a common tax calculus, higher taxes on property/casualty insurers will probably not be passed to customers fully, so insurers will bear much of the burden.
A January 1987 'fresh start' tax adjustment converting loss reserves to a discounted basis gives Berkshire a double deduction for incurred-but-unpaid losses already deducted earlier.
The fresh-start benefit, expected at $30-40 million, will flow into earnings through lower tax charges over several years, a one-time gain versus ongoing, worsening insurance tax burdens.

Repeal of the General Utilities Doctrine creates double taxation on corporate liquidations from 1987, sharply cutting what shareholders would receive and affecting Berkshire's evaluation of prospective investments.
Repeal of the General Utilities Doctrine cuts values sellers can realize, for instance in oil and gas, media and real estate, though operating economics are unchanged; investors have missed it.
The new tax law will hurt Berkshire's results, especially property/casualty insurers, but the negative impact cannot be quantified precisely.
Berkshire bought a used corporate jet for $850,000; its capital cost plus depreciation runs close to $200,000 a year versus about $3 million for a new $15 million plane.
Buffett, previously critical of corporate jets, bought one, making travel easier and costlier, and concedes it is an open question whether Berkshire will get its money's worth.
About 97% of eligible shares joined the 1986 designated-contributions program, giving $4 million to 1,934 charities; shares must be registered to owners by September 30, 1987 for the next program.

Berkshire paid $315 million for Scott Fetzer net assets carried at $172.4 million, a $142.6 million premium that GAAP requires allocating through purchase-price adjustments.

The residual $24.3 million premium was assigned to goodwill, transforming Scott Fetzer's balance sheet from column O to N; assets and liabilities are the same in real terms.

The 1986 purchase-accounting charges: $4.98 million inventory costs, $5.05 million extra depreciation for twelve more years, $595,000 goodwill amortization for 39 years, and $998,000 deferred-tax charges.
The $11.6 million of new purchase-accounting costs are not tax deductible, so 'new' and 'old' Scott Fetzer pay identical tax despite very different GAAP earnings.

Did Berkshire buy a business earning $40.2 million or $28.6 million, and are the $11.6 million of new charges a real economic cost? The questions frame owner earnings.

Owner earnings equal reported earnings plus depreciation, amortization and certain other non-cash charges, minus the average capital expenditures needed to maintain competitive position and unit volume.

stance.quote: we consider the owner earnings figure, not the GAAP figure, to be the relevant item for valuation purposes

summary: Owner earnings require guessing maintenance capital spending and so are imprecise, but Berkshire considers them, not GAAP earnings, the relevant measure for valuing stocks or businesses.
Owner earnings are identical for old and new Scott Fetzer, as are valuations, because earnings plus non-cash charges and required capital spending are the same in both columns.
Buffett and Munger see Scott Fetzer's required capital spending near the old company's $8.3 million depreciation, so owner earnings exceed reported GAAP earnings.
When maintenance capital spending exceeds depreciation, GAAP earnings overstate owner earnings, often substantially; major oil companies spending only depreciation would have shrunk in real terms.

stance.quote: All of this points up the absurdity of the "cash flow" numbers that are often set forth in Wall Street reports.

summary: Wall Street 'cash flow' adds depreciation to earnings without subtracting capital spending, depicting businesses as pyramids needing no replacement; investment bankers' brochures present such deceptive numbers.

Cash flow suits only businesses with huge initial outlays and tiny later ones; in manufacturing, retailing, extraction and utilities it is meaningless because capital spending cannot be deferred long.

stance.quote: we believe these numbers are frequently used by marketers of businesses and securities in attempts to justify the unjustifiable

summary: Marketers push 'cash flow' to justify junk-bond debt service or foolish stock prices when GAAP earnings look inadequate, but ignoring required capital spending leads to trouble.
Believing debt-servicing ability or equity value can be measured by earnings plus non-cash charges while ignoring capital spending leads a company or investor to certain trouble.

Berkshire believes historical-cost depreciation is close to required capital spending, so unit earnings excluding purchase adjustments approximate owner earnings better than GAAP; See's capex exceeds depreciation by $0.5-1 million.
Accountants record while investors and managers must evaluate; accounting numbers are the starting point but only an aid to business thinking, never a substitute for it.
Net worth rose $464 million or 19.5% in 1987; per-share book value grew from $19.46 to $2,477.47, 23.1% compounded; what counts is business value, which can differ widely from book.

Berkshire's business value has tracked book value, with business value growth moderately outpacing it over the last decade and in 1987, because it owns remarkable businesses run by remarkable managers.
CEOs rarely admit weak managers, often praising 'our most precious asset' managers at the end of letters detailing woefully inadequate corporate performance.
Berkshire's seven largest non-financial units (Buffalo News, Fechheimer, Kirby, NFM, Scott Fetzer, See's, World Book) had combined 1987 operating earnings before interest and taxes of $180 million.
The seven units had only $2 million net interest expense in 1987, giving $178 million pre-tax earnings on just $175 million of historical-cost equity.
The seven units would have earned about $100 million after tax in 1987, a 57% equity return; Fortune found only six of 1,000 large firms above 30% over a decade.
Berkshire's returns on the seven units are lower than their underlying returns because it paid about $222 million above historical asset values; managers should be judged on underlying capital.
The seven units' business value far exceeds book and carrying value, they need little capital so earnings are redeployable, and their extraordinary managers achieve exceptional financial results.

stance.quote: Despite these problems, we like the business and it will almost certainly remain our largest operation.

summary: Insurance, Berkshire's other major unit, likely has business value well above net assets, though valuing property-casualty insurers is imprecise given volatility, inaccurate earnings and harmful tax changes.
Buffett and Munger leave operations to managers, with no corporate meetings, budgets or performance reviews, since more involvement would accomplish less.

Little change at Berkshire's businesses is good: severe change and exceptional returns rarely mix, yet investors give the highest price-earnings ratios to exotic businesses promising feverish change.
The best business returns usually come from companies doing what they did five or ten years ago; constant change brings chances for error and hinders building a durable franchise.
Fortune found only 25 of 1,000 companies averaged over 20% return on equity with no year below 15% over 1977-1986, and 24 of them beat the S&P 500.
The 25 Fortune champions use little leverage and mostly sell mundane products as they did ten years ago, showing that exploiting a strong franchise produces exceptional economics.

Berkshire's managers get extraordinary results by doing ordinary things exceptionally well: protecting franchises, controlling costs and building on strengths; Nebraska Furniture Mart's 94-year-old chairman is the example.
Mrs. B started Nebraska Furniture Mart with $500 fifty years ago; it is now the country's largest home furnishings store, and Berkshire scrapped its mandatory retirement-at-100 policy.
Nebraska Furniture Mart's 1987 net sales were $142.6 million, up 8%; customers saved about $30 million versus buying elsewhere, thanks to the Blumkin family's management.
A competitor's letter says NFM leaves 10-20% on the table; NFM instead follows Mrs. B's maxim 'Sell cheap and tell the truth' to keep growing.
The Buffalo News leads dominant papers of its size nationally in weekday and Sunday household penetration and in the percentage of the paper devoted to news.
A news-rich, fresh, relevant product gives the Buffalo News broad appeal and high penetration; it publishes seven edited editions a day, even redoing the obituary page each time.
The Buffalo News kept a news hole near 50% in 1987; cutting it to 40% would save about $4 million of newsprint yearly, which Berkshire declines even if margins shrink.
Berkshire rejects flexible operating budgets: it would not cut news hole or See's quality when profits dip, nor add unneeded staff when money rolls in.
Adding unneeded people when profits boom or cutting essential ones when they shrink is neither business-like nor humane; Berkshire does what makes sense for customers and employees at all times.

stance.quote: Margins will, without question, shrink in 1988 and profit may fall as well.

summary: Buffalo News revenues grew moderately since 1984 but profit grew strongly; Buffett predicts margins will shrink in 1988 and profit may fall because of skyrocketing newsprint costs.
Fechheimer, the Heldman family's uniform maker and distributor, had record profits in 1986 and substantially higher earnings in 1987, with a good outlook for 1988.
See's 1987 volume hit a new high of nearly 25 million pounds, same-store pounds were flat for a second year, and about 85% of profit was earned in December.

stance.quote: practically no one besides See's has made significant profits in recent years from the operation of candy shops.

summary: Practically no candy shop operator but See's has made significant profits recently; its record rests on an excellent product and genuine customer orientation, not an industry tide.
See's raised prices only slightly in 1986-87 and somewhat more in 1988, but sales have been weak so far and improving 1988 earnings may be difficult.

stance.quote: Results in 1987 were even better.

summary: Scott Fetzer, run by Ralph Schey over 19 businesses including World Book and Kirby, raised pre-tax earnings 10% in 1987 while average capital employed fell significantly.
World Book launched its most revised edition since 1962 at the end of 1987; U.S. unit sales rose a fifth straight year and international sales and profits grew substantially.

The combined ratio compares losses plus expenses to premiums; counting float income, a ratio of 107-111 typically yields overall break-even before earnings on shareholder funds.
When industry premiums grow only 4-5%, underwriting losses mount; social and judicial inflation, with skyrocketing verdicts and expanded coverage, are the culprits, so revenues must grow about 10%.
Berkshire continues to believe industry revenues must grow about 10% annually to hold profitability, even with general inflation considerably lower.

stance.quote: Clearly, the party is over.

summary: Strong 1985-87 revenue gains made 1987 a banner underwriting year, but quarterly volume growth slowed from 12.9% to 5.6%, and 1988 gains will fall far below the 10% equilibrium.
With one-year policies, price changes reach earnings with a lag; absent a major catastrophe Berkshire predicts a small rise in the industry combined ratio in 1988, then larger ones.

stance.quote: The insurance industry is cursed with a set of dismal economic characteristics that make for a poor long-term outlook

summary: Insurance has dismal economics: hundreds of competitors, easy entry and an undifferentiable product, so only a very low-cost operator or protected niche sustains high profitability.
Even commodity businesses flourish in shortages, but managers rush to expand capacity, as insurers did in 1985-87, ending the favorable climate.

Berkshire escapes commodity insurance economics first by differentiating on financial strength, which exceeds all others but matters little in personal lines and often in commercial lines when times are good.
When buyers focus on whether a $10 million claim can be paid years later amid poor underwriting and depressed markets, few insurers can be trusted and Berkshire leads.
Berkshire's second differentiator is indifference to volume: it would write five times or one-fifth as much business in 1989 as in 1988, depending on prices, unlike any other major insurer.
Berkshire can flex volume because market share does not drive insurance profitability, distribution channels are easily entered, and idle capacity, mostly people, is not intolerably costly.
Berkshire prices on exposure, not competition, staying available at adequate prices to write huge volumes when others are 'out', acting as standby capacity but often pricing above the market.
When the insurance market softened sharply in 1987 a large broker placed business with cheaper insurers, not Berkshire, yet bought more Berkshire stock, showing the cost of its pricing policy.
Berkshire's 1987 combined ratio was 105 versus 103 in 1986, yet profitability improved on far more float; insurance profits should rise in 1988-89 though the ratio is expected to rise.
Mike Goldberg built talent for larger risks and unusual coverages; reserve development looks better, but with long-tail business like product liability and D&O one year of development says little.

stance.quote: You should be very suspicious of any earnings figures reported by insurers

summary: Insurers' reported earnings have often proved wildly erroneous over the last decade, mostly innocently, because the unpredictable legal system prevents judging the cost of long-tail claims.
Auditors certify insurers' numbers as 'presenting fairly' though they know from experience those earnings may differ dramatically from true earnings, yet investors rely on the opinions.
The new standard audit wording still understates casualty-insurer audit limits; Berkshire suggests an opinion stating auditors rely on management for loss reserves and cannot opine on their accuracy.
Auditors would say in court that they cannot assess loss reserves, so they should say so upfront; Berkshire faults only their failure to acknowledge this limitation.

Beyond innocent reserving mistakes, charlatans exploit auditors' inability to evaluate reserves, since long-tail insurance lets earnings be created by a pen stroke; audit wording would warn investors.
Insurers' taxes rose after the Tax Reform Act of 1986 and worsened again at end-1987; the temporary 'fresh start' adjustment inflated Berkshire's 1987 earnings by $8.2 million.
The 1986 Act was the most important event for insurers in a decade; the 1987 Bill cut the dividends-received credit from 80% to 70% from 1988, except for 20%-plus stakes.

Owning securities through corporate intermediaries, especially insurers, is penalized more heavily by the 1986 and 1987 tax laws, so pre-tax investment returns now translate into poorer after-tax results for shareholders.

Berkshire expects uneven but good insurance results, with substantially lower volume and reasonable earnings improvement now; premium decline accelerates when the Fireman's Fund quota share expires in 1989.
Berkshire buys stocks as if buying a private business, judging economics, people and price with no planned sale; Buffett and Munger see themselves as business analysts, not market analysts.
An active trading market is useful for bargains but not essential; Berkshire's economic fate will follow the businesses it owns, whether partially or fully.
Ben Graham's Mr. Market allegory: imagine quotations from an accommodating partner who daily names a price to buy your interest or sell you his.
Mr. Market's quotations swing between euphoria, naming very high prices, and depression, naming very low ones, even when the business's economics are stable.
Mr. Market does not mind being ignored and returns daily with a new quote; transactions are at the investor's option, so his manic-depressive behavior benefits the investor.
Mr. Market serves, not guides: use his pocketbook, not his wisdom; an investor who cannot value the business far better than he does doesn't belong in the game.
Mr. Market seems dated to professionals and academics who talk of efficient markets, dynamic hedging and betas, techniques whose mystery benefits advisers like a witch doctor.

stance.quote: investment success will not be produced by arcane formulae, computer programs or signals flashed by the price behavior of stocks and markets.

summary: Investment success comes from good business judgment plus insulating oneself from market emotions, not arcane formulae or price signals; the Mr. Market concept helps Buffett stay insulated.
Berkshire judges its stocks by operating results, not price quotations; the market is a voting machine short-term and a weighing machine long-term, and delayed recognition can allow cheaper buying.
Berkshire sells when the market values a business above the facts, or sells fairly valued holdings to fund a more undervalued or better-understood investment.
Berkshire sells not because holdings appreciated or were held long, but holds while return on equity is satisfactory, management competent and honest, and the market does not overvalue the business.
Berkshire's insurers hold three stocks it would keep even if far overpriced, treating them as permanent, though it would sell portions only if needed to pay extraordinary insurance losses.
Buffett and Munger's determination to buy and hold mixes personal and financial considerations and looks eccentric on a Wall Street that treats companies and stocks as raw material for trades.
Berkshire accepts somewhat lower returns to work with managers it likes and admires, introducing its three permanent holdings.

stance.quote: Our goal is to find an outstanding business at a sensible price, not a mediocre business at a bargain price.

summary: Yearend 1987 permanent holdings (Capital Cities/ABC, GEICO, Washington Post) are listed with cost and market; Berkshire sees little difference between buying controlled businesses and such holdings.
Buffett needed 20 years to learn to buy good businesses; his earlier search for bargains taught him the economics of farm implement makers, third-place department stores and New England textiles.
Berkshire may misread a business's fundamental economics in either a subsidiary or a marketable security, though exiting a security is usually far easier.
Berkshire buys good businesses with talented managers; the control advantage of replacing managers is somewhat illusory, and at Cap Cities, GEICO and the Washington Post it is moot.
A first advantage of control is allocating capital, since many CEOs who rose through marketing, production or politics are not skilled at it.

CAT covers are reinsurance contracts protecting primary insurers against a single catastrophe; the reinsurer usually pays 95% of losses above the insurer's retention up to a limit.
The 5% co-share in each CAT layer leaves the primary insurer a financial stake in settlements and protects the reinsurer.
CAT covers are one-year policies with one automatic reinstatement for an extra premium; an 'event' is limited to a 72-hour span chosen by the primary insurer.
A storm lasting more than 72 hours is split into separate events, with losses outside the worst 72 hours claimed separately.
Hurricane Hugo caused $4 billion or more of insured loss and the California earthquake followed within weeks, exhausting or clouding many insurers' automatic second CAT covers.

By adding capacity when it is short and becoming less competitive when it is abundant, Berkshire acts as a stabilizing force in the insurance industry.

Each $10,000 bond converts into .4515 Berkshire shares ($9,815 per share, a 15% premium); Berkshire can call after September 1992 and holders can put them in 1994 and 1999.
Berkshire deducts the 5.5% accrued interest on its zero-coupon bonds, giving positive cash flow and an effective cost well below 5.5%; taxable holders pay tax on non-cash interest.
Berkshire's zero-coupon bonds differ from most recently issued zeros, which Buffett and Munger criticize as often used deceptively with deadly consequences for investors.
The World War II Series E U.S. Savings Bond was in effect a zero-coupon bond and the most widely sold bond issue ever.
A Series E bond cost $18.75 for $25 due in ten years, a 2.9% compounded return that beat other Government bonds, with little market-fluctuation risk.
Ordinary bonds carry reinvestment risk: a stated 10% yield is not realized if coupons are reinvested at lower rates, a problem for pension funds needing 'Savings Bond Equivalents'.
Large buyers needed huge quantities of Savings Bond Equivalents, which Savings Bonds, issued only to individuals in small amounts, could not supply.
Investment bankers led by Salomon created zero-coupon issues by stripping coupons from Government bonds; at 10% rates a six-month strip sells at 95.24% and a 20-year at 14.20%.
A buyer of any stripped maturity is guaranteed a compounded 10%, so pension funds and IRAs widely adopted these high-grade zero-coupon issues.

stance.quote: what the wise do in the beginning, fools do in the end

summary: Zero-coupon and pay-in-kind bonds have been issued in huge quantities by ever-junkier credits, because it is impossible to default on a promise to pay nothing.
Early leveraged buyouts borrowed only against conservatively estimated free cash flow covering interest and modest debt paydown; promises of nothing now let borrowers avoid default for long.
As buyout prices rose, all free cash flow went to interest, leaving nothing for principal, and original-issue junk bond buyers accepted debt to be refinanced rather than repaid.
To finance even sillier deals, borrowers introduced EBDIT, earnings before depreciation, interest and taxes, as the test of interest-paying ability, ignoring depreciation as an expense.
Ignoring depreciation is delusional: at 95% of American businesses, capital expenditures roughly equal to depreciation are as real an expense as labor or utilities.
Skipping capital outlays routinely weakens a business like skipped meals, and Buffett and Munger relish competitors unable to fund capital expenditures.
Promoters seeking to justify pricier acquisitions and avoid losing deals to more 'imaginative' rivals found a way beyond waving away depreciation.
Promoters and bankers measured EBDIT against cash interest only, ignoring accruing interest on zero-coupon or PIK bonds, and many professional managers went along with clients' money.
Example: a business earning $100 million pre-tax with $90 million cash interest adds $60 million of accruing zero/PIK interest, compounding to $69 million the next year.

Bankers offer five-year projections for barely-known companies; compare their past one-year budgets with outcomes. Galbraith's 'bezzle' is undiscovered embezzlement making embezzlers richer while victims feel no poorer.
Galbraith's logic would add the bezzle to the national wealth, so wealth balloons without any productive work.
With zeros, a company able to earn only $100 million magically creates $150 million of 'income' for bondholders, limited only by investors' willingness to believe.

The 'cigar butt' approach buys stocks cheap enough to sell at a profit after some hiccup, even if the business's long-term performance is terrible.

Buying Hochschild Kohn through Diversified Retailing at a discount to book value, with first-class people, ended three years later in a sale for about the purchase price.

Sticking with the easy and obvious pays better than resolving the difficult; exceptions include the Buffalo Sunday paper and American Express and GEICO when marvelous businesses hit solvable problems.
Buffett's most surprising discovery is the 'institutional imperative': rationality in business frequently wilts even with decent, intelligent managers.
The institutional imperative: institutions resist change, projects expand to soak up funds, leaders' cravings get supporting studies, and peers' acquisitions and pay are mindlessly imitated.
After costly mistakes, Buffett organizes Berkshire to minimize the institutional imperative and prefers investees that seem alert to it.
Berkshire partners only with people it likes, trusts and admires, though that cannot rescue a second-class business; it has never made a good deal with a bad person.
Buffett's worst mistakes were unpublicized: big purchases within his competence that he understood but passed on, at huge cost to shareholders.
Higher conventional leverage would have lifted Berkshire's 23.8% average return on equity, but Berkshire's conservative financial policies were not a mistake.
Berkshire rejects 99:1 odds of extra returns versus distress, since a small chance of disgrace cannot be offset by extra returns; leverage only speeds sensible results.

Management quality rarely affects a bond's coupon but can dramatically affect equity 'coupons'.
Buy the investment that discounted cash flow shows cheapest regardless of growth, volatility or price ratios; equities usually but not always beat bonds on that test.
Best business employs large incremental capital at very high returns; worst needs ever more capital at low returns. High-return, low-capital businesses should pay out earnings or repurchase stock.
Berkshire sticks to simple, stable businesses it understands because future cash flows are hard to estimate; realistically defining what you don't know matters most.
Berkshire insists on a margin of safety in price, as Ben Graham stressed, calling it the cornerstone of investment success.

The secondary market, periodically ruled by mass folly, sets clearing prices that can value shares worth x at half x or less.
The new-issue market is ruled by sellers who control timing and offer no bargains, and selling shareholders often unload when the market is overpaying.
Negotiated preferred purchases have met but not exceeded the expectation of returns modestly above fixed-income portfolios; open-market buying would have done better.

Many managers committed their companies to open-ended post-retirement health promises that no insurer would underwrite, creating liabilities that threaten major American industries.
Cash-basis accounting understated post-retirement health liabilities, encouraging reckless promises with an out-of-sight, out-of-mind attitude.
Managers should remember that calling a tail a leg does not make it a leg, even if an auditor certifies it.
Stock options are accounted for illogically; business executives have long fought accounting rulemakers to keep option costs out of reported profits.
Executives argue options are hard to value, would hurt start-ups, or that out-of-the-money options have no value when issued, to avoid recording option costs.
The claim that options are no cost because they are not cash would let companies cut insurance costs by paying in options; Buffett offers to sell insurance for options.
Costs arise when something of value is delivered, not only when cash moves, and imprecise items such as depreciation, loan losses and insurance reserves are still recorded.
Hard-to-measure costs should be estimated by honest, experienced people and recorded; stock options are the only major such cost accountants say to ignore.
Options are not that hard to value; Berkshire would pay executives for the future gain on restricted options and is more confident valuing options than depreciating its corporate jet.
If options are compensation and compensation is an expense, expenses belong in earnings; the accounting profession and SEC were muscled by executives on option accounting.

Buffett values Berkshire managers who work well past retirement age and achieve results superior to younger competitors.

Book value measures capital put into a business; intrinsic value is present value of cash extractable. Berkshire's book value tracks intrinsic value, both up about 14% in 1993.
Berkshire's 1993 market price rose 39%, far above its roughly 14% intrinsic value gain; price and value diverge short term, as with Coca-Cola and Gillette in 1991.
From 1991 to 1993 Coke and Gillette grew operating earnings per share 38% and 37% but their stocks rose only 11% and 6%; long-run earnings performance is what counts.
Coke IPO'd in 1919 at $40, fell over 50% by 1920, yet one share with reinvested dividends was worth over $2.1 million in 1993; the market weighs long term.
Berkshire sold at a higher percentage of intrinsic value at end-1993, defensible with 6-7% long-term rates only if it keeps growing intrinsic value 15% annually, which grows harder with size.
Berkshire's operating businesses range from good to terrific economics under terrific managers; the uncertain part is parent capital allocation, finding new businesses and managers.
Berkshire built on H.H. Brown, which exceeded expectations, with Lowell Shoe in late 1992 and then Dexter Shoe in 1993, a manufacturer of popular-priced shoes needing no fixing.

Harold Alfond and Peter Lunder built Dexter into a producer of over 7.5 million pairs a year; Dexter and H.H. Brown make U.S. plants competitive despite low-wage imports.
Dexter has 77 retail outlets, makes about 15% of U.S. golf shoes, and mainly supplies traditional shoes to retailers such as Nordstrom and J.C. Penney.

Private owners find diversification hard; Dexter's owners solved a reinvestment problem and, with Buffett's net worth committed to Berkshire and no options issued to him, share owners' results.
Because Berkshire issues Buffett neither restricted shares nor stock options, his gain-loss equation always matches that of other owners.
Berkshire keeps promises of no change of control or culture for decades and lets sellers like Dexter's owners run their business as before; Buffett invites similar large private businesses.

CEOs would never sell a crown-jewel subsidiary yet churn personal portfolios on superficial broker arguments such as taking profits; investors should hold outstanding businesses tenaciously.
Investors should hold a small piece of an outstanding business with the tenacity of an owner of the whole.
