Buffett and Munger concluded it is too hard to make hundreds of smart decisions, so as capital grew they adopted a strategy needing only one good idea a year.
Berkshire's concentrated portfolio may reduce risk by forcing deeper thought and comfort with each business, defining risk as the possibility of loss or injury.
Academics define risk as beta, relative past volatility, and build theories on it, forgetting that it is better to be approximately right than precisely wrong.
Under beta theory a stock that fell sharply, like Washington Post when bought in 1973, becomes riskier at the lower price, which makes no sense to an owner.
A true investor welcomes volatility: Ben Graham's Mr. Market offers irrationally low prices for solid businesses, which the investor can exploit or ignore.
A beta purist ignores the business and studies price history, while Berkshire studies the business and would not mind markets closing for a year or two.
The real investment risk is that after-tax receipts will not return the investor's original purchasing power plus a modest interest rate over the holding period.
Risk factors include certainty that management channels rewards to shareholders, the purchase price, and the levels of taxation and inflation that reduce purchasing-power return.
Risk factors are hard to quantify but still important; investors can 'see' risks in certain investments without complex equations or price histories.

summary: Coke and Gillette have raised worldwide market shares; brand names, product attributes and distribution give them a protective moat, unlike commodity-like businesses.

Beta cannot tell a pet-rock toy firm from a Monopoly or Barbie firm, but informed investors can judge such durability if they stay within easy-to-understand cases.
Buffett and Munger cannot tell pet rocks from Barbies in many industries; fast-moving technology resists reliable evaluation, as television and computer makers showed.
Having failed to foresee television and computers, Berkshire sticks with easy cases rather than predicting rapidly evolving businesses.
Strategies like arbitrage and venture capital require wide diversification across independent bets, with the outlook of a casino owning a roulette wheel.
A casino with a favorable roulette wheel wants lots of action but refuses a single huge bet.
An investor who does not understand business economics should own many equities and space out purchases, such as through an index fund, and can beat most professionals.
A know-something investor who can find five to ten sensibly priced companies with long-term advantages gains from concentration; conventional diversification only hurts results and raises risk.
Shareholders ask what happens to Berkshire if Buffett is hit by a truck, a question that leads into corporate governance.
Directors have stiffened their spines and owners are treated better; governance differs across three manager/owner situations, with Berkshire in the second and later the third.
In companies with no controlling shareholder, directors should act as an absentee owner, replacing mediocre management and restraining greedy managers.
Directors must slap the hands of able but greedy managers who dip too deeply into shareholders' pockets.
A dissenting director should first persuade the board, and if unsuccessful may inform the absentee owners, which seldom happens.
Boards should have ten or fewer mostly outside directors who set CEO standards; directors should be chosen for business savvy and owner-orientation, not prominence or diversity.
Where the controlling owner is also manager, as at Berkshire, directors can only persuade or object, since the board cannot act as agent between owners and management.
If an owner/manager's shortcomings persist and are serious, outside directors should resign to signal their doubts.
With a controlling owner not in management, such as Hershey or Dow Jones, outside directors can report concerns directly to the owner, or resign.
The third governance case should best ensure first-class management; in the second case owners won't fire themselves and in the first directors struggle with mediocrity.
In the third case the controlling owner can pick useful directors, decide meritocratically in shareholders' favor, and correct mistakes readily.
Berkshire stays in the second governance mode while Buffett remains functional; on his death his stock goes to his wife or a foundation without requiring consequential sales.
After Buffett's stock transfers, Berkshire will have a vitally interested non-management owner; Susie and son Howard joined the board, and other directors are significant owners.

Berkshire's formula of buying good businesses with honest, able managers at sensible prices should keep producing reasonable success.

Berkshire will stick with its approach and wait for opportunities well within its own happy zone rather than lower standards.

Macro shocks did not dent Graham's principles; the best purchases came when fear of macro events peaked, and Berkshire will not predict future shocks.
Buffett and Munger promise owners share downside as well as upside, no skewed compensation arrangements, and fortunes concentrated in Berkshire shares.

Berkshire's partial stakes give it look-through economics: 7.8% of Coca-Cola (about $200 million), 7% of Gillette (about $250 million of sales), 13% of Wells Fargo (about $100 million earnings).
Owning part of rare-gem businesses beats owning all of a mediocre one; stock prices fluctuate, but intrinsic value, not book value, is what counts.
In 1964 Berkshire's $19.46 book value per share overstated intrinsic value because the capital sat in a sub-profitable textile business.
Today many controlled businesses are worth far more than carrying value, so book value understates intrinsic value; in 1994 both gained roughly 13.9%.
Intrinsic value is the discounted cash that can be taken out of a business over its life; subjective but the only logical basis for comparing investments.
A college education illustrates book value versus intrinsic value: cost including forgone earnings is book value, the future earnings benefit is intrinsic value.
An education's economic value is the lifetime excess earnings over a non-graduate, discounted back to graduation day at an appropriate interest rate.
Book value is meaningless as an indicator of intrinsic value; Scott Fetzer, a huge acquisition winner, will illustrate how the relationship changes and give an accounting lesson.

Ralph Schey's success comes from handling the basics and setting the right goals; as Graham taught, extraordinary results need no extraordinary actions.
Berkshire judges managers on performance, not age; many managers are over 65 and Berkshire scorns mandatory retirement ages.
Managers' capital allocation, including share repurchases, must increase per-share intrinsic value; violations of this principle are common and hurt shareholders.
Managers wrongly judge mergers by immediate earnings or book-value dilution; an MBA-student share-for-share merger with a day laborer shows why that focus is silly.
Berkshire rejected many deals that would have lifted near-term earnings but cut per-share intrinsic value, leaving shareholders many billions richer than standard practice would have.

stance.quote: they usually reduce the wealth of the acquirer's shareholders, often to a substantial extent.

CEO ego and animal spirits, encouraged by advisors, drive deal-making that executives do not need pushing toward.
An insurance CEO's joking justification for buying a life insurer, 'all the other kids have one', illustrates the pathology of many big deals.
Berkshire managers redeploy earnings in their own businesses first and send the rest to Buffett and Munger, who buy businesses they understand to build per-share intrinsic value.

Scott Fetzer's symmetrical bonus charges a hurdle on extra capital, so Ralph Schey is paid to send surplus cash to Omaha when he cannot use it profitably.

Berkshire quotes prices on coverage up to $500 million the same day, while brokers elsewhere must spread large risks across many small policies slowly.

Writing large coverages makes results lumpy, which Berkshire accepts; insurers that smooth reported earnings follow suboptimal strategies, while accepting volatility should earn higher long-term returns.
Buffett and Ajit Jain focus on a worst case of several catastrophes in one year, possibly coinciding with drops in the value of See's, Wells Fargo and Freddie Mac holdings.
Worst-case super-cat loss is about $600 million after tax, slightly above annual earnings from other sources; super-cat volume will probably fall in 1995 as prices drop and capital chases premiums.

Berkshire's other insurance units (homestate, workers' compensation, credit card, National Indemnity auto and liability) had significant underwriting profits and float in 1994; the insurance business is volatile but valuable.
Lead-in to the table of common stock holdings worth over $300 million at yearend 1994.
Table: yearend 1994 common stock holdings over $300 million with shares, cost and market value, led by Coca-Cola, Gillette, Capital Cities/ABC and GEICO.
Berkshire's investments are few and simple: a business with enduring competitive advantages, able owner-oriented managers and a sensible price makes it hard to go wrong.

stance.quote: We try to price, rather than time, purchases.

summary: Degree of difficulty does not count in investing; Berkshire prices rather than times purchases and will not skip an outstanding business over short-term worries about an unpredictable economy or market.
Berkshire bought National Indemnity, See's, Buffalo News, NFM and Scott Fetzer when available at acceptable prices, judging the business, not the Dow or Fed; same logic applies to stocks.
Berkshire first considers adding to existing holdings; it cannot add to 100% owned See's or Scott Fetzer, but in 1994 it enlarged its Coca-Cola and American Express stakes.
Buffett's early associations with GEICO, the Washington Post and Coca-Cola preceded Berkshire's later large purchases of each, showing current decisions drawn from past familiarity.
Buffett's first venture was reselling Coke bottles at a markup; it took fifty years to realise the real money in Coca-Cola was in the syrup.
Buffett Partnership put 40% of capital into American Express after the salad-oil scandal; Berkshire now owns nearly 10% at $1.36 billion cost, and annual Amex earnings rose to $1.4 billion.
Buffett first bought IDS in 1953 at a price-earnings ratio of 3; IDS now supplies about a third of American Express earnings; long familiarity with a company aids evaluation.
Mistakes occur at decision time but are only recognised when the foolishness becomes obvious; 1994 was a vintage year for Buffett's own investment mistakes.
Buffett sold 10 million Cap Cities shares at $63 in late 1993; the stock was $85.25 at yearend 1994, a $222.5 million difference, repeating his 1978-80 sale at $4.30.
The $358 million USAir preferred bought in 1989 was Buffett's biggest mistake, an unforced error from sloppy analysis; its dividend was suspended in September 1994.
Buffett failed to see that USAir's high, hard-to-lower costs were embedded under regulation and stayed hidden after deregulation because low-cost carriers were small.

stance.quote: In an unregulated commodity business, a company must lower its costs to competitive levels or face extinction.

summary: As low-cost airlines expanded, old-line carriers had to cut fares; in an unregulated commodity business a company must cut costs to competitive levels or die, which Buffett missed.
USAir's CEO has not yet fixed its costs because rivals gained labor concessions or fresh-start costs from bankruptcy, and employees with above-market pay resist cuts.
Berkshire wrote its USAir investment down to $89.5 million, 25 cents on the dollar, at yearend 1994, reflecting both possible recovery and worthlessness.
Under GAAP insurers carry stocks at market value, so by third quarter 1994 net worth already reflected USAir preferred at $89.5 million versus $358 million cost.
In the fourth quarter the USAir decline was judged other than temporary, sending a $269 million writedown through income without further net worth effect; Buffett and Munger leave USAir's board.

CEOs Dan Burke and Carl Reichardt retired after leading Capital Cities/ABC and Wells Fargo to record earnings; 95.7% of eligible shares joined the 1994 designated contributions program, giving $10.4 million.
Shares must be registered in the owner's own name, not a nominee, by August 31, 1995 to take part in the designated contributions program; no exceptions are made.
Berkshire made only one minor acquisition in 1994, a small retail shoe chain, and continues looking for candidates under the criteria in the appendix.

After a failed merger offer including Berkshire convertible preferred, the proxy asks shareholders to authorize preferred stock for quick deals, used only if intrinsic value received equals that given.
1995 net worth rose $5.3 billion or 45.0%, book value per share 43.1%; per-share book value grew from $19 to $14,426 over 31 years; a rising market made gains easy.
Berkshire made three acquisitions in 1995-96: Helzberg's, R.C. Willey and GEICO; they roughly double revenues without materially adding shares or debt.
Berkshire buys either 100% of businesses through negotiation or small stakes through the stock market at lower pro-rata prices, a double-barrelled approach that gives it an advantage.
Introduction to a table of marketable securities per share and per-share operating earnings excluding investment income, at ten-year intervals.
The per-share table ignores purchase-price accounting adjustments, which previous reports explained at length.
Table: marketable securities per share and pre-tax earnings per share excluding investment income for 1965-1995; securities grew 33.4% yearly, operating earnings 14.7%.
Berkshire's advantages are outstanding managers and experienced capital allocation; its giant disadvantage is size, which makes finding good big ideas harder as success grows.

stance.quote: We believe most deals do damage to the shareholders of the acquiring company.

summary: Despite three acquisitions, Buffett remains skeptical: most deals harm acquirers' shareholders, and sellers' financial projections are more entertaining than educational.
Buffett and Munger never look at sellers' projections; a business that is currently doing fine is exactly what sellers choose to sell.
Berkshire shares the usual difficulty of acquirers: the seller knows far more about the business and picks the time of sale.
Berkshire has no strategic plan and compares every acquisition with buying pieces of the best businesses in the stock market, a discipline expansion-focused managers lack.
Peter Drucker's quote: dealmaking is exciting while running a business is grubby detail work, which is why deals that make no sense happen.
Berkshire stock is attractive payment for sellers wanting to defer taxes, which helped the two acquisitions paid in shares in 1995.
Sellers value Berkshire as an enduring home with extraordinary manager autonomy and a real promise to buy to keep.
Berkshire invites owners of businesses earning $25 million or more pre-tax that fit its criteria to call; it will never lose its appetite for good companies.
A tale of a company whose consultant-advised diversification acquisitions left it earning 150% of earnings from the original business after ten years.
Berkshire's acquisition of Helzberg's Diamond Shops began when owner Barnett Helzberg, a Berkshire shareholder, approached Buffett in New York in May 1994.
Helzberg's, started in 1915, had 134 stores in 23 states; sales grew from $10 million in 1974 to $53 million in 1984 and $282 million in 1994.
Barnett Helzberg wanted to be free of the business and diversify his family's holdings, after hiring a president in 1988 who proved a homerun.
Berkshire would not have bought Helzberg's without manager Jeff Comment; buying a retailer without good management is like buying the Eiffel Tower without an elevator.
Helzberg was bought in 1995 in a tax-free stock exchange; its stores average $2 million sales, far above competitors', driving excellent profits and growth potential.
Helzberg's will run independently of Borsheim's, whose sales rose 11.7% in 1995 under CEO Susan Jacques.
R.C. Willey's owners wanted to sell for estate tax and diversification reasons; after Irv Blumkin's introduction, Buffett and Bill Child agreed a price quickly and merged by mid-1995.
R.C. Willey grew from $250,000 sales in 1954 to $257 million in 1995, over 50% of Utah's furniture business, with a sixth major store opening.

stance.quote: In retailing, to coast is to fail.

summary: Retailing is tough: many retailers enjoy superb returns then nosedive into bankruptcy, because competitors copy and top you and shoppers are constantly lured to new merchants.
A have-to-be-smart-once business such as a network TV station survives weak management for decades, whereas a retailer must be smart every day.
Berkshire's two new retailers will operate autonomously with no second-guessing; Berkshire tries to behave with managers as it likes owners to behave with it.
Berkshire completed the purchase of 100% of GEICO, the seventh largest US auto insurer with 3.7 million cars, just after yearend; many good managers can report to Buffett.
In 1951 Lorimer Davidson taught Buffett that GEICO's direct marketing gave it an enormous cost advantage over agent-sold competitors.
In 1951 Buffett wrote a report recommending GEICO as the security he liked best and bought its stock for his own account.
Buffett bought 350 GEICO shares in 1951 for $10,282, worth $13,125 at yearend and over 65% of his net worth.
Buffett financed his GEICO shares by delivering the Washington Post, the company that later let Berkshire turn $10 million into $500 million.
Buffett sold GEICO in 1952 for $15,259 to buy Western Insurance at one times earnings; the stake later grew to about $1.3 million, a lesson against selling wonderful companies.
After 1970s underpricing nearly bankrupted GEICO, Berkshire bought in from 1976 (33.3% and $45.7 million by 1980) and reached about 50% through GEICO's share repurchases.
Berkshire agreed in 1995 to pay $2.3 billion for the other half of GEICO, a steep price for an exceptional business run by Tony Nicely and Lou Simpson.
Lou Simpson's GEICO equities returned 22.8% annually from 1980 to 1995 versus 15.7% for the S&P; he takes a conservative, concentrated approach and is Berkshire's investment backup.

stance.quote: GEICO's moat widened in 1995.

summary: GEICO's key is rock-bottom operating costs; 1995 underwriting and loss adjustment expenses fell to 23.6% of premiums, nearly a point below 1994, widening its moat.
Besides acquiring GEICO, 1995 brought other favorable insurance developments; float is money held but not owned, arising from prepaid premiums and the delay in resolving claims.
An underwriting loss is the cost of float; insurance is profitable over time if that cost is below other funding costs, and has negative value if above market rates.
Float is loss reserves, loss adjustment reserves, funds held under reinsurance and unearned premiums less certain prepaid items; underwriting profits in the last three years made its cost negative.
Table: Berkshire's insurance underwriting loss, average float, cost of funds and long-term government bond yield by year, 1967-1984.
Table: insurance underwriting loss, average float, cost of funds and government bond yield by year, 1982-1995, with float reaching $3,607.2 million in 1995.
Since 1967 Berkshire's float has grown 20.7% a year compounded, usually at less than zero cost, boosting performance in a major way.
Profitability depends on asset earnings, liability cost and leverage; Berkshire's float costs very little, whereas many property-casualty insurers pay more for float than it is worth.
Cost-free float acts like equity: replacing $3.4 billion of float with equity would have meant more shares, equal assets and lower earnings, reducing the stock's value.
Float wonderfully benefits a business if it is obtained at a low cost.
Acquiring GEICO adds nearly $3 billion of float, which GEICO should hold at a decent underwriting profit, though Berkshire paid a very substantial price for it.
1995 was a third straight lucky super-cat year; since huge catastrophes are rare, results take many years to measure and a terrible year will partially offset the gains.
No insured super-cat occurred in 1995: Hurricane Opal weakened before landfall and the Kobe earthquake was mostly uninsured, close calls the industry will not always get.
Ajit Jain also writes single-large-loss policies; in 1995 Berkshire insured Mike Tyson's life, Lloyd's against deaths of over 225 names, and two Chinese satellite launches.
All three unusual 1995 policies ended well: both satellites orbit, Lloyd's names avoided abnormal mortality, and Mike Tyson stayed healthy.
Insureds seek Berkshire for super-cat and large single risks due to unmatched financial strength, the fastest quotes and the largest limits; competitors' reinsurance reduces their flexibility.
Large coverages intensify Berkshire's interest; it offered a policy with a $1 billion potential loss, and the largest coverage a client accepted was $400 million.
Berkshire accepts volatile results for better long-term earnings, preferring a lumpy 15% to a smooth 12%, while monitoring aggregate exposure to keep its worst case comfortable.
Berkshire's once-in-a-century super-cat loss is capped and small relative to net worth, whereas primary insurers' many small policies could blow through reinsurance and threaten survival.

stance.quote: A bad reinsurance contract is like hell: easy to enter and impossible to exit.

summary: Super-cat prices are weakening as capital flows in; Berkshire will not knowingly write inadequate rates, having paid for bad early-1970s reinsurance for over 20 years.
Berkshire and GEICO both suffered from reinsurance in the early 1970s and 1980s; Lloyd's problems show insurers fail when writers' interests are not aligned with capital providers.
When the interests of those writing insurance are not symmetric with the capital providers', insurers almost invariably run into trouble, though it may stay hidden for some time.
An insurance CEO's story of low rates, inadequate reserves for asbestos and environmental claims, and failed reinsurers ends with 'it could be my money'; at Berkshire it is.

In 1995 National Indemnity's traditional business had an 84.2 combined ratio and the homestate operation 81.4; California workers' compensation lost volume refusing inadequate rates but earned excellent underwriting profit.
Central States Indemnity's 1995 premium volume rose 23% and underwriting profit 59%; Berkshire's insurance managers are all under 45.
Adding GEICO made Berkshire's insurance business better in quality, faster growing and doubled in size entering 1996; insurance is its core strength.
Berkshire's earnings table aggregates purchase-premium charges separately to show businesses as if unpurchased, which Buffett finds more useful than GAAP; the total equals audited GAAP.

Table: 1995 vs 1994 pre-tax and after-tax operating earnings, first part: insurance underwriting and investment income, Buffalo News, Fechheimer, finance, home furnishings, jewelry, Kirby, Scott Fetzer.
Table: 1995 vs 1994 earnings continued: Kirby, Scott Fetzer, See's, shoes, World Book, premium charges, interest, contributions, operating earnings $814.7 million, securities sales, USAir writedown.
Table: end of the 1995 vs 1994 earnings table: USAir preferred decline and total earnings of all entities, $1,008.8 million in 1995 versus $662.2 million.
Berkshire reports three operations that still earned decent returns on capital but had lower 1995 earnings, in keeping with Charlie's 'just tell me the bad news'.
Shoe industry earnings were depressed in 1995 but Berkshire's shoe units kept or widened their competitive superiority; the decline is viewed as cyclical, not secular.

stance.quote: Over time, we expect the competitive strength of newspapers to gradually erode, though the industry should nevertheless remain a fine business for many years to come.

summary: Buffalo News still does well relative to peers, but newspaper industry trends are poor and its franchise has lost another notch of economic attractiveness.

World Book remains profitable but faces tough CD-ROM and on-line competition with worsening sales and earnings; it changed distribution, pushed electronic products and cut overhead at the end of 1995.
Berkshire's operations, even those with falling earnings, have exceptionally talented managers; Buffett would not replace any of them with other executives in their industries.
Many Berkshire managers work for love of the job; no key manager has left Berkshire to join another employer between 1965 and 1995.
Table: yearend 1995 common stock holdings above $600 million with shares, cost and market value; total common stocks cost $5,745.1 million, market $22,000.3 million.
Five of six top positions were untouched in 1995; American Express rose to about 10%. In early 1996 Berkshire took full ownership of GEICO and swapped Cap Cities for Disney.
Cap Cities holders could take one Disney share plus $65 each; Berkshire sought stock for its 20 million shares, will get over 20 million Disney shares, and bought more.
Buffett Partnership bought Disney in 1966 at a market value under $90 million, about five times rides, and sold in 1967 at 48 cents; Berkshire is again a large owner.
Table: Berkshire's five convertible preferred purchases of 1987-91 (Champion, First Empire, Gillette, Salomon, USAir) with dividend rate, cost and market value.
Berkshire's convertible preferreds were valued mainly as fixed-income securities; the option to convert into common was a kicker.
The $300 million American Express Percs are excluded because they were modified common stock that automatically converted after three years, unlike optional-conversion preferreds.

Convertible preferreds beat the expected moderate return over fixed income only through one issue, trailed wonderful-business returns, and the claim that losing money was almost impossible proved wrong.
Buffett's assertion that Berkshire could almost not lose money on its preferreds caused him well-deserved heartburn.
Gillette has been the best convertible holding, yet it was also Buffett's biggest mistake, of a kind never recognized on financial statements.
Berkshire paid $600 million in 1989 for Gillette preferred convertible into 48 million shares; buying about 60 million common shares at a discount likely would have been possible.
Choosing Gillette preferred over common cost Berkshire about $625 million less $70 million of extra dividends by 1995; Champion called its preferred at 115% of cost in August.
Berkshire offered its converted Champion shares to the company, earning about 19% after tax over six years, and good dividend yields; press accounts overstate insurers' after-tax dividend yields.
A 1987 tax-law change significantly reduced the dividends-received credit of insurers, which press accounts of insurers' after-tax dividend yields ignored.
First Empire preferred will be called March 31, 1996 and converted and kept; the Salomon preferred modestly beat fixed income but absorbed far more management time than its economic significance.
The Salomon conversion option has not proven valuable while the Dow doubled; deciding on it was graded very poor, though the 9% preferred keeps delivering as fixed income.
Salomon preferred requires redemption of 20% yearly from 1995 to 1999; $140 million of the original $700 million was redeemed in 1995, leaving four conversion chances.
USAir's 1995 results improved but problems remain; Berkshire's preferred is well designed, with unpaid dividends since June 1994 compounding at 5% over prime, but the credit is weak.
Berkshire carried its USAir preferred at 60% of par at yearend 1995, while the inferior junior preferred traded at 82% of par and later 97%.
Berkshire's preferreds did well only because of Gillette; excluding it they matched medium-term fixed income. A recapitalization into Class A and new Class B common will be proposed.
Class B shares will carry 1/30th of an A share's economic rights, 1/200th of its vote, and no designated-contributions eligibility; A converts into 30 B but not the reverse.
Berkshire plans to list Class B on the NYSE and sell at least $100 million of new B shares publicly; the price should be near 1/30th of A.
Class A holders can convert shares into B for gifts, and arbitrage conversions would occur if B trades slightly above 1/30th of A.
Class A's full votes and contributions access make it superior to B, so most holders, including Buffett and Munger families, will keep A, giving it a more liquid market.
At $36,000 a share Buffett and Munger do not consider Berkshire undervalued, so the B offering will not dilute intrinsic value; they would not buy it at that price.
Class B adds costs of handling more shareholders but offers convenience for gifts and a do-it-yourself split.
Berkshire is creating Class B mainly because expense-laden unit trusts imitating Berkshire were about to be marketed at low dollar prices.
Tripling small stakes would need a $43 billion market cap to reach $129 billion; Berkshire hopes only to double per-share intrinsic value every five years and wants knowledgeable shareholders.
Unit trusts would be sold for big commissions with burdensome costs to unsophisticated buyers; Class B is meant to make such clones unmerchandisable.
Over the past five years Berkshire's market price grew faster than its per-share intrinsic value, so the stock outperformed the business.
Market overperformance cannot persist; Buffett would prefer Berkshire's price to track intrinsic value exactly so holders gain in proportion to the business's progress.
Informed shareholders not exposed to high-commission salesmanship bring the price closer to intrinsic value, which is why Class B is created to blunt unit-trust marketing.
Disney CEO Michael Eisner and Buffett met by chance in Sun Valley on July 14, 1995, the moment a Disney and Cap Cities combination was raised.
Earlier Disney-Cap Cities talks stalled as Disney wanted cash and Cap Cities stock; after the Sun Valley chat both bent, and a contract was drawn up within weeks.
The Disney/Cap Cities deal makes sense but, without the chance Sun Valley meeting, would not have occurred in that time frame; both should benefit.
Buffett sold a third of Cap Cities for $635 million, versus $1.27 billion in the Disney merger; 96.3% of eligible shares joined the 1995 program giving $11.6 million.
Some shareholders miss the designated-contributions program through unregistered shares or missing the 60-day form deadline; no exceptions are made, even for friends.
To join future contributions programs, Class A shares must be registered in the owner's name by August 31, 1996, not in a broker's nominee name.
Berkshire has no investor relations department and gives no earnings guidance through analysts; the Annual Meeting is its channel for direct manager-to-owner communication.
adjudication_note: The passage states Berkshire's owner-communication policy (no investor relations, no guidance), which is shareholder_programs content rather than meeting arrangements, so it is financial despite the meeting invitation.

summary: 1996 net worth rose $6.2 billion or 36.1%, per-share book value 31.8% after shares issued for FlightSafety and Class B; book value grew from $19 to $19,011 in 32 years.
Each Class B share has 1/30th of a Class A share's economic interest, and per-share figures are stated in Class A equivalents; 1995 statements were restated for technical accounting reasons.
GEICO's January 1996 conversion to a wholly-owned subsidiary required a $478.4 million writedown of the 51% already owned, reducing book value despite its economic value increasing.
After the step-acquisition writedown, the original 51% of GEICO is carried below its market value at the purchase of the remaining 49% and below that 49%'s carrying value.
Two 1996 share issues at a premium to book, B shares for cash in May and stock for FlightSafety in December, offset the GEICO writedown; net effect under one point.
Per-share book value roughly shows economic progress, but intrinsic value is what counts; the Owner's Manual sent in June defined key terms and set out Berkshire's economic principles.
The annual report reproduces the entire Owner's Manual on pages 58-67, including definitions of intrinsic value on pages 64-65.

A table tracks per-share investments and per-share pre-tax operating earnings excluding investment income, two columns to help estimate Berkshire's intrinsic value as if it were broken into two parts.
Table: investments per share and pre-tax operating earnings per share excluding investment income, 1965-1996; in 1996 investments rose 29.0% to $28,500 and operating earnings 63.2% to $421.39.
Past growth rates cannot be matched because Berkshire's large equity capital dampens returns; progress will be uneven with securities markets and swings in catastrophe-reinsurance profitability.

Designated contributions and all corporate expenses are charged against operating earnings; after-tax headquarters expense is under two basis points of net worth, probably lowest among large American companies.
Costs matter: equity mutual funds average about 100 basis points of expenses, cutting investor returns by 10% or more over time, whereas virtually all Berkshire gains stay with shareholders.
In the prior letter, with shares at $36,000, Buffett said market gains had outstripped intrinsic value gains, could not continue, and Berkshire was not undervalued.

Intrinsic value rose significantly in 1996, helped by stunning GEICO performance, while the share price changed little, so the stock underperformed the business and the price/value relationship is more appropriate.
Shareholders' aggregate gains must match business gains; when the stock over- or underperforms, a few buyers or sellers gain at others' expense, usually the sophisticated at the innocents'.
Berkshire wants to maximize owners' total gains while minimizing transfers between shareholders; fairness prevails when market price and intrinsic value are in sync.
The longer shareholders hold, the more business results matter; Berkshire likely leads large companies in long-term owners. It made two acquisitions in 1996 with excellent economics and managers.
Berkshire acquired Kansas Bankers Surety, an insurer with an extraordinary underwriting record under manager Don Towle, and placed it with 80%-owned Wesco, which wanted to expand insurance.
After a chance party conversation and a letter with its financials, Buffett offered $75 million for Kansas Bankers Surety on February 13, 1996 and a deal followed.

FlightSafety International, the world's leading pilot trainer, was Berkshire's other 1996 acquisition at about $1.5 billion, far larger than Kansas Bankers Surety, and arose from a shareholder's suggestion.
A long-time shareholder of both companies saw that FlightSafety fit Berkshire's criteria and that its CEO might want a secure home and Berkshire stock as payment.
The FlightSafety deal let holders choose cash or stock, with terms nudging tax-indifferent holders to cash; about 51% took cash, 41% Berkshire A and 8% Berkshire B.
FlightSafety, founded 1951, trains pilots at 41 locations with 175 simulators costing up to $19 million, making it capital intensive; about half of revenues come from corporate pilot training.
Berkshire hires and retains managers past 70 out of self-interest, since they still perform as well as when young.
Berkshire invites owners of large, good businesses to call it; its 1996 insurance business was terrific, with outstanding results in both primary insurance (GEICO) and super-cat reinsurance.
Float and its cost drive insurance value, and float is a major component of Berkshire's intrinsic value not reflected in book value.
Float is money held but not owned, arising as premiums arrive before losses are paid; an underwriting loss is its cost, and it is an albatross above market rates.
Float is loss reserves, loss adjustment reserves, funds held and unearned premiums less certain prepaid items; underwriting profits in the last four years mean Berkshire is paid to hold money.
Table: Berkshire's insurance underwriting loss, average float, cost of funds and long-term government bond yield by year, 1967-1983.
Table: insurance underwriting loss, average float, cost of funds and government bond yield by year, 1982-1996, with float reaching $6,702.0 million in 1996.
Since 1967 float has grown 22.3% a year compounded, often at less than zero cost, and the GEICO acquisition makes continued growth of free funds more likely.
1996's good results again partly reflect a lucky super-cat year; a truly terrible super-cat year is a certainty, with only the timing unknown.
Shareholders should not panic and sell Berkshire after a large catastrophe loss; selling fine businesses on scary news is usually a bad decision.
Super-cat clients pay Berkshire to absorb earnings volatility; Buffett and Munger prefer a lumpy 15% to a smooth 12% and want shareholders who accept volatility.
Berkshire wrote an Allstate Florida hurricane contract in mid-1996, then a California Earthquake Authority policy from April 1997 exposing it to over twice the loss, retaining all risk.
Berkshire's after-tax worst-case mega-catastrophe loss is probably no more than $600 million, under 3% of book value and 1.5% of market value, less volatile than securities markets.
First super-cat advantage: buyers know Berkshire can and will pay under the worst circumstances, partly because it never lays off risk to reinsurers that might fail in a panic.
Second advantage: after a mega-catastrophe Berkshire would have substantial capacity for long-standing clients, and reinsurers already pay it sizable standby fees to secure coverage.
Third advantage: Berkshire offers firm, immediate coverage sizes no one else matches; California earthquake is its largest risk, and Northridge 1994 losses exceeded insurers' model expectations.
Berkshire reinsures about a $1 billion layer of the new California Earthquake Authority, payable if aggregate losses through March 2001 exceed about $5 billion; only 72% of insurers joined.
Buffett distrusts computer models for super-cat odds, since their false precision can lull decision-makers into huge mistakes, as portfolio insurance did in the 1987 crash.
Perfect risk assessment is unattainable but insurers can underwrite sensibly; Berkshire prices super-cat so about 90% of premiums are eventually paid out in losses and expenses.
Ajit Jain is the best super-cat manager; Buffett's 1970s reinsurance mistakes and GEICO's early-1980s runoff contracts show how disastrous reinsurance propositions abound.
A California quake large enough to tap Berkshire's coverage could also hurt See's, Wells Fargo and Freddie Mac, but Berkshire can handle the aggregated exposures.
Berkshire avoids intolerable outcomes by inverting, per Munger: it does not borrow big amounts and keeps super-cat losses from denting intrinsic value.

stance.quote: our expectations were high - and they are all being exceeded.

summary: Since Berkshire took full ownership of GEICO in early 1996, results are exceeding high expectations under operating chief Tony Nicely.
GEICO's strength is low costs, leading to low prices and good policyholders; over one million annual referrals produce over half of new business, cutting acquisition expenses.
GEICO's voluntary auto policies grew 10% in 1996, versus a best prior year of 8%, led by nonstandard gains; involuntary assigned-risk business is unprofitable.
GEICO hit its 1996 underwriting targets; its goal is a larger price advantage rather than wider margins, so 1997 growth should easily top 1996's.

stance.quote: GEICO's sustainable cost advantage is what attracted me to the company way back in 1951

summary: GEICO's economies of scale should maintain or widen its moat against new entrants; Berkshire paid $2.3 billion for the other 49%, versus $7 million for the whole company in 1951.
GEICO bonuses and profit-sharing now depend only on voluntary auto policy growth and underwriting profit on seasoned business, so everyone knows what counts.

stance.quote: we shun "lottery ticket" arrangements, such as options on Berkshire shares

summary: Berkshire incentive pay should fit the business's economics, be simple and relate to daily activities; it shuns option 'lottery tickets' outside managers' control.
GEICO's 1996 profit-sharing contribution hit a record 16.9% ($40 million) versus under 10% on average earlier; Berkshire enlarges the chart rather than raising the bar.
Lou Simpson's equities beat the S&P 500 by 6.2 points in 1996; his pay is tied to four-year investment results, not underwriting or overall GEICO results.

National Indemnity's traditional business had a 74.2 combined ratio in 1996 and the homestate operation 87.1; California workers' compensation expanded into six states with an excellent underwriting profit.
Central States Indemnity set premium records with good underwriting earnings; Berkshire's smaller insurance units, now including Kansas Bankers Surety, have a virtually unmatched underwriting record.
Berkshire was told to pay $860 million in 1996 income taxes, enough that 2,000 similar taxpayers would have balanced the federal budget.
Buffett and Munger find Berkshire's large tax payments fitting, as society's contribution to Berkshire's prosperity is greater; Berkshire prospers in America as nowhere else.
The earnings table aggregates purchase-accounting adjustments separately so businesses show earnings as if unpurchased, a view Buffett finds more useful than GAAP; the total equals audited GAAP.
Table: 1996 vs 1995 pre-tax and after-tax operating earnings, first part: insurance underwriting and investment income, Buffalo News, Fechheimer, finance, home furnishings, jewelry, Kirby.

Table: earnings continued: Kirby, Scott Fetzer, See's, shoes, World Book, purchase-accounting adjustments, interest, contributions; operating earnings $1,221.4 million and securities sales $2,484.5 million in 1996.
Table: end of the 1996 vs 1995 earnings table: total earnings of all entities were $3,705.9 million pre-tax and $2,488.6 million after tax in 1996.
Buffalo News, the shoe group and World Book, which reported lower 1995 earnings, all recorded gains in 1996.
World Book's unit volume fell and it spent heavily on a CD-ROM launched with IBM in 1997, but cutting distribution and overhead costs preserved earnings and its long-term viability.
Helzberg's earnings fell in 1996 because expenses assumed higher same-store sales; Borsheim's did fine. Berkshire's operating businesses overall far outdid industry norms.
Reported earnings understate Berkshire's progress because they include only investees' dividends; Berkshire values undistributed earnings more, since investees can reinvest at high returns.

Look-through earnings equal operating earnings plus Berkshire's share of investees' retained operating earnings less hypothetical tax, excluding purchase-accounting adjustments, capital gains and non-recurring items.
Introduction to the approximate 1996 look-through earnings table of major investees; investee dividends are already in operating earnings under insurance net investment income.
Table: 1996 look-through earnings: Berkshire's ownership and share of undistributed operating earnings in major investees, hypothetical tax, and total look-through earnings of $1,522 million.
Table: yearend 1996 common stock holdings above $500 million with shares, cost and market value; total common stocks cost $7,910.2 million, market $27,750.6 million.
Berkshire's portfolio showed little change in 1996: it continues to make more money when snoring than when active.
Inactivity is intelligent: Berkshire would not trade subsidiaries on Fed predictions, so it should not trade minority stakes in wonderful businesses; just monitor that quality is preserved.
Capable investing in outstanding businesses leads to a few holdings dominating the portfolio; selling winners because they dominate would be like trading Michael Jordan.
Berkshire favors businesses and industries unlikely to change, seeking virtually certain competitive strength ten or twenty years out; fast-changing industries preclude that certainty.
Buffett welcomes change as a citizen, but as an investor prefers to skip fermenting industries, applauding the endeavor without taking the ride.
See's has changed in details since 1972, but why people buy boxed chocolates from it is virtually unchanged since the 1920s and unlikely to change for 20 to 50 years.

stance.quote: who has done an absolutely incredible job in creating value for his shareholders.

summary: Coca-Cola's sales zeal has grown under Roberto Goizueta, yet the fundamentals behind its competitive dominance and stunning economics have stayed constant.
Coke's 1896 report showed its century-long blueprint already drawn, with sales of $148,000 and 116,492 gallons of syrup; it relies on the same basic theme today.
Coca-Cola syrup sales were 116,492 gallons in 1896 versus about 3.2 billion gallons in 1996.
In 1896 Coca-Cola employed ten traveling salesmen who covered almost the whole territory of the Union, in Asa Candler's description.

stance.quote: Coke and Gillette will dominate their fields worldwide for an investment lifetime.
Coke and Gillette will dominate their fields worldwide for an investment lifetime.

summary: Coca-Cola and Gillette are 'The Inevitables', certain to dominate their fields worldwide for an investment lifetime despite continuing operating work.
Coke and Gillette have significantly expanded their already huge market shares over the past ten years, and all signs point to repeating that in the next decade.
High-tech and embryonic industries will grow faster than The Inevitables, but Buffett would rather be certain of a good result than hopeful of a great one.
Leadership alone gives no certainty, as General Motors, IBM and Sears showed; for every Inevitable there are dozens of Impostors, so Berkshire can find only a few.
Buffett and Munger will never assemble a Nifty Fifty or even a Twinkling Twenty, so they add a few 'Highly Probables' to the Inevitables in the portfolio.

stance.quote: The overpayment risk surfaces periodically and, in our opinion, may now be quite high for the purchasers of virtually all stocks, The Inevitables included.

summary: You can overpay for even the best businesses; overpayment risk may now be quite high for nearly all stocks, and recovery to price can take an extended period.
A bigger risk than overpaying is great companies losing focus and buying so-so businesses, as Coke (shrimp) and Gillette (oil) once did; current managements will not repeat it.

stance.quote: the best way to own common stocks is through an index fund that charges minimal fees.

summary: Most investors should own stocks through a minimal-fee index fund, which is sure to beat the net results of the great majority of investment professionals.
Intelligent investing is not complex but requires correctly evaluating selected businesses within your circle of competence; knowing that circle's boundaries matters more than its size.
Investors need not understand beta, efficient markets, portfolio theory or option pricing; students need only two courses, How to Value a Business and How to Think About Market Prices.
Buy a part interest in an understandable business at a rational price, with earnings certain to be higher in ten years; if unwilling to hold ten years, do not buy.
Berkshire's gains came from this approach: look-through earnings grew at a good clip and the stock price rose correspondingly; without earnings growth there would be little increase in value.
Berkshire's enlarged earnings base means future gains will lag the past; it will keep building earnings by running present businesses well and buying businesses with competitive advantages.

stance.quote: Start as a billionaire and then buy an airline.

summary: Buffett invested $358 million in 1989 in a 9.25% USAir preferred stock, framing it with the joke that airlines destroy fortunes.
Buffett's USAir analysis was superficial and wrong: he overlooked that revenues would face unregulated competition while its cost structure was a holdover from regulated days.
USAir needed major labor contract improvements that airlines rarely get short of bankruptcy; in 1990-94 it lost an aggregate $2.4 billion, wiping out common book equity.
USAir's dividend was suspended in 1994 and the investment written down 75% to $89.5 million; the penalty-dividend provision compounded unpaid amounts at 13.25% to 14%.
USAir turned profitable in late 1996 and paid Berkshire $47.9 million of arrears, helped by a possibly cyclical industry tailwind, though basic cost problems remain.
USAir's preferred is now probably worth its $358 million par, and Berkshire has collected $240.5 million of dividends; Buffett twice failed to sell it, once at about $335 million.
Berkshire paid Salomon four fees in 1996: for the FlightSafety purchase, a small debt offering for its finance subsidiary, and two large offerings.
Berkshire's May sale of 517,500 Class B shares raised $565 million net, answering threatened Berkshire look-alike unit trusts that would charge naive investors high fees.
Unit trusts would have poured offering proceeds into Berkshire's fixed share supply, creating a self-validating speculative bubble in the stock and burdening continuing shareholders.
Exiting shareholders could have profited at buyers' expense, but continuing shareholders would have suffered with hundreds of thousands of unhappy indirect owners and a stained reputation.
The B share offering stopped the trusts and gave a low-cost way to invest, with a 1.5% commission and an open-ended size to repel short-term flippers.
B stock trading volume after the offering was far below normal for a new issue; about 40,000 shareholders were added, mostly long-term owners who understand what they own.
Salomon tailored the B offering to Berkshire's goals even though a standard offering would have earned it perhaps ten times the fee.
Berkshire sold $500 million of five-year notes for $447.1 million, exchangeable into Salomon shares at 17.65 per $1,000 note, with a 1% coupon and about 1.1% interest cost if exchanged.
Buffett and Munger are not unhappy about all investment-banking fees; they gladly pay fees commensurate with performance and more than got their money's worth from Salomon in 1996.
Berkshire will post quarterly and annual reports on the Internet on Saturdays before trading, with a 1997-98 schedule of May 17, August 16, November 15 and March 14.
Berkshire may stop mailing quarterly reports and only post them online, saving significant costs and avoiding erratic delivery to street-name holders.
Internet-only distribution would hurt shareholders without computers; Buffett asks for input, will make no quarterly change in 1997, and will keep delivering the annual report.
97.2% of eligible shares joined the 1996 shareholder-designated contributions program, giving $13.3 million to 3,910 charities; late replies are rejected, with no exceptions.
To join future contributions programs, Class A shares must be registered in the owner's own name, not a nominee, by August 31, 1997.
Nebraska Furniture Mart did about $265 million of business in 1996, a record for a single-location home furnishings operation; store hours and a visit to Mrs. B are noted.
Berkshire's 1997 net worth gain was $8.0 billion, per-share book value rose 34.1%, and 24.1% compounded annually over 33 years.
Berkshire's 34.1% gain in 1997 was no triumph because the S&P Index rose almost as fast in a booming market.
Berkshire lags the S&P Index in booms because it bears taxes; it paid or accrued $4.2 billion of federal income tax in 1997, about 18% of beginning net worth.
Berkshire must overcome corporate tax drag; management expects only a modest long-run advantage over the S&P Index, the yardstick for judging it.
Per-share intrinsic value, not book value, is what counts; in 1997 both grew at nearly the same pace, led by GEICO.
A table splits value into per-share investments and per-share pre-tax operating earnings, the two components central to estimating Berkshire's intrinsic value.
The two columns show Berkshire split into an investment entity and an operating entity bearing all corporate costs.
Table: per-share investments and pre-tax per-share operating earnings excluding investment income for 1967, 1977, 1987 and 1997.
Pre-tax operating earnings grew from $1 million in 1967 to $888 million in 1997, after charging all corporate expenses to the operating businesses.
Per-share investments and operating earnings grew 25.6% and 24.2% annually 1967-1997; 1997 operating earnings rose 70.3%, helped by lucky super-cat results and GEICO's underwriting gain.
Size erodes returns: a $500 million pre-tax profit adds one percentage point to Berkshire's performance, so its rate of progress will fall.
Berkshire's operating subsidiaries and passive investments have splendid prospects, and its managers are motivated by accomplishment rather than pay.

stance.quote: Prices are high for both businesses and stocks.

summary: Prices of businesses and stocks are high, so fresh money earns little prospective earnings, though Buffett has no view on whether prices will fall.
Using Ted Williams's strike-zone lesson, Berkshire waits for the fat pitch rather than swinging at every investment.
Business pitches today barely catch the strike zone and would lock in low returns, yet passing on them carries no assurance of better ones.
Lacking a well-run, sensibly priced business, Berkshire parks money in top-quality short-term instruments, or occasionally makes unconventional commitments that can lose.
Oil derivative contracts for 14.0 million barrels remain from a 1994-95 position; settled contracts earned $61.9 million pre-tax, with $11.6 million unrealized at yearend 1997.
Berkshire bought 111.2 million ounces of silver in 1997, earning a $97.4 million pre-tax gain, because supply and demand needed a higher price; inflation expectations played no part.
Berkshire's largest unconventional position was $4.6 billion of zero-coupon Treasuries, which carried a $598.8 million unrealized pre-tax gain after rates fell in 1997.
Buying zeros instead of cash equivalents risks looking foolish, but owners pay for judgment, and Munger and Buffett hold most of their net worth in Berkshire.
Buyers of beef or cars want lower prices; the same logic is set up for people buying stocks.

stance.quote: Prospective purchasers should much prefer sinking prices.

summary: Net savers who will buy stocks for years should prefer lower stock prices; only near-term sellers benefit from rising prices.
Berkshire owners are automatic savers because earnings are retained to buy businesses and securities, so cheaper purchases make their savings more profitable.
Investee buybacks raise Berkshire's ownership more when prices are low; Coca-Cola, Washington Post and Wells Fargo repurchases at low prices helped far more than today's.
About 97% of Berkshire shares are held by the same owners all year, so they are savers who should welcome falling markets, since every seller's loss is a buyer's gain.
Berkshire gained enormously from low equity and business prices in the 1970s and 1980s, but now finds few exciting opportunities to deploy capital.

stance.quote: GEICO is flying, and we expect that it will continue to do so.

summary: Insurance excites Berkshire, and understanding float and its cost is needed to judge intrinsic value.
Float is money held but not owned; an underwriting loss is its cost, and the business has value only if that cost is below market rates for money.
Insurers have wide latitude in estimating loss costs, so true cost of float is hard to calculate and reserving errors can be huge.
Berkshire tries to present underwriting results conservatively because surprises in insurance are virtually always unpleasant.
Berkshire's insurance has been a huge winner; float is defined and cost of float is negative in years of underwriting profit, such as the last five.
Table: underwriting loss, average float, cost of funds and long-term government bond yield by year, 1967-1989.
Table: underwriting loss, average float, cost of funds and long-term government bond yield by year, 1987-1997.
Float has grown 21.7% a year since 1967 at no cost, and is worth more than equal net worth; it will dip in early 1998 but should grow.
Super-cat insurance is the most volatile line and can spike the cost of float; Berkshire is the preferred market for sophisticated buyers.
Super-cat business should show large profits most years and a huge loss occasionally; a terrible year is certain, only the timing is unknown.
Berkshire was lucky in super-cat in 1997 with no major catastrophes; uninformed investors entering through catastrophe bonds are a concern.
Catastrophe bonds were structured to avoid insurance-licensing laws, and the bond label may make unsophisticated buyers underestimate the risk.
Underpriced catastrophe risk can go undiscovered for years: a dice example shows a 75.4% chance of no payout over a decade before eventual ruin.
A seller who underprices catastrophe risk will go years without paying out but eventually go broke.
Hurricane and earthquake odds are fuzzy, and promoters of catastrophe bonds rely on paid experts who bear no losses if wrong.
The catastrophe-bond expert likely believes his own odds, which makes him less reprehensible but more dangerous.
Catastrophe-bond money has eroded super-cat prices, so Berkshire writes less in 1998; worst-case loss stays about $600 million after tax, under the California Earthquake Authority policy.
The $600 million worst-case loss is about 1% of Berkshire's market value, and Berkshire would raise exposure at appropriate prices.
Ajit Jain built the super-cat business from scratch and has the discipline to walk away from inadequately priced business.

adjudication_note: A tribute to Tony Nicely's vision and energy with no sales, earnings or growth figures is a manager tribute without financial content, which the scope rules put in personal_anecdote; the GEICO results follow in later passages.

summary: GEICO's voluntary auto policies in force grew 16% in 1997 after 10% in 1996; the table gives new and in-force policies, 1993-1997.
GEICO's 1997 underwriting profit was 8.1% of premiums, above its 4% goal, so it cut average rates; the table lists new and in-force voluntary auto policies, 1993-1997.
The auto insurance industry earned unsustainably high profits in 1997; intensified competition will squeeze margins, which long term helps the low-cost operator GEICO.
GEICO paid its 10,500 associates a 26.9% profit-sharing contribution ($71 million) in 1997, up from 16.9%, driven by policy growth and seasoned-business profitability.

stance.quote: We distribute merit badges, not lottery tickets

summary: Berkshire ties subsidiary bonuses to each unit's business performance, not to Berkshire's stock price, which managers cannot affect; GEICO's terrific results earn big checks.
GEICO's underwriting profit should fall in 1998 while growth accelerates: marketing tops $100 million, up 50%, against a 3% share of a $115 billion industry.
Other primary insurers had stunning 1997 results: National Indemnity's traditional business earned a 32.9% underwriting profit and the homestate operation 14.1%, with strong three-year records.
Workers' compensation had a modest 1997 underwriting loss, Central States Indemnity set a volume record, and Kansas Bankers Surety met expectations.
The five other primary insurance operations together recorded a 15.0% underwriting profit in 1997 and have created significant value.
The earnings table separates purchase-accounting adjustments instead of charging them business by business, showing earnings as if the businesses had not been bought; the total matches GAAP.

Operating businesses far outdid industry norms; Helzberg's profits recovered in 1997 after a disappointing 1996, and early 1998 sales were strong.
Buffalo News and Scott Fetzer paid 100% of earnings to Berkshire while public peers retain two-thirds or more, so their records look less impressive than they are.
Buffalo News, See's and Scott Fetzer have paid Berkshire $1.8 billion in earnings, which were then employed elsewhere to build earning power.
Business details and GAAP segment earnings are on later pages, with a non-GAAP four-segment rearrangement matching how management thinks about Berkshire.
Reported earnings understate Berkshire's progress since they include only investee dividends; undistributed investee earnings are more valuable because they are reinvested at high returns.
Look-through earnings equal operating earnings plus Berkshire's share of investees' retained operating earnings, less an allowance for tax on those earnings.
The 1997 look-through earnings table is only approximate because of judgment calls; investee dividends are already in operating earnings.
Table: 1997 look-through earnings, listing major investees' ownership and undistributed earnings, tax allowance and operating earnings totalling $1,930 million.
Berkshire agreed to buy Star Furniture and International Dairy Queen in 1997, both meeting its criteria: understandable, excellent economics, outstanding people.
The Blumkins' referrals led Berkshire to merge with R.C. Willey and later to Star Furniture of Houston.
Buffett bought Star Furniture from Melvyn Wolff in a single two-hour session, relying on the seller's integrity instead of checking leases or contracts.
Star operates 12 stores in Texas, is moving into San Antonio, and could be many times its present size in a decade.
The Star sale closed July 1, 1997, with sellers funding special payments to all employees; sales and earnings growth accelerated afterwards.
International Dairy Queen has 5,792 stores in 23 countries, nearly all franchised; management since 1970 rationalized a precarious operation and built a strong organization.
Berkshire offered IDQ holders cash or slightly lower-valued Berkshire shares to encourage cash; only 45% of IDQ shares elected cash.

stance.quote: when I've issued stock, I've cost you money.

summary: Berkshire strongly prefers cash for acquisitions because its stock-only mergers, excluding two affiliates, left shareholders slightly worse off.
The cost of stock-financed mergers did not come from sellers misleading Berkshire or managing poorly; sellers were candid and effective.
Issuing shares in a merger dilutes owners' stake in all of Berkshire's marvelous businesses, like trading a .380 hitter to get a .350 hitter.
Cash acquisitions such as National Indemnity, See's, Buffalo News, Scott Fetzer and GEICO have delivered far more value than Berkshire anticipated.
Trading up from Berkshire's present businesses is almost impossible, so management will be reluctant to issue shares and will include a cash option when it must.
A premium to a public acquiree needs an overvalued acquirer stock or real synergies; Berkshire seldom is overvalued and expects no synergies from acquirees.

stance.quote: standard -- but, in our view, dead wrong -- accounting practice of ignoring the cost to a business of issuing options

summary: Acquirees that grant options overstate earnings by ignoring option costs; Berkshire replaces options with equivalent cash compensation so the true cost hits earnings.
A takeover premium makes sense only if the acquirer's stock is overvalued or the combination earns more; share-issuing serial buyers concede overvaluation.
Merger synergies are often illusory, and staff and advisors will justify whatever acquisition the CEO favors; introduces the yearend 1997 common stock holdings above $750 million.
Table: yearend 1997 common-stock holdings over $750 million with shares, cost and market value, totalling $36,247.7 million market.
Net sales in 1997 were about 5% of the beginning portfolio, partly to shift the bond-stock ratio moderately in response to relative values.
Lou Simpson independently runs a GEICO equity portfolio of nearly $2 billion that may overlap or differ from Buffett's holdings.

stance.quote: If they stay there -- and if interest rates hold near recent levels -- there is no reason to think of stocks as generally overvalued

summary: Stocks are not overvalued if rates stay low and returns on equity stay high; rates have fallen, but returns on equity may not hold.

stance.quote: Today's price levels, though, have materially eroded the "margin of safety" that Ben Graham identified as the cornerstone of intelligent investing.

summary: Consensus is now cheery, unlike 1979; higher earnings and lower rates support prices, but today's price levels have eroded Graham's margin of safety.

stance.quote: The Coca-Cola Company will be the same steamroller under Doug as it was under Roberto.

summary: Coca-Cola's CEO prepared a seamless succession to Doug Ivester well in advance, so the company's momentum should continue.
Update on the five convertible preferreds bought privately in 1987-1991: Champion sold at a small profit, Gillette and First Empire converted, USAir and Salomon were trouble-prone.
By yearend 1997 the $600 million put into Gillette in 1989 had grown to $4.8 billion and the $40 million in First Empire in 1991 to $236 million.
Salomon merged into Travelers Group, rewarding shareholders after managers saved the firm from extinction after its 1991 scandal and restored its vitality.

stance.quote: I was wrong in originally purchasing the stock

summary: Salomon will pay off far better than expected; USAir's rebound is miraculous after Buffett wrongly bought it and repeatedly tried to sell at 50 cents on the dollar.

stance.quote: Stephen Wolf's accomplishments at the airline have been phenomenal.

summary: USAir rebounded under CEO Stephen Wolf, paid dividend arrearages on Berkshire's preferred in 1997, and its stock rose from $4 to $73.
USAir's preferred was called for redemption in March; the stock's rise made Berkshire's conversion rights valuable, so a decent or even indecent profit is almost certain.
The $300 million of American Express Percs bought in 1991 paid extra dividends for three years with capped appreciation, and proved extraordinarily profitable.
Berkshire considered selling its American Express Percs on conversion in 1994 because of relentless card competition, despite CEO Harvey Golub's quality.

stance.quote: Amex's corporate card was a terrific franchise

summary: Learning that Amex's corporate card is a terrific franchise, Buffett kept the Percs and bought more until Berkshire owned 10%, now a $3 billion gain.
Printing and mailing quarterly reports costs more and is hard for street-name holders, though quarterlies are also posted on Berkshire's website.
Because publishing costs balloon, Berkshire will mail quarterlies only on request, while shareholders still receive the printed annual report and web information.
Berkshire files quarterly information with the SEC and posts it simultaneously on the Internet so all shareholders are on equal footing.
About 97.7% of eligible shares took part in 1997 shareholder-designated contributions: $15.4 million to 3,830 charities.
Over 17 years Berkshire has given $113.1 million as shareholders directed; subsidiaries gave $8.1 million in 1997, including $4.4 million in kind.
Shareholders miss the contributions program if shares are not registered on the record date or forms return late; no exceptions are made.
Only Class A shares registered in the owner's name, not a nominee, by August 31, 1998 can take part in the 1998 contributions program.

adjudication_note: Tickets to the ball game, the local hot-spots packet and the invitation to Omaha are meeting-weekend arrangements, so meeting_logistics, with has_personal true for the curve-ball joke.

summary: Berkshire's 1998 net worth gain was $25.9 billion, raising per-share book value 48.3%; since 1964 book value grew from $19 to $37,801, 24.7% compounded.
Most of the 48.3% 1998 book-value gain came from issuing shares in acquisitions, which raises book value but not intrinsic value because the stock trades above book.
Per-share intrinsic value, not book value, is what counts; 1998 intrinsic value grew substantially but well short of 48.3%, and still far exceeds book value.

stance.quote: GEICO, once again, simply shot the lights out.

summary: Berkshire entered 1999 with its best businesses after buying General Re and Executive Jet; GEICO excelled, but several major investees had shortfalls and the equity portfolio lagged the S&P 500.
The key-value table, restated with General Re pro forma, tracks per-share investments and per-share pre-tax operating earnings, the two components central to intrinsic value.
The table splits Berkshire into an investment entity and an operating entity bearing all corporate costs, excluding investment income from the operating earnings column.
Table: per-share investments and pre-tax per-share earnings excluding investment income for 1968, 1978, 1988 and 1998, with growth rates by decade.
Per-share investments rose 25.2% in 1998 but operating earnings per share fell 33.9%, both because of General Re's large investments and underwriting loss; growth rates by decade are tabulated.
Future gains will fall far short of the past because Berkshire's capital base is too large for outsized returns, though management keeps working to raise both value columns.
Berkshire's $57.4 billion net worth is the largest of any American corporation, though General Electric and Microsoft have market values over three times larger.
Management aims for 15% average annual intrinsic value growth, a peak outcome that needs $58 billion more net worth in five years, with down years certain.
Berkshire needs big acquisitions ('elephants') in unfriendly markets; its payroll reached 47,566 including 7,074 from 1998 acquisitions.
Headquarters has 12.8 staff and after-tax overhead of about $3.5 million; Berkshire and General Re owe $2.7 billion of federal income taxes for 1998.
Berkshire's taxes are so large that 625 similar taxpayers could fund all federal taxes; Buffett says Berkshire prospered in America as it would nowhere else.
Berkshire pays a 35% corporate rate on capital gains, so its tax on a long-term gain is 75% higher than an individual's tax on the same gain.
Berkshire's dividends exclusion is 59.5%, not 70%, because nearly all equity investments sit in insurance companies; paid a $30 million SEC fee on General Re shares.

stance.quote: Quite simply, there is no one in the business world who could run GEICO better than Tony does.

summary: The General Re merger required a record $30 million SEC fee; GEICO combines a low-cost direct-marketing idea with manager Tony Nicely.

stance.quote: Quite simply, there is no one in the business world who could run GEICO better than Tony does.

summary: GEICO leaves unprofitable first-year direct-marketing costs out of bonuses so associates chase growth; 50% of bonuses rest on seasoned-book earnings.
GEICO's marketing spend rose from $33 million in 1995 to $143 million in 1998 and counselors from 652 to 2,162; table of new and in-force auto policies 1993-1998.
GEICO will spend at least $190 million on marketing in 1999; Berkshire accepts first-year costs if each dollar creates more than a dollar of value.
GEICO's claims handling is rated well (lowest New York complaint ratio) and its 1998 profit margin of 6.7% was higher than anticipated or wished.
Fewer and less severe auto accidents lifted margins; GEICO cut rates 3.3% in 1998 and will cut more, expecting margins near its 4% target but above industry.
GEICO paid all 9,313 eligible associates $103 million of profit sharing, 32.3% of salary, likely a high-water mark as profitability falls.
GEICO's market share rose from 3% to 3.5% in 1998; about 40% of those checking rates find savings, so growth room remains.

stance.quote: At Berkshire we feel that telling outstanding CEOs, such as Tony, how to run their companies would be the height of foolishness.

summary: GEICO offers shareholders an 8% discount in 40 states; Berkshire does not direct outstanding CEOs, who are often independently wealthy.

stance.quote: We want our managers to think about what counts, not how it will be counted.

summary: Berkshire removes CEO rituals and tells managers to run businesses as if they own them for a century, ignoring accounting effects.

stance.quote: We can therefore ask our CEOs to manage for maximum long-term value, rather than for next quarter’s earnings.

summary: Few public-company CEOs get Berkshire's mandate because their owners focus on short-term earnings; Berkshire's long-horizon shareholders let it ask managers to maximize long-term value.
GEICO shows Berkshire's approach: its CEO is freed from boards, analysts, financing and earnings expectations, and knows the framework will endure for decades.
Berkshire invites owners of large profitable businesses to call under its acquisition criteria; introduces Executive Jet Aviation's fractional jet ownership business.
EJA sells fractional jet shares with 100 flying hours per eighth, charging monthly management and hourly fees; it created fractional ownership in 1986.
EJA makes a plane available on a few hours' notice at 5,500 U.S. airports, like phoning for a taxi.
Berkshire bought Executive Jet for $725 million, half cash and half stock; EJA is the largest operator with over 1,000 customers and 163 aircraft.
EJA's pilots train twice yearly at FlightSafety; being the industry leader lowers dead-head costs while giving customers unmatched service through positioned planes.
NetJets offers planes from many manufacturers while its two competitors sell only their owners' aircraft; clients can own fractions of several jets as a virtual fleet.
Large companies use NetJets to supplement their fleets and save money on peak needs and dead-head hours; personal users either sign up now or their heirs will.

stance.quote: Rich and I believe that the potential of fractional ownership has barely been scratched.

summary: EJA took 31% of world corporate jet orders in 1997; Buffett believes fractional ownership has barely been tapped, since full ownership needs 350-400 hours annually.
Berkshire completed its $22 billion General Re acquisition on December 21, 1998; General Re is the largest U.S. property-casualty reinsurer and owns 82% of Cologne Re.
Berkshire expects General Re's earnings in a decade to exceed what it could achieve alone, because Berkshire gives it operating freedom a public reinsurer lacks.
Public reinsurers are judged on smooth earnings, so volatility hurts credit ratings and p/e ratios and pushes them to lay off business or reject good risks.
Berkshire accepts earnings volatility and, with its capital strength, can write and retain reinsurance in any amount; General Re adds distribution, technical facilities and management.
General Re and Cologne Re can accelerate international expansion; Berkshire takes over General Re's investment portfolio and brings tax and investment benefits.

stance.quote: we prefer a lumpy 15% return to a smooth 12%.

summary: Berkshire will not manage General Re's underwriting but asks it to retain more business, because it prefers a lumpy 15% return to a smooth 12%.
With General Re and GEICO growing, owners must judge insurers by float, its cost and the long-term outlook for both; float is money held but not owned.
Underwriting loss is the cost of float; an insurer has value if that cost is below market money rates; estimating loss costs gives wide latitude.
Reserving errors flow into earnings and outsiders can only accept them; Berkshire reports conservatively; introduces a table of float since entering insurance 32 years ago.
Float is reserves and unearned premiums less prepaid items; table of average float every fifth year to 1997, and $22,762 million at yearend 1998 with General Re.
Float grew 25.4% a year, and its cost over 32 years has been well under zero, so float is worth more than an equal amount of net worth.
Float growth may be modest as the reinsurance market is soft; General Re is about two thirds of float, and Berkshire's cost of float should stay attractive.

stance.quote: earned a record $96.5 million after-tax on its $112 million net worth.

summary: Operating managers deliver earnings at the top of what their industries allow; Scott Fetzer earned a record $96.5 million after tax on $112 million net worth without leverage.
Berkshire's managers include legends, boosted by General Re and EJA; Buffett and Munger mainly allocate capital and wait for the phone to ring, since activity does not correlate with achievement.
Managers are motivated by a vision for their business more than pay; later pages give GAAP segment earnings and a non-GAAP four-segment view.
