stance.quote: my decision to sell McDonald’s was a very big mistake.

summary: Buffett's 1998 portfolio actions reduced the year's gain; selling McDonald's was a very big mistake.
Berkshire held over $15 billion of cash equivalents at yearend 1998 and sees no large investment or acquisition; General Re sold its equities in the merger.
General Re eliminated about 250 stock positions at a $935 million tax cost, reflecting the 'clean sweep' principle; last year's disclosure of unconventional investments was exceptional.
Berkshire disclosed silver and zero-coupon bond positions because of regulators' questions and their size, but normally sees no advantage in discussing investment actions.
Berkshire's never-comment policy on investments protects owners since talking would lower share value; media speculation about its moves is usually wrong; General Re raised an accounting flaw.
The General Re merger pro forma showed $63 million of extra compensation expense for 1997, not from a General Re accounting problem but from replacing its option plan.
Berkshire replaces General Re's stock option plan with a cash plan of matching economics tied to operating performance rather than the stock price.

stance.quote: existing accounting principles ignore the cost of stock options when earnings are being calculated

summary: Cash and option plans are an economic wash, but accounting ignores the cost of stock options, letting managements pay in options and not count the cost.

stance.quote: Whatever the merits of options may be, their accounting treatment is outrageous.

summary: Options can be ideal pay but are capricious and costly to shareholders; their accounting is outrageous, since paying GEICO's $190 million ad bill in options would still be a cost.
Berkshire subtracts the value of options from an investee's reported earnings and includes the cost of replacing option plans when evaluating acquisitions.
Arguments that employee options cost less than public options, such as forfeitures and tax deductions, are offset because employee options are often repriced.
A non-transferable option's lower value to the employee does not reduce its cost to the employer, just as a restricted company car costs the same.
Option-cost adjustments often cut reported per-share earnings 5% and sometimes 10%, enough to change Berkshire's buy or sell decisions; the questions about options remain unanswered.

stance.quote: many managements purposefully work at manipulating numbers and deceiving investors.

summary: Managements and auditors fought FASB's option-accounting reform and enlisted Congress, and behaved worse in restructuring and merger accounting, manipulating numbers to deceive investors.
The late 1960s brought an orgy of 'bold, imaginative accounting', once easy to tell from honest accounting.

stance.quote: In recent years, probity has eroded.

summary: Probity in accounting has eroded: a growing number of high-grade CEOs now believe manipulating earnings to satisfy Wall Street is acceptable or even their duty.

stance.quote: a premise with which we adamantly disagree

summary: CEOs who assume their job is the highest possible stock price resort to accounting stratagems when operations fall short, rationalizing that deal currency must be fully priced.

stance.quote: The distortion du jour is the “restructuring charge,”

summary: Restructuring charges are often a device for manipulating earnings by dumping multi-year costs into one disappointing quarter; bad accounting drives out good.
Restructuring charges are timed on the cynical bet that Wall Street forgives a big shortfall if later quarters beat expectations slightly.
A golf scorecard analogy mocks the restructuring 'reserve': record a terrible first round, then charge bad holes to it so later results look consistently good.
A variant of the scorecard analogy: defer bad results, report consistency, then take a 'big bath' without returning gains already collected.
CEOs who fiddle with earnings become addicted, and managements use mergers to rearrange assets and liabilities dishonestly, smoothing and swelling future earnings.
Major auditing firms sometimes point out accounting magic at deal time, pushing first-class people to third-class tactics.
Property-casualty acquirers sometimes raise loss reserves at deal time, setting up later reserve releases that flow into earnings.
Berkshire left acquired insurers' loss reserves as found, since immediate large liability increases suggest a lack of knowledge, honesty or groundwork for future earnings.
Two bank CEOs discussing a merger joked that the deal's huge charge was the point; a 1998 tally found 1,369 special charges totaling $72.1 billion.

stance.quote: the attitude of disrespect that many executives have today for accurate reporting is a business disgrace.

summary: The $72.1 billion of 1998 special charges compares with $324 billion 1997 earnings of the Fortune 500; auditors kowtow to managers rather than the investing public.
SEC chairman Arthur Levitt's September speech called for an end to 'earnings management', and Buffett urges support for his clean-up effort.
Berkshire sends quarterly reports only on request and posts them online; Levitt's job of cleaning up corporate reporting is the most important one he could take on.
Berkshire's reporting aims are to give owners what it would want, simultaneously to all; the Internet helps, and Levitt deplored selective disclosure to analysts.
Berkshire treats a B share holder as equal to large institutions, offering the owner's manual and annual reports instead of earnings guidance.
Berkshire plans to post 1999 quarterly reports and the annual report online after market close and promptly posts press releases on its website.
GEICO, Borsheim's, See's and Buffalo News now do substantial Internet business, and Ajit Jain launched annuity products online; 97.5% of eligible shares joined 1998 contributions of $16.9 million.
Over 18 years the contributions program has given $130 million as shareholders directed; subsidiaries gave $12.5 million in 1998, including $2.0 million in kind.
Only Class A shares registered in the owner's name by August 31, 1999 can take part in the 1999 contributions program; late designations are not honored.
Nebraska Furniture Mart did $300 million of business in 1998; NetJets will show a Boeing Business Jet, with deliveries to fractional owners starting in early 2000.
Berkshire's corporate office has 11.8 people; in 1998 6,106 shareholders designated 3,880 charities for contributions.

stance.quote: We had the worst absolute performance of my tenure and, compared to the S&P, the worst relative performance as well.

summary: Berkshire's 1999 net worth gain was $358 million, raising per-share book value 0.5%; the worst absolute and relative performance of Buffett's tenure, though 24.0% compounded since 1964.
Buffett blames himself for 1999: his capital allocation grade is a D because the equity portfolio performed poorly, though relative results are what concern Berkshire.
Several largest investees lagged the market in 1999 on disappointing operations, hurting Berkshire's results; the stock fell more than the business, reversing 1998.
Management expects Berkshire's intrinsic value to modestly outgain the S&P over the next decade, and Buffett keeps over 99% of his net worth in Berkshire.
Large superiority over the S&P is a thing of the past, because Berkshire once bought at more attractive prices and had a much smaller capital base.

stance.quote: the S&P will do far less well in the next decade or two than it has done since 1982

summary: Buffett is virtually certain the S&P will do far less well in the next decade or two than since 1982; Berkshire bought Jordan's Furniture and contracted for MidAmerican Energy.
Jordan's Furniture and MidAmerican Energy were bought for cash with no Berkshire shares issued, the acquisition method management vastly prefers.
Intrinsic value is a key but imprecise measure; an updated table traces per-share investments and per-share operating earnings as guides to Berkshire's intrinsic value.
The two-column table shows Berkshire as if split into an investment entity and an operating entity bearing all corporate costs, excluding investment income from operating earnings.
Table: per-share investments and per-share pre-tax earnings excluding investment income for 1969, 1979, 1989 and 1999 (a $458.55 loss in 1999), with decade growth rates.
Per-share investments barely changed in 1999 while operating earnings fell, as a huge General Re underwriting loss and lower GEICO underwriting profit outweighed managers' fine results.

stance.quote: GEICO’s overall performance, though, was terrific, outstripping my ambitious goals.

summary: General Re's huge 1999 underwriting loss was aberrational; GEICO's underwriting profit fell as predicted but overall performance was terrific, and underwriting should weaken in 2000.
General Re is raising rates, so its underwriting loss should fall absent a mega-catastrophe, but rate effects take time and another unsatisfactory year is likely.
Goodwill amortization of about $500 million a year widens the gap between intrinsic value and book value, though it is an accounting matter unrelated to economic goodwill.
Berkshire's intrinsic value far exceeds its $57.8 billion book value; See's and Buffalo News are worth fifteen to twenty times their carrying value.
Berkshire's managers are in charge with no budgets approved by headquarters or capital expenditure dictums, and are asked to run companies as the family's sole asset for a century.
Berkshire's managers love their work and choose to serve the company; R. C. Willey, Utah's dominant home furnishings business, closes on Sundays for religious reasons.
R. C. Willey grew from $250,000 of sales in 1954 to $342 million in 1999 without Sunday sales; CEO Bill Child proposed a Boise store in 1997.
Bill Child offered to build the Boise store for about $9 million and sell it at cost only if successful, taking the downside personally.
The Boise store opened in August 1999 as a huge success; Berkshire paid Bill Child his cost and he refused any interest on the capital tied up.
Boise sales far exceeded expectations, making it the largest home furnishings store in Idaho; Buffett praises partners like Bill Child.
To understand Berkshire one must judge insurers by float, its cost and the long-term outlook for both; float is money held but not owned.
Underwriting loss is the cost of float, and an insurer has value only if that cost is below market rates; loss estimates give insurers wide latitude.
In 1999 several insurers announced reserve adjustments that made a mockery of earlier earnings; Berkshire reserves conservatively but warns of possible unpleasant surprises.
The float table covers segments since Berkshire entered insurance 33 years ago by buying National Indemnity; float is reserves and unearned premiums less prepaid costs.
Table: yearend float by segment (GEICO, General Re, other reinsurance, other primary) for 1967-1999, totalling $25,298 million in 1999; cost of float has usually been low.

stance.quote: our overall result must be judged extremely poor

summary: A $1.4 billion underwriting loss in 1999 produced a 5.8% cost of float, partly welcome but overall extremely poor; float cost should fall in 2000 absent a mega-catastrophe.
Ajit Jain built an outstanding reinsurance business from scratch that has earned an underwriting profit and now holds $6.3 billion of float.
Ajit's super-cat reinsurance is volatile and has benefitted from luck; the other primary insurers delivered a $192 million underwriting profit over five years.
General Re had an exceptionally poor 1999 underwriting year from underpriced business; incentive pay at General Re and Cologne Re is now tied to float growth and cost.

stance.quote: GEICO made exceptional progress in 1999.

summary: Reinsurance is volatile and prices can be bad, but General Re's distribution, skills and Berkshire's backing can make it the world's most profitable reinsurer; GEICO progressed in 1999.

stance.quote: We have a terrific business idea being implemented by an extraordinary manager, Tony Nicely.

summary: GEICO made exceptional progress in 1999; table of new auto policies and policies in force, 1993-1999.
GEICO's marketing spend rose from $33 million in 1995 to $242 million in 1999 and will rise in 2000; inquiries are costlier because of rising media rates and diminishing returns.

stance.quote: Both of these major competitive advantages are sustainable.

summary: GEICO's cost of new business, though rising, is below the industry's and its renewal operating costs are lowest among national auto insurers; these advantages are sustainable.
GEICO's apparent falling retention reflects a shift to standard and non-standard policyholders and more new customers; adjusted, retention is little changed.
Auto insurer underwriting margins fell in 1999 as predicted and may deteriorate about three points in 2000 as accident frequency and severity worsen.
Rate increases take effect slowly and the reserve releases that boosted auto insurers' earnings have dried up; GEICO bonuses depend on policy growth and seasoned-business earnings.
GEICO paid associates a 28.4% profit-sharing contribution ($113.3 million) for 1999, based on policyholder growth and seasoned-business earnings.
GEICO's bonus plan does not charge new-business costs to associates and rewards policyholder growth and cost control; word of mouth brings most new business.
GEICO's complaint ratio is well below major competitors', referrals are strong, and it could probably hold policy count with $50 million of annual advertising.
GEICO will spend $300-350 million on advertising in 2000, much of it aimed at future growth rather than holding current policies.

stance.quote: Personally, I think these expenditures are the best investment Berkshire can make.

summary: GEICO's optional advertising and counselor spending builds direct relationships with households sending $1,100 yearly; Buffett calls it Berkshire's best investment.
GEICO added 766,256 customers in 1999 and gained $590 million of cash from earnings and float growth; market share rose from 2.7% to 4.1% in three years.
About 40% of people checking GEICO rates save money, and shareholders get a discount, usually 8%, in 40 states; GEICO's former chairman Lorimer Davidson died.
Aviation services leaders EJA (fractional jets, larger than its next two rivals combined) and FlightSafety (pilot training) lead their fields; Buffett also mourns Lorimer Davidson.
EJA is larger than its next two competitors combined and FlightSafety about five times its nearest rival; both are run by founding entrepreneurs.
FlightSafety is capital-intensive: 222 simulators costing up to $15 million each, $215 million of 1999 capital expenditures, so high operating margins are needed for good returns.
At EJA customers own the planes: 1,412 customers own fractions of 169 planes, so modest pre-tax margins give good returns on equity, though a core fleet is needed.
Customers own over $2 billion of EJA planes and $4.2 billion more are on order; aircraft supply is the limit on EJA's growth.
EJA takes about 8% of world business jet output; supply-constrained in 1999, its recurring revenues rose 46%; it is spending heavily to build scale in Europe.
EJA's two largest competitors sell only their parents' aircraft while EJA offers planes from five suppliers, an important advantage.
Buffett and two outside directors buy EJA service at the same prices as any customer under a most-favored-nations policy; his EJA and Borsheim's spending equals ten times his salary.
About 65% of new EJA aircraft owners come from referrals, as at GEICO, and Berkshire's acquisitions usually arise the same way.
Investment banker sale 'books' project earnings precisely for years ahead while the same bankers refuse to forecast their own next month, a mismatch Buffett mocks.
In 1985 a banker failed to sell Scott Fetzer, then Buffett wrote CEO Ralph Schey and agreed a deal within a week.
The banker still claimed a $2.5 million fee on the Scott Fetzer sale; Berkshire's acquisition strategy is to wait for the phone, often prompted by earlier sellers' referrals.
Nebraska Furniture Mart (1983) led to R. C. Willey (1995) and Star Furniture (1997); sellers recommended the Tatelman brothers' Jordan's.
Berkshire agreed to acquire Jordan's, family-run since 1927 and the largest furniture retailer in New Hampshire and Massachusetts.

stance.quote: Jordan’s has the highest sales per square foot of any major furniture operation in the country.

summary: Jordan's 'shoppertainment' produces the highest sales per square foot of any major U.S. furniture operation; the brothers also paid employees from their own pockets.
The Tatelmans paid employees $9 million themselves; each Berkshire furniture operation is number one in its territory, and Star entered San Antonio and enlarged its Austin store.
Buffett thanks the Blumkins for starting Berkshire's furniture group; a second 1999 deal came through Walter Scott, a director with holdings in utility MidAmerican Energy.
After a conversation with Walter Scott and a review of public reports, Buffett agreed to seek a large investment in MidAmerican Energy at an appropriate price.
To avoid voting control under utility regulation, Berkshire is buying an 11% fixed-income security plus stock and exchangeable preferred: under 10% of votes, about 76% of equity, about $2 billion.
Walter Scott and family will invest about $280 million in MidAmerican and control it; Berkshire may make further, possibly large, utility commitments.
GAAP allows acquisitions as purchase or pooling; managements prefer pooling because purchase accounting creates goodwill that is charged against earnings for decades.

stance.quote: we agree with the many managers who argue that goodwill amortization charges are usually spurious

summary: FASB proposed ending pooling; Buffett agrees with managers that goodwill amortization charges are usually spurious.

stance.quote: For accounting rules to mandate amortization that will, in the usual case, conflict with reality is deeply troublesome

summary: Mandating goodwill amortization that conflicts with reality is troubling, unlike depreciation or bad-debt charges, which describe costs that truly occur.
Economic goodwill usually grows rather than diminishes, as at See's for 78 years; managers escape goodwill charges through the fiction of pooling.
Pooling pretends merged companies were always one unit, so no goodwill arises and no charges hit earnings, which Buffett calls poetry.
In most mergers one company is clearly the purchaser, so FASB is right to require purchase accounting; Berkshire proposes an approach satisfying FASB and managements.
Buffett proposes recording acquisitions at fair value, leaving the resulting goodwill unamortized and writing it down only on impairment, applied retroactively.
Under the proposal managements would choose cash or stock for real shareholder consequences rather than for reported earnings effects.
Buying Jordan's assets for cash lets Berkshire amortize goodwill over 15 years for tax, raising cash but lowering reported earnings; stock purchases get no such deduction.
A stock-for-stock acquisition is the worst deal for the acquirer, with no tax-basis step-up; Berkshire has accepted poor tax structures at sellers' insistence but never to flatter its figures.
The earnings table separates purchase-accounting adjustments rather than charging them business by business; its total equals the GAAP total in the audited statements.

Table: 1999 total earnings of all entities were $2,450 million pre-tax against $4,314 million in 1998, after purchase-accounting adjustments, interest, contributions and capital gains.
Dexter Shoe was the one weak business in 1999 because 93% of the 1.3 billion pairs of shoes bought in the U.S. came from low-labor-cost imports.
Berkshire, the leading U.S. shoe manufacturer, is sourcing more output abroad at significant severance costs; Helzberg's restored its margins under Jeff Comment.

stance.quote: See’s Candies deserves a special comment, given that it achieved a record operating margin of 24% last year.

summary: See's achieved a record 24% operating margin in 1999 and, bought for $25 million in 1972, has earned $857 million pre-tax with little added capital.
Under Chuck Huggins See's pre-tax profit grew from about 10% of his age in millions to 100% of it; further pages give GAAP segment data.
Reported earnings understate Berkshire's progress by including only investee dividends; undistributed investee earnings are worth more because they can be reinvested at high returns.
Look-through earnings add Berkshire's share of investees' retained operating earnings to its operating earnings, less a tax allowance, excluding capital gains.
The 1999 look-through earnings table is approximate because of judgment calls; investee dividends are already in operating earnings.

Table: rest of the yearend 1999 holdings (Wells Fargo, others) totalling $8,203 million cost and $37,008 million market; Berkshire made few portfolio changes in 1999.

stance.quote: why we don’t own stocks of tech companies, even though we share the general view that our society will be transformed by their products and services

summary: Large investees had disappointing 1999 results but durable competitive advantages; Berkshire holds no tech stocks because it cannot identify their advantages with conviction.

stance.quote: we have no insights into which participants in the tech field possess a truly durable competitive advantage

summary: Buffett has no insight into which tech companies have durable competitive advantages and, like patents or geology, stays out of fields where he has no capital-allocation expertise.
Berkshire sticks within its circle of competence and does not try to predict the long-term economics of fast-changing industries, neither envying nor emulating those who claim to.

stance.quote: Right now, the prices of the fine businesses we already own are just not that attractive.

summary: Prices of the fine businesses Berkshire owns are not attractive, so it has not added to holdings, though it prefers a comfortable business at a questionable price.

stance.quote: equity investors currently seem wildly optimistic in their expectations about future returns

summary: Berkshire never forecasts the market, but equity investors seem wildly optimistic: profits should grow with real GDP of about 3% plus 2% inflation, the market's own TIPS-implied view.

stance.quote: the market adjustment is apt to be severe, particularly in sectors in which speculation has been concentrated

summary: If profits grow about 5% with GDP, equity returns will be far below what investors expect, and the market adjustment would be severe, especially where speculation is concentrated.
Berkshire expects to deploy cash in equities someday; Buffett scorns explanations of the manic market; a repurchase discussion begins after shareholders requested buybacks.
A repurchase is advisable only when a company has funds beyond business needs and its stock sells below conservatively calculated intrinsic value, with shareholders fully informed.
Business needs are maintenance outlays (Helzberg's remodeling) and growth spending returning over a dollar per dollar (R. C. Willey in Idaho); excess funds go to deals or repurchases.
In the mid-1970s repurchases were obviously wise but few managements acted; those that did made owners much wealthier.

stance.quote: Now, repurchases are all the rage, but are all too often made for an unstated and, in our view, ignoble reason: to pump or support the stock price.

summary: Buffett once looked for big repurchasers as undervalued, shareholder-oriented companies, but now buybacks mostly aim to support stock prices and penalize continuing holders when above intrinsic value.
Many companies repurchasing now overpay departing shareholders at the expense of those who stay, to show confidence or follow fashion rather than raise per-share value.
Buying back shares to offset option exercises is a 'buy high, sell low' strategy; repurchase and issuance decisions should stand on their own.
Buffett admits erring at times by not repurchasing Berkshire shares because he was too conservative on value, though light trading would have limited the gain.
Repurchasing 2% of shares at a 25% discount adds at most half a percent to per-share value; holders who want the stock to rise misread what benefits continuing owners.
Berkshire will repurchase only if its stock sells well below conservatively calculated intrinsic value and will not talk the stock up or down; it gives all holders equal information.
With A shares below $45,000 Berkshire considered buying back but waited; any repurchases would be by direct offers, favor B shares at over a 2% discount, and skip tiny lots.
Berkshire will never buy to stem a price decline but only as an attractive use of money, and repurchases would barely affect its intrinsic value growth.
About 97.3% of eligible shares joined the 1999 contributions program, giving $17.2 million; cumulative gifts reached $147 million and subsidiaries gave $13.8 million.
Only Class A shares registered in the owner's name by August 31, 2000 can take part in the 2000 contributions program; late designations are not honored.
Nebraska Furniture Mart did more than $300 million of business in 1999 at its Omaha location, an absolute miracle in a metropolitan area of 675,000.

S&P 500 numbers are pre-tax while Berkshire's are after-tax; owning the index with taxes accrued would lag in up years and lead in down years.
Net worth rose $3.96 billion in 2000, lifting per-share book value 6.5%, beating the S&P; book value rose 23.6% annually over 36 years, intrinsic value moderately more.
Eight acquisitions cost about $8 billion, 97% in cash, with aggregate sales of $13 billion; no debt was incurred and shares outstanding rose only 1/3 of 1%.

stance.quote: policyholder growth at GEICO slowed to a halt as the year progressed

summary: GEICO policyholder growth stalled in 2000 because new business became costlier despite more advertising; the equity portfolio looks only mildly attractive and is fully priced.

stance.quote: The longterm prospect for equities in general is far from exciting.

summary: Most holdings are fully priced and unlikely to deliver more than moderate returns; long-term prospects for equities in general are not exciting.
Goal is per-share value growing modestly faster than the S&P 500; requires adding a few good businesses yearly, value gains in existing ones, and no material share increase.
Operating managers run their businesses splendidly, leaving Buffett to spend his time allocating capital rather than supervising.

stance.quote: Our managers are a very special breed.

summary: Berkshire's divisional managers hold the jobs they want, focus on long-term value of their businesses, and none of significant size has voluntarily left in 36 years.
Headquarters staff of 13.8 people handled eight acquisitions, a 4,896-page tax return and the annual meeting, for a workforce of about 112,000.
Berkshire has a $40 billion revenue run-rate and over 300,000 owners; checks went to 3,660 designated charities; acquisition technique is simply answering the phone.
Berkshire holds 76% of MidAmerican Energy and, because of regulatory limits on voting, consolidates it on one line of its financial statements.
Full consolidation of MidAmerican would add $5 billion to 2000 revenues with unchanged net income; Buffett spotted CORT through a faxed article on a failed buyout.

stance.quote: a fine though unglamorous business, an outstanding manager, and a price

summary: CORT, national leader in rent-to-rent office furniture with 117 showrooms, was bought for its unglamorous business, outstanding manager and sensible price.

stance.quote: CORT looks like a good bet to beat our original expectations.

summary: Wesco paid about $386 million cash for CORT; Berkshire agreed a half-stock, half-cash deal for U.S. Liability, a specialist surplus-lines insurer.

stance.quote: Few property-casualty companies are outstanding businesses. We have far more than our share

summary: U.S. Liability has combined excellent growth with unusual profitability, and Ben Bridge Jeweler, a 65-store West Coast retailer, was also bought by phone.

stance.quote: a truly remarkable record

summary: Ben Bridge was bought half for cash and half for stock; same-store sales rose 9%, 11%, 13%, 10%, 12%, 21% and 7% over seven years.
The Bridge family kept management control after the sale, without synergy or cost-cutting schemes, and shared a substantial part of the proceeds with co-workers.
Berkshire acquired Justin Industries in July 2000, maker of Western boots (Justin, Tony Lama, Nocona, Chippewa) and Texas brick, after a stranger's fax offering a deal.
Berkshire bought Justin Industries for $570 million in cash; managers Harrold Melton at Acme and Randy Watson at Justin Boot run their companies autonomously.

stance.quote: Acme enjoys unquestioned leadership

summary: Acme makes over one billion bricks a year at 22 plants, 11.7% of U.S. output; 75% of Texans name Acme as a brick brand versus 16% for the runner-up.
Berkshire is a clicks-and-bricks business via GEICO's internet sales and Acme; Shaw's CEO visited about a merger whose partner faced huge asbestos liabilities.
Berkshire would write an exceptionally large asbestos policy but never one without a cap, so the proposed Shaw merger died; Berkshire then arranged to buy Shaw.

stance.quote: This leaves us associated with the best in the business

summary: Shaw has annual sales of about $4 billion and Berkshire owns 87.3%, making it by far its largest non-insurance business; Benjamin Moore Paint also approached Berkshire.

stance.quote: We liked them; we liked the business

summary: Berkshire made a $1 billion cash offer for Benjamin Moore, completed in December, and agreed to buy Johns Manville for about $1.8 billion.
Johns Manville went bankrupt in 1982 from asbestos claims; its victims' trust, the controlling owner, agreed to an LBO sale that failed for lack of financing.

stance.quote: the business has earned good, if cyclical, returns

summary: Berkshire made an all-cash offer without financing contingencies after the LBO collapsed; Johns Manville leads in insulation and roofing with sales above $2 billion and cyclical returns.
Sellers foresaw slowdowns, so Berkshire bought companies whose earnings will fall from 1999-2000 peaks; Berkshire ignores such bumps and expects all businesses to have ups and downs.

stance.quote: junk bond purchasers had relaxed their standards, buying the obligations of everweaker issuers at inappropriate prices

summary: The junk bond market dried up in 2000 after lax standards produced rising defaults, so leveraged buyers could not borrow what they wanted.
LBO operators bid less aggressively in 2000; Berkshire analyzes purchases on an all-equity basis so became more competitive, and is often the seller's preferred buyer.
Berkshire prefers sellers who love their company, a sign of honest accounting and loyal staff; owners who auction off a dressed-up business are a warning sign.
Berkshire offers an almost unique permanent home for businesses built over lifetimes, and its ownership structure ensures promises to sellers are kept.
Sellers can rely on Berkshire's promises, such as keeping a business headquartered where it is or unmerged; owners should choose a business's permanent home rather than leave it to auction.
An insurer is valued by float generated, its cost and their long-term outlook; float is money held but not owned because premiums precede loss payments.
Underwriting loss is the cost of float; an insurer has value only if that cost is below market money rates, but estimated loss costs obscure it.

stance.quote: Both the income statements and balance sheets of insurers can be minefields.

summary: Reserving errors can be huge and flow into earnings, auditors sometimes bless dubious numbers, and Berkshire aims to be consistent and conservative but warns surprises in insurance are unpleasant.
Berkshire's float table covers 34 years since National Indemnity; float is net loss and unearned premium reserves, reinsurance funds held, less receivables and prepaid costs.

stance.quote: We’re pleased by the growth in our float during 2000 but not happy with its cost.

summary: Yearend float by segment (GEICO, General Re, reinsurance, other primary) from 1967, reaching $27.9 billion in 2000; cost of float has been near zero, 19% in 1984.
A $1.6 billion underwriting loss in 2000 gave a 6% float cost; Berkshire expects it to fall in 2001 from General Re repricing, barring a mega-catastrophe.

stance.quote: When these policies are properly priced, we welcome the pain-today, gain-tomorrow effects they have.

summary: Insurers offloading large losses onto Berkshire produced $400 million (27.8%) of the 1999 and $482 million (34.4%) of the 2000 underwriting loss, in exchange for usable float.
Other reinsurers avoid policies whose reported losses hurt results even though the economics are favorable; Berkshire also assumes past losses of insurers wanting to exit troubles.
Retroactive reinsurance contracts are always capped; under GAAP they do not hit current earnings but create a deferred-charge asset equal to expected losses above the premium.
The deferred charge is amortized into annual underwriting losses for years or decades, offset by large float; retroactive insurance is less desirable than profitable float but decent business.

stance.quote: I expect our cost of float to be very attractive in the future

summary: Cost of float should be attractive but rarely zero because of retroactive reinsurance charges; benefits depend on deploying float well; Ajit Jain wrote the retroactive business.
Ajit Jain wrote a $2.4 billion retroactive reinsurance premium for a major U.K. company, plus record disability cover for the Texas Rangers on Alex Rodriguez's $252 million contract.
Berkshire insured a $1 billion Grab.com prize; such a policy brings modest premium, a small chance of a huge loss and good odds, and cannot be laid off through reinsurance.

stance.quote: At General Re, the news has turned considerably better

summary: Berkshire likes bets with compelling mathematics regardless of reported earnings; General Re repriced or dropped unprofitable business in 2000, and its float cost should fall if there is no mega-catastrophe.

stance.quote: General Re has several important and enduring business advantages.

summary: General Re's float cost should fall materially in 2001 absent a mega-catastrophe; Berkshire's smaller insurers produced an excellent underwriting profit and significant float in 2000.
Berkshire's smaller insurers would rank as an outstanding insurer if standalone, though the world may not notice; thanks go to their managers, including the new Cypress head.

stance.quote: I was wrong: The extra money we spent did not produce a commensurate increase in inquiries.

summary: Cypress's CEO moved to run uniform maker Fechheimer and is succeeding; Buffett admits GEICO's extra 2000 advertising did not produce commensurate inquiries or sales.

stance.quote: But acknowledging and analyzing them can be useful

summary: GEICO's conversion of inquiries fell and acquisition cost per policy jumped in 2000; table of new auto policies and policies in force 1993-2000, with new policies down in 2000.

stance.quote: The Washington Post Company, which unfailingly and objectively reviews its acquisitions three years after they are made
Elsewhere, triumphs are trumpeted, but dumb decisions either get no follow-up or are rationalized.

summary: Boards rarely hold candid post-mortems on failed decisions, especially acquisitions; The Washington Post Company is an exception, reviewing each acquisition three years later.

stance.quote: write-offs that are casually waved off as “nonrecurring.”

Rate increases that narrow GEICO's price gap reduce acceptance even though it remains the best deal; State Farm, with about 19% of the auto market, was slow to raise prices.

stance.quote: State Farm is one of America’s greatest business stories

State Farm, founded in 1922 as a mutual with no capital-market access, stock options or lavish pay, overcame established insurers with greater capital and distribution.

stance.quote: GEICO has much the better business model

summary: GEICO has significantly lower operating costs than State Farm, an enduring low-cost advantage that should raise market share with excellent profits, though slowly if State Farm keeps absorbing losses.

we would rather purchase businesses than stocks

stance.quote: They are high-grade, talented and loyal.

summary: Subsidiary managers' business behavior is more rational and owner-oriented than at many public companies, one reason Berkshire prefers owning businesses outright to holding stocks.
Owning 80% or more of a business is far more tax-efficient: dividends upstreamed are untaxed and a sale would carry no capital gains on retained earnings.
On a 10% stake earning $10 million, Berkshire's $1 million share bears about $140,000 dividend tax or at least $350,000 capital gains tax, versus none for an 80%-owned subsidiary.
Government is partner twice on stock investments but once on 80%-owned businesses; apart from tax, stocks and businesses are valued by the same formula, like Aesop's bird in the hand.
Valuing any asset needs three answers: how certain the future cash is, when and how much, and the risk-free rate (long-term U.S. bond yield); it applies to all assets.
The valuation formula applies to every asset regardless of technology; dividend yield, P/E, book ratios and growth matter only as clues to cash flows, and growth can destroy value.

stance.quote: are displaying their ignorance, not their sophistication

summary: Growth is just a component of value, so calling growth and value contrasting styles is ignorance; precise inputs are foolish, working with ranges is better.

Usually the range of estimates is too wide to conclude, but conservative estimates occasionally show prices startlingly low; investors need business understanding and independent thinking, not brilliance.
When even broad estimates give no conviction, as with new businesses and rapidly changing industries, any capital commitment is speculative.

stance.quote: But it is not a game in which Charlie and I wish to play.

summary: Speculation focuses on what the next buyer will pay; Berkshire won't play, and recent market triumphs blur the line between investment and speculation.

stance.quote: will eventually bring on pumpkins and mice

summary: Speculators continuing in companies with gigantic valuations relative to future cash will meet pumpkins and mice; last year Buffett called investor expectations irrational, several multiples of probable returns.

stance.quote: That, for sure, was an irrational expectation

summary: A December 1999 survey found investors expected 19% annual returns over the decade, impossible for American business; valuations of businesses likely worthless were even more irrational.

stance.quote: the values of stocks in certain sectors became decoupled from the values of the businesses that underlay them

summary: Stocks in certain sectors became decoupled from their underlying businesses; any business that loses money over its lifetime destroys value, however high its interim valuation.

stance.quote: By shamelessly merchandising birdless bushes, promoters have in recent years moved billions of dollars from the pockets of the public to their own purses

summary: Promoters moved billions from the public to themselves by selling birdless bushes; bubble companies existed to profit from investors, their business model an old chain letter.

stance.quote: speculation is most dangerous when it looks easiest

summary: Wall Street sells investors anything they will buy; Berkshire does not pick winners among unproven enterprises but applies Aesop's equation where it is reasonably confident of cash flows.

summary: Berkshire keeps estimates conservative and focuses on industries without ruinous surprises, yet erred on trading stamps, textiles, shoes and department stores; negotiated whole-business purchases are lately the best bushes.

Berkshire releases annual and quarterly financials on the Internet after Friday's close so its 300,000 owners get simultaneous access with time to digest before Monday trading.

stance.quote: We applaud the work that Arthur Levitt, Jr., until recently Chairman of the SEC, has done

summary: Selective disclosure, guiding analysts to earnings expectations, had become standard and gave speculative institutions an information edge; SEC chairman Levitt cracked down on it.

stance.quote: should be a matter of shame for CEOs and their investor relations departments

summary: Selective disclosure favored institutions over individual investors; thanks to the SEC, corporations must now treat all owners equally, a reform that came by coercion rather than conscience.

stance.quote: it is both deceptive and dangerous for CEOs to predict growth rates for their companies

summary: CEOs should not predict long-term growth rates; hopes with caveats are fine, but forecasting 15% annual per-share earnings growth for a major company courts trouble.

stance.quote: Even more troublesome is the fact that they corrode CEO behavior.

summary: Only a handful of the 200 top-earning companies of 1970 or 1980 grew per-share earnings 15% annually; lofty predictions spread optimism and corrode CEO behavior.

stance.quote: These accounting shenanigans have a way of snowballing

summary: CEOs who announce earnings targets make uneconomic operating moves and then play accounting games to make the numbers; shifting earnings between periods snowballs and can turn fudging into fraud.

summary: Berkshire is leery of companies run by CEOs who woo investors with fancy predictions, who may prove prophetic but are often congenital optimists or charlatans; investors cannot tell in advance.
The Wall Street Journal wrongly reported on December 29 that Berkshire was buying Conseco and Finova bonds, putting 'several hundred million dollars' in each.

The false Berkshire story, repeated on CNBC and by other outlets, sent Conseco stock sharply higher on exceptional volume, ninth on the NYSE most-active list that day.

stance.quote: Trailer leasing is a cyclical business but one in which we should earn decent returns over time.

In 1955 Graham-Newman's Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron bought Union Underwear, maker of Fruit of the Loom, for $15 million, using its excess cash and tax loss carryforward.
Union Underwear earned about $3 million pre-tax, sheltered by P&R's tax position, and $9 million of the price was non-interest notes; Fruit later earned over $200 million pre-tax before 1996.
After its operating head retired in 1996, Fruit of the Loom took on debt for disappointing acquisitions and went bankrupt; his return cut staff from 40,000 to 23,000.
Berkshire's bankruptcy-court proposal for Fruit of the Loom had no financing conditions but required the CEO to stay, since he and the brand are its key assets.
H.H. Brown bought Acme Boot's inventory and trademarks for $700,000; Acme was P&R's 1956 purchase, at $3.2 million for sales of $7 million, later the world's largest bootmaker.
Acme Boot eventually collapsed and Berkshire bought its remnants, illustrating Graham's quote that many shall be restored and many shall fall; R.C. Willey's Boise story gets a postscript.
R.C. Willey does over $300 million in Utah, up from $250,000 under its chairman 48 years ago, with a closed-on-Sundays policy that defied conventional retailing wisdom.
The chairman put $11 million of his own money into the Boise store, to sell to Berkshire at cost if it worked; it succeeded hugely, so Henderson followed.

stance.quote: This store outsells all others in the R.C. Willey chain

summary: The Henderson, Nevada R.C. Willey store outsells all others in the chain and does twice the volume Buffett expected; an insurance-economics section on float then begins.
Understanding Berkshire means understanding insurers: the key factors are float, its cost, and the long-term outlook for both; float is money held but not owned.
Underwriting loss is the cost of float; an insurance business has value if that cost is below what the company would otherwise pay for funds, otherwise it is a lemon.

stance.quote: Over the last few years, however, our cost has been too high, and in 2001 it was terrible.

summary: Berkshire's float cost was below zero in about half its years but too high recently and terrible in 2001; the float table starts with the National Indemnity purchase.

stance.quote: Our float cost therefore came in at a staggering 12.8%.

summary: September 11 produced the insurance industry's largest loss and a 12.8% float cost, worst since 1984, partly self-inflicted; float costing 4% was tolerable when bonds yielded twice as much.

stance.quote: Today, fat returns are nowhere to be found (at least we can’t find them)

summary: With short-term rates under 2% and fat returns scarce, every Berkshire insurer except retroactive reinsurance, which loses about $425 million yearly by design, must earn an underwriting profit.

stance.quote: very few stack up as satisfactory businesses

summary: Size and brand do not determine insurer profitability, underwriting discipline does; the first principle is accepting only risks one can evaluate within one's circle of competence.
Disciplined insurers ignore market share and limit business so no single event or correlated risks threaten solvency, ceaselessly searching for correlation among seemingly unrelated risks.

stance.quote: our implementation of rules 1 and 2 at General Re had been dangerously weak

summary: Insurers must avoid moral risk; September 11 showed General Re applied its first two underwriting rules weakly, overlooking large-scale terrorism losses in pricing and aggregation.

stance.quote: all of us in the industry made a fundamental underwriting mistake by focusing on experience, rather than exposure

summary: The industry priced property cover on past windstorm, fire and quake experience and assumed huge terrorism risk without premium; the largest insured property loss in history came from terrorism.
Experience is a useful underwriting starting point, as for California quakes written by National Indemnity, but dangerous late in a bull market, when D&O losses look rare.
After bull markets end, hidden promotions and earnings manipulation surface and juries can hit D&O insurers with judgments unrelated to earlier experience; even one jumbo verdict can be costly.

stance.quote: Doing that in the case of terrorism, however, could literally bankrupt the industry.

summary: D&O excess cover priced on exposure might cost five or more times the experience-based premium; ignoring terrorism exposure could bankrupt the insurance industry.
Probabilities of nuclear or biological terrorism cannot be measured but are not zero and are rising; an attack on several buildings would produce astronomical workers' compensation claims.

stance.quote: insurers and reinsurers have blithely assumed the financial consequences from the incalculable risks I have described

summary: In a close-to-worst-case terrorism scenario with $1 trillion of damage, the insurance industry would be destroyed unless it limits terrorism risk; only the U.S. Government can absorb such a blow.
If the government will not absorb terrorism losses beforehand, citizens must bear their own risks and rely on government rescue after a disaster.

stance.quote: I violated the Noah rule: Predicting rain doesn’t count; building arks does.

summary: Buffett saw terrorism risk before September 11 but did not act, leaving General Re with uncompensated risk now running off; Berkshire will accept $2-2.5 billion single-event losses if properly paid.

stance.quote: Over time, insuring these jumbo risks should be profitable

summary: Berkshire's tolerance for huge losses is a competitive advantage, backed by liquid resources, non-insurance earnings, a favorable tax position and shareholders accepting volatility; jumbo risks should pay off over time.

stance.quote: we stumbled in a big way in 2001, largely because of underwriting losses at General Re

summary: Berkshire will write some terrorism cover, including a few large non-correlated policies, but cap total exposure; insurance float fueled growth, though General Re's underwriting losses caused a big 2001 stumble.

stance.quote: the company broke each of the three underwriting rules I set forth in the last section and has paid a huge price for doing so

summary: General Re broke all three underwriting rules, under-reserved and so misjudged its costs in long-tail reinsurance, and was overly competitive for business.
Equating winning with market share rather than profit brings trouble; underwriting discipline is being restored at General Re and Cologne Re under new CEO Joe Brandon and president Tad Montross.

stance.quote: General Re should be a huge asset for Berkshire

Ajit Jain, with 18 associates, runs one of the world's largest reinsurance operations by assets and the largest by individual risk size, and never breaks Berkshire's three underwriting rules.
Discipline does not eliminate losses but prevents foolish ones; as in investing, insurers get outstanding long-term results mainly by avoiding dumb decisions rather than making brilliant ones.
After September 11, Berkshire kept for its own account jumbo policies: $578 million refinery cover, $1 billion airline terrorism liability, a North Sea platform and Sears Tower cover.
Berkshire avoids writing policies whose losses could aggregate, such as many towers in one city without nuclear exclusions; its speed in offering huge policies after September 11 is an advantage.
Weak reinsurers reliant on retrocessionaire chains could not survive a second mega-catastrophe; insurers must stress-test every participant, while Berkshire retains its risks and depends on no one.

stance.quote: they want you to unthinkingly accept concepts that are dangerously flawed

stance.quote: “loss development” is a widely used term – and one that is seriously misleading

summary: Loss reserves are a liability for all losses incurred but unpaid, including IBNR losses not yet reported, not funds set aside for a rainy day.
Estimating the cost of reported and unreported losses accurately is vital; GEICO nearly failed in the early 1970s by under-reserving, which left it underpricing and growing at ever-larger losses.
Loss development means past reserve shortfalls hit current earnings; at General Re in 2001 a staggering $800 million of earlier-year loss costs was belatedly recognized.

Under-reserving made General Re underprice for years, overstate profits, pay unjustified incentive compensation and incur taxes too early; Buffett urges dropping the terms loss development and reserve strengthening.
Loss development implies an uncontrollable event, when in fact management misestimated, misreporting earlier results; losses did not develop, management's understanding of them did.

stance.quote: Underreserving, it should be noted, is a common – and serious – problem throughout the property/casualty insurance industry.

summary: Under-reserving is common in property-casualty insurance, especially at struggling firms; Berkshire underestimated in 1984 and 1986 but is generally conservative; insurers essentially grade their own reserves.

Insurers grade their own reserves and auditors get a management letter covering them; companies in financial difficulty are seldom tough graders, and proper reserving is hard even with good intentions.
Insurers' past operations hold hidden 'rented suit' liabilities that can lie dormant for decades, as with asbestos; management must adequately account for all possibilities.
Reserving conservatism is essential because surprises in insurance have been far from symmetrical in their effect on earnings: claims news is rarely good.

stance.quote: FINOVA’s prospects, therefore, are not as good as when we made our proposal to the bankruptcy court

summary: Berkshire ended its FINOVA bond offer when the NYSE closed after September 11, which also cut aircraft collateral values; Berkshire still expects the transaction to be satisfactory.
Leucadia manages FINOVA day to day; in 1969 Berkshire's Boston bank promptly offered the $10 million needed to buy Illinois National Bank, unlike its New York bank.

stance.quote: Debt is a four-letter word around Berkshire.

summary: Berkshire borrowed almost nothing from banks for three decades until the February 2001 FINOVA structuring, when FleetBoston again agreed to provide the money and settle details later.
FleetBoston syndicated a $6 billion loan, oversubscribed by 17 banks; Berkshire's reported purchases are sometimes made by Lou Simpson, who runs a $2 billion GEICO portfolio independent of Buffett.
Lou Simpson runs GEICO's portfolio independently, thinks like Buffett but buys smaller companies because he has less money, and in recent years his performance has been far better than Buffett's.

stance.quote: it’s one that Charlie and I believe is both rational and fair to owners

summary: Subsidiaries make their own charitable decisions, totaling $19.2 million in 2001, while the parent contributes only what shareholders designate; managers must use company funds to benefit their operations.
Berkshire does not match employee gifts or support the Buffetts' or Mungers' charities; registered A-share holders (86.6% of equity capital) direct a per-share contribution to up to three charities.
Berkshire gave $16.7 million at the direction of 5,700 shareholders naming 3,550 charities, cumulatively $181 million; shareholders named 437 churches and synagogues and 790 schools.
Critics of Berkshire's gifts to Planned Parenthood overlook that owners, not Berkshire, make charitable decisions, and the owners are diverse in their opinions.

Berkshire follows shareholder instructions for any 501(c)(3) charity, as if paying a dividend that the shareholder then donated, but more tax-efficiently; it never weighs personal characteristics in hiring or purchasing.
Berkshire added about 40,000 employees in 2001, bringing its workforce to 110,000, while headquarters, in 5,246.5 square feet, grew by one person.
Headquarters has 14.8 employees for a workforce of 110,000 and also handles unusual duties such as the shareholder gala and designated-gifts program.

stance.quote: In all respects 2002 was a banner year.

summary: Net worth rose $6.1 billion in 2002, lifting per-share book value 10.0%; 22.2% annual growth over 38 years; non-insurance pre-tax earnings, $272 million a decade ago, now arrive monthly.

stance.quote: GEICO shot the lights out in 2002, and underwriting discipline was restored at General Re
GEICO shot the lights out in 2002, and underwriting discipline was restored at General Re
Getting back to low-cost float feels good

summary: Float rose $5.7 billion to $41.2 billion at a cost of only 1%; reinsurance and GEICO excelled and General Re discipline returned; acquisitions need good economics, great managers, sensible price.

stance.quote: we have no “exit” strategy – we buy to keep

summary: Unlike LBO firms Berkshire has no exit strategy; marketable securities beat most indices after dismal years; book value beat the S&P 500 by 32.1 points, aided by market conditions.
The 32.1-point outperformance is aberrational; Berkshire hopes for an annual edge of a few points and will trail in strong bull markets because fewer assets are in stocks.

stance.quote: Often, a forget-all-this-bad-stuff message is delivered year after year without management so much as blushing.

summary: Pro-forma earnings statements show managers' earnings far above audited figures, telling owners to ignore bad items, often year after year without embarrassment.
On a pro-forma basis Berkshire's 2002 earnings were lower than reported, because no megacatastrophe occurred and insurers earned more than normal; insurers like to adjust for 'except for' disasters.

stance.quote: That is deceptive nonsense.

summary: 'Except for' megacat losses will always be paid with shareholders' money; Berkshire's 2002 underwriting was flattered by no disasters, and bond-market gains in finance strategies will diminish.

stance.quote: We continue to be blessed with an extraordinary group of managers

summary: Excluding two favorable breaks, 2002 pre-tax earnings would have been about $500 million lower; no subsidiary CEO has left in 38 years, and six managers are over 75.

stance.quote: Berkshire’s operating CEOs are masters of their crafts

summary: Berkshire's CEOs run their businesses as if their own and Buffett's job is to stay out of the way and allocate their excess capital.
Berkshire completed Albecca (Larson-Juhl), the U.S. leader in custom picture frames, and Fruit of the Loom, with about 33.3% of U.S. men's and boys' underwear, both pending at yearend 2001.

Fruit of the Loom's CEO rescued the company after returning; two smaller 2002 acquisitions together earn over $60 million pre-tax in tough industries but with competitive strengths yielding decent returns.
Berkshire bought CTB (poultry, hog and grain equipment), Garan (children's apparel) and, its largest 2002 deal, The Pampered Chef, started in 1980 by a home economics teacher.
Pampered Chef began with $3,000 borrowed against a life insurance policy, all the capital ever injected, selling kitchenware through in-home presentations.
Pampered Chef did $50,000 in its first year and over $700 million annually 22 years later through 67,000 kitchen consultants, selling largely proprietary, well-styled products.

stance.quote: Berkshire shareholders couldn’t be luckier than to be associated with Doris and Sheila.

summary: Pampered Chef sells largely proprietary kitchenware through knowledgeable consultants; its founder and new CEO met Buffett in Omaha in August and a deal was made within seconds.

stance.quote: the company is a key part of Berkshire

summary: Berkshire owns 80.2% of MidAmerican Energy Holdings but PUHCA limits voting to 9.9%, so it is not consolidated; MEHC has $18 billion of assets and Berkshire's largest non-insurance earnings stream.
MEHC bought the Kern River pipeline, moving 900 million cubic feet a day with a $1.2 billion expansion to double throughput, and the 16,600-mile Northern Natural Gas pipeline.
Northern Natural, once an Omaha business as InterNorth, merged with Houston Natural Gas in 1985; promises to stay in Omaha were broken and the renamed company, Enron, moved to Houston.
After Enron pledged Northern Natural to Dynegy, which also faced distress, MEHC signed a cash purchase on July 29; Kern River's expansion will carry about 8% of U.S. gas.
MEHC deliberately expanded HomeServices of America, a residential brokerage operating under local names such as Edina Realty and Iowa Realty, which is market leader in most areas it serves.

HomeServices, the second-largest U.S. residential brokerage, took part in $37 billion of transactions in 2002, up 100%, driven by three acquisitions including Prudential California Realty with $16 billion of closings.

stance.quote: it’s one we like and in which we continue to have an appetite for sensible acquisitions

summary: HomeServices' CEO sharply increased revenues and profits in a cyclical business Berkshire likes; MEHC's CEO and deputy are dealmakers and managers, and Berkshire stands ready to inject massive capital.
Understanding Berkshire means understanding insurers: float, its cost and the long-term outlook for both determine value; float is money held but not owned.
Underwriting loss is the cost of float; falling interest rates have turned formerly tolerable underwriting losses into burdens that push insurance businesses deeply into lemon territory.

stance.quote: burdens that move insurance businesses deeply into the lemon category

summary: Berkshire's float cost was below zero in many years but 12.8% in 2001, half from World Trade Center losses; cheap float is not automatic, as 1983-84 showed.
Yearend float by segment (GEICO, General Re, reinsurance, other primary) from 1967, reaching $41.2 billion in 2002 from $35.5 billion in 2001.
Berkshire's 2002 cost of float was 1%, but with no megacatastrophe that year enthusiasm should be tempered, since periodic disasters will spike the cost.

stance.quote: Absent a megacatastrophe, I expect our cost of float in 2003 to again be very low

summary: A General Re charge for earlier-year losses plus the retroactive insurance charge cost $1.75 billion, 4.6% of float, yet 2002 came near no-cost; 2003 float cost is expected very low.

stance.quote: enormous progress has been made on each of the fronts described

summary: Low-cost float requires underwriting discipline, conservative reserving and no aggregation of exposures; all major Berkshire insurers meet these tests except General Re, where progress under new management has been enormous.

stance.quote: I was dead wrong.
the company was grossly mispricing its current business

summary: When Berkshire merged with Gen Re in 1998, Buffett believed it followed Berkshire's underwriting rules, but its culture had changed and it was grossly mispricing business.
Gen Re had accumulated exposures that terrorist nuclear attacks would have made fatal, and the World Trade Center loss alone would have threatened an independent Gen Re.
Gen Re cut its nuclear, chemical and biological aggregation to a tolerable level during 2002 and now writes only properly priced business, judging itself on underwriting profit, not size.
Berkshire is making every effort to get Gen Re's reserving right, since an insurer that does not know its costs is heading for big trouble.

stance.quote: but we failed badly

summary: General Re failed to reserve adequately at yearend 2001, so 2002 underwriting results bore an extra $1.31 billion to correct earlier estimates; avoiding under-reserving is the top priority.

stance.quote: I believe General Re is now well positioned to deliver huge amounts of no-cost float to Berkshire

summary: Casualty managers naturally under-reserve and reinsurers find proper reserving harder; Buffett believes Gen Re is now well positioned to deliver no-cost float with sink-the-ship catastrophe risk eliminated.
General Re's three biggest rivals lost AAA ratings, leaving it unique among giants in financial strength; one large reinsurer has nearly stopped paying valid claims.

stance.quote: “Cheap” reinsurance is a fool’s bargain
At GEICO, everything went so well in 2002 that we should pinch ourselves.

summary: Cheap reinsurance is dangerous because insurers depend on a reinsurer's promise to pay decades later; GEICO had strong growth and profits in 2002.
GEICO saves policyholders about $1 billion a year versus other insurers, ranked above major competitors, and paid associates profit-sharing of 19% of salary.
GEICO premiums grew from $2.9 billion in 1996 to $6.9 billion in 2002, Internet new business up 75%; a 1981-83 footnote shows why insurers need the strongest reinsurers.
In 1981-83 GEICO wrote $3.05 million of umbrella and product liability, reinsuring almost all of it, yet its losses from that venture now total $94.1 million.

stance.quote: So much for “cheap” reinsurance.

summary: Of GEICO's $94.1 million loss on that venture, $90.3 million is uncollectable receivables from reinsurers, including $19 million charged in 2002: cheap reinsurance proved costly.
Ajit Jain's reinsurance division built $13.4 billion of float since 1986 with 20 employees and earned a 2002 underwriting profit of $534 million after a $428 million retroactive-insurance charge.
Retroactive insurance assumes already-incurred losses for a large premium below expected payouts; Berkshire accepts the gap because payments are capped and it holds the money for years.

About 80% of Berkshire's $6.6 billion asbestos and environmental reserves are capped; the difference between premium and reserve on retroactive policies is a $3.4 billion deferred charge, amortized to income.

stance.quote: we love taking on short-term volatility that others wish to shed

summary: Amortization charges of $440 million in 2002 are intentional underwriting losses; Ajit's division carries risks far larger than any other insurer, and Berkshire prefers lumpy 15% to smooth 12%.

stance.quote: Collectively, these operations would make one of the finest insurance companies in the country.

summary: Smaller insurers' float grew 38% with a $32 million underwriting profit, 4.5% of premiums; California workers' compensation had terrible results from under-reserving and will stay small until fixed.
Purchase-accounting adjustments fell sharply in 2002 because GAAP stopped requiring goodwill amortization, which raises reported but not economic earnings.

stance.quote: Shoes are a tough business, but we have terrific managers

summary: Shoes earned $24 million in 2002, a $70 million swing from 2001, as Dexter was turned around and Justin raised margins while trimming invested capital.

stance.quote: In a so-so year for home-furnishing and jewelry retailers, our operations did well.

summary: Berkshire's eight retailers did well in a so-so year; NFM will open a 450,000 square foot Kansas City store in August that could be the second-largest furniture store by volume.

stance.quote: Bob Shaw and Julian Saul are terrific operators.

summary: Home and construction businesses earned $941 million pre-tax in 2002; Shaw rose from $292 million to $424 million through productivity and cost control despite carpet prices up only 1%.

stance.quote: FlightSafety training continues to be the gold standard for the industry, and we expect growth in the years to come.

summary: Flight services earnings rose only through a $60 million pre-tax gain on selling a 50% interest in FlightSafety Boeing; underlying training earnings dipped with business aviation.

stance.quote: we are the runaway leader of the four-company field

summary: NetJets held a 75% industry share in 2002, triple its three rivals combined by plane value, flying 132.7 million nautical miles to 130 countries.

stance.quote: Overall, the fractional-ownership industry lost significant sums last year, and that is almost certain to be the outcome in 2003 as well.

summary: NetJets revenue hit a record but it lost money again as European losses exceeded a small U.S. profit; the industry lost significantly and will in 2003, yet economics favor NetJets.

stance.quote: Many businesses could save millions of dollars annually by flying with us.

summary: Large companies could save over $10 million annually by using NetJets, and fractional ownership lets clients have several planes in the air and interchange among 12 other models.

General Electric is NetJets' largest customer; finance and financial products earned highly in 2002 from high-grade fixed-income activities that will probably continue briefly but are certain to shrink.

stance.quote: a highly satisfactory
On the minus side, the Finance line also includes the operations of General Re Securities

summary: Berkadia's Finova income is satisfactory but diminishing; General Re Securities lost $173 million pre-tax in 2002, partly a belated acknowledgment of faulty standard accounting; derivatives deserve closer examination.

stance.quote: We view them as time bombs, both for the parties that deal in them and the economic system.

summary: Buffett and Munger view derivatives and related trading as time bombs for parties and the economic system; they are contracts exchanging money later, based on reference items.
Derivatives contracts can run 20 years, depend on counterparty creditworthiness unless collateralized, and let parties book huge profits or losses in current earnings before any cash changes hands.
Derivatives contracts can cover anything, as Enron's newsprint and broadband contracts showed; Berkshire inherited General Re Securities, a derivatives dealer it judged dangerous.

stance.quote: Like Hell, both are easy to enter and almost impossible to exit.

summary: Berkshire is terminating General Re Securities, an unwanted derivatives dealer; exiting derivatives takes many years because long contracts stick.

stance.quote: the parties to derivatives also have enormous incentives to cheat in accounting for them

summary: Reinsurance and derivatives both leave residual liability and generate overstated earnings built on estimates; derivatives traders have strong incentives to cheat since pay depends on mark-to-market earnings.

stance.quote: mark-to-model degenerates into what I would call mark-to-myth

summary: Without real markets, derivatives are valued by models; long, multi-variable contracts let counterparties use fanciful assumptions and both show profits for years, so mark-to-model becomes mark-to-myth.
Auditors face a hard job valuing derivatives: General Re Securities, after ten months of winding down, still had 14,384 contracts outstanding.

stance.quote: some huge-scale frauds and near-frauds have been facilitated by derivatives trades

summary: The 14,384 contracts with 672 counterparties could be honestly valued very differently; derivatives enabled near-frauds in energy and utilities, where reported earnings vanished when receivables had to become cash.

stance.quote: the marking errors in the derivatives business have not been symmetrical

summary: Derivative marking errors favored bonus-seeking traders and CEOs; contracts requiring collateral on a credit downgrade can pile cash demands onto a troubled company.

stance.quote: It all becomes a spiral that can lead to a corporate meltdown.

summary: Downgrade-triggered collateral demands can create a liquidity crisis and spiral into meltdown; derivatives also create daisy-chain risk like reinsurers laying off business, building huge receivables from many counterparties.
Gen Re Securities still holds $6.5 billion of receivables after nearly a year of liquidation; apparent diversification fails in a crisis because counterparty problems correlate.
The Fed now insulates strong banks from weak ones, but no central bank stops dominoes in insurance or derivatives, so Berkshire minimizes links in reinsurance and exits derivatives.

stance.quote: Charlie and I believe, however, that the macro picture is dangerous and getting more so.

summary: Defenders say derivatives transfer risk to stronger hands and stabilize the economy, often true individually, and Berkshire sometimes uses large derivatives; Buffett and Munger find the macro picture dangerous.
Credit risk is concentrated in a few derivatives dealers who trade with each other and are owed huge sums by linked counterparties, so one event could trigger systemic problems.

In 1998 the leveraged, derivatives-heavy Long-Term Capital Management alarmed the Federal Reserve, which orchestrated a rescue; officials later said its trades could threaten American market stability.
The Fed acted fearing the LTCM domino would topple other institutions; LTCM used total-return swaps, giving 100% leverage with the counterparty bank supplying all the money.

stance.quote: Total-return swaps of this type make a joke of margin requirements.

summary: Total-return swaps mock margin requirements and derivatives curb regulators' ability to monitor leverage and risk; even long footnotes on banks' derivatives leave readers unable to gauge risk.

stance.quote: until some event makes their toxicity clear

summary: Derivatives will multiply until an event reveals their toxicity; electricity and gas businesses cut use after troubles, elsewhere the business expands unchecked and central banks cannot monitor it.

stance.quote: derivatives are financial weapons of mass destruction, carrying dangers that, while now latent, are potentially lethal

summary: Berkshire aims to be a fortress of financial strength and is wary of megacatastrophe risk; long-term derivatives and growing uncollateralized receivables are potentially lethal weapons of mass destruction.
