Table end: Washington Post, Wells Fargo and others; total common stocks at yearend 2002 were $9,164 million cost and $28,363 million market; Berkshire is doing little in equities.

stance.quote: Though these enterprises have good prospects, we don’t yet believe their shares are undervalued.

summary: Berkshire is comfortable with major holdings whose earnings rose as valuations fell, but is not adding because shares are not yet undervalued; stocks generally remain unattractive.

stance.quote: That dismal fact is testimony to the insanity of valuations reached during The Great Bubble.

summary: Few stocks interest Berkshire after bubble valuations; it needs a likely 10% pre-tax return before buying and accepts inactivity with short-term money earning under 1% after tax.

Berkshire's junk bond and loan commitments sextupled to $8.3 billion in 2002; both junk bonds and stocks need price-value calculations, but stocks are chosen for conservatively financed, strong businesses.

stance.quote: These businesses are usually overloaded with debt and often operate in industries characterized by low returns on capital.

summary: Berkshire's equity gains have exceeded losses about 100 to one over 38 years; junk issuers are marginal and debt-laden, so occasional large losses are expected though results are reasonable.

stance.quote: So far, however, we have done reasonably well in this field.

summary: Managers' ability and fidelity need monitoring; accountability and stewardship withered during the Great Bubble, as managers' behavioral norms fell while stock prices rose.

stance.quote: Too many of these people, however, have in recent years behaved badly at the office, fudging numbers and drawing obscene pay for mediocre business achievements.

summary: Too many otherwise decent CEOs fudged numbers and took obscene pay for mediocre results in the late 1990s; corporate boards in theory should have prevented the deterioration.
Per the 1993 letter, directors should act as single absentee owners and remove mediocre managers however likable; the 1993 discussion on directors' responsibilities is available on request.

stance.quote: over-reaching has become common but few hands have been slapped

summary: Directors must slap the hands of greedy managers who dip into shareholders' pockets, yet few have; directors failed because of boardroom atmosphere, not inadequate laws.

Social pressure keeps directors from questioning CEO replacement, CEO-backed acquisitions or megagrants of options recommended by paid consultants, which argues for outside directors meeting without the CEO.

stance.quote: I doubt, however, that most of the other new governance rules and recommendations will provide benefits commensurate with the monetary and other costs they impose.

summary: Buffett endorses outside directors meeting without the CEO but doubts most new governance rules pay off; directors must be independent-minded, business-savvy, interested and shareholder-oriented.

stance.quote: their contribution to shareholder well-being was minimal at best and, too often, negative

summary: Of about 250 directors Buffett has met across 19 boards, most were technically independent yet lacked business knowledge or shareholder focus to question foolish acquisitions or pay; collegiality trumped independence.
Federal law since 1940 has required 40-50% independent directors on investment-company boards, whose real duties are choosing the best investment manager and negotiating the lowest fee.

stance.quote: their record has been absolutely pathetic

summary: Independent fund directors should obtain the best manager at the lowest fee but their record is pathetic; each year Fund A's board selects manager A, Fund B's selects B.

stance.quote: in a zombie-like process that makes a mockery of stewardship

summary: Fund directors rarely consider other managers even after persistently substandard performance, yet look elsewhere with their own money; when a management company is sold they suddenly switch to the buyer.
When Manager B buys fund manager A, directors suddenly find B the best, though B was available cheaper earlier; B recoups its purchase cost through fees from A's shareholders.
A fund family offered Buffett's daughter a directorship worth about 50% of her income, expecting no independent view on advisors; she declined and the fund kept its managers.

stance.quote: Investment company directors have failed as well in negotiating management fees

summary: Fund directors have failed to negotiate management fees; with a share of any savings, fees would fall fast, but today reductions mean nothing to independent directors and everything to managers.
Choosing the right manager matters more than the fee, yet independent fund directors failed at both over six decades while earning six-figure fees; real reform needs action by big owners.

stance.quote: that’s the missing element in today’s corporate governance

summary: Because ownership is concentrated, twenty or fewer large institutions acting together could reform a company's governance by withholding votes from directors tolerating odious behavior, the only meaningful improvement.
Institutions have glass-house problems arguing for governance since they fear scrutiny of their own performance and fees; Bogle, Davis and Miller offer leadership that pension funds should support.

stance.quote: compensation committees too often have been tail-wagging puppy dogs meekly following recommendations by consultants

summary: CEO compensation is the acid test of reform: managers accept board diversity and SEC attestations but fight scrutiny of pay, and compensation committees meekly follow consultants and write boilerplate.

stance.quote: The upshot is that CEOs have often amassed riches while their shareholders have experienced financial disasters.

summary: Compensation committees must negotiate for owners, explain pay and performance measures and treat money as their own; in the 1990s CEOs amassed riches while shareholders suffered disasters.

stance.quote: It would be a travesty if the bloated pay of recent years became a baseline for future compensation.

summary: Pay should be high only for exceptional performance, otherwise directors should demand less; coming rules will oblige Berkshire to add directors meeting codified independence requirements.
Berkshire will select directors with large genuine ownership stakes bought, not granted; director pay of about $50,000 makes independence questionable when it is 20% of income.
A director earning trivial legal fees from Berkshire may be deemed non-independent, while directors reliant on fee income are unlikely to offend CEOs; regulators overlook that class.
Berkshire pays directors only a pittance and provides no directors' liability insurance, saving shareholders millions, so directors' behavior is driven by the effect on their family's net worth.

New directors will come from long-time shareholders with large Berkshire holdings, plus business savvy; Buffett family members stay on the board, unpaid, to preserve Berkshire's culture after Buffett.
Board changes will not alter how Berkshire is run; the board's most important job is selecting successors, and new directors must be devoted to its economic principles.

stance.quote: Reforms that ignore this reality and that instead focus on the structure and charter of the audit committee will accomplish little.
far too many managers have fudged their company’s numbers in recent years

summary: Only outside auditors can judge whether reported earnings are suspect; many managers fudged numbers while auditors stayed silent, so the audit committee must get auditors to divulge what they know.

stance.quote: They have instead generally viewed the CEO, rather than the shareholders or directors, as their client.

summary: Auditors treat the CEO, who pays their fees, as their client, and new rules will not change that; audit committees must put auditors on the spot with liability for silence.

Audit committees should ask auditors four recorded questions; the first asks whether the auditor, if solely responsible, would have prepared the financial statements differently, with both sides' arguments disclosed.

More audit committee questions: whether investors received essential information in plain English, whether internal audit matches what the auditor would do as CEO, and whether earnings were shifted between periods.
If audit committees ask these questions, their composition matters little; auditors put on the spot do their duty; questions should be asked at least a week before the earnings release.

stance.quote: Charlie and I believe that rule is a mistake and should be rescinded.

summary: Audit committees should ask the four questions a week before earnings so rushed releases do not force rubberstamping; the SEC's shortened reporting deadlines hurt information quality and should be rescinded.
Requiring auditors to affirmatively endorse management's actions makes them resist misdoings early, before specious figures are embedded in the books, out of fear of the plaintiffs' bar.

stance.quote: accounting standards and audit quality have eroded in recent years

summary: Arthur Andersen's elite standards group insisted in 1992 that option costs be expensed, but rainmaking partners reversed it, since clients wanted higher reported earnings.

stance.quote: It was not a sight for a civics class.

summary: After FASB voted 7-0 to expense options, auditing firms and CEOs lobbied the Senate, using corporate money for political contributions, to block it, because megagrants of options would shrink.

stance.quote: To its shame, the Senate voted 88-9 against expensing.

summary: The Senate voted 88-9 against expensing options and threatened FASB's existence; SEC chairman Levitt later called bowing to Congressional and corporate pressure his greatest regret.

stance.quote: The licentious behavior that followed quickly became an air pump for The Great Bubble.

summary: Corporate America won control of accounting; the resulting anything-goes earnings reports, blessed by big-name auditors, pumped up The Great Bubble, and FASB retreated to an honor system on option expensing.

stance.quote: The disheartening result: Of the 500 companies in the S&P, 498 adopted the method deemed less desirable

summary: Of the S&P 500 companies, 498 chose not to expense options, reporting higher earnings; CEOs' self-serving behavior has cost business leaders their credibility.

stance.quote: First, beware of companies displaying weak accounting.

summary: CEOs must regain trust through stewardship and treating owners as partners; investors should beware companies that do not expense options or use fanciful pension assumptions.

stance.quote: Trumpeting EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) is a particularly pernicious practice.

summary: Touting EBITDA implies depreciation is not a real expense, yet it is paid up front before an asset delivers any benefit; prepaid ten-year wages would show the absurdity.

stance.quote: unintelligible footnotes usually indicate untrustworthy management

summary: If a ten-year prepaid cost were treated as non-cash after year one, that would be absurd; unintelligible footnotes, as in Enron's transactions, usually signal untrustworthy management.

stance.quote: be suspicious of companies that trumpet earnings projections and growth expectations

summary: Be suspicious of companies trumpeting earnings projections: earnings do not advance smoothly, Berkshire cannot predict even next quarter, and CEOs who always hit targets may eventually make up numbers.
About 97.3% of eligible shares joined the 2002 designated-contributions program, totaling $16.5 million; cumulative giving over 22 years is $197 million, with subsidiaries giving separately.
Subsidiaries gave $24 million in 2002 including $4 million in kind; to join the 2003 program Class A shares must be registered in the owner's name by August 31, 2003.

Companies are pushed by history and shareholders into capital-allocation policies they would not choose; at Berkshire neither constrains decisions, so mistakes are unforced errors.
When valuations are similar Berkshire prefers businesses to stocks; it tilted to equities when stocks were cheaper, but large funds make undervalued stocks hard to find.

Berkshire will buy stocks if cheaper than businesses, load up on attractive bonds, and buy qualifying businesses; capital is underutilized now.
Future performance will fall far short of the past, though Buffett hopes for modestly above average results; introduces the Clayton Homes purchase.
Buffett lost on distressed Oakwood Homes junk debt, learning how bad manufactured-housing financing was, while seeing Clayton as the industry's class act.

stance.quote: I did not understand how atrocious consumer-financing practices had become throughout most of the manufactured housing industry.

summary: Manufactured housing gives good value, but distribution and financing practices were poor; Oakwood went bankrupt.

stance.quote: Much of its volume a few years back came from buyers who shouldn’t have bought, financed by lenders who shouldn’t have lent.

summary: Securitization worsened manufactured-housing lending, with many repossessions and low recoveries; Clayton behaved better than competitors.
Buffett offered for Clayton based on Jim Clayton's book, Kevin Clayton, public financials and Oakwood lessons; Clayton's board was receptive.
Clayton's board welcomed Berkshire because lenders had fled manufactured housing and securitizations had become costlier and more restrictive, hurting Clayton's earnings.

stance.quote: Today, the manufactured housing industry remains awash in problems.

summary: Manufactured housing still has high delinquencies, many repossessions and half the retailers; the model must stop retailers pocketing money on loans destined to default.
Under a model with real down payments and shorter loans the industry stays smaller; Clayton agreed to buy Oakwood's assets, so Berkshire's discounted Oakwood debt may return a small profit.
Introduces Berkshire's purchase of McLane, a grocery and nonfood distributor Wal-Mart wished to sell, brought by a Goldman Sachs banker.
McLane distributes groceries and nonfood goods with about $23 billion of sales at roughly 1% pre-tax margin, adding more to Berkshire's sales than income; CEO Grady Rosier is winning accounts.

stance.quote: For several years, I have given my vote to Wal-Mart in the balloting for Fortune Magazine’s “Most Admired” list.

summary: The McLane deal took one two-hour meeting, a handshake and 29 days with no due diligence; Buffett admires Wal-Mart and the banker who brought three Berkshire deals.
Buffett criticized the Bush tax proposals in a 2003 op-ed, and a Treasury official said he was safe retaining all his earnings.
Berkshire will send the Treasury $3.3 billion of tax on 2003 income, 2.5% of all U.S. corporate income tax, while being about 1% of corporate market value.
540 Berkshires paying $3.3 billion would cover all federal tax receipts of $1.782 trillion; Berkshire's 2002 federal return paid $1.75 billion and ran 8,905 pages.
Berkshire's huge tax return contrasts with Buffett's three-page first 1040 in 1944; he asks the Treasury official to credit Berkshire's contribution.
Corporate income tax was 7.4% of federal receipts in fiscal 2003, down from a 32% peak in 1952; corporate tax breaks were part of 2002-03 initiatives.

stance.quote: If class warfare is being waged in America, my class is clearly winning.

summary: Many large corporations pay far below the 35% statutory rate; Berkshire paid $132 million of federal tax in 1985, $286 million in 1995 and about $3.3 billion for 2003.

stance.quote: To date, the results aren’t encouraging.

summary: Buffett hopes Berkshire's taxes keep rising while the rest of corporate America pays up; CEO pay remains the test of governance reform, with GE's Immelt a rare good example.
CEO pay got out of hand because CEOs care far more about pay bargains than compensation committees do, especially when options carry no earnings charge.

stance.quote: Overreaching by CEOs greatly accelerated in the 1990s

summary: CEO overreaching accelerated in the 1990s, spread by compensation consultants; calls for independent directors neglect what motivates independence.
Statutorily independent mutual fund directors were examined on two tasks: obtaining an able and honest manager and compensating the manager fairly.

stance.quote: Year after year, at literally thousands of funds, directors had routinely rehired the incumbent management company, however pathetic its performance had been.

summary: Fund directors routinely rehired incumbent managers and approved excessive fees, even switching to the buyer when a management company was sold at a huge price.
Fund directors are not bad people but boardroom atmosphere sedates them; after an industry head wished they had done something wrong, fund-management abuses surfaced.

stance.quote: they trampled on the interests of fund shareholders in an appalling manner.

summary: Fund-management companies with enviable margins and returns on tangible equity hurt fund owners to boost their own fees.
Directors of the looted funds have not fired the offending managers, and one wrongdoing manager offered itself for sale, collecting a payoff for delivering the funds.
A winning bidder spared the payoff could manage the funds for lower fees; a truly independent director would obtain the new manager this way.
Rules treat directors earning all income from director fees as independent but not Berkshire director Ron Olson, whose legal fees are about 3% of his income.
Directors getting 20-50% of income from fees lose independence, as at mutual funds; Buffett suggests fund directors affirm they compared managers and negotiated fees.
Fund directors paid over $100,000 should declare the two points; many funds are well run and a director would gladly make the declarations.

stance.quote: those index funds that are very low-cost (such as Vanguard’s) are investor-friendly by definition and are the best selection for most of those who wish to own equities.

summary: Very low-cost index funds such as Vanguard's are the best choice for most equity owners; Buffett blames industry insiders who knew of the wrongdoing until Spitzer acted.
Spitzer's probe started the fund-industry housecleaning; fund directors must decide whether they work for owners or managers; true independence in a director is rare and valuable.
Berkshire's eleven directors each hold over $4 million of stock with family, bought in the market, never granted options or restricted shares.
Berkshire director fees are nominal, so directors share exactly the same upside as any shareholder.
Berkshire carries no directors and officers liability insurance, so directors lose big if shareholders do; Buffett calls this owner-capitalism and says directors also need business savvy.
Directors need business savvy, the rarest quality, alongside shareholder orientation and genuine interest; people lacking it do not belong on corporate boards.
Berkshire invited shareholder self-nominations for its board and received over twenty applications from owner-oriented holders worth over $1 million.
Four shareholders not self-nominated joined the board; the directors' primary job is to select Buffett's successor.
The board mainly discusses four internal successor candidates, who must keep the culture, allocate capital and retain managers; Buffett has over 99% of his net worth in Berkshire.
Buffett keeps over 99% of his net worth in Berkshire; consolidated statements obscure businesses with different economics, so results will be shown for four major categories.
Berkshire will give sector financials with commentary and explain its limited use of debt, but not data irrelevant to intrinsic value; view Berkshire as an unfolding movie.
Insurance float is money held that belongs to others, arising from upfront premiums and delayed loss settlement such as asbestos.
Float is wonderful if cheap; the cost depends on underwriting results; Berkshire has made an underwriting profit in 18 of 37 years though five years cost over 10%.

Table: yearend float by segment (GEICO, General Re, other reinsurance, primary) for selected years 1967-2003, reaching $44.2 billion; 2003 float came at no cost with a $1.7 billion underwriting profit.
Insurance has no proprietary product or moat, so managerial brains, discipline and integrity decide results; General Re was a problem child after its 1998 acquisition.

stance.quote: That’s behind us: Gen Re is fixed.

summary: Gen Re is fixed under CEO Joe Brandon and Tad Montross, with discipline restored in underwriting and reserving.
Gen Re and National Indemnity are the only AAA-rated major reinsurers after rivals' downgrades; Gen Re retains the risks it writes, though reinsurance still delivers setbacks.
Berkshire retains virtually all the reinsurance risk it assumes, an advantage in a mega-catastrophe; Ajit Jain runs a large reinsurance operation with 23 staff.
Ajit Jain assumes catastrophe risks no other reinsurer would, so results are lumpy; Berkshire wrote a $1 billion PepsiCo prize policy.

stance.quote: GEICO was a fine insurance company when Tony Nicely took over as CEO in 1992. Now it is a great one.

summary: PepsiCo prize policy exposure was $250 million present value; under Tony Nicely GEICO's premiums rose from $2.2 billion to $8.1 billion and auto share to 5.0%.
GEICO's inquiries and closure rates rose in 2003; preferred policies grew 8.2% and standard and non-standard policies 21.4%.
GEICO announced a customer service center in Buffalo as part of expansion needing more employees and facilities.
GEICO's Buffalo expansion will bring 2,500 jobs; Berkshire's smaller insurers raised float 41% with excellent underwriting profit; long-tail insurers can report almost any earnings.

stance.quote: Too often the industry has reported wildly inaccurate figures by misstating liabilities.

summary: Long-tail insurers have often misstated liabilities and auditors and actuaries failed to stop it; Buffett missed Gen Re's underreserving, which also caused premature tax payments.
Buffett believes current Gen Re reserving is adequate; start of table of 2003 versus 2002 pre-tax underwriting results by segment (Gen Re, Ajit's business, GEICO).
Total pre-tax underwriting gain of $1,718 million in 2003 versus a $398 million loss in 2002; retroactive contracts explained; introduces the 80.5% interest in MidAmerican.
Berkshire owns 80.5% of MidAmerican, with U.K. electricity distributors (3.7 million customers), Iowa utility (689,000 customers) and Kern River and Northern Natural pipelines (7.8% of U.S. gas).
Under PUHCA Berkshire's voting interest in MidAmerican is limited to 9.9%, so it is carried as a one-line entry in the balance sheet and income account.
If PUHCA or accounting rules change, MidAmerican's substantial debt, not a Berkshire obligation, would be consolidated; $1.578 billion of junior debt is owed to Berkshire at 11%.
Berkshire's 11% junior debt financed MidAmerican purchases without diluting partners; HomeServices, the second-largest U.S. broker, took part in $48.6 billion of transactions.
HomeServices has 16 brokerage firms and 16,343 brokers and should grow through acquisitions; after 1990 denationalization the U.K. utilities cut staff from 6,800 to 2,539 at similar customer counts.
U.K. utility efficiency gains show profit-motivated managers find savings government never will, though prices stay regulated; start of MidAmerican earnings table.

Table: MidAmerican interest to Berkshire, tax, net earnings $416 million, earnings applicable to Berkshire, and debt owed to others and to Berkshire.
Buffett's AAA fixed-income strategies, financed almost entirely with borrowing, were profitable but are ending; capital gains realized last year will not recur.
Fewer opportunities will cut fixed-income earnings; Gen Re Securities, the derivatives dealer inherited with General Re, had 23,218 tickets with 884 counterparties when liquidation began.
Winding down Gen Re Securities cost pre-tax losses of $173 million in 2002 and $99 million in 2003 despite marking to market, in a benign market.

stance.quote: you can’t possibly learn from reading the disclosure documents of a derivatives-intensive company what risks lurk in its positions.

summary: Derivatives disclosures reveal little about risk, as shown by Gen Re's experience and Freddie Mac's huge accounting problems revealed last year.
Buffett admits a prompt Gen Re Securities shutdown would have saved about $100 million pre-tax; its profits looked illusory and its risks could drain Berkshire's capital.
A derivatives problem would commandeer capital when Berkshire could deploy it best, as in 1974 when an insurance fraud forced extra cash and cost cheap stock purchases.
Buffett dithered on closing Gen Re Securities, so shareholders paid more to exit; life and annuity business shown in finance because it arbitrages money, including long structured settlements.
Annuity earnings were lifted by accelerated principal payments that have ended, so earnings will drop; Berkshire has a $604 million limited-partner investment in Value Capital.
New rules after Enron may force consolidation of Value Capital's over $20 billion of liabilities, which Buffett finds inappropriate; Berkadia with Leucadia winds down Finova.
Leucadia's fast Finova liquidation extinguished Berkshire's $5.6 billion guarantee, cutting future income; XTRA and CORT leasing earnings were poor for two years.
XTRA and CORT should modestly improve; Clayton now retains its loans instead of securitizing, giving up GAAP front-ended income, believing holding consumer paper pays better.
Clayton's retained loan book is financed almost entirely with debt like a bank, with Berkshire borrowing and re-lending to Clayton at cost plus one percentage point.
Berkshire borrowed and re-lent $2 billion to Clayton in 2003 for portfolio purchases; each subsidiary pays for funds under an 'every tub on its own bottom' philosophy.
Subsidiaries should not be subsidized by the parent; Berkshire's cash is for acquisitions or securities, and Clayton's loan portfolio should reach at least $5 billion.

Shaw Industries had a record year, likely another in 2004, adding Dixie carpet operations to approach $5 billion of sales; Fruit of the Loom is the largest apparel unit.
Fruit of the Loom took 42.3% of mass-market men's and boys' underwear; furniture earned $106 million, jewelers $59 million and See's $59 million; new Willey and NFM stores did well.
NFM's new Kansas City store overflowed its 25-acre parking lot, proving Mrs. B's maxim that the lowest price draws customers anywhere.
FlightSafety's normal operating earnings fell from $183 million to $150 million, with a $37 million simulator obsolescence loss in 2003.
Corporate aviation weakness hurt FlightSafety, whose simulators cost $1.2 billion; NetJets lost $41 million pre-tax in 2003 after a $32 million aircraft inventory loss and European losses.
NetJets and its three competitors account for 70% of fractional-ownership sales and NetJets' lead is growing; the Mayo Clinic response program is a free benefit.
The $32 million NetJets inventory write-down came from falling used-aircraft prices; staying in Europe, despite losses, avoids second-tier status.

stance.quote: Overwhelmingly, our owners love the NetJets experience.

summary: NetJets Europe revenues grew 88%, 61% and 77% in 2001-03 but losses continue; Buffett expects the European loss to shrink in 2004 and be offset by U.S. profits.

stance.quote: NetJets will become a very big business over time and will be one in which we are preeminent in both customer satisfaction and profits.

summary: NetJets will become a very big business, preeminent in customer satisfaction and profits.

Table: yearend 2003 common-stock holdings with cost and market; Buffett is neither enthusiastic nor negative about the portfolio at current prices.

stance.quote: The pendulum swung quickly though, and this sector now looks decidedly unattractive to us.

summary: Holdings are fully priced after excellent businesses' gains; Buffett's big mistake was not selling several during the bubble; about $8 billion of junk bonds bought in 2002 now look unattractive.
Realized gains are meaningless for analysis because Berkshire holds huge unrealized gains; table of 2003 gains by category begins with common stocks at $448 million.
Table end: 2003 pre-tax gains of $4,129 million; common stock profits came from the edges of the portfolio, not major holdings.

stance.quote: I should note that the cemetery for seers has a huge section set aside for macro forecasters.

summary: Gains came from selling volatile long-term government strips and junk bond calls; Berkshire entered currencies as Buffett grew bearish on the dollar, having made few macro forecasts.
The U.S. trade deficit force-feeds claims on America to foreigners, the dollar began sliding late in 2002, and the flood of dollars could have troublesome consequences.
Buffett holds foreign-exchange contracts as a partial offset to Berkshire's dollar cash; contract value changes run through capital gains each quarter.
Open foreign exchange contracts were about $12 billion across five currencies, plus about $1 billion of euro junk bonds; the default position is Treasuries, never reaching for yield.
Berkshire never reaches for yield by lowering credit standards or extending maturities; Buffett recommends books by Mahar, McLean and Elkind, and Rubin.
Jason Zweig revised The Intelligent Investor; Berkshire's shareholder-designated gifts program disbursed $197 million from 1981 to 2002 and was terminated in 2003.
Berkshire ended its shareholder-designated gifts program in 2003 because of the abortion controversy, which had drawn boycotts of subsidiaries' products.
Boycotts hurt independent Pampered Chef associates, outweighing the program's modest tax efficiency and its fit with the Owner's Manual partnership principle.
Berkshire now makes no contributions at the parent level; subsidiaries keep their prior philanthropic policies, with former owners' personal gifts now funded personally.

Net worth gained $8.3 billion in 2004, raising per-share book value 10.5%; book value grew from $19 to $55,824 over 40 years, 21.9% compounded.
Intrinsic value, not book value, counts; Berkshire became worth far more than book, so 40-year intrinsic value gain somewhat exceeds the 21.9% book gain.
Book value slightly understates intrinsic value growth and matters less for single years against the S&P; equities fell from 114% of net worth in the 1980s to under 50%.
Because stocks are a smaller share of net worth, Berkshire will underperform in years stocks rise sharply and outperform when they fall.
Berkshire's long-term record against the S&P is what counts, since owners can buy the S&P cheaply through an index fund.
Book value gained 10.5% in 2004 versus the S&P's 10.9%; operating CEOs carried their load and send excess cash to Omaha for Buffett to deploy.
Buffett failed to make multi-billion acquisitions in 2004 and found few attractive securities, leaving Berkshire with $43 billion of cash equivalents.
S&P returns averaged 11.2% annually over the 35 years since the 1960s, but only one year before 2004 came near that figure, so 2004's normal return was unusual.

stance.quote: An index fund that they never touched would have done the job.

summary: American business delivered terrific results over 35 years, so an untouched index fund would have earned juicy returns, yet many investors fared mediocre to disastrous.
Investors fail through high costs, tip-and-fad decisions and start-stop timing; excitement and expenses are their enemies, and if timing, be fearful when others are greedy.
Consolidated statements hide very different business economics, so Berkshire will present sector balance sheet and earnings figures with commentary.
Sector figures will show the limited circumstances in which Berkshire uses debt but no data irrelevant to intrinsic value; introduces regulated utility businesses.
Berkshire owns 80.5% of MidAmerican: U.K. electric distributors with 3.7 million customers, an Iowa utility with 698,000 customers, and pipelines carrying 7.9% of U.S. gas.
Three partners own the other 19.5% of MidAmerican; PUHCA limits Berkshire's voting interest to 9.9%, with voting control with Walter Scott.
Berkshire books MidAmerican in one-line entries; if PUHCA is repealed or accounting changes, its substantial debt, not a Berkshire obligation, would be consolidated.
MidAmerican owes Berkshire $1.478 billion of junior debt at 11%, funding acquisitions without diluting partners; it repaid $100 million in 2004.
MidAmerican owns HomeServices, the second-largest U.S. real estate broker, which is cyclical but viewed enthusiastically under Ron Peltier.
HomeServices took part in $59.8 billion of transactions in 2004, up $11.2 billion, with six acquisitions; it has 17 brokerage firms and over 18,000 brokers and should keep growing.
MidAmerican wrote off a major zinc recovery project from its California geothermal brine, begun in 1998 and operational in 2002, after unsolvable problems.
The zinc failure shows the guideline to stay with simple propositions: ten independent 90% variables give only a 35% chance of success.
MidAmerican's 2004 other earnings include a $72.2 million profit from selling an Enron receivable acquired with Northern Natural; start of earnings table.

Property-casualty insurance, started with National Indemnity in 1967, has been Berkshire's core business, providing funds used to acquire securities and businesses.
Float is money held that belongs to others; the $20 million acquired with National Indemnity in 1967 has grown to $46.1 billion.

stance.quote: In aggregate, the property-casualty industry almost invariably operates at an underwriting loss.

summary: Float is wonderful if cheap; Berkshire made an underwriting profit in about half of 38 years, while the industry almost always runs underwriting losses.

stance.quote: Insurers have generally earned poor returns for a simple reason: They sell a commodity-like product.

summary: Insurers earn poor returns because they sell a commodity-like product with standard policies and price-driven buyers, so competition is fierce.
Berkshire's insurance operations try to overcome the industry's dismal economics and build enduring competitive advantage, starting with National Indemnity's strategy.

stance.quote: for almost all of the past 38 years, NICO has been a star performer.

summary: National Indemnity had no apparent advantages when bought, yet has been a star performer for 38 years; without it Berkshire would be worth far less.
NICO priced to make a profit rather than match competitors, so revenue slid from 1986 through 1999 though premiums were available; the mindset is hard for insurers to copy.
Businesses and insurers resist falling volume; optimistic reserving overstates earnings and nearly destroyed GEICO in the early 1970s; start of the NICO disciplined-underwriter table.

Insurance profitability of a year is learned slowly because incurred-but-not-reported claims must be estimated and claims can take decades to settle.
The table's margins are estimates at yearend 2004; years through 1999 are probably close to correct, while 2003 and 2004 may change significantly.
Fear of layoffs makes employees rationalize inadequate pricing during a shrinking business, hoping a recovery is around the corner.
NICO promises no layoffs from declining volume, since it can live with excess overhead but not underpriced business and weak underwriting discipline.
A no-layoff policy requires care not to overstaff; Tom Murphy taught that a $20,000 hire is really a $3 million lifetime decision.
An added employee is unlikely to be dismissed unless the company falls on hard times, however marginal the contribution.
Operating as NICO does takes fortitude embedded in culture, living with dwindling volume from 1986 to 1999 while rivals boast of growth; four CEOs since 1940 never bent.
Don Wurster, running NICO since 1989, has built $950 million of float likely to prove negative-cost and will accept volume declines as insurance prices fall.
GEICO is the low-cost operator among broad-scale auto insurers; insurance was once a bureau-rate cartel that rewarded agents with high commissions and consumers with high prices.
State Farm, formed in 1922 with captive agents, cut acquisition costs and captured about 25% of personal lines; Allstate followed in 1931 with a similar system.
Leo Goodwin started GEICO in 1936 with $200,000, eliminating agents to sell directly to auto owners, a powerful low-cost insight.
GEICO originally mailed to government employees, then shifted marketing to phone inquiries from advertising, and the Internet is now coming on strong.
GEICO grew from 1936 to a 4% share by 1975, but underreserving after 1970 caused inadequate pricing and brought it to the brink of failure by 1976.
Jack Byrne saved GEICO with price increases, but share fell to 1.8% by 1980 and unwise diversification kept it at 1.9% in 1993, until Tony Nicely took charge.

stance.quote: Tony has matched growth with profitability.

summary: GEICO should reach a 6% share in 2005; in 2004 customers saved about $1 billion, associates got a $191 million bonus and Berkshire earned excellent returns.
GEICO left New Jersey in 1976 when rates were refused; a 2003 law curbing fraud and allowing fair rates opened the way to re-entry.
GEICO re-entered New Jersey with the commissioner's cooperation and now serves 140,000 policyholders, about 4% of the market, with a higher closure rate than nationally.

stance.quote: we believe GEICO offers the lowest price more often than any other national company that serves all segments of the public.

summary: GEICO offers the lowest price more often than other national insurers, though not for everyone, and gives Berkshire shareholders an 8% discount in most states.
Reinsurance should not be a commodity product because a policy is a promise and promises vary greatly in quality.
At the primary level an insurer's promise matters little for the 60% of industry volume protected by state guaranty assessments, which make prudent insurers subsidize reckless ones.
Policies of failed insurers Reliance and Home proved worthless; reinsurer insolvency risk is worse, and GEICO lost tens of millions on careless reinsurer choices in the early 1980s.
A mega-catastrophe could sink some reinsurers; World Trade Center cost insurers about $35 billion, Andrew $15.5 billion, and four 2004 Florida hurricanes about $25 billion.
Hurricanes Charley and Ivan could have caused at least three times the damage had they landed slightly differently.
Many insurers will not plan for a $100 billion industry loss, but Berkshire is prepared: its share would be 3-5% and covered by other earnings.
The 2004 hurricanes cost Berkshire $1.25 billion yet reinsurance did well; Joe Brandon restored Gen Re's underwriting discipline and Ajit Jain keeps writing huge risks others refuse.
Table: 2004 underwriting profit of $1,551 million and yearend float of $46,094 million by segment: General Re, B-H Reinsurance, GEICO and other primary.
Float rose $1.9 billion in 2004 and Berkshire was paid over $1.5 billion to hold about $45.2 billion; 2005 pricing is less attractive but no-cost float is still possible.
Berkadia, Value Capital and trading matter less now; leasing rebounded, CORT earnings are inadequate but rising and XTRA sold container businesses to focus on trailer leasing.

stance.quote: Like Hell, derivative trading is easy to enter but difficult to leave.

summary: Gen Re Securities still had 2,890 derivative contracts at yearend, down from 23,218, showing derivatives are easy to enter and hard to leave.

stance.quote: It’s small wonder that phantom profits are often recorded.

summary: Derivative marks are fuzzy when settlement is decades away and they drive bonuses, so phantom profits are often recorded.
Rapid growth can mask problems in financial institutions and a derivatives operation is tested in a no-growth mode; Clayton benefits from its association with Berkshire.

stance.quote: continues to reside in the intensive care unit of Corporate America

summary: Manufactured home sales of under 135,000 were the lowest since 1962 and about 40% of 1995-99 levels; lenders fled, and Berkshire funds Clayton.
Berkshire's borrowing re-lent to Clayton at a one-point markup rose from $2 billion to $7.35 billion by January 2005, including a bank portfolio Clayton bought December 30, 2004.
Clayton's receivables should hover near $9 billion with steady earnings instead of front-ended securitization income; the securitization market has dried up.
Clayton completed buying Oakwood Homes, becoming the largest manufactured-home producer and retailer, with 11,837 employees versus 7,136 at purchase; start of the finance earnings table.

stance.quote: The company is a powerhouse and has a bright future.

summary: Shaw absorbed over $300 million of fiber cost increases, with price rises lagging and margins narrowing, yet earned 25.6% on tangible equity in 2004.
Fruit of the Loom raised unit sales 14%, women's intimate apparel up 31%; Garan, Ben Bridge and R. C. Willey had excellent years.
Ben Bridge same-store sales grew 11.4% in 2004, the best among public jewelers, with a wider margin and an 8.8% average gain over the past decade.
Ben Bridge expanded by good locations and knowledgeable staff, entering Minneapolis-St. Paul; 41.9% of R.C. Willey's 2004 sales came from out-of-state stores opened since 1999.
Buffett thought R.C. Willey's out-of-state expansion and Sunday closing were mistakes, but the first Las Vegas store opened in 2001 became its number one unit.
A second Las Vegas Willey store, which Buffett expected to cannibalize, now does 26% more volume than any other chain store; Reno is next.

FlightSafety's profits rose as corporate aviation rebounded; 283 simulators costing $1.2 billion need $3.50 of capital per $1 of revenue, so utilization matters; return on tangible equity rose to 15.1%.
FlightSafety's founder Al Ueltschi, who started it in 1951 with $10,000, handed the CEO job to veteran Bruce Whitman, who shares his insistence on rigorous pilot training.
NetJets is FlightSafety's top customer, its 2,100 pilots training 18 days a year on one aircraft type each; Buffett chose NetJets for its safety standards and CEO Rich Santulli.
NetJets again gained about 70% of new business among the four dominant fractional-ownership firms, helped by Marquis Jet's 25-hour card.
NetJets' U.S. contracts rose from 3,877 to 4,967 in 2004 and European contracts from 364 to 693; U.S. earnings were offset by European losses, which will continue in 2005.
Europe has been costlier than expected but is essential for NetJets, with U.S. owners' European flights up 22%; introduces the table of common stock investments over $600 million.

Valuation gains on the big holdings slightly exceeded earnings growth as P/E ratios rose; during the Great Bubble prices outran business results, afterwards the reverse.
Buffett admits he merely clucked about nose-bleed valuations during the Bubble rather than acting, underestimating the overvaluation, and big positions make nimble selling hard.
Berkshire dislikes holding $43 billion of low-yielding cash and wants to buy fractional interests or whole businesses, but only at prices offering a reasonable return.
Realized gains are meaningless for analysis given huge unrealized gains, and GAAP marking of foreign exchange contracts sends unrealized gains through earnings.

stance.quote: Our economy is far and away the strongest in the world and will continue to be.

summary: Buffett's currency stance does not reflect doubts about America, whose economy is the world's strongest and will remain so.

stance.quote: our country’s trade practices are weighing down the dollar.

summary: Trade practices weigh on the dollar, likely to keep falling and perhaps become disorderly; a study of deficits was ignored while the deficit grew from $263 billion to $618 billion.
The trade deficit rose from $263 billion in 1999 to $618 billion in 2004 while a congressional study of its consequences gathered dust.
True trade of $1.15 trillion benefits all sides, but the U.S. also bought an extra $618 billion of goods and services from abroad without reciprocation.
The deficit transfers American wealth abroad at $1.8 billion daily, up 20% in a year, so foreigners own a net $3 trillion of the U.S., negligible a decade ago.
The current account deficit and the budget deficit are not twins: budget deficits leave all output owned by Americans, unlike trade deficits.
Budget deficits only redistribute national output among Americans through taxes, benefits or internal debt, with no slice sent abroad.
Persistent current account deficits cut Americans' ownership of what they produce, like a family overspending and working more for its finance company.
At current deficits foreigners would own about $11 trillion of the U.S. in a decade, requiring about 3% of an $18 trillion GDP as annual tribute at 5% returns.
Unlike budget deficits, the sons would truly pay for the sins of their fathers through output sent abroad.

stance.quote: But that’s precisely where our trade policies, supported by Republicans and Democrats alike, are taking us.

summary: The annual royalty to foreign owners would cause political unrest; Buffett says trade policies are taking America toward a Sharecropper's Society.
Officials, including the Fed's 2004 minutes, say current-account deficits cannot persist, yet offer no substantive suggestions to tame the imbalance.
A gently declining dollar has not fixed the deficit; structural problems will keep it huge unless trade policy changes or the dollar falls enough to unsettle markets.
Adam Smith defended trade of product for product, not the wealth-for-product exchange of $.6 trillion annually, like a family selling parts of its farm to overconsume.
A $.6 trillion U.S. surplus would be condemned as mercantilism; in effect the world practices it on the U.S., which uses a home-currency credit card beyond any other country's limit.
Foreign investors view the U.S. as spending junkies but know it is a rich one, so they remain sanguine.
The trade problem will not be tolerated forever and is unlikely to lift the dollar; a fix could cost Berkshire currency losses, yet it favors a strong dollar.

stance.quote: macro-economics is a tough game in which few people, Charlie and I included, have demonstrated skill.

summary: Macro-economics is a tough game and Berkshire's currency judgments may prove wrong and publicly so, whereas staying all in dollars would hide any mistake.
Citing Keynes, Buffett accepts reputational risk from the foreign-exchange commitment because he manages Berkshire as if he owned all of it, which would not mean a dollar-only policy.
Tennessee finance students visiting Omaha spotted Clayton Homes, which Berkshire bought for $1.7 billion.
Buffett tells visiting students how Tennessee students found Clayton Homes, hoping new scouts bring deals, though none have so far.
Under accounting rules Berkshire's purchases of life insurance policies, whose premiums it pays until collecting face value at death, mildly distort its statements.
Berkshire pays well above cash surrender value for policies from holders who would otherwise surrender them, often a large multiple when the holder borrowed against the value.
Accounting forces an immediate realized capital loss for the price paid above cash surrender value, plus yearly charges, which Buffett says are not economic losses.
Berkshire recorded $207 million of net losses in 2004 from buying and maintaining life policies, charged against realized gains; later proceeds above surrender value will be gains.
Buffett faults himself for not adopting regular director meetings without the CEO earlier; having sat on 19 boards he sees no downside and many benefits.
Berkshire's whistleblower line lets employees of its 180,000-person decentralized group report problems to Buffett and the audit committee, and would have added value if started decades earlier.
Berkshire would be more valuable today had Buffett installed a whistleblower line decades ago, since issues raised concern personnel and business practices audits miss.

stance.quote: So far, however, the moves made by institutions have been less than awe-inspiring.

summary: Institutional owners should lead on three questions: the right CEO, overreaching pay, and whether acquisitions create per-share value, but they focus on minutiae.

stance.quote: Directors, moreover, sometimes lack the knowledge or gumption to overrule the CEO.

summary: Large owners must judge CEO and board questions themselves; checklist voting led institutions to oppose Buffett as a Coca-Cola director.
Institutions that sought to remove Buffett from Coca-Cola's audit committee failed and he was re-elected, since directors must serve on some committee.
Institutions questioned Buffett's independence because McLane and Dairy Queen buy Coke products, though his $8 billion Coke stake means his interests lie with Coke's owners.
Citing Matthew 6:21, Buffett argues $8 billion of Coke stock is the treasure that dwarfs profits from Berkshire's routine Coke transactions, ensuring independence.
Berkshire's board meets the biblical standard: directors' families own at least $4 million of stock bought without options, fees are tiny, and there is no liability insurance.

stance.quote: the least independent directors are likely to be those who receive an important fraction of their annual income from the fees they receive for board service

summary: Directors relying on board fees for much of their income are least independent, yet are most often classed as independent.
In a non-Berkshire example, management, bankers and some directors backed a premium acquisition proposal, but fee-dependent directors blocked it.
Directors paid about $100,000 annually scuttled a multi-billion offer so shareholders never saw it, though they owned little stock and had declined to buy shares far below the offer.

stance.quote: At the same meeting at which the deal was rejected, the board voted itself a significant increase in directors’ fees.

summary: Fees of $100,000 meet the Matthew 6:21 'treasure' test; the deal would have ended them, and the board raised directors' fees at the meeting rejecting it.

stance.quote: the most important accounting mechanism still available to CEOs who wish to overstate earnings: the non-expensing of stock options.

summary: Not expensing stock options is the main tool for CEOs to overstate earnings, perpetuated by Congress against auditors, FASB and investment professionals.
A House bill passed 312-111 would have blocked option expensing, but the Senate refused and SEC Chairman Donaldson held firm against pressure from CEOs, as in 1993.
No one proposes restricting options; Buffett's successor may be paid via well-structured options, and recording their cost should not reduce use if the company gets value.
Some CEOs fight option expensing since it would lower their pay and stock price, using shareholder funds; expensing becomes mandatory June 15, so expect intensified efforts to stall it.

2005 net worth rose $5.6 billion, 6.4% per share; book value grew 21.5% annually over 41 years; Katrina cost $2.5 billion, Rita and Wilma $.9 billion.

stance.quote: Credit GEICO – and its brilliant CEO, Tony Nicely – for our stellar insurance results in a disasterridden year.

summary: GEICO raised productivity 32% in two years, cut employment 4% while policy count grew 26%, gained market share, earned good profits and strengthened its brand.
The report aims to help owners estimate Berkshire's intrinsic value, which is imprecise but easier to calculate for Berkshire given stable earnings, liquidity and minimal debt.
With 68 unrelated businesses plus large investments, consolidated statements alone no longer let owners estimate intrinsic value as they could in 1965 with one textile operation.
Businesses are clustered into four groups; Berkshire's value may exceed or fall short of the parts depending on whether holding-company ownership improves capital allocation.
Whether Berkshire ownership adds value beyond holding the 68 businesses directly is a question owners must answer for themselves.
Introduces per-share investments including cash, excluding the finance operation's investments because they are offset by borrowings, as one measure of Berkshire's progress.

Investment growth and operating earnings growth rates have shifted in the last decade because of Berkshire's growing emphasis on acquisitions; the aim is to raise both.

stance.quote: When a management proudly acquires another company for stock, the shareholders of the acquirer are concurrently selling part of their interest in everything they own.

summary: Existing businesses give only modest growth so major acquisitions are needed; five 2005 purchases involved no Berkshire shares, since stock deals cost acquirer shareholders.

stance.quote: MedPro nevertheless should do well.

summary: Bought MedPro, a malpractice insurer, on June 30; a hard line to underwrite, but Berkshire's discipline and financial strength should help it.
Forest River, an RV maker with $1.6 billion of sales, was bought after a two-page fax matched Berkshire's criteria; the deal was struck within a week.
Forest River has 60 plants and 5,400 employees and has consistently gained RV share; owner-manager Pete Liegl will run it without Buffett's interference.
Business Wire's president wrote to Buffett after a Wall Street Journal article on Berkshire's unusual acquisition practices, offering her company as a fit.
Business Wire's president described a tight-ship company that spends big only on technology advantage, which convinced Buffett it fit Berkshire.
Berkshire agreed to buy Business Wire, which serves 25,000 clients in 150 countries, and in December agreed to buy 81% of Applied Underwriters, payroll and workers' comp for small businesses.
Applied Underwriters grew from 12 employees in 1998 by acquiring an Omaha operation; 400 of its 479 employees are now in Omaha.
Applied signed a large reinsurance contract with National Indemnity, which led to Berkshire buying 81% while the two founders keep 19%.

stance.quote: You can’t expect to earn outsized profits in regulated utilities, but the industry offers owners the opportunity to deploy large sums at fair returns

summary: MidAmerican agreed to buy PacifiCorp, funded by $3.4 billion of Berkshire stock and $1.7 billion of debt; regulated utilities offer fair returns on large sums, and Berkshire wants more.
Shaw spent about $550 million on two bolt-on purchases; Berkshire buys to keep, has no exit strategy, and seeks businesses meeting six criteria at reasonable prices.
Float is money held temporarily because premiums are paid upfront and claims settle slowly; Berkshire's float grew from $20 million in 1967 to $49 billion.

stance.quote: In aggregate, the property-casualty industry almost invariably operates at an underwriting loss.

summary: Float's cost equals underwriting results; Berkshire profited in about half its 39 insurance years, making float better than free, while the industry usually loses.
Despite $3.4 billion of hurricane losses, 2005 float was costless thanks to other units, especially GEICO, whose policies grew 12.1% and share rose from 5.6% to 6.1%.
GEICO's brand strength grew; its advertising spending rose from $31 million when Berkshire took control in 1996 to $502 million in 2005.
GEICO's advertising works because more people can save with it than with any other national carrier; its conversion rate of quotes into sales was the highest ever.
GEICO prices are more attractive relative to competitors than ever; shareholders who ask for a quote often qualify for a discount.

stance.quote: I called GEICO “The Security I Like Best.”

summary: GEICO's low costs allow low prices and steady profitable gains; its New Jersey retention is the highest of any state and it may become third largest there by 2007.
General Re and National Indemnity, Berkshire's major reinsurance units, performed well in 2005 despite extraordinary industry hurricane losses.
About 59 Category 3 or stronger hurricanes hit the Southeast in 100 years before 2004, but seven came in 2004-05, including Katrina; whether storm frequency changed is an open question.
Berkshire's reinsurers do not know whether climate or other changes could produce disasters dwarfing Katrina, so like Pascal they must act cautiously.
Berkshire will write mega-cat policies only at far higher prices and with limited aggregate exposure, but remains willing to be the world's largest writer if prices are right.
Smaller insurers including MedPro had outstanding 2005 results, understated because MedPro's loss reserves were raised about $125 million right after the purchase.

stance.quote: Too often, however, insurers react to looming loss problems with optimism.

summary: Malpractice is a long-tail line whose reserves are uncertain; insurance surprises are asymmetrical, about one pleasant for every ten bad, and insurers often respond with optimism.
Excluding prior-period reserve additions MedPro had an underwriting profit; other primary insurers earned $324 million underwriting profit on $1,270 million of volume.

stance.quote: Long contracts, or alternatively those with multiple variables, are the most difficult to mark to market (the standard procedure used in accounting for derivatives)

summary: The unit was meant to serve insurance clients, yet one liquidated contract ran 100 years; long, multi-variable contracts are hardest to mark to market and invite imaginative valuation.

stance.quote: A business in which huge amounts of compensation flow from assumed numbers is obviously fraught with danger.

summary: Counterparties value the same derivative contract differently and each tends to report a profit, so compensation based on assumed numbers is dangerous.
Buffett says he cost owners a lot of money by not moving immediately to close down the derivatives trading operation.
Buffett wasted years trying to sell the Gen Re trading operation, which could not be sold given open-ended liabilities likely to correlate with trouble elsewhere in markets.

stance.quote: The number and value of derivative contracts outstanding in the world continues to mushroom and is now a multiple of what existed in 1998

summary: Delay was a mistake: act at once on problems; Berkshire's experience is a warning because outstanding derivative contracts are now a multiple of 1998.
Gen Re was a minor derivatives player that unwound in a benign market with conservative accounting, so its experience is a best case for exiting gracefully.
Firms with positions many times larger liquidating in chaotic markets would fare worse; the risk deserves attention now, as levees did before Katrina. Gen Re Securities results follow.

summary: Building products and Shaw face soaring petrochemical and natural gas costs with lagging price increases, yet delivered respectable 2005 results thanks to strong franchises.
Fruit of the Loom raised earnings and share: 48.7% of mass-marketer men's and boys' underwear (44.2% in 2002) and 24.7% of women's and girls' intimate apparel (13.7% in 2002).

stance.quote: Our never-on-Sunday approach at R. C. Willey continues to overwhelm seven-day competitors as we roll out stores in new markets.

summary: R. C. Willey's Boise store gained 21% in 2005 after 10% in 2004, the new Reno store opened strongly, and Sacramento opens in June.

stance.quote: I said last year that this business would earn money in 2005 – and I was dead wrong.

summary: FlightSafety earnings rose as corporate aviation rebounded, with 42 training centers and over $100 million invested in a new England facility; NetJets did not earn money in 2005.
NetJets Europe grew, with contracts up 37% and a smaller loss, but the U.S. operation fell deep into the red as efficiency fell and costs soared.
Rich Santulli will fix NetJets' revenue and expense problem without impairing service, security and safety quality.
See's, bought in 1972, saw profits rise more than tenfold in Chuck Huggins' 34-year tenure in an industry growing slowly at best.
At yearend 2005 Brad Kinstler, previously running Cypress Insurance and Fechheimer, succeeded Chuck Huggins as head of See's, an unusual move of managers between Berkshire businesses.
Each business grows stronger or weaker daily depending on delighting customers and cutting unnecessary costs; small actions are imperceptible but cumulatively enormous.

stance.quote: But when short-term and long-term conflict, widening the moat must take precedence.

summary: Widening the moat is essential for the business wanted in a decade or two; bad decisions made to hit short-term earnings targets damage costs, customers and brands beyond repair.
Auto and airline managers struggle with huge problems left by predecessors; sometimes no cure overcomes past mistakes, so prevention matters.
Berkshire's managers are passionate moat-wideners who usually ran their businesses before Berkshire arrived; Berkshire's only function is to stay out of their way.

stance.quote: Wells Fargo, a company that Dick Kovacevich runs brilliantly

summary: Total common stocks cost $15,947 million and were worth $46,721 million; Gillette merged into P&G, American Express spun off Ameriprise, and Berkshire raised Wells Fargo and bought Anheuser-Busch and Wal-Mart.

stance.quote: Expect no miracles from our equity portfolio.

summary: Berkshire's equities are strong businesses but not at bargain prices; they may double in ten years as per-share earnings grow 6-8% annually and prices match.

stance.quote: This bookkeeping entry, dictated by GAAP, is meaningless from an economic standpoint

summary: The P&G-Gillette merger forced a $5.0 billion pre-tax GAAP capital gain, economically meaningless and tax-free, which should be ignored when evaluating 2005 earnings.
CEO identity matters hugely: Gillette's Duracell acquisition cost shareholders billions that conventional accounting never showed, because business value received was less than value given up.

stance.quote: it’s difficult to overpay the truly extraordinary CEO of a giant enterprise. But this species is rare.

summary: CEO Jim Kilts raised Gillette's intrinsic value through discipline and marketing and earned his generous pay; Berkshire, a 9.7% owner, effectively paid that share of his compensation.

stance.quote: Too often, executive compensation in the U.S. is ridiculously out of line with performance.

summary: CEO pay is stacked against investors; with ten-year fixed-price options a CEO profits by skipping dividends and using all earnings to repurchase stock.
In a stagnant company earning $1 billion on $10 billion, a CEO withholding dividends and buying back shares gets $158 million from options as EPS rises to $25.80.
The option-holding CEO earns his $158 million with no business improvement, and could make more than $100 million even if earnings fell 20% over the decade.

stance.quote: still can provide lush rewards for managers who achieve nothing.

summary: Fixed-price options let a manager profit from retained earnings invested at a paltry 5% return, while shareholders lose the promised alignment of interests.

stance.quote: they somehow forget to tell shareholders that fixed-price options give them capital that is free.

summary: Every dividend reduces the value of outstanding options, a conflict never disclosed in proxy materials; CEOs preach that capital has a cost but fixed-price options make it free.

stance.quote: But – surprise, surprise – options of that kind are almost never issued.

summary: Boards could easily adjust option strike prices for retained earnings, yet such options are almost never issued, and compensation experts favor management-friendly plans.

stance.quote: Today, in the executive suite, the alltoo-prevalent rule is that nothing succeeds like failure.

summary: Fired CEOs can collect enormous severance in a single day, so executive rewards now often follow failure rather than success.

stance.quote: When comp committees follow this “logic,” yesterday’s most egregious excess becomes today’s baseline.

summary: Compensation committees, bombarded with ever-rising comparative pay data and perks, grant huge severance and outsized pay for ho-hum performance, ratcheting up CEO pay.
Compensation committees should adopt a strict pay-for-performance attitude; Buffett, a director of twenty public companies, has been put on a comp committee by only one CEO.
Buffett's trade-imbalance conviction cost $955 million pre-tax in 2005 through currency marks in earnings, while stock holdings like Coca-Cola ($13.4 billion to $8.1 billion) never hit earnings.
Long-term currency positions are marked to market daily and hit earnings each period; since the first contract Berkshire is $2.0 billion ahead.
Berkshire cut direct currency positions in 2005 and bought foreign-currency equities instead, since higher U.S. rates make holding foreign currencies a negative carry costing money in 2005 and 2006.

stance.quote: The underlying factors affecting the U.S. current account deficit continue to worsen, and no letup is in sight.

summary: The trade deficit hit a record in 2005, investment income balance will soon turn negative as foreigners own more U.S. assets, and unilateral transfers are always negative.

stance.quote: I doubt, however, that the situation will forever remain benign.

summary: The rich U.S. may run huge current account imbalances for a long time without harm, but Americans must address the problem on their own terms or face an unpleasant outcome.
The Dow rose from 66 to 11,497 over the 20th century because American businesses prospered, but shareholders' self-inflicted wounds are now cutting the returns they will realize.
Owners in aggregate can earn at most what their businesses earn; one investor's gain from clever trading comes at another's expense, and no outside money can boost total wealth.
Owners earn less than their businesses because of frictional costs, which now reach amounts that will make shareholders earn far less than historically.
Gotrocks parable: if one family owned all American corporations, earning about $700 billion a year, everyone would grow wealthier together and compound savings harmoniously.
When broker-Helpers get family members to trade among themselves for fees, the family's gain equals business earnings minus commissions, and more trading shrinks their share.

stance.quote: Overall, a bigger slice of the pie now goes to the two classes of Helpers.

summary: Investment managers hired to beat relatives increase trading for brokers, so two classes of Helpers take a bigger slice and the family's finances worsen.

stance.quote: By now its members know they can pick neither the right stocks nor the right stock-pickers.

summary: Investors who cannot pick stocks or stock-pickers add consultants as further fee-charging helpers, with no reason to expect better results.
With three classes of expensive Helpers and worse results, a fourth group, the hyper-Helpers, claims existing Helpers are insufficiently motivated.

stance.quote: The more observant members of the family see that some of the hyper-Helpers are really just manager-Helpers wearing new uniforms

summary: Hyper-Helpers such as hedge funds and private equity demand huge contingent payments on top of stiff fixed fees, though they are often just rebranded managers.

stance.quote: Particularly expensive is the recent pandemic of profit arrangements under which Helpers receive large portions of the winnings

summary: A record share of business earnings now goes to Helpers, especially under profit-sharing deals where owners bear all losses plus large fixed fees.

stance.quote: the family’s frictional costs of all sorts may well amount to 20% of the earnings of American business.

summary: Frictional costs may equal 20% of American business earnings, so equity investors overall may earn only about 80% of what they would by sitting still.
Newton lost heavily in the South Sea Bubble; the proposed fourth law of motion is that for investors as a whole, returns decrease as motion increases.

stance.quote: Except for token amounts, we shun debt, turning to it for only three purposes

summary: The Dow's 20th-century gain was 5.3% compounded; matching it needs 2,011,011 by 2099. Consolidating MidAmerican does not raise Berkshire's tolerance for borrowing, which has three limited purposes.
First borrowing purpose: opportunistic repos tied to short-term holdings of highly liquid U.S. government or agency securities; the related debt has been cut and may soon be gone.

Second purpose: borrowing against understood receivables, such as the $5.6 billion guaranteed for FINOVA (repaid) and Clayton's manufactured-home loans, instead of securitizing, which would show less debt and faster earnings.

stance.quote: Until then, we prefer better profits to better cosmetics.

summary: Securitizing receivables would remove debt from the balance sheet and accelerate reported earnings but ultimately earn less money, so Berkshire prefers actual profits to cosmetics.

stance.quote: this debt is unquestionably secure because it is serviced by MidAmerican’s diversified stream of highly-stable utility earnings

summary: Third purpose: MidAmerican's debt is its own obligation, not guaranteed by Berkshire, and is secure given stable diversified utility earnings; MidAmerican retains all earnings.

Ten diverse, uncorrelated utilities covering interest 2:1 are safer than one utility with higher coverage; MidAmerican's widening diversity of regulated earnings means it will always use major amounts of debt.

stance.quote: We are not interested in incurring any significant debt at Berkshire for acquisitions or operating purposes.

summary: Berkshire will not borrow significantly for acquisitions or operations, though conventional wisdom says moderate leverage could earn more safely.
Many investors, board members and managers hold large parts of their net worth in Berkshire, and insurance payments stretch fifty years, so Berkshire promises total security through any panic.
Berkshire writes high-limit catastrophe policies and holds a volatile portfolio, yet keeps the net worth, earnings and liquidity to cope; any other approach risks a zero.
If Buffett died tonight, Berkshire's businesses with strong market positions, momentum, terrific managers and an ingrained culture would not miss a beat.
Three young managers could be CEO; a separate person would handle marketable securities, as GEICO has done for 26 years with terrific results.
The board has discussed the three CEO candidates and unanimously agreed on a successor, and stays updated so it always knows what to do.
The board must be willing to replace the CEO if age-related decline sets in, since managers' self-assessment fades along with their abilities and someone else must blow the whistle.

stance.quote: I know of no other board in the country in which the financial interests of directors are so completely aligned with those of shareholders.

summary: Berkshire's directors are financially aligned with shareholders and motivated to act, though telling a friend he can no longer do the job is personally hard.
Because all of Buffett's Berkshire shares will go to philanthropy, the board shirking its duty to replace him would hurt society; he trusts the directors to act for shareholders.
Borsheim's gross margin, even before the shareholder discount, is twenty percentage points below major rivals; shareholder-period business rose 9% in 2005 after a 73% gain in 2004.
