2006 net worth rose a record $16.9 billion, 18.4% per share, and book value compounded at 21.4% over 42 years; Exxon earns more but pays it out.

stance.quote: What management accomplished there was simply extraordinary.

summary: Insurance benefited from luck in 2006 as the absence of hurricanes turned super-cat losses very profitable; most of 73 businesses did outstandingly, with GEICO extraordinary.

stance.quote: Tony has delivered staggering productivity gains in recent years.

summary: GEICO policies grew 42% from 5.7 to 8.1 million between 2003 and 2006 while full-time employees fell 3.5%, lifting productivity 47%.
Productivity gains keep GEICO a low-cost producer despite ad spending of $631 million in 2006, up from $238 million in 2003 and $31 million in 1995, far above rivals.
Berkshire has grown into a big business with 217,000 employees and annual revenues approaching $100 billion, which Buffett and Munger never planned; a director jokes about GEICO's performance.

stance.quote: Size seems to make many organizations slow-thinking, resistant to change and smug.

summary: Buffett and Munger doubt big entities function well; of the ten largest non-oil companies by market value in 1965, only one made the 2006 list.
Buffett admires giant-company managers such as Ken Chenault of American Express, Jeff Immelt of G.E. and Dick Kovacevich of Wells Fargo, but would not want their duties.
Buffett works through great managers who run their own shows; his tasks are cheering them on, shaping corporate culture and making major capital-allocation decisions.
No single criterion measures Berkshire's progress and intrinsic value; key unquantifiable factors include having younger managers ready to succeed Buffett.
One key statistic is per-share investments including cash, excluding finance operation holdings offset by borrowings; the record since present management took control follows.
Table: Berkshire per-share investments for 1965 to 2006 ($80,636 in 2006) with compound growth of 27.5% since 1965 and 12.6% since 1995.
Early retained earnings and float went into securities; later emphasis on buying operating businesses slowed investment growth and accelerated non-insurance pre-tax earnings, the second yardstick.
Table: non-insurance pre-tax earnings per share for 1965 to 2006 ($3,625 in 2006) with compound growth of 17.9% since 1965 and 31.7% since 1995.
Non-insurance earnings rose 38% in 2006; further large gains need major sensible acquisitions, and Berkshire is increasingly the buyer of choice, now beyond U.S. borders.
Berkshire completed three pending 2005 deals early in 2006, spending about $6 billion on PacifiCorp, Business Wire and Applied Underwriters, all performing very well.
The year's highlight was buying most of Israeli ISCAR, a cutting-tool business in 61 countries, after its chairman wrote Buffett an introductory letter in October 2005.
ISCAR's owners, facing generational transfer of a family enterprise, concluded Berkshire would be the ideal home and the company would thrive as part of its portfolio.
After meeting ISCAR's talented managers in Omaha and learning tax and jurisdictional matters for a first foreign business purchase, Berkshire agreed to buy 80%.
Berkshire purchased 80% of ISCAR for $4 billion, with the remaining 20% staying with the Wertheimer family as partner.

stance.quote: ISCAR makes money because it enables its customers to make more money.

summary: ISCAR sells small consumable cutting tools used with expensive machine tools; managers who constantly develop more productive tools make its customers more money, a recipe for continued success.

stance.quote: We – and I mean every one of us – have never been more impressed with any operation.

summary: After a September visit to ISCAR in Israel, Buffett and Munger were more impressed than with any other operation; shareholders are lucky to have joined with its managers.
Berkshire was again the buyer of choice via John Roach, who brought TTI, an electronic components distributor its owner built from $112,000 to $1.3 billion of sales in 35 years.
TTI's owner, seeing how a founder's death disrupts a private company, wanted to choose his successor owner himself rather than leave an auction to a trust officer or lawyer.
TTI's owner rejected a strategic buyer seeking synergies and a debt-loading private equity firm, leaving Berkshire; the deal was made before lunch on November 15.
Tuck-in 2006 deals included Fruit of the Loom buying Russell for about $1.2 billion and VF's intimate apparel business, together adding about $2.2 billion of sales and 23,000 employees.
Tuck-ins leverage proven Berkshire managers, such as MiTek's 14 acquisitions since 2001; but a flood of incoming cash means Berkshire needs elephants and must ignore mice.
Buffett invites acquisition candidates that fit his criteria; Berkshire's insurance entry began March 9, 1967 with the $8.6 million purchase of National Indemnity and National Fire & Marine.
Buffett bought the Ringwalt insurers in the mid-1960s on a handshake within minutes, waiving any audit or due diligence.
The two insurers bought in 1967 had $17 million of float; float is money held that is not Berkshire's but which it gets to invest.

Float reached $50.9 billion at yearend 2006 and a huge retroactive contract with Equitas adds $7 billion; growth came from acquisitions and strong internal growth at Ajit Jain's reinsurance operation.

Float from retroactive reinsurance drifts down, so growth needs insurance acquisitions; Berkshire's float cost over time should stay well below the industry's, perhaps below zero, with bad years periodically.
Everything went right in 2006 insurance: Berkshire's managers delivered results generally superior to competitors in a year when the overall industry also had a terrific result.
Table: 2006 and 2005 underwriting profit or loss and yearend float for General Re, B-H Reinsurance, GEICO, other primary and total ($3,838 million profit, $50,887 million float in 2006).
Bread-and-butter insurance results will deteriorate in 2007; super-cat is the unknown, since 2006's calm may precede devastating storms if the 2004-05 hurricanes signaled climate change.
Neither Ajit Jain nor Buffett knows what lies ahead; betting that atmospheric changes are benign for insurers would be a huge mistake.
Berkshire will risk $6 billion on one event if paid properly but refuses underpriced exposure; with rates falling on new capital, it sharply cut wind exposure.
Berkshire agreed to a huge retroactive reinsurance contract, which protects an insurer against losses already incurred whose cost is unknown; the background in insurance history follows.
Lloyd's began in a London coffee house around 1688 where capitalists underwrote sea risks; it is not an insurer but a marketplace where member-insurers transact business.
Lloyd's underwriters raised passive investors into syndicates and broadened from marine risks into every form of insurance; the backers became known as names.

Thousands of names joined Lloyd's expecting easy income despite unlimited, everlasting liability for syndicate underwriting, a warning that came to seem perfunctory after three centuries without calamity.
Asbestos, environmental and product claims of the 1980s caused decades-old Lloyd's policies to develop tens of billions of dollars of losses, making Lloyd's implode and ruining many names.
In 1996 Lloyd's allotted £11.1 billion to a new company, Equitas, to pay all claims on pre-1993 policies, pooling losses; names stayed liable for any shortfall.
Pooling in Equitas cut squabbling and improved claims handling; after £11.3 billion of claims paid by spring 2006, Berkshire concluded Equitas would survive and offered it a huge reinsurance policy.
For $7.12 billion of cash and securities, Berkshire will pay Equitas' future claims up to $13.9 billion, $5.7 billion above Equitas' own liability estimate, giving its names large protection.
Berkshire's result on Equitas depends on known and unknown claim costs, payment timing and earnings on the cash received; Buffett and Ajit Jain think the odds favor Berkshire.
Equitas' CEO said the deal buys its names the world's best mattress; an optional section follows explaining the accounting for retroactive reinsurance.
Berkshire writes far more retroactive policies than any insurer and is reinsurer of choice, since obligations lasting 50 years or more require the certainty only it can guarantee.

Retroactive reinsurance accounting is unintuitive, so Berkshire lays out the debits and credits; murky footnotes about important transactions, like Enron's, leave Buffett suspicious that the company wanted it that way.
Equitas accounting: debits to cash, reinsurance recoverable and deferred charges (DCRA), a credit to loss reserves; no initial profit or loss, then annual underwriting losses as DCRA is amortized.
Retroactive contracts always produce underwriting losses, worthwhile if investment income on the cash exceeds them; DCRA charges of about $300 million rise to roughly $450 million after Equitas.
For float to be cost-free, other insurance operations must earn underwriting gains of at least the $450 million DCRA cost, a hurdle Buffett expects to clear most years.

stance.quote: Shaw, however, remains a powerhouse and a major contributor to Berkshire’s earnings.

summary: Shaw's founder retired at 75, succeeded by a 31-year veteran; weak housing has slowed carpet, but Shaw remains a major contributor to Berkshire's earnings.
Berkshire bought MiTek in 2001 for $420 million, lending $200 million at 9% and buying $198 million of stock; 55 employees bought shares at the same price.
In five years MiTek's sales tripled and its stock rose to $71,699 per share, while it made 14 acquisitions for $291 million, repaid Berkshire and holds $35 million of cash.

stance.quote: And fundamentals are definitely eroding in the newspaper industry, a trend that has caused the profits of our Buffalo News to decline.

summary: Declining industry economics eventually overwhelm management brilliance; newspaper fundamentals are eroding, Buffalo News profits are falling, and the skid will almost certainly continue.
Newspapers were once an easy way to huge returns because they were the main source of news and the easiest ad channel; a one-paper city paper gushed profits however poor.
Families wanted one daily paper, and advertisers and readers favored the biggest, creating a circularity of circulation and ads: survival of the fattest.
Once rivals vanished, the leading paper gained pricing power over advertisers and readers, raising rates annually for years of economic heaven, which papers never reported on themselves.

stance.quote: the media businesses . . . will prove considerably less marvelous than I, the industry, or lenders thought would be the case only a few years ago

summary: Buffett warned in his 1991 letter that media businesses would be less marvelous, yet newspapers kept selling like indestructible slot machines and executives were blind or indifferent to the change.

stance.quote: Nevertheless, this operation faces unrelenting pressures that will cause profit margins to slide.

summary: Newspaper owners are losing the battle for eyeballs to cable, satellite and the internet; Buffalo News has top market penetration and outperforms peers but faces margin pressure.

stance.quote: is at best a small fraction of that existing in the past for a print newspaper facing no competition.

summary: Buffalo News has the leading local online news site, but its economics are a fraction of the print monopoly; ownership still gives prominence and power that attract wealthy local buyers.

stance.quote: There’s no rule that says a newspaper’s revenues can’t fall below its expenses and that losses can’t mushroom.

summary: Non-economic individual buyers may emerge for newspapers, but high fixed costs make losses mushroom as volume falls, and a paper's psychic value will wane.

stance.quote: But the days of lush profits from our newspaper are over.

summary: Berkshire will keep the Buffalo News unless it faces an irreversible cash drain and will work on a sustainable print-plus-online model, but lush newspaper profits are over.

stance.quote: Under Mark Booth’s brilliant leadership, NetJets is now operating profitably in Europe, and we expect the positive trend to continue.

summary: NetJets' flight revenues are up 596% since 1998 though profits were erratic; its costly European move lost $212 million by mid-2006, but demand exploded and Europe now profits.

stance.quote: Today, the value of the fleet we manage is far greater than that managed by our three largest competitors combined.

summary: NetJets earned $143 million pre-tax worldwide in 2006 despite a $19 million first-quarter loss; Rich Santulli and Mark Booth turned it around and widened its lead over competitors.
NetJets is the runaway leader thanks to safety and service, and an indispensable tool for Berkshire and its subsidiaries; Buffett, his family and directors use it without a discount.
Berkshire holds 86.6% of MidAmerican, whose units serve U.K., Iowa and six western states with electricity and whose two pipelines carry about 8% of U.S. natural gas.
MidAmerican is run as a unanimous partnership with Walter Scott, Dave Sokol and Greg Abel; HomeServices' volume fell 9% to $58 billion and its profits fell 50% in 2006.

stance.quote: Naturally, there are few defaults when virtually nothing is required of a borrower.

summary: Weak lending, with optional contracts and teaser rates, let borrowers pay less than interest costs, adding to principal; many homeowners now face above-normal payments, slowing residential real estate.
As homeowners' mortgage payment adjustments arrive, there is a huge overhang of homes offered for sale in several HomeServices markets.
Berkshire will keep buying brokerage operations, expecting HomeServices to be much larger in a decade; introduces MidAmerican's key earnings figures.

summary: Berkshire exited Value Capital; manufactured-housing sales in 2006 were the lowest since 1962 and one-third of 1999's, and outside Clayton the industry probably made no money.
Clayton earned $513 million pre-tax and paid Berkshire $86 million for financing its $10 billion receivables portfolio; headcount grew from 6,661 at purchase to 14,787 through acquisitions.
CORT's furniture-rental earnings improved significantly in 2006 and XTRA's trailer-leasing earnings stayed at 2005's high level; Berkshire seeks tuck-in acquisitions and new leasing ideas.

Direct currency positions suited early interest-rate differentials, but the spread turned negative in 2005, so Berkshire now gains foreign exposure through foreign equities.

stance.quote: As our U.S. trade problems worsen, the probability that the dollar will weaken over time continues to be high.

summary: Buffett favors real trade ($1.44 trillion in 2006) but the U.S. also ran $.76 trillion of unreciprocated pseudo-trade imports, 6% of GDP, transferring assets or IOUs abroad.

stance.quote: Like a very wealthy but self-indulgent family, we peeled off a bit of what we owned in order to consume more than we produced.

summary: By consuming more than it produced, the U.S. sold off a bit of what it owned.
The U.S. can run these deficits because it is rich and behaved responsibly, so the world accepts its bonds, real estate, stocks and businesses.

stance.quote: In effect, we’ve used up our bank account and turned to our credit card.

summary: The U.S. investment income account, positive every year since 1915, turned negative in 2006, so foreigners earn more on U.S. assets than Americans abroad, bringing reverse compounding.

stance.quote: Americans will live better ten or twenty years from now than they do today.

summary: Americans will still grow wealthier, but must ship part of their output abroad to service a huge debtor position, likely triggering political backlash; a soft landing is wishful thinking.

All direct currency profits came from forward contracts, which are derivatives, and Berkshire has other derivatives too, despite the Gen Re unwinding experience and systemic concerns about derivatives growth.

stance.quote: derivatives, just like stocks and bonds, are sometimes wildly mispriced.

summary: Berkshire selectively writes mispriced derivative contracts, 62 outstanding, managed personally and free of counterparty credit risk, producing pre-tax profits in the hundreds of millions of dollars.
Three much younger CEO candidates exist, but Berkshire is less prepared on investing: Lou Simpson, GEICO's successful portfolio manager, is only six years younger than Buffett.
The board plans to hire a younger person, possibly after trying several candidates, to become chief investment officer; brains and recent performance alone are not enough.

stance.quote: Independent thinking, emotional stability, and a keen understanding of both human and institutional behavior is vital to long-term investment success.

summary: A single big mistake can wipe out many successes, so the investment successor must recognize serious risks that models miss and have the right temperament.
Berkshire must retain its new investment manager, whose resume would be more marketable and who could earn much more elsewhere.
Lou Simpson was found in 1979 and paid for sustained overperformance, yet never left for larger sums; Berkshire needs younger people of the same stuff.

stance.quote: many directors who are now deemed independent by various authorities and observers are far from that

summary: Berkshire's director criteria are owner-oriented, business-savvy, interested and truly independent; fees of $150,000 to $250,000 compromise many so-called independent directors, and director pay has soared.
Director compensation has soared in recent years, pushed up by recommendations from corporate America's favorite consultants.

stance.quote: Yet these criteria are usually ignored.

summary: Directors must faithfully represent owners, yet boards are stocked by demographic quotas; nobody asks whether a candidate thinks like an intelligent owner.
Director selection should seek the specific talents a specialized job requires; at Berkshire, running a business well, that means business judgment.
Susan Decker, Yahoo!'s CFO, will join the board, scoring high on all four director criteria and being young; more young directors will come without slighting those qualities.
Berkshire will pay about $4.4 billion of federal income tax on 2006 earnings; with U.S. government spending of $2.6 trillion, 600 such taxpayers could fund all federal expenditures.
Berkshire's 9,386-page federal return and all other requirements are handled by 19 headquarters employees in 9,708 square feet with a total payroll of $3,531,978.
Buffett and Munger bought control of trading-stamp operation Blue Chip Stamps in 1970, thinking they had spotted the rewards trend early; sales that year were $126 million.
Blue Chip Stamps went straight downhill after Buffett and Munger joined: sales fell to $19.4 million by 1980 and $1.5 million by 1990.
Blue Chip sales fell another 98%, contributing only $25,920 of Berkshire's $98 billion revenue in 2006; Buffett sets pay for about 40 CEOs but has been outvoted on comp committees.
Buffett sets CEO pay at Berkshire in virtually no time, no CEO has voluntarily left in 42 years, and incentives vary with business economics but stay simple and fair.

stance.quote: We issue no lottery tickets that carry payoffs unrelated to business performance.

summary: Berkshire ties incentives to the operating results a CEO controls, not to $6 billion swings in its $61 billion equity portfolio, so a .300 hitter is paid as one.
Beyond astronomical pay for mediocre results, American CEOs also live like royalty; Buffett jokes that Berkshire will keep it that way, via Pampered Chef wordplay.

stance.quote: CEO perks at one company are quickly copied elsewhere.

summary: Consultants advising compensation committees use the 'all the other kids have one' argument, so CEO perks spread from company to company.

stance.quote: Irrational and excessive comp practices will not be materially changed by disclosure or by “independent” comp committee members.

summary: Pay reform will come only if a few large institutional shareholders demand it; consultants' selection of peer companies perpetuates excesses.
Buffett arranged for most of his Berkshire holdings to go to five charitable foundations, as part of a lifelong plan; taxes did not influence the decision or its timing.
Under Buffett's will, proceeds of his remaining Berkshire shares go to philanthropy within ten years of the estate closing, so all his shares likely distribute over about 25 years.
Foundation sales of Berkshire shares should not depress the stock: Berkshire's annual trading volume is only 15% of shares, and the sales would add at most three points.

Business performance determines Berkshire's price, usually within a zone of reasonableness; Buffett and Munger will use policies and shareholder communications to avoid a large discount or premium to intrinsic value.

Foundation ownership will not influence decisions on dividends, repurchases or share issuance, guided by what best serves shareholders over time; the Gotrocks family kept paying fees to helpers in 2006.

stance.quote: using investment assumptions that are likely to be out of reach

summary: Unrealistic return expectations persist; private pension plans overstate earnings and public plans defer tax increases with unreachable assumptions that actuaries and auditors accept.

stance.quote: The hapless Gotrocks will be assured that they all can achieve above-average investment performance – but only by paying ever-higher fees.

summary: Wall Street's performance promoters assure investors they can all beat the average, but only by paying ever-higher fees, the adult version of Lake Wobegon.

stance.quote: It’s a lopsided system whereby 2% of your principal is paid each year to the manager even if he accomplishes nothing

summary: In 2006 money flowed to the '2-and-20' crowd: a 2% annual fee on principal plus 20% of profits, so a 10% gross return nets investors only 6.4%.
On a $3 billion fund, a 6.4% net return still earns the manager $108 million, though an index fund might have returned 15% to investors at a token fee.

stance.quote: The inexorable math of this grotesque arrangement is certain to make the Gotrocks family poorer over time

summary: The math of 2-and-20 arrangements makes investors poorer than avoiding hyper-helpers would, yet the practice spreads; the experienced end up with the money and the moneyed with the experience.
Walter Schloss, a Wall Street good guy now 90, ran an investment partnership from 1956 to 2002 and took nothing unless investors made money.

stance.quote: We try to buy stocks cheap.

summary: Schloss worked with no secretary, never used inside information, and picked securities by simple statistical methods learned from Ben Graham; his approach was summarized as trying to buy stocks cheap.

stance.quote: So much for Modern Portfolio Theory, technical analysis, macroeconomic thoughts and complex algorithms.

summary: Schloss's simple 'buy stocks cheap' approach dismisses Modern Portfolio Theory, technical analysis, macroeconomic thoughts and complex algorithms.

stance.quote: There is simply no possibility that what Walter achieved over 47 years was due to chance.

summary: Investing with no real risk in about 1,000 mostly lackluster securities, Schloss dramatically beat the S&P 500 over 47 years, a record that cannot be luck.

stance.quote: When I talked about Walter 23 years ago, his record forcefully contradicted this dogma.

summary: Efficient market theory, taught at most business schools in 1984, held that no investor can beat the averages using public information; Schloss's record contradicted it.

stance.quote: Rather than opening their minds, they closed their eyes.

summary: Business schools teaching efficient market theory never studied Schloss's record and presented the theory as scripture; questioning it harmed an instructor's promotion chances.

stance.quote: attempts to evaluate businesses – that is, stocks – were useless.

summary: Tens of thousands of students were taught that stock prices are always right and valuation is useless, which made Schloss's outperformance easier.

stance.quote: Some major financial institutions have, however, experienced staggering problems

summary: Some major financial institutions suffered staggering problems from weakened lending practices; the Wells Fargo CEO says the industry invented new ways to lose money.

stance.quote: what we are witnessing at some of our largest financial institutions is an ugly sight

summary: Belief that house prices would keep rising led lenders to ignore income and equity; falling prices now expose widespread financial folly at large institutions.

stance.quote: Iscar is as impressive a manufacturing operation as I’ve seen

summary: TTI and Iscar performed magnificently in 2007; insurance had an excellent year helped by a second year without major insured catastrophes.

stance.quote: insurance-industry profit margins, including ours, will fall significantly in 2008

summary: Insurance margins will shrink about four points in 2008; Berkshire values itself by investments, $141 billion at yearend, and non-insurance earnings.
Insurance float of $59 billion funds investments and is free if underwriting breaks even; Berkshire has been profitable overall and expects breakeven or better.

The tables help valuation but mislead as forecasts; Berkshire’s record cannot be repeated because its asset base is too large.
Most Berkshire managers have no financial need to work, sold for large sums and run businesses for love of the job.

stance.quote: our rare and hard-to-replicate managerial structure gives Berkshire a real advantage

summary: Berkshire CEOs have the job they want long-term and are judged on their business’s long-term performance, a managerial structure Buffett sees as an advantage.
Little acquisition progress in 2007 until Christmas day, when Berkshire contracted its largest cash purchase ever.
In 1954 Jay Pritzker took control of Rockwood Chocolate and tendered 80 pounds of cocoa beans per share, a tax-efficient deal later described as arbitrage in 1988.
Pritzker family is selling Marmon: 125 businesses, Union Tank Car with 94,000 leased rail cars costing $5.1 billion, $7 billion sales, about 20,000 employees.
Berkshire will buy 60% of Marmon for $4.5 billion and the rest within six years at a price based on an earnings formula.
Marmon price was set from its financial statements with no advisors; Marmon CEO Frank Ptak works with John Nichols, formerly ITW’s CEO.
Goldman Sachs banker Byron Trott facilitated the Marmon purchase, which was code-named Indy 500.
Berkshire bought Dennis Ulrich’s jewelry maker and a similar supplier in 2007 to form Richline, well below the usual earnings threshold for purchases.
Acquisition criteria: an understandable business, favorable long-term economics, trustworthy management and a sensible price; buy all or at least 80%, else small parts of great businesses.
A great business needs an enduring moat, such as low cost or a powerful brand, to protect high returns on capital from competitors.
Berkshire rules out industries prone to rapid change and businesses whose success depends on a great manager, because the moat must be enduring.
A business needing a superstar is not great: a brain surgeon’s partnership loses its moat when he leaves, while the Mayo Clinic’s moat endures.
Buffett seeks long-term advantage in a stable industry and redeploys its earnings in other businesses, since great businesses cannot reinvest much internally at high returns.

stance.quote: Let’s look at the prototype of a dream business, our own See’s Candy.

summary: See’s Candy is a dream business in an unexciting, no-growth boxed-chocolate industry, earning nearly half of the industry’s profits.
See’s volume rose from 16 million pounds when Blue Chip bought it in 1972 to 31 million pounds, about 2% a year, on a durable advantage.
Bought for $25 million with $30 million sales and under $5 million pre-tax earnings; $8 million capital gave a 60% pre-tax return.
See’s 2007 sales were $383 million and pre-tax profit $82 million on $40 million capital; only $32 million was reinvested since 1972 against $1.35 billion pre-tax earnings.
See’s earnings have spawned multiple new streams of cash for Berkshire.
Few firms match See’s; companies lifting earnings from $5 million to $82 million typically need about $400 million of capital investment.
Earning $82 million on $400 million of tangible assets is satisfactory, but a growing earnings stream with almost no capital needs, like See’s, is far better.

stance.quote: It also possesses a durable competitive advantage

summary: FlightSafety delivers customer benefits equal to any business and has a durable competitive advantage, but is only good, not sensational, economics.
FlightSafety needs heavy reinvestment: capex $1.635 billion vs depreciation $923 million since 1996; pre-tax earnings rose from $111 million to $270 million.

The dollar fell further in 2007 because America ships about $2 billion of IOUs and assets abroad daily to pay for its trade deficit.

The weak dollar is not the fault of OPEC or China; U.S. trade policy should not single out countries or industries or invite retaliation.
Trade imbalances are unsustainable and legislators should reduce them soon, or the $2 billion of dollars sent abroad daily may cause global indigestion.

The 363 S&P companies with pension plans assumed an average 8% return in 2006; with 28% in bonds and cash earning under 5%, the rest must earn 9.2%.
The Dow rose from 66 to 11,497 in the 20th century, only 5.3% a year compounded, so a 9.2% return on pension equities is unrealistic.
To match last century’s 5.3% annual gain the Dow would need to reach about 2,000,000 by 2099, versus under 2,000 points gained in eight years.
With dividends near 2% and 5.3% appreciation less 0.5% costs, pension equity assets would earn about 7% at best; adviser layers may cost more.
Investors in total earn the average minus costs; passive investors’ costs are low and active investors’ are high, so the active group trails.

stance.quote: the passive group – the “know-nothings” – must win

summary: Passive index investors must beat active investors as a group because active investors bear far higher costs.
Expecting 10% yearly from equities this century implies a Dow near 24,000,000 by 2100; advisers promising double-digit returns fill their pockets with fees.
Companies assume U.S. pension plans earn more than non-U.S. plans, and CEOs choose high return assumptions to report higher earnings, which Buffett thinks will prove wrong.
After decades of pushing to report the highest current earnings, Corporate America should ease up, as Charlie advises.

In 2008 Berkshire Hathaway Assurance began insuring tax-exempt municipal bonds, after the major monoline bond insurers all fell into trouble by yearend 2007.

stance.quote: the monoline industry quickly became a basket case

summary: Monolines took ever-riskier business, including mortgage obligations, and collapsed when house prices fell; Berkshire offered to assume tax-exempt insurance of the three largest.
Berkshire offered to take over guarantees on about $822 billion of bonds at a 1.5% rate; the monolines refused, and Buffett realized the offer was severely underpriced.
Berkshire wrote $15.6 billion of secondary-market bond insurance, 77% on already-insured bonds, at average second-to-pay rates of 3.3% versus the 1.5% once offered.
Two of the three monolines raised capital, lowering Berkshire’s claim risk; it also wrote $3.7 billion of primary municipal bond insurance for $96 million of premium.
Berkshire has far more capital behind its bond insurance than other monolines, so bondholders prefer it, but Buffett remains cautious that the business will be profitable.
Low premium rates assume the few defaults of uninsured tax-exempts; fully insured bonds would behave differently, as the uninsured New York City bonds were solved by local holders in 1975.
Had New York City’s bonds been insured by Berkshire, no belt-tightening or concessions would have come; Berkshire would have been asked to share substantial sacrifices.
Local governments face tougher fiscal problems, with pension liabilities staggeringly above assets; communities with fully insured bonds will favor solutions worse for bondholders.

stance.quote: Insuring tax-exempts, therefore, has the look today of a dangerous business

summary: Municipal bond losses will be correlated, and insuring tax-exempts resembles catastrophe insurance: loss-free years can be followed by devastating losses; Berkshire will be careful.
Berkshire avoids many bond classes monolines insure; projecting loss history from uninsured bonds onto insured ones is a fallacy shared by back-tested financial models.

stance.quote: flawed, history-based models used by salesmen, rating agencies and investors

The “past” and “current” housing universes differed, and lenders, government and media failed to recognize it.

stance.quote: Beware of geeks bearing formulas.

stance.quote: In my opinion, the Fed was right to do so.

Derivatives often go unsettled for years, building hard-to-value paper assets and a web of mutual dependence among highly leveraged large dealers.
Derivative receivables and payables of billions are concentrated in a few large dealers, so a participant’s risk depends on its counterparties’ counterparties.
Large derivative dealers are assured government aid if trouble hits; Berkshire is party to 251 derivative contracts despite the dangers.

stance.quote: I believe each contract we own was mispriced at inception

Berkshire’s derivatives “float” is $8.1 billion, premiums received less losses paid; it expects to do better than break even, and collateral posted in Q4 2008 was under 1%.
Collateral-posting terms are a lethal threat, seen at financial institutions in 2008; Berkshire’s derivatives fall into four categories, starting with equity puts.

Credit-loss derivative contracts cover 100 companies in high-yield indices over five years, averaging 2⅓ years remaining, with expirations from September 2009 to December 2013.

stance.quote: the possibility of an eventual loss has increased

summary: Payments on the credit contracts were only $97 million in 2008 but losses are accelerating with bankruptcies; Berkshire also began writing credit default swaps on individual companies.

Berkshire writes a few tax-exempt bond insurance contracts structured as derivatives, which need mark-to-market accounting unlike the accrual accounting at BHAC; it will not post collateral.
Mark-to-market forced a $631 million loss on state-bond derivative contracts that BHAC accrual accounting would show as a small profit; results converge eventually.
Mark-to-market derivatives cause wild earnings swings that do not bother Buffett; declines let Berkshire expand positions; Black-Scholes values equity puts.

stance.quote: it can produce absurd results

summary: Black-Scholes gives absurd results over long periods; a 100-year $1 billion S&P put struck at 903 would carry a theoretical premium of $2.5 million.
A 100-year S&P put at 903 has a Black-Scholes premium of $2.5 million; inflation shrinks the dollar to 14 cents, but retained earnings raised the Dow 175-fold last century.
Buffett puts the chance of a 100-year index decline well under 1%, a $5 million expected loss, covered if the $2.5 million premium earned 0.7% yearly.
Such a put equals borrowing for 100 years at 0.7%, or 6.2% even in the worst case, so either the assumptions are crazy or the formula inappropriate.

stance.quote: This metric is simply irrelevant

summary: Black-Scholes premiums are inflated by past volatility, which is irrelevant to the value of American business a century ahead, like valuing a farm from a neighbor’s daily quotes.
Historical volatility loses usefulness for long options, so Black-Scholes overstates Berkshire’s put liability, but Berkshire keeps using it as conventional wisdom.
CEOs who invent their own valuations for esoteric financial instruments seldom err on the conservative side; Buffett and Munger do not wish to join that club.

A’s CEO gives $125 of intrinsic value for $100 and B’s holders end up owning 55.6%, yet the CEO gains prestige and pay from running a bigger company.

Iscar outperformed its competitors; Johns Manville, MiTek, Shaw and Acme Brick earned $362 million pre-tax in 2010 versus $1.3 billion in 2006, with 9,400 fewer employees.

stance.quote: These businesses entered the recession strong and will exit it stronger.

summary: Expecting a housing recovery, MiTek made five bolt-ons, Acme bought an Alabama brick maker for $50 million, Johns Manville is building a $55 million plant, Shaw will spend $200 million.
BNSF and MidAmerican hold long-lived regulated assets funded by long-term debt not guaranteed by Berkshire; BNSF's 2010 interest coverage was 6:1 despite weak car loadings.
Both regulated companies need continuous heavy investment and fair returns; rail moves 42% of U.S. inter-city freight and BNSF carries about 28% of that, over 11% of the total.
BNSF must maintain 23,000 miles of track and will spend $2 billion more than depreciation in 2011; Buffett expects appropriate returns on the incremental investments.
MidAmerican operates under a social compact: it must keep investing for customers' needs and expects a fair return if it operates reliably and efficiently.

stance.quote: MidAmerican has delivered outstanding results for both its owners

summary: MidAmerican supplies 2.4 million customers, its pipelines carry 8% of U.S. gas, and Northern Natural rose from last place in 2002 to second, behind Kern River.
MidAmerican's Iowa rates have not risen since 1999 while a rival raised prices over 70%; it will have 2,909 megawatts of wind generation by the end of 2011.
MidAmerican has invested or committed $5.4 billion to wind, possible because it retains all earnings unlike utilities that pay most out; earnings tables for MidAmerican and BNSF follow.

Buffett expects market gains to at least equal the earnings investees retain; normal earning power was estimated with three adjustments for future investment income, the first negative.
The Swiss Re note was redeemed in early 2011 and the Goldman Sachs and General Electric preferred stocks will likely be called by yearend, reducing investment income.
Redemptions will pay Berkshire about $1.4 billion in premiums but cut earning power; $38 billion of cash earns a pittance, and normal rates would add at least $500 million.
Dividends on Berkshire's stock holdings should rise; the Federal Reserve froze major banks' dividends, forcing Wells Fargo to keep an artificially low payout despite great earning power.
When the Fed lifts its restriction, Wells Fargo's dividends to Berkshire should rise by several hundred million dollars a year; Coca-Cola paid $88 million in 1995.

stance.quote: Time is the friend of the wonderful business.

summary: Coke raises its dividend every year, with $376 million due in 2011 and expected to double within ten years; Berkshire's normal investment income should at least equal 2010.
Lou Simpson, GEICO's investment manager since 1979, is retiring at 74; Buffett calls him one of the investment greats.
Berkshire needs younger investment managers as backup; past records matter less than how results were achieved and understanding of risk, which beta does not measure.
Berkshire wanted an investment manager able to anticipate effects of unprecedented economic scenarios and who regards working for Berkshire as far more than a job.
Todd Combs gets a salary plus performance pay relative to the S&P with deferrals and carryforwards, unlike hedge-fund general partners who collect on upside and walk away on losses.

stance.quote: Investors who put money with such managers should be labeled patsies, not partners.

summary: Buffett will keep managing most holdings; Todd Combs starts with one to three billion dollars, mainly equities, with no style-box restrictions.
Further managers may be paid 80% on their own portfolio and 20% on the others'; after Buffett and Munger, investment managers run the portfolio and are consulted on acquisitions.
Berkshire hired the little-known Todd Combs; its derivatives contracts (excluding subsidiaries' operating ones) fell from 251 in 2008 to 203 now.
Berkshire's 203 derivatives contracts are insurance-like activities in which it receives premiums for assuming risks others shed, with Buffett personally responsible for them.
Premiums received up front mean no counterparty risk; contracts written in 2004-2008 cover defaults in high-yield indices of 100 companies each, bringing $3.4 billion of premiums.
Buffett had said the high-yield default contracts should deliver an underwriting profit, losses below the $3.4 billion of premiums, plus the benefit of float.
Defaults in the financial panic cost $2.5 billion but an underwriting profit is almost certain, with about $2 billion of average float; equity puts were introduced.
Equity puts insure against falls in U.S., U.K., European and Japanese equity indices; Berkshire received $4.8 billion of premiums for 47 mostly 15-year contracts, payable only at termination.
In 2010 Berkshire unwound eight equity puts, receiving $647 million of premiums, paying $425 million and gaining $222 million; 39 contracts remain with $4.2 billion of premiums.
At yearend 2010 prices Berkshire would owe $3.8 billion settlement value on the equity puts, against a carried liability of $6.7 billion.
Unchanged index prices would produce a $2.9 billion gain; Berkshire expects equity prices to rise and keeps $4.2 billion of float for about ten more years, outside the $66 billion.
Almost all derivatives contracts need no collateral, reducing premiums but giving comfort in the financial crisis; Buffett turns to net earnings as a reporting number.
Net income is almost always meaningless at Berkshire, because Buffett and Munger could legally make it almost any number they like in a given period.
Realized gains and losses enter net income while unrealized gains are excluded, so net income can fall even when the business improves and unrealized gains soar.

stance.quote: We both have a deep disgust for “game playing” with numbers

summary: Berkshire never sells securities to manage reported net income; operating earnings are a reasonable guide, and readers should ignore net income.
Book value fully reflects realized and unrealized gains, so watch it and operating earnings; equity-put liabilities show net income's caprice, with $6.4 billion owed at June 30, 2010.
Black-Scholes raised the equity-put liability from $8.9 billion to $9.6 billion in a rising market quarter, cutting net income by $455 million; Buffett thinks it badly misvalues long-dated options.
Berkshire still uses Black-Scholes in its statements because it is the accepted standard and its auditors could not attest to values far from its counterparties' values.
Berkshire believes the true liability of its equity puts is far below the Black-Scholes figure but cannot give an exact number; approximately right beats precisely wrong.

stance.quote: Witness the tenacity with which almost all clung to the theory of efficient markets throughout the 1970s and 1980s, dismissively calling powerful facts that refuted it “anomalies.”

summary: University finance departments clung to efficient-market theory through the 1970s and 1980s, dismissing contrary evidence as anomalies.

stance.quote: However, that’s also been a way to get very poor.

summary: Investors need not value options to succeed; students should learn to value a business. Borrowed money has made some rich but has also made others very poor.

stance.quote: History tells us that leverage all too often produces zeroes, even when it is employed by very smart people.

summary: Leverage is addictive and can wipe out gains when a single zero multiplies them, as relearned in 2008; companies assuming debt can be refinanced face risk.
Credit is like oxygen: unnoticed when abundant, fatal when missing, and its overnight disappearance in September 2008 nearly brought the country to its knees; maturities need cash.
Berkshire will not risk its wellbeing for a few points of extra return, because owners' savings, philanthropy and accident victims' long-dated claims depend on its prudence.
Following his grandfather's liquidity lesson, Berkshire pledges to hold at least $10 billion of cash, excluding utility and railroad cash, and customarily keeps at least $20 billion.
Keeping $20 billion of cash lets Berkshire withstand unprecedented insurance losses, the largest so far about $3 billion from Katrina, and quickly seize opportunities in turmoil.
Cash sits mostly in Treasury bills, with no reliance on bank lines or collateral contracts; no cash has left Berkshire for dividends or buybacks in 40 years.

stance.quote: Having loads of liquidity, though, lets us sleep well.

summary: Retained earnings of about $1 billion a month grew net worth from $48 million to $157 billion in four decades; liquidity allowed $15.6 billion of investing after Lehman.
Berkshire's liquidity let it invest $15.6 billion in 25 days of panic following the Lehman bankruptcy in 2008.
In his biennial memo to managers, Buffett makes guarding Berkshire's reputation the top priority: it can afford to lose money but not reputation, tested by a front-page standard.
'Everybody else is doing it' is never an acceptable rationale; any action that causes hesitation about propriety is too close to the line and should be abandoned.
Managers must report significant bad news promptly; delay turned a small problem at Salomon into one that nearly destroyed a firm with 8,000 employees.
With over 250,000 employees some bad behavior is inevitable; managers' immediate response to impropriety shapes their culture, which determines behavior more than rule books.

Managers run their operations independently and need to clear with Buffett only post-retirement benefit changes and unusually large capital expenditures or acquisitions; succession letters are requested.
Buffett asks each manager for a private written recommendation of a successor with strengths and weaknesses, since Berkshire has added so many businesses.
Succession letters may be short and informal, except where co-managers run an operation; Buffett also asks managers to refuse proposals for him to speak or donate.

Berkshire bought Lubrizol, whose pre-tax profit rose from $147 million to $1,085 million since 2004, and agreed three bolt-ons costing $493 million; five major businesses set records.

Operating companies spent a record $8.2 billion on property, plant and equipment in 2011, 95% in the U.S., with another record in 2012; insurance float is costless capital.
Nine underwriting-profit years totaled $17 billion; float grew from $41 billion to $70 billion. Berkshire bought $5 billion of Bank of America preferred and $10.9 billion of IBM.

stance.quote: We view these holdings as partnership interests in wonderful businesses, not as marketable securities to be bought or sold based on their near-term prospects.

summary: Berkshire owns 13.0% of American Express, 8.8% of Coca-Cola, 5.5% of IBM and 7.6% of Wells Fargo, whose undistributed earnings are not reflected in Berkshire's income.
Dividends from the Big Four would have been $862 million against $3.3 billion of Berkshire's share of their earnings; $2.4 billion unreported creates at least that much value.
The Big Four might earn $7 billion in a decade, paying Berkshire $2 billion of dividends; Buffett's $2 billion purchase of Energy Future Holdings bonds was a big mistake.
Energy Future Holdings bonds, tied to weak natural gas prices, pay about $102 million a year; written down $1 billion in 2010 and $390 million in 2011 to $878 million.
Further loss on the Energy Future bonds is likely if gas prices stay low, though a rise could recoup some write-down; Buffett calls his misjudged probabilities a major unforced error.

Swiss Re, Goldman and General Electric paid $12.8 billion to redeem securities earning $1.2 billion pre-tax; Lubrizol offset most. Buffett's housing-recovery call was wrong; Clayton builds 7% of U.S. homes.

stance.quote: Housing will come back – you can be sure of that.

summary: Five housing-related companies earned $513 million pre-tax in 2011, similar to 2010 but down from $1.8 billion in 2006; the 2008 bubble came from building more units than households.
Oversupply of housing units burst the bubble and household formation fell in 2009; now more households than units form each day, reversing the supply-demand balance.

At 600,000 housing starts the old oversupply is being absorbed; Berkshire's housing companies employ 43,315 people versus 58,769 in 2006, and housing's depression explains the lagging employment recovery.

stance.quote: America’s best days lie ahead.

summary: Monetary and fiscal policy cannot fix excess housing; demographics will restore balance and one million units a year; Berkshire measures performance by per-share intrinsic business value against the S&P 500.
Berkshire is judged by gain in per-share intrinsic value versus the S&P 500; book value, an understated proxy, roughly tracks business value because the gap between them is stable.
The excess of intrinsic value over book value will grow in absolute terms but stay reasonably steady as a percentage.
Book value should beat the S&P in bad years and trail in strong ones; all 42 earlier five-year periods and 2007-11 beat the S&P, but the streak may snap.
Per-share investments rose 4% to $98,366 and per-share pre-tax earnings outside insurance and investments rose 18% to $6,990; eight subsidiaries would be Fortune 500 companies.
Berkshire announced buybacks up to 110% of book value but bought only $67 million before the price passed the limit; Buffett favors repurchases below intrinsic value.
Repurchases are justified only when ample funds exist and the stock sells at a material discount to conservative intrinsic value; offsetting dilution or spending excess cash is not enough.

stance.quote: The first law of capital allocation – whether the money is slated for acquisitions or share repurchases – is that what is smart at one price is dumb at another.

summary: Repurchases hurt continuing shareholders unless made below intrinsic value; Jamie Dimon at J.P. Morgan stresses price versus value; Berkshire has mixed feelings when its shares sell well below value.
Buying Berkshire's own stock below intrinsic value is the surest way to benefit continuing shareholders, and at 110% of book value repurchases clearly raise per-share value.
Berkshire will likely repurchase aggressively at or below the limit, will not support the stock and will not buy if cash equivalents are under $20 billion.
Berkshire hopes for rising earnings and a long-underperforming stock price when it owns a company that is repurchasing shares; talking its book would be harmful.

stance.quote: I can think of no major company that has had better financial management

summary: Gerstner and Palmisano rescued IBM, and its financial management, using debt wisely, buying companies for cash and repurchasing stock aggressively, benefited shareholders; Berkshire owns 63.9 million shares, 5.5%.
IBM may spend $50 billion on buybacks over five years, so Berkshire should wish for a weak stock price: at $200 it retires 250 million shares, lifting Berkshire to 7%.
At a $300 average price IBM retires only 167 million shares and Berkshire owns 6.5%; the lower-price scenario would add $100 million to Berkshire's share of fifth-year earnings.
A net buyer of stocks, directly or through a repurchasing company, is hurt when prices rise and benefits when they fall, though most people take comfort in rising prices.
Buffett learned from Ben Graham to welcome low prices; the success of the IBM investment depends mainly on future earnings and secondarily on how many shares IBM repurchases.
Buffett jokes of a paid holiday if repurchases cut IBM to 63.9 million shares; Berkshire will compare intrinsic value with carrying value in each of its four sectors.
P/C insurers collect premiums upfront and pay claims later, leaving float that grows with the business and is stable relative to premium volume; a float table begins.
Float reached $65.8 billion in 2010 and $70.6 billion in 2011 and is unlikely to grow; underwriting profit makes it free money, but industry competition usually causes underwriting losses.
State Farm lost money underwriting in eight of eleven years, while Berkshire had nine consecutive underwriting profit years totaling $17 billion.
Float of $70.6 billion should be better than cost-free; book value deducts it fully as a liability, but it is really a revolving fund whose true value is far lower.
Insurance goodwill of $15.5 billion in book value is the price paid for float-generating capability; it is worthless if underwriting losses are large and sustained.

stance.quote: In most years, including 2011, the industry’s premiums have been inadequate to cover claims plus expenses.

summary: Berkshire's insurance goodwill is worth far more than its carrying value, a huge reason intrinsic value exceeds book value; Berkshire-quality float is rare because industry premiums are inadequate.

stance.quote: industry’s overall return on tangible equity has for many decades fallen far short of the average return realized by American industry

summary: Industry returns on tangible equity lag American industry; Berkshire's economics depend on terrific managers. Ajit Jain's reinsurance group is first by float size and takes risks others avoid.
A $250 billion industry mega-catastrophe would likely still leave Berkshire with a moderate profit; Ajit built reinsurance float to $34 billion with significant underwriting profits.
Ajit added billions to Berkshire's value from a standing start in 1985; General Re, managed by Tad Montross, follows four insurance disciplines.

stance.quote: Many insurers pass the first three tests and flunk the fourth.

summary: A sound insurer must walk away when premiums are inadequate, yet many cannot turn down business competitors write, which spells trouble especially in insurance.
General Re under Tad Montross follows all four insurance disciplines; its huge float has been better than cost-free, and it went from major headache to treasure.

stance.quote: GEICO’s much-envied record comes from Tony’s brilliant execution

summary: Under Tony Nicely GEICO's market share rose from 2.0% to 9.3%, lifting 2011 premiums to $15.4 billion versus $3.3 billion had share stayed flat.

stance.quote: Don’t bet against Tony acquiring chunks of it year after year in the future.

summary: GEICO still has over 90% of the auto-insurance market to win; low costs permit low prices, and its Gecko needs no agent. Berkshire's smaller insurers are introduced.
Berkshire's smaller insurers, in odd corners of the insurance world, have been consistently profitable in aggregate and provide substantial float.
Berkshire bought Princeton Insurance at yearend, adding over $600 million of float to Medical Protective's operations; a table of 2011 and 2010 underwriting profit and float by insurance unit begins.

stance.quote: Among large insurance operations, Berkshire’s impresses me as the best in the world.

summary: Insurance float totaled $70.6 billion in 2011 on $248 million of underwriting profit; BNSF and MidAmerican hold long-lived regulated assets funded by long-term debt not guaranteed by Berkshire.
BNSF's 2011 interest coverage was 9.5x; MidAmerican's debt service is secure thanks to stable essential-service earnings and diverse regulatory exposure; BNSF carries about 37% of rail freight.

stance.quote: It is no exaggeration to characterize railroads as the circulatory system of our economy.

summary: BNSF carries about 15% of all U.S. inter-city freight ton-miles and must maintain 23,000 miles of track, 13,000 bridges and thousands of locomotives and cars with ample financial resources.

stance.quote: It is pouring money – funds from the private sector – into the investment projects needed to provide better and more extensive service in the future.

summary: BNSF invested $1.8 billion more than depreciation in 2011 and the other major railroads similarly, with private funds that spare the public highway system worse congestion.

BNSF's massive investments would be foolish without appropriate returns, but Buffett is confident it will earn them given the value it delivers; good behavior toward customers earns regulators' goodwill.
MidAmerican, 89.8% owned by Berkshire, serves 2.5 million customers and its pipelines carry 8% of U.S. gas; Northern Natural was ranked last of 43 when bought in 2002.
Northern Natural now ranks second among pipelines behind Kern River, MidAmerican's utilities rank second in customer satisfaction, and it will have 3,316 megawatts of wind generation by end 2012.
MidAmerican has invested or committed $6 billion to wind and began two solar projects costing about $3 billion, funded by retaining all earnings unlike utilities that pay most out.

Berkshire holds on to Buffett's mistakes rather than dumping laggards, as its economic principles (Number 11) state a general reluctance to sell poor performers.
Berkshire commits to sellers that it will retain their businesses through thick and thin; the cost has been small and builds goodwill among prospective sellers seeking a permanent home.
Sellers know what they get from Berkshire cannot be delivered by others and that its commitments will be good for many decades.
Berkshire acts promptly if a business is a long-term cash drain or has endemic labor strife, which happened only a couple of times in 47 years; the economy has recovered.
Four housing-related companies earned $227 million, $362 million and $359 million pre-tax in 2009-2011, while non-housing operations earned $1,831 million, $3,912 million and $4,678 million.

stance.quote: housing-related businesses remain in the emergency room

summary: Lubrizol added $291 million of 2011 earnings; the remaining $4,387 million shows most businesses recovered from the 2008 panic while housing-related ones remain depressed.
CTB, bought for $139 million in 2002, has distributed $180 million, earned $124 million pre-tax in 2011 and holds $109 million cash; TTI's sales hit a record $2.1 billion.

stance.quote: Iscar, our 80%-owned cutting-tools operation, continues to amaze us.

summary: TTI beat its larger public competitors and made a bolt-on in 2012; Iscar's growth is unique in its industry, and it bought Tungaloy in November 2008.
Tungaloy set a sales record in 2011 despite tsunami damage; McLane set a $370 million pre-tax record and has earned $2.4 billion pre-tax since its $1.5 billion purchase in 2003.
McLane increased its LIFO reserve by $230 million as product prices rose, runs an unmatched logistical machine, and may add bolt-ons in its new wine-and-spirits business.
NetJets earned $227 million pre-tax in 2011 despite slow new-plane sales; it was once Buffett's number one worry with costs far above revenues and would have failed without Berkshire.

stance.quote: No other fractional-ownership operator has remotely the size and breadth of the NetJets operation, and none ever will.

summary: NetJets plans to enter China, widening its moat; Marmon grows internally and made three bolt-on acquisitions costing about $270 million in the last few months of 2011.

stance.quote: “Buy commodities, sell brands” has long been a formula for business success.

summary: Marmon formed an Indian crane joint venture and ten of its eleven sectors grew earnings; 'buy commodities, sell brands' has produced enormous profits for Coca-Cola, Wrigley and See's.
See's earned a record $83 million pre-tax, $1.65 billion since its $25 million purchase; Nebraska Furniture Mart's 2011 earnings were over ten times its 1983 level.
NFM bought 433 acres north of Dallas for a likely highest-volume home-furnishings store; its Omaha and Kansas City stores each had record 2011 sales over $400 million.
The Dallas store's drawing power and surrounding land should attract other major stores; Mrs. B founded NFM in 1937 with $500.
Intrinsic value of this sector's businesses significantly exceeds book value, though not for many smaller companies, where Buffett erred; large purchases have worked well overall.
Subsidiaries are normally carried at cost plus retained earnings, except for the odd GAAP treatment of Marmon.
Berkshire bought 64% of Marmon in 2008 for $4.8 billion and 16% more in 2011 for $1.5 billion, then wrote off $614 million, widening intrinsic value over carrying value.
The finance sector holds leasing companies XTRA and CORT, Clayton Homes, financial assets and half of Berkadia; the two lessors' combined pre-tax earnings were $13 million in 2009.
Leasing earnings recovered to $155 million in 2011 from $13 million in 2009, while manufactured housing sales stayed depressed at 51,606 homes versus 146,744 in 2005; Clayton remained profitable.

Old-fashioned loan policies with meaningful down payments and sensible payments kept Clayton's losses acceptable despite negative borrower equity; U.S. home-ownership and mortgage policies caused a huge economic price.
Government, lenders, borrowers, media and rating agencies all fed the folly that house values would always rise, justifying any price and fueling refinancing-driven consumption.
Many people who lost homes to foreclosure actually profited because earlier refinancings gave them more cash than their cost; the lender was the victim.

After the 2007 bubble burst, household formations exceed housing starts; Clayton's earnings should improve, and intrinsic value of the three sector businesses roughly equals book value. A holdings table begins.

summary: Key 2011 moves: buying IBM and Bank of America and adding $1 billion to Wells Fargo, which is prospering; Bank of America is cleaning up prior management's mistakes.
Bank of America's warrants to buy 700 million shares should prove valuable; Buffett was late to IBM, as with Coca-Cola in 1988 and railroads in 2006.
Todd Combs built a $1.75 billion portfolio in 2011 and Ted Weschler will build a similar one; each gets 80% of performance pay from own results, 20% from the partner's.
Combs and Weschler will help the next CEO make acquisitions; new derivatives rules require collateral, so Berkshire will initiate no major derivatives positions.
Berkshire shuns contracts that could require instant collateral postings, inconsistent with redundant liquidity; its high-yield default contracts are ending.
High-yield default contract payments, $86 million in 2011, total $2.6 billion against $3.4 billion of premiums, so a final underwriting profit is almost certain; float averaged $2 billion.
Equity puts should produce a significant profit given $4.2 billion of float and $222 million already realized; the book liability was $8.5 billion versus $6.2 billion if due at yearend.

stance.quote: The riskiness of an investment is not measured by beta

summary: Berkshire defines investing as forgoing consumption now to gain more purchasing power after taxes later; risk is the probability of losing purchasing power, not volatility or beta.
Price fluctuation is not risk if purchasing power is reasonably certain to grow, and non-fluctuating assets can be risky; the first of three investment categories is currency-denominated instruments.

stance.quote: In truth they are among the most dangerous of assets.

summary: Currency-based investments seen as safe are among the most dangerous: despite zero beta, governments' inflationary policies have destroyed investors' purchasing power over the past century even as interest was paid.
The dollar has lost 86% of its value since 1965, so a tax-free institution needed 4.3% annual bond interest merely to maintain purchasing power; none of it was true income.
Rolling Treasury bills returned 5.7% a year over 47 years, but income taxes took 1.4 points and the inflation tax 4.3 points, leaving a taxpayer no real income.

stance.quote: Right now bonds should come with a warning label.

summary: High rates in the early 1980s compensated for inflation risk but current rates do not; Buffett dislikes currency-based investments yet Berkshire holds mainly short-term ones for liquidity.
Berkshire meets liquidity needs mainly with Treasury bills, keeping $20 billion as a working level and $10 billion as the minimum; other securities only if unusual gains are possible.

stance.quote: Bonds promoted as offering risk-free returns are now priced to deliver return-free risk.

summary: Berkshire would buy credit only when mispriced, as in junk-bond debacles, or high-grade bonds before rate falls; neither exists now, as bonds priced as risk-free deliver return-free risk.
The second category is assets that produce nothing and depend on an expanding pool of buyers, like tulips; today's major example is gold, favored by those who fear paper money.

stance.quote: Gold, however, has two significant shortcomings, being neither of much use nor procreative.

summary: Gold has limited industrial demand and produces nothing; buyers are motivated by growing fear and by the rising price itself, which attracts bandwagon purchasers.
Bandwagon investors create their own truth for a while; Internet stocks and houses showed how rising prices expand the pool of buyers until bubbles pop.
The world's 170,000 tons of gold at $1,750 an ounce would be worth $9.6 trillion, equal to all U.S. cropland plus 16 Exxon Mobils and $1 trillion left over.
Annual gold production is worth about $160 billion that buyers must absorb; in a century farmland and Exxon Mobil would have produced trillions while gold stays unproductive.

Hypothetical: a business with $2 million net worth earns 12% and outsiders buy at 125% of net worth; owners consider paying out one-third of earnings as dividends.
Dividend case: paying one-third out, dividends and stock value both grow 8% a year; after ten years net worth is $4,317,850 and each owner's shares are worth $2,698,656.

The sell-off math assumes 12% returns on net worth and sales at 125% of book, plausible for Berkshire; over its history sell-off would have beaten dividends dramatically.

stance.quote: You don’t need to be an expert in order to achieve satisfactory investment returns.

summary: Non-experts should know their limits, keep investing simple, say no to quick profits, and focus on an asset's future productivity, dropping any investment whose earnings they cannot roughly estimate.

stance.quote: the fact that a given asset has appreciated in the recent past is never a reason to buy it

Wildly fluctuating stock quotes are an advantage, like a moody neighbor shouting daily prices for a farm: buy when absurdly low, sell or ignore when absurdly high.
Stock owners too often copy other owners' irrational behavior and heed pundits, turning liquidity into a curse; people who sit quietly on a farm become frenetic with constant stock quotations.

stance.quote: A climate of fear is your friend when investing; a euphoric world is your enemy.
