summary: Berkshire sold 114 million Tesco shares in 2013 for a $43 million profit, delayed selling the rest, and exited in 2014 as market share, margins and accounting deteriorated.
Tesco cost $444 million after tax, 1/5 of 1% of net worth; the only losses of 1-2% came in 1974-75. S&P 500 returned 11,196% over 1964-2014.
From 1964 to 2014 the S&P 500 returned 11,196% with dividends while the dollar lost 87% of its purchasing power; investing means gaining purchasing power after tax.

stance.quote: currency-denominated instruments are riskier investments – far riskier investments – than widely-diversified stock

summary: Over the past fifty years, and the half-century before, diversified American businesses were far safer than Treasuries tied to the dollar; stock prices are more volatile than cash.
Volatility is not risk; business schools wrongly equate them. Low-fee diversified stock portfolios bought over time are far less risky than currency-denominated instruments.
Investors facing near-term cash needs or forced selling should hold Treasuries or insured deposits; long-horizon investors can ignore price declines and focus on purchasing-power gains.
Investors who feared volatility and bought Treasury bills or CDs six years ago earn a pittance, while the S&P 500 rose from below 700 to about 2,100.

stance.quote: Market forecasters will fill your ear but will never fill your wallet.
borrowed money has no place in the investor’s tool kit

summary: Active trading, market timing, poor diversification, high fees and borrowed money make stock ownership risky; no one can predict when chaos will occur.

stance.quote: And that is a fool’s game.

summary: Large institutions have long underperformed a patient index-fund investor, mainly through fees paid to consultants who recommend high-fee managers; skilled managers are few and hard to identify.
Most advisors are better at generating fees than returns; Buffett recommends Jack Bogle's index-fund book and Graham's view that investors, not markets, are to blame for failure.
Berkshire gives all shareholders simultaneous access to new information, issuing data late Fridays or early Saturdays, and does not talk one-on-one with large institutions or analysts.
Berkshire's operating managers run businesses as if they were their families' only asset, with a shareholder-oriented mindset; most have no financial need to work.
Managers are shareholder-oriented; the 24-person corporate office handles regulatory filings, a 24,100-page federal tax return, 3,400 state returns, shareholder inquiries and the annual meeting.
Acquisition criteria: at least $75 million pre-tax earnings, consistent earning power, good returns with little debt, management in place, simple businesses, and a stated price.
Berkshire wants $5-20 billion acquisitions, no unfriendly takeovers or auctions, prefers cash, and issues stock only when it receives as much intrinsic value as it gives.
Berkshire is approached with deals far outside its criteria; it avoids new ventures, turnarounds and auction-like sales.
In 1964 Berkshire offered to repurchase 225,000 of its 1,583,680 shares at $11.375; Buffett Partnership owned about 7% and, irritated by the price, did not tender.
Berkshire was a New England textile maker in a declining industry; its 1954 board minutes already described the trend of the industry going out of business.
After the 1955 merger Berkshire lost money for seven years and net worth fell 37%; it closed nine plants, sometimes using proceeds to repurchase shares.
BPL bought Berkshire at $7.50 versus $10.25 working capital and $20.20 book value, a cigar-butt purchase; Berkshire used plant-closure proceeds to repurchase shares.
The 1964 repurchase offer was 50% above Buffett's original cost, but he ignored it and bought more Berkshire shares instead.
By April 1965 Buffett Partnership owned 392,633 of 1,017,547 shares and took control; net worth had fallen from $55 million in 1955 to $22 million, with $2.5 million bank debt.
Berkshire's earnings after 1964 were tax-free thanks to a loss carry-forward; 18 years of struggle ended when the textile business was closed in 1985.
In 1967 Berkshire paid $8.6 million for National Indemnity; Buffett calls buying it for Berkshire rather than for his partnership a colossal mistake.
Buying NICO through Berkshire, only 61% owned by partners, hindered growth for two decades and diverted about $100 billion from partnership holders to Berkshire's legacy shareholders.
The 1975 purchase of Waumbec Mills looked like a bargain on assets and synergies but proved a disaster and was closed; the northern textile industry is now extinct.
Buffett's cigar-butt strategy of buying cheap mediocre companies worked well on small sums in the 1950s; the exception was GEICO, where he put 65% of his net worth in 1951.
Cigar-butt investing does not scale and marginal businesses are the wrong foundation for an enduring enterprise; taking the $11.375 offer would have earned the partnership about 40% annually.

stance.quote: buy wonderful businesses at fair prices

summary: Munger's blueprint for Berkshire: forget buying fair businesses at wonderful prices; buy wonderful businesses at fair prices.
Berkshire was built to Munger's blueprint, with subsidiary CEOs doing the real work; 1972 was a turning point, when Blue Chip Stamps could buy See's Candy.

stance.quote: a broad and durable competitive advantage that gave it significant pricing power

summary: Blue Chip Stamps could buy See's Candy, earning about $4 million pre-tax on $8 million of net tangible assets, with durable pricing power and minimal reinvestment needs.
Berkshire paid $25 million for See's, three times net tangible assets; See's has since earned $1.9 billion pre-tax needing only $40 million added investment, funding other acquisitions.
See's taught Buffett the value of powerful brands; his worst post-Waumbec mistake was Dexter Shoe, bought in 1993 and undone by foreign competition he failed to foresee.

stance.quote: As a financial disaster, this one deserves a spot in the Guinness Book of World Records.

summary: Berkshire paid $433 million in stock for Dexter, whose value went to zero; those shares are now worth about $5.7 billion. Trading stock for so-so businesses destroys value.
Berkshire has also lost when investee companies overpaid in stock; the intrinsic value of shares given in an acquisition must not exceed the intrinsic value of the business received.
Investment bankers rarely quantify intrinsic value in stock deals, focusing on customary premiums and earnings-per-share gains while CEOs conjure fanciful synergies and ignore dis-synergies.

Acquisition post-mortems comparing reality with projections should be standard; Berkshire's CEO and Board will calculate intrinsic value before issuing shares, and overall its acquisitions have worked out well.
Marketable securities are carried at market, but acquired subsidiaries are never revalued upward, leaving huge unrecorded gains that have grown fast in the last decade.
Conglomerates deserve their poor investor reputation; in the late 1960s CEOs inflated stock prices through promotion and dubious accounting, then issued shares to buy lower-multiple businesses.
Conglomerates issued 20-times-earnings stock to buy ten-times-earnings businesses and used pooling accounting to raise per-share earnings automatically, then promised to repeat the process endlessly.
Wall Street and auditors embraced conglomerates' per-share earnings maneuvers, which generated huge merger fees for investment bankers, while easy money washed away ethical concerns.
Conglomerates exploited p/e differences, which pushed CEOs to buy mediocre low-multiple businesses; deal velocity and pooling accounting mattered more to investors than quality.
Accounting shenanigans were excused in the 1960s conglomerate boom, and accounting wizards at the helm were seen as guaranteeing reported earnings would never disappoint.
Analysts approved an acquisitive CEO's 'bold, imaginative accounting' as a way to guarantee that forecasts would be met whatever the business results.

stance.quote: business models based on the serial issuances of overpriced shares – just like chain-letter models – most assuredly redistribute wealth, but in no way create it.

summary: Serial issuance of overpriced shares redistributes rather than creates wealth, like chain letters; neither BPL nor Berkshire has invested in companies hell-bent on issuing shares.
Heavy share issuance signals promotional management, weak accounting and overpriced stock; used judiciously, the conglomerate form is an ideal structure for long-term capital growth.
Capital often moves irrationally slowly because CEOs of declining businesses rarely redeploy capital into unrelated activities, as Berkshire's own textile history showed.
Shareholders reallocating capital between businesses face heavy taxes and frictional costs paid to bankers, accountants, consultants, lawyers and leveraged-buyout operators.

stance.quote: Our structural advantages, however, are formidable.

summary: Berkshire can shift huge sums from low-opportunity businesses to promising ones without taxes or much cost, free from industry bias and colleagues' vested interests.
Berkshire's capital allocation is free of pressure from colleagues with a vested interest in the status quo; horses would not have built the auto industry.
Berkshire can buy pieces of wonderful businesses (stocks) as well as whole companies; market offerings are often more attractive, and securities gains have financed large acquisitions.
Berkshire's opportunities are broad but limited to businesses whose prospects it can evaluate; that limit is smaller than for single-industry executives, and it can scale far larger.
See's excess cash, unusable for expansion, was redeployed into other acquisitions without taxes or frictional costs, unlike a stand-alone company that would have to distribute earnings to investors.
Berkshire has become the home of choice for owners and managers of outstanding businesses; families often best do nothing rather than sell.
Owners selling outright usually choose a competitor seeking synergies, which cuts associates' jobs, or a Wall Street buyer such as a leveraged buyout firm.

stance.quote: Equity is dramatically reduced and debt is piled on in virtually all private-equity purchases.

summary: Leveraged-buyout firms renamed themselves private equity but still cut equity and pile debt on acquired companies; the offer price partly reflects the maximum debt that can be added.
Private-equity buyers re-leverage and pay huge dividends that drive equity toward zero, treating businesses as merchandise; Berkshire offers sellers a permanent home keeping people and culture.
Acquired businesses gain financial strength and end dealing with banks and analysts; spin-off proposals make no sense because Berkshire moves funds between businesses instantly and tax-free.
Splitting off subsidiaries would multiply board, regulatory and administrative costs, and utilities' tax credits are usable only because other Berkshire units generate large taxable income.
Berkshire's taxable income gives Berkshire Hathaway Energy an advantage in wind and solar; bankers urge acquirers to pay 20-50% premiums for supposed control value.
Bankers urge paying control premiums to acquire companies and later urge spinning them off to unlock value, which strips control value without payment; fees lead to transactions.
Berkshire spun off a bank in Rockford, Illinois in 1979 because new bank-holding-company regulations required it; only a regulator-required spin-off would be conceivable at Berkshire.
Voluntary spin-offs would cost Berkshire control value, capital-allocation flexibility and tax advantages, and subsidiaries would likely incur moderately greater costs and operate less effectively.
Jimmy Ling took LTV from $36 million of sales in 1965 to number 14 on the Fortune 500 two years later through acquisitions and planned partial spin-offs.
Ling bought meatpacker Wilson & Co. in 1967 and split it into three parts for partial spin-offs, justified by an '2 plus 2 equals 5' acquisition formula.
LTV collapsed by the early 1970s and Ling was fired; markets periodically detach from reality, and investors should hold that 2+2 equals 4 and buy stocks cheap afterward.

Berkshire's strengths: favorable businesses, devoted managers, diverse earnings, premier financial strength and liquidity, first-choice status among sellers, and a rock-solid culture built over 50 years.
Buffett believes patient Berkshire shareholders face as low a chance of permanent capital loss as any single-company investment, since per-share intrinsic value is almost certain to advance.
Buying Berkshire near double book value could take years to profit; purchases modestly above the repurchase price should pay, since directors authorize buybacks only well below intrinsic value.
Repurchases only well below intrinsic value are an essential criterion; short-term buyers' results depend on market movements, as Graham said the market is a voting machine short-term.

stance.quote: Berkshire shares should not be purchased with borrowed money.

summary: Buy Berkshire only with a five-year horizon since markets cannot be predicted; the stock fell about 50% three times since 1965, so leverage could be disastrous.
Buffett sees essentially zero chance of financial problems at Berkshire; it was a first responder in 2008-09 and has since more than doubled balance-sheet strength and earnings potential.

Financial staying power needs reliable earnings, massive liquid assets and no significant near-term cash requirements; many managements wrongly assumed they could always refund maturing debt in 2008-09.
Berkshire's diversified earnings from companies with durable competitive advantages assure continued profitability even if catastrophe insurance losses far exceed any experienced before.
Cash is a business's oxygen; in a three-week span in late 2008 Berkshire supplied $15.6 billion of fresh money to American businesses.

stance.quote: When bills come due, only cash is legal tender. Don’t leave home without it.

summary: Berkshire always holds at least $20 billion in Treasury-bill cash equivalents and avoids large short-term debt maturities or derivative contracts that could trigger collateral calls.
Earlier mispriced derivatives with minor collateral proved profitable, but fully collateralized new contracts ended Berkshire's interest; it will not write insurance policyholders can cash out.
Property-casualty float has no run risk and would decline only slowly if premiums shrank; Berkshire's conservatism reflects that the timing of panics cannot be predicted.
Berkshire will never play financial Russian roulette with owners' funds even at 1-in-100 odds, and still expects to build per-share earning power each year.

stance.quote: In most years, moreover, our country’s economy will provide a strong tailwind for business.

summary: Berkshire will add to underlying earning power annually through organic gains, bolt-on acquisitions and new fields, though operating earnings will fluctuate with the economy.

stance.quote: We are blessed to have the United States as our home field.

summary: The U.S. economy will provide a strong tailwind for Berkshire in most years; America is Berkshire's home field.
Berkshire's percentage gains will fall well short of the past 50 years; in 10-20 years earnings may exceed reinvestment needs, and excess earnings go to dividends or repurchases.

If shares trade below intrinsic value, massive repurchases will be the best use of excess earnings; Berkshire reaffirms its partnership-attitude Shareholder Principles, and directors take only token fees.
Berkshire directors earn token fees, own shares bought in the market rather than granted by options, and the company carries no directors and officers liability insurance.
Buffett suggests his son Howard succeed him as unpaid nonexecutive Chairman to ease replacing a wrong CEO, since a mediocre CEO who is also Chairman is hard to remove.
Howard Buffett would be an unpaid safety valve for directors' concerns; managing Berkshire is chiefly capital allocation plus choosing and retaining outstanding subsidiary managers.
A Berkshire CEO must be rational, calm, decisive, know his limits and be 'all in' for the company, with character above ego or avarice.
A CEO should not reach for pay matching lavishly-compensated peers; his shareholder-first behavior shapes managers down the line.
A successor must fight arrogance, bureaucracy and complacency, which brought down GM, IBM, Sears and U.S. Steel despite their financial strength and historical earning power.
Berkshire's economic value depends on keeping its noneconomic values; extraordinary delegation of authority makes it a collection of large companies, an antidote to bureaucracy.
Headquarters has no committees, subsidiary budgets, legal office or HR, PR, investor-relations, strategy or acquisitions departments, only an audit function, trusting managers as stewards.
Trust yields better results than directives; directors want future CEOs to come from internal candidates, relatively young, averaging well over ten years in the job.
Counterparties in acquisitions and tailored investments must feel comfortable with Berkshire's CEO; the board has a successor ready to take over the day after Buffett dies or steps down.
Investments will be handled by several specialists with great autonomy, reporting to the CEO; Todd Combs and Ted Weschler can help evaluate acquisitions.
Berkshire is positioned for life after Buffett and Munger: the right directors, managers and successors, an embedded culture and a regenerative system attracting like-minded owners.
A shareholder proxy resolution asked the board to consider paying a meaningful annual dividend; the sponsor never appeared but the proxy votes were tallied.
A shares voted 89 to 1 against a dividend and B shares 660,759,855 to 13,927,026, about 47 to 1; 98% of votes said reinvest all earnings.
Owners large and small are in sync with Berkshire's managerial philosophy of reinvesting earnings.
Munger sets out to describe the management system that turned a doomed textile business into Berkshire, why it did well, and whether results would continue after Buffett.
Berkshire system: a diffuse conglomerate averse only to what it cannot predict, working through separately incorporated subsidiaries with extreme CEO autonomy and a tiny headquarters.

Subsidiaries always include casualty insurers expected to produce underwriting gains and float; no system-wide personnel, stock option, incentive or retirement systems; the Chairman reserves few activities.
The Chairman manages security investments in the insurers, chooses and pays subsidiary CEOs with successor recommendations, and deploys spare cash ideally into new subsidiaries.
The Chairman stays available to subsidiary CEOs, writes a useful annual letter, models the culture, and prioritizes quiet reading and thinking.
New subsidiaries are bought with cash, not stock; no dividends while each retained dollar creates over a dollar of market value; buy good businesses at fair prices.
Berkshire almost never sells subsidiaries, moves or retires their CEOs for age, keeps little debt for perfect creditworthiness and cash for opportunities, and treats large sellers promptly.
Berkshire treats offers of large businesses confidentially; Munger notes few large corporations share half the Berkshire system, which Buffett installed while controlling about 45% of shares at 34.
Buffett designed the Berkshire system to maximize rationality and devotion of key people, win/win loyalty and long-term decisions by long-tenured managers; subsidiaries need not use the same system.
The Berkshire system aimed at long-term decisions by managers who stay to bear consequences, minimal headquarters bureaucracy, and spreading wisdom; some benefits arose through practice evolution.
Munger credits Berkshire's success to Buffett's peculiarities, the Berkshire system, luck and shareholder devotion; limiting activities to a few kinds for 50 years was a lollapalooza.
Like Wooden concentrating playing time, Buffett concentrated skill in himself and power in long-serving subsidiary CEOs, improving their skills and the achievements of subsidiaries.
Autonomy and Berkshire's success attract better subsidiaries and CEOs, who need less headquarters attention, creating a virtuous circle.
Including casualty insurers worked marvelously: their stock holdings about equal equity, the S&P 500 returned roughly 10% pre-tax annually over 50 years, and early stock picks beat the index.
As stock outperformance faded with size and taxes, Ajit Jain built a huge reinsurance business with float and underwriting gain, GEICO joined Berkshire and quadrupled share, other insurers improved.
Berkshire's reputation gave its insurers attractive opportunities to buy privately issued fixed-maturity securities; its insurance outcome was far above the usual mediocre casualty results.
Being a diffuse conglomerate enlarged opportunities; Berkshire bought with cash since nothing received was as valuable as its stock, and its non-insurance acquisitions worked out well.
Berkshire had no acquisitions department under pressure to buy, did not rely on prejudiced advisers, and Buffett showed great patience, seldom buying.
Berkshire's big mistakes were mostly omissions, such as not buying Walmart stock; net worth would be at least $50 billion higher had it seized several near-certain opportunities.

Berkshire would likely remain a better-than-normal company if Buffett left, thanks to subsidiaries' durable competitive advantages, large fixed-asset opportunities in railroad and utilities, and bolt-on acquisitions.
Even with moderate successors and no more large purchases, Berkshire would stay better than normal; Munger rates Ajit Jain and Greg Abel as world-leading executives who would stay.

New acquisitions would continue after Buffett as activism creates opportunities, reducing Berkshire's $60 billion of cash; avoiding bureaucracy and relying on one thoughtful leader solved Berkshire's early task.
Typical corporations have headquarters bureaucracy and CEOs forced out by a fixed retirement age; Munger urges trying versions of the Berkshire system and treating bureaucracy like cancer.

A corporation simply owning the S&P 500 and accruing taxes would lag the index in up years and beat it in down years, with a substantial aggregate lag over time.
Net worth rose $15.4 billion in 2015, up 6.4% per share; book value grew from $19 to $155,501 over 51 years, 19.2% compounded. Early on, net worth tracked intrinsic value.
By the early 1990s Berkshire shifted to owning businesses outright, where accounting writes down losers but never writes up winners, so book value became less relevant.

stance.quote: we would be delighted to repurchase our shares should they sell as low as 120% of book value

summary: Asymmetric accounting widens the gap between intrinsic value and book value; Berkshire would gladly repurchase shares at as low as 120% of book value.
Repurchases at 120% of book would raise per-share intrinsic value; unrecorded business gains make market-value gains exceed book-value gains over time, though 2015 book value did better.
Normalized earning power should rise every year despite occasional dips; BNSF dramatically improved service in 2015 after a poor 2014, investing about $5.8 billion in capital expenditures.
BNSF's $5.8 billion capex was a railroad record, nearly three times depreciation; it moves about 17% of U.S. intercity freight, 45% more ton-miles than its closest competitor.
BNSF maintained volume as rail ton-miles fell, with record pre-tax income of $6.8 billion; the 'Powerhouse Five' earned $13.1 billion in 2015, up $650 million.
Three of the Powerhouse Five were bought with cash; BNSF was 70% cash and 6.1% share dilution, so $12.7 billion of added annual earnings came with minor dilution.

stance.quote: PCC fits perfectly into the Berkshire model and will substantially increase our normalized per-share earning power.

summary: Berkshire bought Precision Castparts, the premier aerospace components supplier, for over $32 billion of cash, adding a sixth 'Powerhouse'; CEO Mark Donegan is compared to IMC's Jacob Harpaz.
PCC supplies key components for most large aircraft under multi-year contracts, with 30,466 employees at 162 plants in 13 countries; its CEO has made many acquisitions Berkshire will fund.
Todd Combs brought PCC to Buffett's attention; Combs and Weschler each manage about $9 billion. With PCC, Berkshire owns 10-1/4 Fortune 500-size companies, counting its 27% of Kraft Heinz.
Smaller non-insurance businesses earned $5.7 billion in 2015, up from $5.1 billion; earnings distribution ranges from one earning over $700 million to eleven earning $50-100 million.
Berkshire invested $16 billion in property, plant and equipment in 2015, 86% in the U.S.; BHE invested $16 billion in renewables, owning 7% of U.S. wind generation.
BHE made major renewables commitments after the Paris conference; insurance had an underwriting profit for the 13th year, with float growing from $41 billion to $88 billion.
Underwriting profit totaled $26 billion over 13 years, $1.8 billion in 2015; insurance is Berkshire's largest unrecorded wealth. Subsidiaries contracted 29 bolt-ons costing $634 million.
Bolt-on acquisitions deploy capital in fitting businesses run by existing managers, adding earnings with no extra work; Berkshire will make many dozens more if sensibly priced.
Heinz merged with Kraft; Berkshire's $4.25 billion cost for 53% of Heinz became 325.4 million Kraft Heinz shares (about 27%) costing $9.8 billion, in a company with $27 billion sales.
GAAP required a $6.8 billion write-up of the Kraft Heinz stake; Berkshire's Kraft Heinz preferred pays $720 million yearly and will probably be redeemed for $8.32 billion in June.
Partners at 3G buy companies, promptly cut unnecessary costs and boost productivity, the key to economic growth; Berkshire shares their passion for buying large businesses meeting basic needs.
Berkshire avoids bloat by buying businesses long run by cost-conscious managers and then leaving them alone to maximize effectiveness, unlike 3G's cost-cutting approach.
Berkshire will keep extreme decentralization but may partner with 3G, as financing partner on Tim Horton's or equity-and-financing partner at Heinz, and with others such as Berkadia.
Berkshire will join only partners making friendly acquisitions, leaving hostile offers for CEOs who forget shareholders or are inept to others; it goes only where welcome.
Berkshire raised its Big Four stakes: IBM 8.4%, Wells Fargo 9.8%, Coca-Cola 9.3%, American Express 15.6%; each ownership point adds about $500 million of annual earnings.

stance.quote: we much prefer owning a non-controlling but substantial portion of a wonderful company to owning 100% of a so-so business

summary: The Big Four earned Berkshire's share of $4.7 billion in 2015 but only about $1.8 billion in dividends is reported; the unreported nearly $3 billion is equally valuable.

Investees' retained earnings fund buybacks, raising Berkshire's share of future earnings at no cost, and profitable opportunities; their per-share earnings should grow, lifting dividends and unrealized gains.

Willingness to invest passively in non-controlled businesses as well as buy operating companies doubles Berkshire's chances of using its cash sensibly; marketable securities provide funds for an elephant-sized acquisition.

stance.quote: The babies being born in America today are the luckiest crop in history.

summary: Despite election-year pessimism, American GDP per capita of about $56,000 is in real terms six times the 1930 level.

stance.quote: America’s economic magic remains alive and well.

summary: Americans produce far more through efficiency, not harder work, and the trend will continue; 2% real GDP growth still delivers astounding gains.
With population growing 0.8%, 2% real GDP growth yields 1.2% per-capita growth, a 34.4% gain in a generation, or a $19,000 increase in GDP per capita.
Today's families live better than Rockefeller did in 1930, and the next generation's economic pie will be far larger though contentious to divide.
Future output will be fought over between workers and retirees, investors and workers, skilled and unskilled, with Congress the battlefield, yet even losing sides will enjoy far more goods.
The market system is unrivaled in producing what people want and don't yet know they want, so even losing sides will get more and better goods.

stance.quote: For 240 years it’s been a terrible mistake to bet against America, and now is no time to start.

summary: Betting against America has been a mistake for 240 years; social security promises will be honored, kids will live better, and the tailwind should help Berkshire prosper.

Successors build intrinsic value by improving subsidiaries' earning power, bolt-on acquisitions, investee growth, buybacks at a meaningful discount to intrinsic value, occasional large acquisitions, and rarely issuing shares.
In 2015 Berkshire's per-share cash and investments rose 8.3% to $159,794 and per-share business earnings rose 2.1% to $12,304, two quantitative factors for estimating intrinsic value.

Business earnings per share are pre-tax after overhead, interest, depreciation, amortization and minority interests, excluding investment income; insurance underwriting income is now included for the first time.
Underwriting was previously assumed to break even because of catastrophe coverages; results are now more stable after deemphasizing cats, and underwriting contributed $1,118 of the $12,304 per share.
Underwriting income averaged $1,434 per share over a decade but can be unprofitable in a year; since 1970 per-share investments grew 18.9% and earnings 23.7% annually.
Berkshire's stock price tracked its two value measures over 45 years; the main goal is building operating earnings, and operations are presented as four separate businesses.
Property-casualty insurance has propelled Berkshire since the 1967 purchase of National Indemnity and National Fire & Marine for $8.6 million; NICO is the world's largest P/C insurer by net worth.
P/C insurers collect premiums upfront and pay claims later, holding float that stays stable relative to premium volume; the passage begins a table of Berkshire's float.
Float reached $87,722 million in 2015 and further gains will be tough; run-off reinsurance contracts could shrink it at most 3% a year, and contracts impose no near-term cash demands.

An underwriting profit adds to float's investment income, giving paid use of free money; intense industry competition sometimes causes underwriting losses, which is what the industry pays for its float.

stance.quote: will continue its dismal record of earning subnormal returns on tangible net worth as compared to other American businesses

summary: Competition keeps insurers' returns on tangible net worth subnormal, and low interest rates will steadily decrease float earnings; industry results over the next ten years will fall short, especially reinsurance.
Berkshire has had an underwriting profit for 13 consecutive years totaling $26.2 billion pre-tax because disciplined risk evaluation is a religion; poor underwriting can drown float's benefits.
Book value deducts float in full as a liability, but float is a revolving fund: Berkshire paid $24.5 billion to six million claimants in 2015 while adding new float.
If float is costless and long-enduring, its true value is far below the GAAP liability; a $15.5 billion insurance goodwill asset partly offsets the overstated liability.

Insurance goodwill of $15.5 billion reflects the price paid for float-generating capability; its true economic value far exceeds carrying value, though prolonged underwriting losses would make goodwill worthless.
Nearly all the $15.5 billion insurance goodwill was on the books in 2000 while float tripled, a major reason intrinsic value exceeds book value; Ajit Jain's group leads in float.
Ajit Jain writes risks others avoid yet stays appropriate to Berkshire's resources; after a $250 billion industry mega-catastrophe loss, Berkshire would likely still profit and have abundant cash.
Other insurers would face red ink or insolvency after a mega-catastrophe; Ajit Jain, hired in 1986 with no insurance experience, has created tens of billions of value for shareholders.

General Re is a reinsurance powerhouse; a sound insurer must understand exposures, assess likelihood and cost conservatively, price for profit after expenses, and walk away when the premium is inadequate.

stance.quote: General Re’s huge float has been considerably better than cost-free under his leadership

summary: Many insurers fail to walk away from underpriced business; General Re under Tad Montross has float better than cost-free, and its international life reinsurance has grown profitably since 1998.

stance.quote: General Re is now a gem.

summary: Early problems at General Re after the 1998 purchase are long gone; GEICO, run by Tony Nicely since 1993, has been flying since then.

stance.quote: GEICO would succeed because it deserved to succeed.

summary: GEICO's huge cost advantage over giant insurers means savings on auto insurance, a major family expenditure; at least 40% of readers can save by switching.

stance.quote: The company’s low costs create a moat – an enduring one – that competitors are unable to cross.

summary: GEICO's cost advantage drove its U.S. auto market share from 2.5% in 1995, when Berkshire acquired control, to 11.4% at the end of 2015.
Smaller commercial insurers earned $4 billion of underwriting profit over 13 years, about 13% of premium volume, while float grew from $943 million to $9.9 billion.
Berkshire Hathaway Specialty Insurance, formed less than three years ago under Peter Eastwood, already writes $1 billion of annual premiums and may become a leading P/C insurer.
Table: 2015 and 2014 underwriting profit and yearend float by division (BH Reinsurance, General Re, GEICO, Other Primary); total float $87,722 million in 2015.
BNSF and BHE, regulated capital-intensive businesses, together provided 37% of Berkshire's 2015 after-tax operating earnings and invest heavily in very long-lived regulated assets.

stance.quote: a commonly used measure we view as seriously flawed

summary: BNSF and BHE carry long-term debt not guaranteed by Berkshire; BNSF's 2015 interest coverage (EBIT to interest) exceeded 8:1, and Berkshire views EBITDA-based coverage as flawed.

With Berkshire's backing Clayton kept financing home buyers and even non-Clayton dealers through the 2008-2009 panic, a quieter rescue than funds Berkshire gave Goldman Sachs and General Electric.
Clayton's retail outlets inform home buyers in plain language of alternative financing sources, mostly local banks, and obtain signed acknowledgments.
Reckless mortgage practices caused the 2008 panic and Great Recession: originators sold loans to banks that packaged them into mortgage-backed securities sold to unwitting institutions worldwide.
Investment bankers built a second layer of securities on junkier tranches; originators and packagers had no skin in the game, and borrowers lied on applications.
Rating agencies rated complex structures they may not have understood; Barney Frank said regulators erred in not imposing risk retention on all residential mortgages under Dodd-Frank.

stance.quote: At Clayton, our risk retention was, and is, 100%.

summary: Clayton retains 100% of the mortgages it originates; in 2015 it foreclosed on 8,444 manufactured-housing mortgages at a $157 million cost.

Clayton financed its fixed-rate mortgage portfolio with floating or short-term debt, so low short-term rates widened its spread; borrowers' strong desire for a home helped performance.
Clayton's widening spread between short-term interest cost and fixed mortgage income is similar to buying long-term bonds financed short-term.

Lending long and borrowing short is normally risky, but Berkshire's $20-60 billion of short-term cash equivalents offset Clayton's $13 billion portfolio, making Berkshire asset-sensitive and a beneficiary of rising rates.
Berkshire will always benefit from rising interest rates; after the Great Recession mortgage originators faced fines, and Clayton's practices are continuously reviewed by regulators.

Productivity gains drive America's rising living standards; in 1900 farming employed 11 million of 28 million workers and corn yielded 30 bushels per acre on 90 million acres.
Tractors and innovations raised corn yields to over 150 bushels per acre on about 85 million acres, lifting annual output from 2.7 billion to 13-14 billion bushels.
Farm employment fell to about three million, 2% of the 158-million workforce, freeing tens of millions of workers to produce non-farm goods and services.
Agricultural productivity benefited society though displaced farm hands lost jobs; Buffett turns to three efficiency stories affecting Berkshire subsidiaries and the flip side of productivity gains.
From 1947 to 2014 Class I railroads' ton-miles rose 182% to 1.85 trillion while employees fell 86% to 187,000; inflation-adjusted freight prices fell 55%.
Lower inflation-adjusted rail freight prices save shippers about $90 billion annually; at 1947 staffing levels, over three million rail workers would be needed.
BNSF raised ton-miles 71% to 702 million from 1996 to 2015 with only 4% more employees, and injuries fell by half; auto insurance traditionally went through high-commission agencies.
Agency-based auto insurance spent about 40 cents of each premium dollar on commissions and expenses with cartel-like pricing; G. J. Mecherle's captive sales force became State Farm.
State Farm cut commissions and became volume leader in auto and homeowners insurance, with Allstate second; both run about 25% underwriting expenses. USAA sold directly to officers in the 1930s.
USAA's direct distribution had lower costs than State Farm and Allstate; Leo and Lillian Goodwin, with $100,000 of capital, founded GEICO in 1936 to broaden direct auto insurance.

Federally subsidized wind and solar and tax credits may erode high-cost incumbent utilities; BHE's efficiency emphasis keeps it competitive. Its Iowa utility cut staff while output rose.
BHE's Iowa utility raised output from 19 to 29 million megawatt-hours with fewer employees, avoiding a rate increase for 16 years while industry rates rose 44%; PacifiCorp purchased in 2006.
PacifiCorp raised output with 5,700 versus 6,750 employees and far fewer accidents; regulators welcome BHE as efficient and well capitalized, and it has never paid Berkshire a dividend.
Productivity gains benefit society but largely helped the wealthy recently and cause upheaval for capital and labor; investors should bear losses from wrong choices.
Widely diversified investors who sit tight are certain to prosper in America, where winners offset clunkers; the Dow rose from 66 to 11,497 during the 20th Century.

Productivity gains obsolete long-employed workers; when Asian competition closed Dexter, Berkshire lost its entire investment and 1,600 Maine jobs, as slowly happened at its New England textile operation.
Outlawing productivity gains would hurt living standards; safety nets, such as a reformed and expanded Earned Income Tax Credit, should support those whose skills the market undervalues.
Prosperity for most should not mean penury for the unfortunate; Buffett finds the SEC-required 10-K risk factors section never helped him evaluate a business, since important risks are well known.
Risk catalogs rarely help assess probability, cost or timing of threats; a threat 50 years away is not an investor's financial problem, and Berkshire's many industries have hard-to-evaluate risks.
Known threats include lost coal volume at BNSF, driverless cars hurting GEICO and auto dealerships, falling newspaper circulation, and storage-driven changes for renewables and online retailing.
Online retailing threatens Berkshire retailers and consumer brands, but none of these problems is crucial to long-term well-being; in 1965 its single risk was the dying textile business.
Berkshire's 1965 risk, a textile business destined for losses, was no death knell because it adapted and will continue to adapt.
Berkshire's money, talent and culture and flexible capital deployment let it survive adversity; the one present danger is a cyber, biological, nuclear or chemical attack on the U.S.
The annual probability of a mass-destruction attack on the U.S. is likely very small, but Berkshire shares the risk with all American business.
A one-in-thirty annual chance becomes 96.6% over a century; American corporations and investors cannot shed this risk, and mass devastation would decimate all equity investments.
A proxy proposal asks Berkshire for a report on climate-change dangers to its insurance operation; Buffett finds it highly likely climate change poses a major problem for the planet.
Buffett argues it is foolish to demand 100% proof of huge damage when prompt action might thwart a danger, comparing climate change to Pascal's Wager.
Noah's Law says build the ark early; a sponsor fears Berkshire as a huge insurer is exposed to weather losses, which would matter only with ten- or twenty-year fixed-price policies.
Insurance policies are customarily written for one year and repriced annually, so increased loss possibilities translate promptly into higher premiums.
GEICO's loss cost per policy rose from about $30 in 1951 to $1,000 in 2015, matched by higher premiums; GEICO now does $23 billion of business, not $600 million.

stance.quote: climate change should not be on your list of worries.

Berkshire gives all shareholders simultaneous access to new information, issuing data late Fridays or early Saturdays, and does not talk one-on-one with large institutions; shareholders of limited means matter most.

Berkshire's operating managers are shareholder-oriented and run businesses as if they were their families' only asset; the 24-person corporate office handles regulatory filings and a 30,400-page federal tax return.
The corporate office files a 30,400-page federal tax return, up 6,000 pages, and oversees 3,530 state returns, alongside regulatory filings, shareholder inquiries and the annual report.
Berkshire's revenues increased by $16 billion in 2015 while its home-office crew of 25 people stayed identical.

Buying back Berkshire shares has proved hard, perhaps because the policy signals intrinsic value well above 120% of book; management prefers a narrow price range around intrinsic value.
Buying out partners at a discount is not gratifying, but Berkshire will repurchase if market conditions let it benefit both continuing and exiting shareholders.

summary: Despite huge performance incentives at both levels, honest managers delivered dismal results to investors while charging huge fixed fees unwarranted by performance.

Disappointing hedge-fund results are expected to recur; the bet's statement says the S&P 500 will beat funds of hedge funds net of fees, costs and expenses over 2008-2017.

Passive investors get about average results, so active investors must too before costs; large annual, performance and trading fees make their aggregate results worse, especially for funds of hedge funds.

stance.quote: Investors, on average and over time, will do better with a low-cost index fund than with a group of funds of funds.

summary: Hedge-fund managers' efforts largely neutralize each other and their intelligence will not overcome the costs imposed on investors, who do better in a low-cost index fund.
If active and do-nothing investors both earn average results before costs, the lower-cost group wins; Buffett identified only about ten professionals expected to beat the S&P over long stretches.
Skilled outperformers exist but the great majority of managers who try will fail, and the one soliciting your funds is unlikely to be an exception.
Short-term luck misleads: of 1,000 managers making market calls, one will likely be right nine years running; success also breeds failure because a good record attracts a torrent of money.
Huge sums anchor investment performance while managers still seek money because their fees grow with assets; in 1966, managing $44 million, Buffett closed his partnership to new partners.

stance.quote: Both large and small investors should stick with low-cost index funds.

summary: When trillions are managed by Wall Streeters charging high fees, managers rather than clients reap outsized profits; investors should use low-cost index funds, as Jack Bogle urged for decades.

stance.quote: he helped millions of investors realize far better returns on their savings than they otherwise would have earned.

summary: Bogle's crusade for ultra-low-cost index funds gave millions better returns than managers' promised rewards did; Buffett regularly recommends a low-cost S&P 500 index fund.

stance.quote: My regular recommendation has been a low-cost S&P 500 index

summary: Buffett regularly recommends a low-cost S&P 500 index fund, and friends of modest means usually follow it.

Mega-rich individuals, institutions and pension funds ignore index-fund advice and chase high-fee managers or consultants, who earn large fees by recommending small managerial shifts every year or so.
Wealthy investors, pension funds and endowments resist an index fund available to small savers even though it is clearly the best choice on an expectancy basis.
Buffett roughly estimates the elite's search for superior advice wasted over $100 billion in a decade, as even a 1% fee on trillions adds up; public pension funds suffered much.

Underfunded public pension funds suffered poor returns plus huge fees, leaving taxpayers to cover shortfalls for decades; advisors who promise something extra, like hedge funds, will keep getting rich.
When a person with money meets one with experience, the experienced one ends up with the money; a stockyard agent's anecdote shows that persuasion, not skill, wins clients.

The stockyard lesson applies to Wall Street; Berkshire happily pays even outrageous fees to investment bankers who bring acquisitions and has paid substantial over-performance sums to its two investment managers.
Buffett says he will cheerfully write a big check for Wall Street fees whenever they deliver value to Berkshire.
All shareholders should get new information at the same time, so Berkshire releases data late Friday or early Saturday and does not talk one-on-one with large institutions or analysts.

Berkshire paid a $1.9 million premium over $6.7 million net worth for National Indemnity, gaining an underwriting-profit business and $19.4 million of float that it could invest.
Berkshire keeps all dividends, interest and gains (and bears losses) on invested float, which arises because premiums come upfront while losses occur over the policy life and beyond.
Float also arises because some losses, like asbestos exposure, take years to surface and settle, and workers' compensation payments can stretch over decades.
Float grows with premium volume and long-tail lines like malpractice generate far more of it; Berkshire leads in jumbo reinsurance of incurred long-tail losses, driving extraordinary float growth.

Float will rise slowly and any decline would be at most about 3% a year; unlike deposits it cannot be withdrawn, so no runs; Berkshire never depends on strangers.
Treasury Bills protected Berkshire from relying on bank lines in 2008-2009; float carries oceans of risk, as 1980s long-tail problems at Lloyd's nearly destroyed it.

Lloyd's recovered; Berkshire's careful underwriters usually earn underwriting profits, making the cost of float below zero, but the catastrophe-light period was no new norm, as three hurricanes showed.
The catastrophe-light period was not a new norm; three significant hurricanes hit Texas, Florida and Puerto Rico last September.

Berkshire bore about 3% of industry hurricane losses, under 1% of net worth versus 7% to 15% at other reinsurers; annual odds of a $400 billion mega-cat are about 2%.
Mega-cat risk rises as more structures sit in vulnerable areas; Berkshire's share of a $400 billion loss, about $12 billion, is below non-insurance earnings, while much of the industry fails.
After 14 straight underwriting profit years totalling $28.3 billion pre-tax, Berkshire lost $3.2 billion from underwriting in 2017; it expects profits in most years but occasional losses.

American Express repurchases lifted Berkshire's stake from 12.6% to 17.9% with unchanged shares; Berkshire's share of its 2018 earnings, $1.2 billion, was about 96% of cost; shared-control companies follow.

summary: Berkshire stays a financial fortress and never risks being short of cash; with business prices sky-high, 2019 will likely bring more marketable equities while it hopes for an elephant acquisition.

stance.quote: Predictions of that sort have never been a part of our activities.

summary: More stock purchases are not a market call; Berkshire does not predict markets but compares a business's worth with its price; intrinsic value approximates the sum of four groves.

stance.quote: Truly good businesses are exceptionally hard to find. Selling any you are lucky enough to own makes no sense at all.

summary: Intrinsic value is roughly the four groves summed less eventual tax on marketable securities; no tax allowance is made for selling wholly-owned businesses, which would be foolish.
Non-insurance earnings are after interest; float from insurers, expected to be cost-free, funds much of the other groves; combining the five groves in one entity maximizes value.

A single entity lets Berkshire allocate capital objectively, eliminate enterprise risk, avoid insularity, fund assets cheaply, use tax efficiencies and minimize overhead; the whole exceeds the sum of the parts.

Repurchases below intrinsic value benefit both leaving and staying shareholders; the benefit to sellers is slight, while continuing holders gain per-share intrinsic value on each repurchase at a discount.

stance.quote: Obviously, repurchases should be price-sensitive

summary: Repurchases should be price-sensitive, since blind buying of overpriced stock destroys value; owners must receive the information needed to estimate value so no partner sells because of being misled.
Some sellers disagree on value or find better investments, and some holders turn into net consumers; Buffett and Munger have no interest in joining them.
Berkshire decisions favor staying shareholders; it prepares no monthly company-wide earnings reports or balance sheets and has no company-wide budget, so no quarterly number to hit.

Meeting Wall Street expectations induces bad behavior like trade-loading, ignoring rising insurance losses or cookie-jar reserves, which can grow into fraud; Berkshire's lack of a quarterly number reinforces its culture.
If bosses cheat a little, subordinates rationalize similar behavior; Berkshire works for shareholder-partners, not analysts, and the numbers that flow to management are those sent to owners.
Non-insurance businesses earned $20.8 billion pre-tax in 2018, up 24%, with acquisitions adding little; after-tax gain was 47%, largely from the corporate tax rate cut.
The U.S. Treasury is like a holder of special AA shares taking 35% of earnings through the corporate tax rate; those payments went from nothing in 1965 to billions yearly.

stance.quote: America is Exhibit A.

Berkshire shareholders participated in the American miracle by forgoing dividends and reinvesting; tiny early reinvestment mushroomed through savings culture and long-term compounding.
Berkshire's results were possible only in America; Buffett thanks the Treasury, hopes to pay larger taxes later, and says a stable currency requires wisdom and vigilance from government.

In long-tail lines like malpractice and product liability, insurers can report fictitious profits for decades; Berkshire has invested float while generally earning a small underwriting profit.
Berkshire prices to absorb growing losses and contests fraud; Ajit made it a world insurance leader with Gibraltar-like strength, and executives use no options, sharing owners' losses.
P/C growth depends on rising economic risk; 300 million U.S. vehicles and massive, increasingly unpredictable hurricane, tornado and wildfire damage drive insurance needs.

Ten-year policies on catastrophe risks would be madness, but one-year policies are manageable; Berkshire must shrink when prices are inadequate, since underpricing to stay in the game is corporate suicide.

stance.quote: All things considered, we like the P/C insurance business.

summary: Pricing P/C insurance is not for optimists; Berkshire can absorb extreme losses, needs no reinsurers, has outstanding managers, and generated $32 billion of after-tax underwriting profit in two decades.
Insurance earned $32 billion after tax from underwriting over two decades, about 3.3 cents per sales dollar, while float grew from $46 billion to $171 billion.
Berkshire's Japanese investment is in five large companies: Itochu, Marubeni, Mitsubishi, Mitsui and Sumitomo, each owning interests in many businesses in Japan and worldwide.
Berkshire first bought the five Japanese firms in July 2019 at amazingly low prices; they raise dividends, repurchase shares sensibly and pay managers far less aggressively than U.S. peers.
Berkshire's Japanese holdings cost $13.8 billion and were worth $23.5 billion; it keeps stakes near 10% and raises fixed-rate yen borrowings seeking currency neutrality.
GAAP counted $2.3 billion of after-tax yen-borrowing gains, $850 million in 2024; Japanese dividends of about $812 million in 2025 exceed roughly $135 million of yen interest.
Annual dividend income from the Japanese holdings should total about $812 million in 2025 against about $135 million of interest on yen debt.
